slides.title: 1. Meaning of Tax
slides.html:
A tax is a compulsory payment that the State collects under the authority of law to meet public expenditure, without giving the payer any specific service in return. The absence of a direct return (no quid pro quo) is what separates a tax from a fee or a price.

In Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, AIR 1954 SC 282 (the Shirur Mutt case), Mukherjea J. adopted the definition given by Latham C.J. in Matthews v. Chicory Marketing Board (1938) 60 CLR 263: a tax is a compulsory exaction of money by a public authority for public purposes, enforceable by law, and is not a payment for services rendered. Five features follow.

  1. Compulsory: the payer has no choice; non payment leads to recovery, interest and penalty.
  2. Imposed by law: no tax can be levied or collected except by authority of law (Article 265).
  3. For public purposes: the proceeds go to the Consolidated Fund (Article 266) and meet general public needs.
  4. No quid pro quo: the payer cannot demand a special service in return.
  5. Enforceable: the law provides machinery to assess, collect and punish evasion.

Article 366(28) adds that “taxation” includes the imposition of any tax or impost, whether general, local or special.

slides.title: 1.1 The four components of a tax
slides.html:
In Govind Saran Ganga Saran v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, 1985 Supp SCC 205, the Supreme Court held that every tax has four components, and if any of them is uncertain the levy fails.

  1. The taxable event that attracts the levy.
  2. The person liable to pay.
  3. The rate of tax.
  4. The measure or value to which the rate applies.

Under the 2025 Act, the taxable event is earning total income in a tax year (section 4(2)), the person is “every person” (section 2(77)), the rate comes from the Finance Act (section 4(1)) or section 202(1), and the measure is total income computed under the Act (sections 2(108) and 5).

slides.title: 2. History of Taxation
slides.html:
1. Ancient India. The Manusmriti (Chapter VII) asks the king to take moderate taxes, little by little, as the leech, the calf and the bee take their food, and allows him a share of the crop of one sixth, one eighth or one twelfth. Kautilya’s Arthashastra describes an organised revenue system with officials such as the samaharta (collector general) and the sannidhata (treasurer). Kalidasa’s Raghuvamsha praises King Dilipa, who taxed his subjects only for their welfare, as the sun draws up water only to return it a thousandfold as rain.
  2. Medieval period. Land revenue was the main source of income. Under Akbar, Raja Todar Mal reorganised it on the basis of measurement of land and average produce.
  3. British period. Income tax was first introduced in 1860 by James Wilson, the first Finance Member, to meet the financial strain after the revolt of 1857. The Income Tax Act, 1886 gave it a lasting form, followed by the Acts of 1918 and 1922. The Government of India Act, 1935 placed taxes on income other than agricultural income in the Federal List (Entry 54) and left agricultural income to the provinces.
  4. After Independence. The Constitution gave Parliament taxes on income other than agricultural income (Entry 82, List I) and the States taxes on agricultural income (Entry 46, List II). Nicholas Kaldor’s report (1956) led to the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, the Expenditure Tax Act, 1957 and the Gift Tax Act, 1958. Gift tax ceased to apply to gifts made on or after 1 October 1998, and wealth tax was abolished by the Finance Act, 2015. The Income Tax Act, 1961 came into force on 1 April 1962, after the Law Commission’s Twelfth Report (1958) on the 1922 Act. A Direct Taxes Code Bill introduced in 2010 lapsed in 2014.
  5. The 2025 Act. The Income Tax Bill, 2025 was introduced on 13 February 2025 and examined by a Select Committee of 31 members chaired by Baijayant Panda, which reported on 21 July 2025. The Bill was withdrawn on 8 August 2025. The Income Tax (No. 2) Bill, 2025 was passed by the Lok Sabha on 11 August and by the Rajya Sabha on 12 August 2025, received assent on 21 August 2025 and came into force on 1 April 2026.

slides.title: 3. Types of Taxes
slides.html:
1. Direct and indirect. In a direct tax, such as income tax, the person on whom the tax is imposed also bears it. An indirect tax, such as GST or customs duty, can be passed on to others through prices. Direct taxes are administered by the Central Board of Direct Taxes and indirect taxes by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, both under the Central Boards of Revenue Act, 1963.
  2. Progressive, proportional, regressive and degressive. A progressive tax rises with income: section 202(1) charges nil up to Rs. 4,00,000 and then 5% to 30%. A proportional tax uses one rate: section 195 taxes unexplained income at a flat 30%. A regressive tax takes a larger share of the income of the poor, as a uniform tax on necessities does. A degressive tax rises up to a point and then stays flat.
  3. By level of government. Union taxes (income tax, customs), State taxes (agricultural income tax, taxes on lands and buildings), local taxes (municipal property tax), and GST levied by both the Union and the States under Article 246A.

slides.title: 4. Purposes of Taxation
slides.html:
Richard Musgrave described three functions of public finance: allocation, distribution and stabilisation. In practice, taxation serves these purposes.

  1. Revenue to finance defence, administration, justice, infrastructure and welfare.
  2. Redistribution through progressive rates, supported by Article 38(2) (minimise inequalities in income) and Article 39(b) and (c) (prevent concentration of wealth).
  3. Regulation of behaviour, such as high taxes on tobacco or deductions for donations (section 133) and health insurance (section 126).
  4. Economic stabilisation and growth, such as additional depreciation on new plant and machinery (section 33(8)).
  5. Formalisation, such as disallowing large cash payments (section 36(4)), a lower presumptive rate on digital receipts (section 58), and tax deduction at source (sections 392 and 393).

slides.part: 5. Principles of a Good Tax System
slides.title: 5. Principles of a Good Tax System
slides.html:
Adam Smith’s four canons in The Wealth of Nations (1776) remain the starting point.

  1. Equality: contribution in proportion to ability. Progressive slabs serve this canon.
  2. Certainty: the amount, time and manner of payment should be clear. The single “tax year” and the tables in the 2025 Act serve this canon.
  3. Convenience: collection at a convenient time and in a convenient manner, as with deduction of tax from salary at source.
  4. Economy: low cost of collection and minimal harm to productive activity.

Later writers added productivity, elasticity, flexibility, simplicity and diversity. On sharing the burden, the benefit theory says people should pay according to the benefit they receive from the State, while the ability to pay theory, on which income tax mainly rests, says they should pay according to their capacity. Sacrifice theories (equal, proportional or minimum sacrifice) explain ability to pay; minimum sacrifice supports steep progression.

slides.title: 6.1 The duty to pay
slides.html: The usual justification for taxation is that it is the price of an organised society. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, dissenting in Compania General de Tabacos de Filipinas v. Collector of Internal Revenue, 275 U.S. 87 (1927), put it as “Taxes are what we pay for civilized society.” Voluntary compliance improves when people see the system as fair and the money as well used.

slides.title: 6.2 Evasion, avoidance and planning
slides.html:
Evasion is illegal non payment through concealment or fraud, and it attracts penalty and prosecution (Chapters XXI and XXII). Planning means arranging one’s affairs within the law and its purpose, such as claiming a deduction the law offers. Avoidance uses the letter of the law to defeat its purpose, often through artificial arrangements.

IRC v. Duke of Westminster [1936] AC 1 (House of Lords)

Payments to a gardener under a deed of covenant, instead of wages, were held deductible. Lord Tomlin’s speech is the source of the principle that a person may arrange his affairs so that the tax payable is less than it would otherwise be.

McDowell and Co. Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer (1985) 3 SCC 230

Buyers paid excise duty on liquor directly to the excise authorities so that it would not form part of the seller’s turnover for sales tax. The Supreme Court rejected the device. Chinnappa Reddy J. said that colourable devices cannot be part of tax planning.

Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan (2004) 10 SCC 1

A CBDT circular allowing Mauritius residents to claim treaty benefits was upheld. Treaty shopping is not illegal in itself, and legitimate tax planning is permissible.

Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v. Union of India (2012) 6 SCC 613

A sale between non residents of shares in a foreign company that indirectly held an Indian business was held not taxable under the 1961 Act as it then stood. The transaction must be looked at as a whole, and a structure can be disregarded only if it is a sham or colourable device.

Parliament’s answer is the General Anti Avoidance Rule in Chapter XI of the 2025 Act (sections 178 to 184). Section 179 describes an impermissible avoidance arrangement, section 180 explains lack of commercial substance, and section 181 sets out the consequences.

slides.title: 6.3 Other moral questions
slides.html:
1. Fairness of exemptions. Every exemption shifts the burden onto others. The exemption for agricultural income (Schedule II, Sl. No. 1) protects small farmers but also benefits wealthy agriculturists and can be misused to disguise other income.
  2. Retrospective taxation. After Vodafone, the Finance Act, 2012 retrospectively amended the 1961 Act to tax indirect transfers. The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 later provided that no demand would be raised on that basis for transfers before 28 May 2012, subject to conditions. Indirect transfers are now dealt with prospectively in section 9(10).
  3. Privacy. Privacy is a fundamental right (K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1). Linking the Permanent Account Number with Aadhaar was upheld in Binoy Viswam v. Union of India (2017) 7 SCC 59 and in the Aadhaar judgment (2019) 1 SCC 1. The 2025 Act continues the requirement; section 430 levies a fee for default in intimating the Aadhaar number.
  4. Illegal income. Profits of an illegal business are taxable, and its losses can be set off against its profits (CIT v. S.C. Kothari [1971] 82 ITR 794 (SC)). But expenditure for a purpose that is an offence or prohibited by law is not deductible (section 34(2)(a) and (3)).
  5. Sin taxes. Heavy taxes on tobacco or alcohol reduce harmful consumption but are regressive and paternalistic.

slides.title: 7. Impact, Incidence and Shifting
slides.html:
1. Impact is the immediate burden on the person who pays the tax to the Government.
  2. Incidence is the final resting place of the burden, on the person who cannot pass it on.
  3. Effects are the wider consequences on prices, production, savings and distribution.

Shifting passes the burden forward to buyers through higher prices, or backward to suppliers or workers through lower prices or wages. A tax on an asset may also be capitalised into a lower asset price. How far a tax can be shifted depends on the following factors.

  1. Elasticity: the more inelastic side of the market bears more of the tax.
  2. Market power: a monopolist shifts tax more easily than a firm in a competitive market.
  3. Time: shifting is easier in the long run, when supply can adjust.
  4. Coverage: a tax on all close substitutes is harder to escape than a tax on one product.

In a direct tax, impact and incidence usually fall on the same person; in an indirect tax, such as GST, the supplier bears the impact and the consumer the incidence. In income tax, an employer may bear the tax on an employee’s non monetary perquisite. That tax is excluded from the employee’s income (Schedule III, Sl. No. 10) and is not deductible for the employer (section 35(a)(ii)). Where the employer pays tax on an employee’s salary, the amount is the employee’s income (Emil Webber v. CIT (1993) 2 SCC 386; section 17(1)(f)).

slides.title: 8. Taxation and Government
slides.html:
1. Legal basis. Article 265 requires authority of law. The 2025 Act is the permanent law, and the annual Finance Act fixes rates (section 4(1)).
  2. Parliamentary control. The Budget is laid under Article 112. A Bill dealing only with taxation is a Money Bill (Article 110); it is introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations within fourteen days (Article 109). The Income Tax (No. 2) Bill, 2025 was passed in the Lok Sabha as a Money Bill.
  3. Consent of representatives. The English Bill of Rights, 1689 made it illegal to levy money for the Crown without the grant of Parliament. Article 265 carries the same idea.
  4. Administration. The Central Board of Direct Taxes administers income tax. Section 240 requires a Taxpayer’s Charter, and sections 245 and 273 provide for faceless jurisdiction and assessment.
  5. Accountability. The Comptroller and Auditor General audits government accounts (Articles 148 to 151), and the Public Accounts Committee examines the reports.

slides.title: 9. Taxation and Economic Management
slides.html:
1. Demand management: lower taxes raise demand; higher taxes help control inflation.
  2. Automatic stabilisers: progressive income tax collects more in booms and less in slowdowns without new legislation.
  3. Fiscal discipline: the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 sets the path for reducing the fiscal deficit.
  4. Investment incentives: additional depreciation (section 33(8)), Part C deductions of Chapter VIII, and concessional rates for certain domestic companies (sections 199 to 201).
  5. Formalisation: restrictions on cash transactions (sections 36(4) and 185 to 188), tax deduction and collection at source (sections 392 to 394) and the Annual Information Statement (section 510).

slides.title: 10.1 Fee
slides.html:
The Shirur Mutt case explained that a fee is a charge for a special service rendered to individuals by a governmental agency. Two elements were identified: the fee is levied in consideration of a service that individuals accept, willingly or unwillingly; and the amount collected is meant to meet the cost of that service rather than go to general revenue. A tax is a common burden, while a fee is payment for a special benefit. Later decisions treated separate earmarking as a relevant sign rather than an absolute condition, because Article 266 requires all revenues to be credited to the Consolidated Fund.

Kewal Krishan Puri v. State of Punjab (1980) 1 SCC 416

A market fee must bear a close and reasonable relationship to services rendered to the payers, and a good and substantial portion of it must be shown to be spent for their special benefit.

Sreenivasa General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1983) 4 SCC 353

The correlation between a fee and the services need not be exact. A broad and general correlation is enough, and the services may benefit the payers as a class.

Corporation of Calcutta v. Liberty Cinema AIR 1965 SC 1107

A levy called a “licence fee”, for which no service was rendered, was in substance a tax. The label does not decide the nature of a levy.

A regulatory fee, charged to regulate a trade, does not need a strict quid pro quo. Fees have their own entries (Entry 96 of List I, Entry 66 of List II and Entry 47 of List III), and under Article 110(2) a Bill is not a Money Bill merely because it provides for fees for licences or services.

slides.title: 10.2 Cess
slides.html:
A cess is a levy for a specific purpose, usually charged as an addition to an existing tax, such as the Health and Education Cess that the Finance Acts levy on income tax. A cess is normally a tax, but it can be a fee if it has the character of a fee.

Hingir Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa AIR 1961 SC 459

A cess on mine owners, credited to a fund for developing mining areas, was held to be a fee because it was linked to services that benefited the payers.

India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu (1990) 1 SCC 12 and Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India 2024 SCC OnLine SC 1796

India Cement struck down a State cess on royalty and described royalty as a tax. On 25 July 2024, a nine judge bench in Mineral Area Development Authority held by 8 to 1 (Nagarathna J. dissenting) that royalty is not a tax but a contractual consideration, overruled India Cement on that point, and held that the States’ power to tax mineral rights under Entry 50 of List II is not taken away by the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.

Constitutionally, cess matters because Article 270(1) excludes “any cess levied for specific purposes” from the taxes shared with the States, and surcharges under Article 271 belong wholly to the Union. The 2025 Act treats a cess on income tax as part of the tax: section 35(a) denies a business deduction for income tax, including any surcharge or cess.
slides.plain: 10.2 Cess A cess is a levy for a specific purpose, usually charged as an addition to an existing tax, such as the Health and Education Cess that the Finance Acts levy on income tax. A cess is normally a tax, but it can be a fee if it has the character of a fee. Hingir Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa AIR 1961 SC 459 A cess on mine owners, credited to a fund for developing mining areas, was held to be a fee because it was linked to services that benefited the payers. India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu (1990) 1 SCC 12 and Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India 2024 SCC OnLine SC 1796 India Cement struck down a State cess on royalty and described royalty as a tax. On 25 July 2024, a nine judge bench in Mineral Area Development Authority held by 8 to 1 (Nagarathna J. dissenting) that royalty is not a tax but a contractual consideration, overruled India Cement on that point, and held that the States’ power to tax mineral rights under Entry 50 of List II is not taken away by the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. Constitutionally, cess matters because Article 270(1) excludes “any cess levied for specific purposes” from the taxes shared with the States, and surcharges under Article 271 belong wholly to the Union. The 2025 Act treats a cess on income tax as part of the tax: section 35(a) denies a business deduction for income tax, including any surcharge or cess.

slides.title: 10.3 Distinctions in points
slides.html:
1. Purpose: a tax is for general purposes; a fee for a special service; a cess for a specified purpose.
  2. Quid pro quo: none for a tax; a broad correlation for a fee (not for a regulatory fee); none for a cess that is a tax.
  3. Legislative entry: taxes need a taxing entry; fees fall under the fee entries.
  4. Sharing with States: Union taxes are generally shared under Article 270; cesses for specific purposes and surcharges are not.
  5. Money Bill: a Bill imposing a tax is a Money Bill; a Bill providing only for fees is not (Article 110(2)).

Exam focus. Start with Shirur Mutt, explain quid pro quo through Kewal Krishan Puri and Sreenivasa General Traders, show that labels do not matter (Liberty Cinema, Hingir Rampur), and end with the Article 270 consequence of cesses and the 2024 royalty judgment.

slides.title: Practice Questions for Unit I
slides.html:
1. Define a tax. Distinguish a tax from a fee and a cess with reference to decided cases.
  2. Explain impact, incidence and shifting. How do elasticity and market structure affect incidence?
  3. “Tax avoidance is legal, but is it moral?” Discuss with reference to Duke of Westminster, McDowell, Azadi Bachao Andolan, Vodafone and the General Anti Avoidance Rule.
  4. Trace the development of income tax law in India from 1860 to the Income Tax Act, 2025.
  5. State Adam Smith’s canons and examine whether the 2025 Act satisfies the canon of certainty.

slides.part: 1. Sources of the Power to Tax
slides.title: 1.1 Article 265
slides.html:
No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law. This has three consequences.

  1. Only the legislature can impose a tax; delegated legislation (such as rules under section 533) is valid only within the limits of the parent Act.
  2. “Law” means a valid law, made by a competent legislature and consistent with fundamental rights and other constitutional limits.
  3. Both the levy and the collection need legal authority, and money collected without authority of law can be recovered.

Article 265 is in Part XII, so it is a constitutional right but not a fundamental right; a violation is usually challenged under Article 226.

slides.part: 1. Sources of the Power to Tax
slides.title: 1.2 Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule
slides.html:
Taxing entries in the Lists are separate from general entries, and a power to legislate on a subject does not include a power to tax it unless there is a taxing entry (M.P.V. Sundararamier and Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1958 SC 468). The entries most relevant here are these.

  1. List I: Entry 82 (taxes on income other than agricultural income), Entry 83 (customs duties), Entry 85 (corporation tax), Entry 86 (taxes on the capital value of assets, excluding agricultural land), Entry 96 (fees) and Entry 97 (residuary matters, including any tax not mentioned in List II or III).
  2. List II: Entry 45 (land revenue), Entry 46 (taxes on agricultural income), Entry 49 (taxes on lands and buildings), Entry 50 (taxes on mineral rights, subject to Parliament’s law on mineral development), Entry 60 (taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments) and Entry 66 (fees).
  3. List III has no general taxing entry; Entry 44 covers stamp duties (other than judicial stamps, and not rates) and Entry 47 covers fees. Article 246A gives Parliament and the States simultaneous power over GST.

Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1971) 2 SCC 779

Wealth tax on net wealth including agricultural land was upheld. It was not a tax on lands and buildings under Entry 49 of List II, so Parliament could levy it under its residuary power (Article 248 and Entry 97 of List I).

slides.part: 1. Sources of the Power to Tax
slides.title: 1.3 Agricultural income in the Constitution
slides.html:
1. Article 366(1) gives “agricultural income” the meaning it has under the Indian income tax law. So section 2(5) of the 2025 Act decides both what the Union cannot tax and what the States may tax under Entry 46 of List II.
  2. Article 274 requires the President’s recommendation for a Bill that varies the meaning of “agricultural income” for income tax purposes.
  3. Article 366(6) defines corporation tax as a tax on the income of companies that, among other conditions, is not charged on agricultural income.
  4. Article 366(29) provides that “tax on income” includes a tax in the nature of an excess profits tax.

slides.part: 1. Sources of the Power to Tax
slides.title: 1.4 Extra territorial reach
slides.html: Under Article 245(2), a law of Parliament is not invalid because it operates outside India. In GVK Industries Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer (2011) 4 SCC 36, a Constitution Bench held that Parliament may legislate on extra territorial matters that have a nexus with India, but not on matters with no such nexus. This supports the deemed accrual rules in section 9, such as business connection, significant economic presence and indirect transfer.

Income Tax Officer (2011) 4 SCC 36, a Constitution Bench held that Parliament may legislate on extra territorial matters that have a nexus with India, but not on matters with no such nexus. This supports the deemed accrual rules in section 9, such as business connection, significant economic presence and indirect transfer.

slides.part: 1. Sources of the Power to Tax
slides.title: 1.5 Constitutional limits on taxation
slides.html:
1. Part III: taxing laws must respect fundamental rights (Part 3 of this unit).
  2. Article 276: the total tax on professions, trades and employments payable by one person to a State and its local bodies cannot exceed Rs. 2,500 a year. Section 19(1) (Table, Sl. No. 1) allows a deduction for it from salary.
  3. Articles 285 and 289: Union property is exempt from State taxes unless Parliament provides otherwise; the property and income of a State are exempt from Union taxes, but the Union may tax a trade or business carried on by a State (Article 289(2)).
  4. Article 286: States cannot tax sales outside the State or in the course of import or export.
  5. Articles 301 to 304: trade, commerce and intercourse throughout India must be free, subject to Articles 302 to 304.

slides.part: 2. Distribution of Revenues and Centre State Financial Relations
slides.title: 2.1 The main Articles
slides.html:
1. Articles 268, 269 and 269A: certain duties are collected and kept by the States; taxes on inter State sales and consignments are collected by the Union but assigned to the States; GST on inter State supplies is apportioned between the Union and the States on the recommendations of the GST Council.
  2. Article 270: all taxes in the Union List, except those under Articles 268, 269 and 269A, surcharges under Article 271 and any cess for specific purposes, are levied and collected by the Union and shared with the States. Income tax and corporation tax are shared under this Article.
  3. Article 271: surcharges on taxes for Union purposes belong wholly to the Union.
  4. Articles 275 and 282: statutory grants in aid to States in need, and discretionary grants for any public purpose.
  5. Article 279: “net proceeds” means proceeds less the cost of collection, as certified by the Comptroller and Auditor General.
  6. Articles 279A, 280 and 281: the GST Council, the Finance Commission, and the laying of its recommendations before Parliament.

Article 270: all taxes in the Union List, except those under Articles 268, 269 and 269A, surcharges under Article 271 and any cess for specific purposes, are levied and collected by the Union and shared with the States. Income tax and corporation tax are shared under this Article. Article 271: surcharges on taxes for Union purposes belong wholly to the Union. slides.part: 2. Distribution of Revenues and Centre State Financial Relations
slides.title: 2.2 The divisible pool
slides.html: Originally only income tax was compulsorily shared (Article 270), and Union excise duties could be shared under Article 272. The Constitution (Eightieth Amendment) Act, 2000 removed Article 272 and made all Union List taxes, with the stated exceptions, a single divisible pool, following the Tenth Finance Commission’s alternative scheme of devolution.

The Constitution (Eightieth Amendment) Act, 2000 removed Article 272 and made all Union List taxes, with the stated exceptions, a single divisible pool, following the Tenth Finance Commission’s alternative scheme of devolution.

slides.part: 2. Distribution of Revenues and Centre State Financial Relations
slides.title: 2.3 Fiscal imbalance and its correction
slides.html:
The Union controls the most productive taxes, while the States carry heavy spending responsibilities in health, police, agriculture and education (vertical imbalance). States also differ in their capacity to raise revenue (horizontal imbalance). The Constitution corrects this through tax devolution under Article 270, grants under Articles 275 and 282, and borrowing within the limits of Article 293.

Because cesses and surcharges are outside the divisible pool, a larger use of them reduces the States’ share of total Union revenue even when their percentage share of the pool stays the same. This is a recurring source of tension.

slides.part: 2. Distribution of Revenues and Centre State Financial Relations
slides.title: 2.4 GST and cooperative federalism
slides.html:
The One Hundred and First Amendment (2016) introduced Articles 246A, 269A and 279A.

Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (Supreme Court, 19 May 2022)

GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding, on Parliament and the State Legislatures, because Article 246A gives both simultaneous power. The Court described Indian federalism as a dialogue involving both cooperation and contestation.

(Supreme Court, 19 May 2022) GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding, on Parliament and the State Legislatures, because Article 246A gives both simultaneous power. The Court described Indian federalism as a dialogue involving both cooperation and contestation.

slides.title: 3. Fundamental Rights and Tax Statutes
slides.html: Taxing laws are subject to Part III, but courts give the legislature greater freedom in fiscal matters because taxation involves complex economic choices.
slides.plain: 3. Fundamental Rights and Tax Statutes Taxing laws are subject to Part III, but courts give the legislature greater freedom in fiscal matters because taxation involves complex economic choices.

slides.title: 3.1 Article 14
slides.html:
Classification is permitted if it rests on an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the object of the law (Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S.R. Tendolkar, AIR 1958 SC 538).

Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala AIR 1961 SC 552

A flat rate of land tax on all lands, whether productive or barren, with no machinery for assessment or objections, treated unequals as equals and was struck down. It was also held confiscatory.

Suraj Mall Mohta and Co. v. A.V. Visvanatha Sastri AIR 1954 SC 545

A harsher procedure under the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, for persons who could equally be dealt with under the normal procedure of the 1922 Act, was held discriminatory. Procedural provisions of tax laws are also tested under Article 14.

R.K. Garg v. Union of India (1981) 4 SCC 675

The Special Bearer Bonds scheme, which gave immunity to persons investing unaccounted money, was upheld. Laws on economic activities are viewed with greater latitude than laws affecting civil rights.

Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Association of India v. Union of India (1989) 3 SCC 634

The Expenditure Tax Act, 1987, which taxed expenditure in certain hotels with high room charges, was upheld. The legislature has greater freedom of classification in taxation.

slides.title: 3.2 Article 19
slides.html: A tax is not normally an unreasonable restriction on trade under Article 19(1)(g); it becomes open to challenge only if it is confiscatory or prohibitive. In Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641, the Supreme Court held that newspapers are not immune from taxation, but a tax heavy enough to curtail circulation can violate the freedom of the press under Article 19(1)(a).
slides.plain: 3.2 Article 19 A tax is not normally an unreasonable restriction on trade under Article 19(1)(g); it becomes open to challenge only if it is confiscatory or prohibitive. In Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641, the Supreme Court held that newspapers are not immune from taxation, but a tax heavy enough to curtail circulation can violate the freedom of the press under Article 19(1)(a).

slides.title: 3.3 Article 20 and retrospective taxation
slides.html: Article 20(1) bars retrospective criminal laws, not retrospective taxes. In Rai Ramkrishna v. State of Bihar, AIR 1963 SC 1667, the Supreme Court held that a tax law may be retrospective, though the length and effect of the retrospective period may be relevant when its reasonableness is tested. Penal provisions, however, cannot be applied retrospectively.

State of Bihar , AIR 1963 SC 1667, the Supreme Court held that a tax law may be retrospective, though the length and effect of the retrospective period may be relevant when its reasonableness is tested. Penal provisions, however, cannot be applied retrospectively.

slides.title: 3.4 Article 21 and Article 300A
slides.html: Tax laws that collect personal information must satisfy the requirements of the right to privacy (K.S. Puttaswamy, Unit I). The right to property is now a constitutional right under Article 300A; a tax imposed by a valid law satisfies it.

slides.title: 3.5 Fair procedure
slides.html: In Pannalal Binjraj v. Union of India, AIR 1957 SC 397, the power under the 1922 Act to transfer an assessee’s case from one officer to another was upheld because it was given to a high authority and had to be exercised reasonably; an arbitrary transfer in a particular case could still be challenged. The corresponding power is now in section 243.

Union of India , AIR 1957 SC 397, the power under the 1922 Act to transfer an assessee’s case from one officer to another was upheld because it was given to a high authority and had to be exercised reasonably; an arbitrary transfer in a particular case could still be challenged. The corresponding power is now in section 243.

slides.title: 3.6 Freedom of trade (Articles 301 to 304)
slides.html: In Atiabari Tea Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam, AIR 1961 SC 232, a tax that directly restricted the movement of trade was held to be hit by Article 301. Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1962 SC 1406, excluded regulatory measures and compensatory taxes. In Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana (2017) 12 SCC 1, a nine judge bench held that non discriminatory taxes do not offend Article 301 and rejected the compensatory tax test; discrimination against goods from other States remains barred by Article 304(a).

State of Assam , AIR 1961 SC 232, a tax that directly restricted the movement of trade was held to be hit by Article 301. Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan , AIR 1962 SC 1406, excluded regulatory measures and compensatory taxes. In Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana (2017) 12 SCC 1, a nine judge bench held that non discriminatory taxes do not offend Article 301 and rejected the compensatory tax test; discrimination against goods from other States remains barred by Article 304(a).

slides.title: 4.1 The Finance Commission
slides.html:
Under Article 280, the President constitutes a Finance Commission every fifth year or earlier, with a Chairman and four other members. The Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951 lays down their qualifications and gives the Commission certain powers of a civil court. Under Article 280(3) it recommends:

  1. the distribution of the net proceeds of shareable taxes between the Union and the States, and their allocation among the States (vertical and horizontal devolution);
  2. the principles governing grants in aid under Article 275;
  3. measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities (added by the Seventy Third and Seventy Fourth Amendments, 1992); and
  4. any other matter referred to it by the President in the interests of sound finance.

Under Article 281, the President lays every recommendation before Parliament with an explanatory memorandum of the action taken. The Commission’s recommendations are advisory, but those on tax devolution have in practice been accepted.

The Commission’s recommendations are advisory, but those on tax devolution have in practice been accepted.

slides.title: 4.2 The Fifteenth and Sixteenth Finance Commissions
slides.html:
1. The Fifteenth Finance Commission (chaired by N.K. Singh) fixed the States’ share at 41% of the divisible pool, down from 42% because Jammu and Kashmir became Union territories. For distribution among States it used income distance (45%), population as per the 2011 Census (15%), area (15%), forest and ecology (10%), demographic performance (12.5%) and tax and fiscal efforts (2.5%).
  2. The Sixteenth Finance Commission was constituted on 31 December 2023 under the chairmanship of Arvind Panagariya. It submitted its report to the President on 17 November 2025, and the report was laid in Parliament with the Union Budget on 1 February 2026.
  3. The Sixteenth Commission kept the States’ share at 41% for its award period from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031, and the Union accepted this recommendation.

slides.title: 4.3 NITI Aayog
slides.html: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was set up by a Union Cabinet resolution with effect from 1 January 2015, replacing the Planning Commission. It is neither a constitutional nor a statutory body. The Prime Minister is its Chairperson; it has a Vice Chairperson, full time and ex officio members and a Chief Executive Officer, and its Governing Council includes the Chief Ministers of all States and of Union territories with legislatures. It acts as a policy think tank, promotes cooperative federalism and ranks States on development indices, but, unlike the Planning Commission, it does not allocate funds to States. Five Year Plans ended with the Twelfth Plan in 2017.

slides.title: 4.4 The two bodies compared
slides.html:
1. Basis: the Finance Commission is constitutional (Article 280); NITI Aayog is executive.
  2. Function: the Finance Commission recommends sharing of taxes and grants; NITI Aayog advises on policy.
  3. Money: Finance Commission recommendations govern large formula based transfers; NITI Aayog transfers no funds.
  4. Tenure: each Finance Commission covers an award period, usually five years; NITI Aayog is a standing body.

Function: the Finance Commission recommends sharing of taxes and grants; NITI Aayog advises on policy. Money: Finance Commission recommendations govern large formula based transfers; NITI Aayog transfers no funds. Tenure: each Finance Commission covers an award period, usually five years; NITI Aayog is a standing body.

slides.title: 5.1 Strict construction of the charge
slides.html: In Partington v. Attorney General (1869) LR 4 HL 100, Lord Cairns said that a person within the letter of the law must be taxed however great the hardship, and a person not within the letter is free however much he seems to be within its spirit. In Cape Brandy Syndicate v. IRC [1921] 1 KB 64, Rowlatt J. said that in a taxing Act one looks only at what is clearly said: “there is no equity about a tax”, nothing is to be read in and nothing implied. The Supreme Court adopted this approach in A.V. Fernandez v. State of Kerala, AIR 1957 SC 657: no tax can be imposed by inference or analogy.

Attorney General (1869) LR 4 HL 100, Lord Cairns said that a person within the letter of the law must be taxed however great the hardship, and a person not within the letter is free however much he seems to be within its spirit. In Cape Brandy Syndicate v. IRC [1921] 1 KB 64, Rowlatt J. said that in a taxing Act one looks only at what is clearly said: “there is no equity about a tax”, nothing is to be read in and nothing implied. The Supreme Court adopted this approach in A.V. Fernandez v. State of Kerala , AIR 1957 SC 657: no tax can be imposed by inference or analogy.

slides.title: 5.2 Benefit of a real doubt
slides.html: If a charging provision is reasonably capable of two constructions, the one favouring the assessee is adopted (CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd. (1973) 1 SCC 442; [1973] 88 ITR 192 (SC)). This applies only to genuine ambiguity.
slides.plain: 5.2 Benefit of a real doubt If a charging provision is reasonably capable of two constructions, the one favouring the assessee is adopted ( CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd. (1973) 1 SCC 442; [1973] 88 ITR 192 (SC)). This applies only to genuine ambiguity.

slides.title: 5.3 The charge must be complete
slides.html: The charging provision must clearly identify the subject, the person, the rate and the measure; courts cannot fill gaps (Mathuram Agrawal v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1999) 8 SCC 667). The charging section and the computation provisions form one code, so where the computation provisions cannot apply, the charge fails (CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty (1981) 2 SCC 460, on self generated goodwill).

slides.title: 5.4 Exemptions and incentives
slides.html: A Constitution Bench in Commissioner of Customs (Import), Mumbai v. Dilip Kumar and Co. (2018) 9 SCC 1 held that exemptions are construed strictly, the burden is on the person claiming them, and ambiguity in an exemption benefits the Revenue. On the other hand, an incentive provision meant to promote growth is construed liberally to advance its object (Bajaj Tempo Ltd. v. CIT (1992) 3 SCC 78; [1992] 196 ITR 188 (SC)). Together: whether a person falls within an exemption is decided strictly, but once he does, the provision is applied fairly. This matters under the 2025 Act, where most exemptions are in Schedules II to VII with their own conditions.

slides.title: 5.5 Purposive construction
slides.html: In K.P. Varghese v. Income Tax Officer (1981) 4 SCC 173; [1981] 131 ITR 597 (SC), a literal reading of section 52(2) of the 1961 Act would have taxed honest sellers on notional consideration. The Court read it as applying only where consideration was understated, relying on its purpose and the Finance Minister’s speech.

slides.title: 5.6 Substance, avoidance and retrospectivity
slides.html: Courts look at the true nature of a transaction, not its label (Liberty Cinema, Unit I), and tax avoidance is now governed by the General Anti Avoidance Rule (Chapter XI). In CIT v. Vatika Township (P) Ltd. (2015) 1 SCC 1, a Constitution Bench held that a provision imposing a new burden is presumed prospective unless made retrospective expressly or by necessary implication, though a truly clarificatory or curative provision may operate retrospectively.

slides.title: 5.7 Circulars and treaties
slides.html: CBDT circulars bind the department even when they relax the law in the assessee’s favour (UCO Bank v. CIT (1999) 4 SCC 599), but they do not bind the assessee or the courts, and a circular contrary to the statute cannot prevail (Commissioner of Central Excise v. Ratan Melting and Wire Industries (2008) 13 SCC 1). Section 536(2)(j) continues circulars and notifications issued under the 1961 Act so far as they are consistent with the 2025 Act. Section 159 provides for double taxation agreements, and a notified treaty provision more beneficial to the assessee can prevail over the Act (Azadi Bachao Andolan, Unit I).

Ratan Melting and Wire Industries (2008) 13 SCC 1). Section 536(2)(j) continues circulars and notifications issued under the 1961 Act so far as they are consistent with the 2025 Act. Section 159 provides for double taxation agreements, and a notified treaty provision more beneficial to the assessee can prevail over the Act ( Azadi Bachao Andolan , Unit I).

slides.title: 5.8 Reading the 2025 Act
slides.html:
1. A consolidating and amending Act. Where the new words are substantially the same as the old, decisions under the 1961 Act remain good guidance; where the words have changed, the change must be given effect.
  2. Repeal and savings. Section 536(2) preserves the previous operation of the 1961 Act, accrued rights and liabilities, and pending proceedings, and section 536(4) applies section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 to the repeal.
  3. Old years. A reference to a tax year beginning on 1 April 2025 or earlier is read as the corresponding previous year under the 1961 Act (section 536(3)).
  4. Tables and Notes. Conditions in Tables must be read with the Notes below them, just as a section is read with its definitions.

Exam focus. Begin with strict construction of the charge (Cape Brandy Syndicate, A.V. Fernandez), then the refinements: benefit of real doubt (Vegetable Products), exemptions and incentives (Dilip Kumar and Bajaj Tempo), purposive reading (K.P. Varghese) and prospectivity (Vatika Township). End with how consolidation affects the use of old precedents.

slides.title: Practice Questions for Unit II
slides.html:
1. Explain the distribution of taxing powers between the Union and the States. Why are taxing entries separate from general entries?
  2. “Parliament defines agricultural income, but the States tax it.” Explain with reference to Articles 366(1) and 274 and Entry 46 of List II.
  3. Discuss the role of the Finance Commission with reference to the Fifteenth and Sixteenth Finance Commissions. How do cesses and surcharges affect the States?
  4. To what extent are taxing statutes subject to Articles 14 and 19? Discuss with cases.
  5. “There is no equity about a tax.” Explain the rule of strict interpretation and its limits, including the treatment of exemptions.

slides.part: 1. Overview of the Income Tax Act, 2025
slides.title: 1.1 Why a new Act
slides.html: The 1961 Act had been amended almost every year for six decades and had become hard to read because of long provisos, many Explanations, lettered sections and obsolete provisions. The 2025 Act aims to simplify the language and structure of the law rather than to change tax policy fundamentally. Its long title describes it as an Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to income tax. It is Act 30 of 2025, received assent on 21 August 2025 and came into force on 1 April 2026 (section 1(3)).
slides.plain: 1.1 Why a new Act The 1961 Act had been amended almost every year for six decades and had become hard to read because of long provisos, many Explanations, lettered sections and obsolete provisions. The 2025 Act aims to simplify the language and structure of the law rather than to change tax policy fundamentally. Its long title describes it as an Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to income tax. It is Act 30 of 2025, received assent on 21 August 2025 and came into force on 1 April 2026 (section 1(3)).

slides.part: 1. Overview of the Income Tax Act, 2025
slides.title: 1.2 Structure
slides.html:
The Act has 23 Chapters, 536 sections and 16 Schedules. The Chapters most relevant to this course are Chapter I (preliminary, sections 1 to 3), Chapter II (basis of charge, sections 4 to 10), Chapter III (incomes not forming part of total income, sections 11 and 12), Chapter IV (computation of total income, sections 13 to 95, divided into Parts for the heads: salaries in sections 15 to 19, house property in sections 20 to 25, business or profession in sections 26 to 66, capital gains in sections 67 to 91, and other sources in sections 92 to 95), Chapter V (income of other persons included in the assessee’s income, sections 96 to 100), Chapter VI (aggregation of income, sections 101 to 107), Chapter VII (losses, sections 108 to 121), Chapter VIII (deductions, sections 122 to 154) and Chapter XIII (determination of tax in special cases, including the new regime in section 202). Procedure, appeals, collection, penalties and prosecution follow in Chapters XIV to XXII, and Chapter XXIII (miscellaneous) contains the rule making power (section 533) and repeal and savings (section 536).

The Schedules carry much of the detail. Schedule I sets conditions for certain activities not to constitute a business connection in India (section 9(12)). Schedules II to VI list incomes not included in total income, and Schedule VII lists persons exempt from tax (section 11). Schedule VIII covers political parties and electoral trusts. The remaining Schedules deal with specific matters, such as development accounts for tea, coffee and rubber (Schedule IX), recognised provident funds (Schedule XI), insurance business (Schedule XIV) and items qualifying for deduction under section 123 (Schedule XV).

slides.part: 1. Overview of the Income Tax Act, 2025
slides.title: 1.3 Main design features
slides.html:
1. One tax year (section 3) replaces the “previous year” and “assessment year” of the 1961 Act.
  2. Exemptions in Schedules (section 11) replace the long section 10 of the 1961 Act.
  3. Retirement benefits such as gratuity, commuted pension and leave encashment are now deductions in the Table in section 19, not exemptions.
  4. Tables and formulae set out conditions and computations (for example, sections 19, 31, 41(1)(c), 58 and 202).
  5. Relocation: the method of accounting is now section 276; deduction of tax at source is in sections 392 and 393; charitable and religious institutions are dealt with as registered non profit organisations (sections 332 to 355).
  6. Codified positions: for example, section 14(3) (disallowance even where no exempt income is earned), section 26(4) (letting of a residential house is house property income), section 33(7) (depreciation applies whether or not claimed) and section 34(3)(b) (benefits whose acceptance breaches the recipient’s conduct rules).

slides.part: 1. Overview of the Income Tax Act, 2025
slides.title: 1.4 Rules and amendments
slides.html:
The Income Tax Rules, 2026 were notified under section 533 by Notification No. 22/2026, G.S.R. 198(E), dated 20 March 2026, and came into force on 1 April 2026. Many figures, such as the house rent allowance formula and perquisite values, are in the Rules.

The text used here includes amendments by the Finance Act, 2026 (Act 4 of 2026) and Act 21 of 2026. Those relevant to this course include: the interest limit for self occupied houses in section 22(2) now covers pre construction interest as well; section 29(1)(e) now allows employees’ provident fund contributions credited by the due date of the return; section 195 now taxes unexplained income at 30% instead of 60%, and the penalty in section 443 has been omitted; and buy back payments have been removed from the definition of dividend in section 2(40).

Those relevant to this course include: the interest limit for self occupied houses in section 22(2) now covers pre construction interest as well; section 29(1)(e) now allows employees’ provident fund contributions credited by the due date of the return; section 195 now taxes unexplained income at 30% instead of 60%, and the penalty in section 443 has been omitted; and buy back payments have been removed from the definition of dividend in section 2(40).

slides.part: 1. Overview of the Income Tax Act, 2025
slides.title: 1.5 Transition from the 1961 Act
slides.html:
1. The previous operation of the 1961 Act and accrued rights and liabilities are preserved (section 536(2)(a) and (b)).
  2. Proceedings for any tax year beginning before 1 April 2026, whether pending or started later, continue under the procedure of the 1961 Act (section 536(2)(c)).
  3. Options exercised and circulars or notifications issued under the 1961 Act continue so far as consistent (section 536(2)(f) and (j)), and brought forward losses carry over (section 536(2)(m) and (n)).
  4. A reference to a tax year beginning on 1 April 2025 or earlier is read as the corresponding previous year under the 1961 Act (section 536(3)).
slides.plain: 1.5 Transition from the 1961 Act The previous operation of the 1961 Act and accrued rights and liabilities are preserved (section 536(2)(a) and (b)). Proceedings for any tax year beginning before 1 April 2026, whether pending or started later, continue under the procedure of the 1961 Act (section 536(2)(c)). Options exercised and circulars or notifications issued under the 1961 Act continue so far as consistent (section 536(2)(f) and (j)), and brought forward losses carry over (section 536(2)(m) and (n)). A reference to a tax year beginning on 1 April 2025 or earlier is read as the corresponding previous year under the 1961 Act (section 536(3)).

slides.title: 2.1 The statutory definition
slides.html:
Section 2(49) says that “income” includes a list of items. The word “includes” enlarges the ordinary meaning: anything that is income in the ordinary sense is income even if not listed, and the listed items are income even if they would not otherwise be. The list includes:

  1. profits and gains, dividends, and voluntary contributions received by registered non profit organisations and certain institutions;
  2. perquisites and profits in lieu of salary (sections 17 and 18), special allowances for duties, and allowances for personal expenses or cost of living;
  3. benefits obtained from a company by a director or a person with a substantial interest, or their relatives;
  4. capital gains (section 67) and special business receipts under sections 26(2) and 38;
  5. profits of mutual insurance companies and cooperative insurance, and of banking by cooperative societies with their members (clauses (l) and (m));
  6. winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, races, card games and other games, gambling and betting;
  7. employees’ contributions to welfare funds received by an employer, and sums under a Keyman insurance policy;
  8. gifts and property received without or for inadequate consideration (section 92(2)(m)) and compensation connected with termination of employment (section 92(2)(j)); and
  9. any subsidy, grant, incentive, duty drawback, waiver or reimbursement from a government or authority (clause (w)), except a subsidy that reduces the actual cost of an asset under section 39 and a Central Government corpus grant to a government trust or institution.

slides.title: 2.2 The judicial meaning of income
slides.html:
1. Navinchandra Mafatlal v. CIT, AIR 1955 SC 58: “income” in a legislative entry must be given its widest meaning; capital gains could be taxed as income.
  2. CIT v. G.R. Karthikeyan, 1993 Supp (3) SCC 222; [1993] 201 ITR 866 (SC): a prize won in a motor rally was income in the ordinary sense; the inclusive definition does not cut down the natural meaning of income.
  3. Emil Webber v. CIT (1993) 2 SCC 386; [1993] 200 ITR 483 (SC): tax paid by an employer on an employee’s salary is the employee’s income.

slides.title: 2.3 Receipts that are not income
slides.html:
1. Capital receipts, unless a provision taxes them (such as capital gains, or compensation under section 26(2)(b), (c) and (h)).
  2. Gifts, except as taxed by section 92(2)(m), which taxes, among other things, sums of money received without consideration where the total in a tax year exceeds Rs. 50,000.
  3. Loans and deposits, though an unexplained credit can be taxed under section 102.
  4. Reimbursements, such as special allowances for official duties to the extent actually spent (Schedule III, Sl. No. 12).
  5. Amounts diverted at source by an overriding title (Part 3 below) and genuinely mutual surpluses (Part 4 below).

slides.title: 2.4 Capital and revenue receipts
slides.html:
No single test decides the question. The courts ask whether the receipt arose from the fixed capital (the profit making structure) or the circulating capital (stock in trade), and whether it compensates for the loss of a source of income or only for loss of income from a source that continues.

Kettlewell Bullen and Co. Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1965 SC 65; [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC)

The assessee company, which held managing agencies of several companies, received compensation for surrendering the managing agency of Fort William Jute Co. The Supreme Court held it to be a capital receipt, because the agency was a capital asset forming part of the assessee’s business structure and was not given up in the ordinary course of business.

Section 26(2)(b) now taxes as business income compensation received in connection with the termination or modification of a management, agency or business contract, so Kettlewell Bullen matters today mainly for its test. For subsidies, the earlier purpose test (Sahney Steel and Press Works Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 228 ITR 253 (SC): subsidies to run a business are revenue; CIT v. Ponni Sugars and Chemicals Ltd. [2008] 306 ITR 392 (SC): a subsidy to repay loans for expansion is capital) now has a narrow role, because section 2(49)(w) treats most subsidies as income.

slides.title: 2.5 Real income
slides.html:
Income tax is levied on real, not hypothetical, income.

CIT v. Shoorji Vallabhdas and Co. AIR 1962 SC 1281; [1962] 46 ITR 144 (SC)

Managing agents agreed, before the year ended, to accept a lower commission. Only the reduced commission was taxable. If income does not really result, there is no tax, even if a book entry shows hypothetical income.

State Bank of Travancore v. CIT (1986) 2 SCC 11; [1986] 158 ITR 102 (SC)

Interest on doubtful loans that had accrued under the mercantile system was taxable even though credited to a suspense account. The real income theory cannot override the statutory scheme; the remedy is a bad debt deduction if the loan is later lost.

Godhra Electricity Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1997) 4 SCC 530; [1997] 225 ITR 746 (SC)

Enhanced charges that consumers disputed and never paid were not real income of the company, even under the mercantile system.

slides.title: 3. Application and Diversion of Income
slides.html:
1. Diversion by overriding title: if a legal obligation diverts income at its source, so that it never becomes the assessee’s income, it is not taxable in his hands.
  2. Application of income: if income first becomes the assessee’s and he is then obliged to pay part of it to another, the payment is an application of his own income and is taxable in his hands.

Raja Bejoy Singh Dudhuria v. CIT (1933) 1 ITR 135 (PC)

Maintenance payable to the assessee’s stepmother under a decree, and charged on his estate, was diverted at source and was not his income.

CIT v. Sitaldas Tirathdas AIR 1961 SC 728; [1961] 41 ITR 367 (SC)

Maintenance payable to the assessee’s wife and children under a decree, but not charged on his income or property, was an application of income. The true test is whether the amount, in truth, never reached the assessee as his income.

CIT v. Sunil J. Kinariwala (2003) 1 SCC 660; [2003] 259 ITR 10 (SC)

A partner assigned part of his share of the firm’s profits to a trust. The share first became his income and was then applied, so the whole share was taxable in his hands.

The Act also prevents diversion by mere arrangement: income transferred without transferring the asset that produces it remains the transferor’s income (section 96), and income from a revocable transfer of assets is also taxed in the transferor’s hands (section 97).

slides.title: 4. Doctrine of Mutuality
slides.html:
A person cannot make a profit out of himself. If members contribute to a common fund for their mutual benefit, and any surplus can only be spent on them or returned to them, the surplus is not income. The doctrine originated in New York Life Insurance Co. v. Styles (1889) 14 App Cas 381.

Bangalore Club v. CIT (2013) 5 SCC 509; [2013] 350 ITR 509 (SC)

The Supreme Court laid down three conditions: complete identity between contributors and participants; actions of the contributors and participants in furtherance of the mandate of the association; and no scope for profiteering by contributors from a fund that can only be spent on or returned to them. Interest earned by the club on deposits with banks that were its corporate members was held taxable, because the money went out of the closed circle of members into commercial lending.

CIT v. Royal Western India Turf Club Ltd. AIR 1954 SC 85; [1953] 24 ITR 551 (SC)

A club that carried on the business of conducting races and served members and non members alike could not claim mutuality.

Chelmsford Club v. CIT (2000) 3 SCC 214; [2000] 243 ITR 89 (SC)

A club providing facilities only to its members, with any surplus usable only for them, was entitled to the benefit of mutuality.

Statutory limits. Section 2(49)(l) and (m) tax profits of mutual insurance companies and cooperative insurance, and of banking by cooperative societies with their members. Section 26(2)(d) taxes the income of trade, professional and similar associations from specific services to members. Section 50 allows such an association a deduction where its receipts from members fall short of its expenditure for their common interest, limited to 50% of total income.

slides.title: 5.1 The statutory basis
slides.html: Section 5 fixes the scope of total income by reference to income received or deemed received in India, income accruing or deemed to accrue in India, and income accruing outside India. Residents are taxed on all three, subject to the limit for those not ordinarily resident in section 5(1)(c). Non residents are taxed only on the first two (section 5(2)). Income accruing outside India is not received in India merely because it appears in a balance sheet prepared in India (section 5(3)), and income taxed on accrual is not taxed again on receipt (section 5(4)).

Residents are taxed on all three, subject to the limit for those not ordinarily resident in section 5(1)(c). Non residents are taxed only on the first two (section 5(2)). Income accruing outside India is not received in India merely because it appears in a balance sheet prepared in India (section 5(3)), and income taxed on accrual is not taxed again on receipt (section 5(4)).

slides.title: 5.2 When income accrues
slides.html:
E.D. Sassoon and Co. Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1954 SC 470; [1954] 26 ITR 27 (SC)

Managing agents transferred their agencies during the year, and their commission was payable only at the end of the year. The Supreme Court held that income accrues when the assessee acquires a right to receive it, so that it becomes a debt due to him. No commission had accrued to the transferors before the transfer. “Accrue” and “arise” are used in contrast to “receive”: income is received when it reaches the assessee, and accrues when the right to it vests in him.

CIT v. Toshoku Ltd. [1980] 125 ITR 525 (SC)

Commission earned by a non resident for services outside India and credited in the books of an Indian company was neither received in India (a book credit is not receipt) nor accrued in India.

slides.title: 5.3 Deemed receipt: section 7
slides.html: The taxable accretion and transferred balance in a recognised provident fund, and the employer’s contribution to the pension scheme under section 124, are deemed received in the tax year (section 7(1)). A dividend is income of the year in which it is declared, distributed or paid, and an interim dividend of the year in which it is unconditionally made available (section 7(2)).

A dividend is income of the year in which it is declared, distributed or paid, and an interim dividend of the year in which it is unconditionally made available (section 7(2)).

slides.title: 5.4 Deemed accrual in India: section 9
slides.html:
1. General rule (section 9(2)): income accruing directly or indirectly through or from any asset, source or property in India, any business connection in India, or the transfer of a capital asset situated in India. “Through” includes “by means of”, “in consequence of” and “by reason of” (section 9(13)).
  2. Salaries (section 9(3)): salary for services rendered in India (including related rest or leave periods), and salary paid by the Government to an Indian citizen for services outside India.
  3. Dividends (section 9(4)): dividends paid by an Indian company outside India.
  4. Interest, royalty and fees for technical services (section 9(5) to (7)): payable by the Government, by a resident (unless used for business or income outside India), or by a non resident where used for business or income in India. Under section 9(11), these are taxable whether or not the non resident has a residence, place of business or business connection in India, and whether or not he rendered the services in India.
  5. Gifts (section 9(8)): sums of the kind in section 2(49)(u) paid by a resident to a non resident or to a person not ordinarily resident.
  6. Business connection (section 9(9)): includes business through a dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts, keeps stock for delivery or secures orders for the non resident, and a significant economic presence (transactions above a prescribed amount or systematic interaction with a prescribed number of users in India). Business through an independent agent, and purchases of goods in India for export, are excluded.
  7. Indirect transfers (section 9(10)): shares of a foreign company are deemed situated in India if their value is derived substantially from Indian assets, that is, Indian assets exceed Rs. 10 crore and form at least 50% of total assets. Small shareholders holding 5% or less without management rights are excluded.

CIT v. R.D. Aggarwal and Co. AIR 1965 SC 1526; [1965] 56 ITR 20 (SC)

A business connection requires a real and intimate relation between the non resident’s activity outside India and an activity in India that contributes to earning the income, with an element of continuity. A stray or isolated transaction is not normally a business connection.

Ishikawajima Harima Heavy Industries Ltd. v. Director of Income Tax (2007) 3 SCC 481

Income from offshore supply of equipment for an Indian project, with title passing outside India, was not taxable in India, and fees for services rendered outside India needed a sufficient territorial nexus. Parliament responded with the rule now in section 9(11).

slides.title: 5.5 Method of accounting
slides.html: Business income and income from other sources are computed under the cash or mercantile system regularly employed by the assessee, subject to the notified Income Computation and Disclosure Standards (section 276(1) and (2)). If the accounts are unreliable, the method is not regularly followed or the standards are ignored, the Assessing Officer may make a best judgment assessment under section 271 (section 276(3)). Salary has its own timing rule: due or receipt, whichever is earlier (section 15).

slides.part: 6. Assessment Year, Previous Year and Tax Year
slides.title: 6.1 The old position
slides.html: Under the 1961 Act, income of the previous year (the financial year in which it was earned) was assessed in the following assessment year at the rates for that assessment year. Income earned from 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025 was assessed in the assessment year 2025 to 2026. Exceptions taxed income in the year of earning, for example in the case of non resident shipping businesses, persons leaving India and discontinued businesses.

Income earned from 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025 was assessed in the assessment year 2025 to 2026. Exceptions taxed income in the year of earning, for example in the case of non resident shipping businesses, persons leaving India and discontinued businesses.

slides.part: 6. Assessment Year, Previous Year and Tax Year
slides.title: 6.2 The tax year
slides.html:
1. Section 3(1): “tax year” means the twelve month period of the financial year beginning on 1 April.
  2. Section 3(2): for a business or profession newly set up, or a new source of income, the tax year begins on the date of setting up or the date the source comes into existence and ends with that financial year. For example, a lawyer who starts practice on 15 September 2026 has a first tax year from 15 September 2026 to 31 March 2027.
  3. Section 4 charges tax for the tax year at the rates fixed by the Finance Act on the total income of the tax year. The phrase “assessment year” does not appear in the 2025 Act at all.
  4. Where the Act charges income of another period, it is charged accordingly (section 4(4)); examples are sections 316 (shipping business of non residents), 317 (persons leaving India) and 320 (discontinued business).

Section 3(2): for a business or profession newly set up, or a new source of income, the tax year begins on the date of setting up or the date the source comes into existence and ends with that financial year. slides.part: 6. Assessment Year, Previous Year and Tax Year
slides.title: 6.3 The changeover
slides.html: Income earned from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 remains under the 1961 Act (previous year 2025 to 2026, assessment year 2026 to 2027). The first tax year under the 2025 Act runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027. Section 536(2)(c) and (3) govern the transition (Part 1.5 above).
slides.plain: 6.3 The changeover Income earned from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 remains under the 1961 Act (previous year 2025 to 2026, assessment year 2026 to 2027). The first tax year under the 2025 Act runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027. Section 536(2)(c) and (3) govern the transition (Part 1.5 above).

slides.title: 7.1 Why it is special
slides.html: Parliament taxes income other than agricultural income (Entry 82, List I); the States tax agricultural income (Entry 46, List II); and Article 366(1) adopts the income tax definition. Section 2(5) of the 2025 Act therefore fixes the boundary. Agricultural income is excluded from total income by section 11 read with Schedule II, Sl. No. 1, without any conditions.

Section 2(5) of the 2025 Act therefore fixes the boundary. Agricultural income is excluded from total income by section 11 read with Schedule II, Sl. No. 1, without any conditions.

slides.title: 7.2 Section 2(5)
slides.html:
“Agricultural income” means:

(a) any rent or revenue derived from land situated in India and used for agricultural purposes;

(b) any income derived from such land by:

  1. agriculture;
  2. a process ordinarily employed by a cultivator or receiver of rent in kind to make the produce fit to be taken to market; or
  3. the sale by a cultivator or receiver of rent in kind of produce on which no other process has been performed;

(c) income from a farm building on or near the land, required by the cultivator or receiver of rent as a dwelling house, store house or out building because of his connection with the land, where the land is assessed to land revenue or a local rate or, if not so assessed, is not in an urban area described in section 2(22)(iii)(A) or (B); and

(d) income derived from saplings or seedlings grown in a nursery.

It excludes income from such a building or land used for any other purpose (such as letting for residence or business), and income from transferring urban agricultural land.

Urban land. Agricultural land is not a “capital asset” (section 2(22)(iii)) unless it lies within a municipality or cantonment board with a population of at least ten thousand, or within 2, 6 or 8 kilometres of its limits, depending on whether its population is up to one lakh, up to ten lakh, or more. The sale of rural agricultural land therefore gives no taxable capital gain.

slides.title: 7.3 Meaning of agriculture
slides.html:
CIT v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy AIR 1957 SC 768; [1957] 32 ITR 466 (SC)

“Agriculture” requires basic operations on the land itself, such as tilling, sowing and planting, involving human skill and labour. Subsequent operations (weeding, pruning, protection) count only when they follow basic operations. Income from a forest of spontaneous growth was therefore not agricultural income. On the same reasoning, dairy and poultry farming are generally not agriculture.

Mrs. Bacha F. Guzdar v. CIT AIR 1955 SC 74; [1955] 27 ITR 1 (SC)

Dividends from a company owning tea estates are not agricultural income in the shareholder’s hands. Income “derived from” land requires a direct and immediate relation with the land.

slides.title: 7.4 Composite income and partial integration
slides.html:
Where the same person grows and processes a crop, the Rules split the income. Under Rule 271 of the Income Tax Rules, 2026 (formerly Rules 7A, 7B and 8 of the 1962 Rules), the taxable business portion is 35% for rubber, 25% for coffee grown and cured, 40% for coffee grown, cured, roasted and ground, and 40% for tea grown and manufactured. The rest is agricultural income.

Agricultural income is exempt, but for certain assessees it is used to fix the rate on non agricultural income (partial integration). The method is laid down in the Finance Act of each year, which section 405(2) recognises. Under the Finance Acts of the 1961 regime, it applied to individuals, Hindu undivided families and similar persons with net agricultural income above Rs. 5,000 and non agricultural income above the exemption limit: tax is computed on the two incomes together, then on agricultural income plus the exemption limit, and the difference is payable. Confirm the method in the current Finance Act.

slides.title: 8. Basis of Charge
slides.html:
Section 4 charges income tax for each tax year at the rates enacted by a Central Act (the Finance Act), on the total income of the tax year of every person, in accordance with the Act (section 4(1) and (2)). Income tax includes any additional income tax (section 4(3)), and it is collected through deduction or collection at source and advance tax (section 4(5)).

Rates under the new regime (section 202(1)), for individuals, Hindu undivided families, associations of persons (other than cooperative societies), bodies of individuals and artificial juridical persons, unless they opt out: nil up to Rs. 4,00,000; 5% from Rs. 4,00,001 to Rs. 8,00,000; 10% to Rs. 12,00,000; 15% to Rs. 16,00,000; 20% to Rs. 20,00,000; 25% to Rs. 24,00,000; and 30% above that.

Rebate (section 156): under the new regime, a resident individual with total income up to Rs. 12,00,000 gets a rebate of the full tax or Rs. 60,000, whichever is less, with marginal relief just above that level; in other cases, the rebate is the full tax or Rs. 12,500, whichever is less, where total income does not exceed Rs. 5,00,000. Surcharge and cess are imposed by the Finance Act.

slides.title: 9.1 Individuals
slides.html:
An individual is resident in a tax year if he is in India for 182 days or more in that year, or for 60 days or more in that year and 365 days or more in the four preceding years (section 6(2)). The 60 day condition does not apply to:

  1. an Indian citizen leaving India in the year as a crew member of an Indian ship or for employment abroad (section 6(3)); or
  2. an Indian citizen or person of Indian origin visiting India (section 6(4)), except that if his income other than income from foreign sources exceeds Rs. 15,00,000, the condition applies with 120 days in place of 60 (section 6(5)).

An Indian citizen who is not liable to tax in any other country because of domicile or residence, and whose income other than from foreign sources exceeds Rs. 15,00,000, is deemed resident (section 6(7)), unless already resident (section 6(8)).

A resident is not ordinarily resident (section 6(13)) if he (or the manager of a Hindu undivided family) was non resident in nine of the ten preceding years, or was in India for 729 days or less in the seven preceding years; or if he is a citizen or person of Indian origin with such income above Rs. 15,00,000 who stayed 120 days or more but less than 182 days; or if he is a deemed resident citizen.

slides.title: 9.2 Other persons
slides.html:
1. Hindu undivided family, firm or association of persons: resident unless the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly outside India (section 6(9)). Even partial control exercised in India therefore makes it resident.
  2. Company: resident if it is an Indian company or its place of effective management is in India, meaning the place where key management and commercial decisions for the business as a whole are in substance made (section 6(10)).
  3. Every other person: resident unless control and management is wholly outside India (section 6(11)). A person resident for one source is resident for all sources (section 6(12)).

V.V.R.N.M. Subbayya Chettiar v. CIT AIR 1951 SC 101; [1951] 19 ITR 168 (SC)

“Control and management” means the controlling and directive power, “the head and brain” as it is sometimes called, and “situated” implies that this power functions at a place with some degree of permanence. On the facts, the family had not shown that its control and management was wholly outside India, so it was held resident.

CIT v. Nandlal Gandalal [1960] 3 SCR 620

Control and management means de facto control and management, not merely the legal right to control or manage.

The place of effective management test draws on the English “central management and control” test in De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd. v. Howe [1906] AC 455.

slides.title: 9.3 Effect on scope of income
slides.html:
1. Resident and ordinarily resident: income received or deemed received in India, accruing or deemed to accrue in India, and accruing outside India.
  2. Not ordinarily resident: the first two, and foreign income only if derived from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India.
  3. Non resident: only income received or deemed received in India, or accruing or deemed to accrue in India.

Example. Ravi, an Indian citizen working abroad, visits India for 130 days and has Indian rental income of Rs. 18,00,000. Because that income exceeds Rs. 15,00,000, the 120 day version applies to him, so he is resident if he was in India for 365 days or more in the four preceding years. He is then not ordinarily resident under section 6(13)(b), since his stay was 120 days or more but less than 182 days.

Ravi, an Indian citizen working abroad, visits India for 130 days and has Indian rental income of Rs. 18,00,000. Because that income exceeds Rs. 15,00,000, the 120 day version applies to him, so he is resident if he was in India for 365 days or more in the four preceding years. He is then not ordinarily resident under section 6(13)(b), since his stay was 120 days or more but less than 182 days.

slides.title: 10. Person
slides.html:
Section 2(77) says that “person” includes an individual, a Hindu undivided family, a company, a firm, an association of persons or a body of individuals (incorporated or not), a local authority, and every other artificial juridical person. An association, body, local authority or artificial juridical person is a person whether or not formed to earn income.

  1. Individual: a natural person, including a minor or a person of unsound mind, assessed through a representative where necessary.
  2. Hindu undivided family: carries its Hindu law meaning and is a person separate from its members. Joint family property remains such even if held for the time being by a sole male coparcener with female members (Gowli Buddanna v. CIT, AIR 1966 SC 1523), and a family of a father, mother and minor daughters holding ancestral property is assessable as such (N.V. Narendranath v. Commissioner of Wealth Tax (1969) 1 SCC 748). Since the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, daughters are coparceners by birth (Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) 9 SCC 1). Section 99(3) taxes in the individual’s hands income from separate property converted into family property without adequate consideration.
  3. Company: includes Indian companies, foreign bodies corporate and bodies declared by the Board to be companies (section 2(28)). An Indian company is one formed and registered under Indian company law, or a statutory corporation, with its registered or principal office in India (section 2(53)).
  4. Firm: as defined in section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, including a limited liability partnership (section 2(45)).
  5. Association of persons: two or more persons who join in a common purpose or common action whose object is to produce income; merely receiving income jointly is not enough (CIT v. Indira Balkrishna, AIR 1960 SC 1172; [1960] 39 ITR 546 (SC)). A body of individuals consists of individuals only. Co owners with definite shares are not assessed as an association of persons (section 24(1)).
  6. Local authority and artificial juridical person: municipalities and panchayats are local authorities; an artificial juridical person is the residual category for other legal persons.
