slides.title: 11. Assessee
slides.html: Section 2(11) defines “assessee” as a person by whom any tax or other sum is payable under the Act, and includes every person in respect of whom proceedings have been taken for assessing his own income, loss or refund or that of another person, every person deemed to be an assessee, and every person deemed to be an assessee in default. Examples are representative assessees such as a guardian or the agent of a non resident (sections 303 to 306), legal representatives (section 302), and a payer who fails to deduct tax at source or to pay it over (section 398(2)). Every assessee is a person, but a person becomes an assessee only when tax is payable by him, proceedings are taken in respect of him, or the Act deems him to be one.

slides.title: 12.1 Three kinds of relief
slides.html:
1. Exemption: the income is not included in total income at all (sections 11 and 12 with Schedules II to VIII).
  2. Deduction: an amount subtracted while computing income, either under a head (section 19 for salaries, section 22 for house property, sections 28 to 52 for business) or from gross total income under Chapter VIII (sections 122 to 154).
  3. Rebate and relief: a reduction of the tax itself, such as the rebate under section 156 and relief for arrears of salary under section 157.

slides.title: 12.2 Exemptions
slides.html: Section 11(1) excludes from total income the incomes listed in Schedules II to VI, subject to their conditions; if the conditions are not met, the income is taxed (section 11(2)). The persons in Schedule VII are not chargeable on their total income while they meet the conditions (section 11(3) and (4)). Schedule II covers general items (such as agricultural income, life insurance sums and payments from statutory provident funds), and Schedule III covers items for eligible persons (such as sums received by a member from a Hindu undivided family, a partner’s share of firm profits, house rent allowance and leave travel concession).

The persons in Schedule VII are not chargeable on their total income while they meet the conditions (section 11(3) and (4)). Schedule II covers general items (such as agricultural income, life insurance sums and payments from statutory provident funds), and Schedule III covers items for eligible persons (such as sums received by a member from a Hindu undivided family, a partner’s share of firm profits, house rent allowance and leave travel concession).

slides.title: 12.3 Expenditure relating to exempt income: section 14
slides.html: No deduction is allowed for expenditure incurred in relation to income that is not part of total income (section 14(1)). If the Assessing Officer is not satisfied with the assessee’s claim, he determines the amount by the prescribed method (section 14(2)), and the rule applies even if no exempt income is earned in that year (section 14(3)). In Maxopp Investment Ltd. v. CIT (2018) 15 SCC 523; [2018] 402 ITR 640 (SC), the Supreme Court held that the dominant purpose of holding shares does not avoid the disallowance, even for shares held as stock in trade, to the extent the expenditure relates to exempt income.

slides.title: 12.4 Deductions under Chapter VIII
slides.html:
Deductions are allowed from gross total income (section 122(1)), which is total income before these deductions (section 122(10)), and cannot exceed it (section 122(2)). Part C deductions require the return to be filed by the due date with the claim (section 122(5)). Part B covers payments such as life insurance and provident fund (section 123 with Schedule XV), pension scheme (section 124), health insurance (section 126), education loan interest (section 129), donations (sections 133 and 135) and rent paid (section 134). Part C covers profits of specified undertakings and incomes (sections 138 to 152), and Parts D and E cover interest on deposits (section 153) and persons with disability (section 154).

Under the new regime (section 202(2)), most exemptions and deductions are not available, including house rent allowance, leave travel concession, tax on employment, interest on a self occupied house, and Chapter VIII deductions other than those under sections 124(1) and (2), 125(2) and 146. Exemptions are construed strictly and incentives liberally (Unit II, Part 5.4).

slides.title: Practice Questions for Unit III
slides.html:
1. Explain the structure of the Income Tax Act, 2025 and five significant changes from the 1961 Act.
  2. “Every receipt is not income.” Explain with reference to section 2(49) and the distinction between capital and revenue receipts.
  3. Distinguish diversion of income by overriding title from application of income, with cases.
  4. State the doctrine of mutuality and its conditions. How has the 2025 Act limited it?
  5. When does income accrue? Explain the deemed accrual rules in section 9 for non residents.
  6. Explain the tax year under section 3 and the transition from the 1961 Act.
  7. Is income from (a) a forest of spontaneous growth, (b) a nursery, (c) dividends from a tea company, and (d) sale of urban agricultural land, agricultural income? Give reasons.

slides.title: 1. Heads of Income
slides.html:
Section 13 classifies all income under five heads: Salaries (sections 15 to 19); Income from house property (sections 20 to 25); Profits and gains of business or profession (sections 26 to 66); Capital gains (sections 67 to 91); and Income from other sources (sections 92 to 95). The heads are mutually exclusive. Each has its own computation rules, and income that falls under a specific head must be computed under it.

United Commercial Bank Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1957 SC 918; [1957] 32 ITR 688 (SC)

Interest on securities held by a bank as part of its business had to be computed under the specific head then provided for interest on securities, not as business income. Each head deals with a particular source.

East India Housing and Land Development Trust Ltd. v. CIT [1961] 42 ITR 49 (SC)

Rent from shops and stalls built by a company dealing in land was taxable under the property head, whatever the object of the company.

“Income from other sources” is the residuary head: it covers income of every kind, not excluded from total income, that is not chargeable under the other four heads (section 92(1)).

slides.part: 2. Total Income and How It Is Computed
slides.title: 2. Total Income and How It Is Computed
slides.html:
Total income is the income referred to in section 5, computed in the manner laid down in the Act (section 2(108)). The steps are:

  1. determine residential status (section 6) and the scope of income (section 5);
  2. leave out exempt income (sections 11 and 12 with the Schedules);
  3. compute income under each head, with the deductions allowed under that head;
  4. add the income of other persons included by sections 96 to 100 (clubbing);
  5. set off losses and brought forward losses (sections 108 to 121), giving the gross total income (section 122(10));
  6. subtract Chapter VIII deductions, unless the new regime bars them, giving the total income, rounded off under section 516; and
  7. apply the rates (Finance Act or section 202, and special rates such as section 195), then the rebate and reliefs (sections 156 to 160), surcharge and cess, and credit for tax deducted or collected at source and advance tax.

The steps are: determine residential status (section 6) and the scope of income (section 5); leave out exempt income (sections 11 and 12 with the Schedules); compute income under each head, with the deductions allowed under that head; add the income of other persons included by sections 96 to 100 (clubbing); set off losses and brought forward losses (sections 108 to 121), giving the gross total income (section 122(10)); subtract Chapter VIII deductions, unless the new regime bars them, giving the total income , rounded off under section 516; and apply the rates (Finance Act or section 202, and special rates such as section 195), then the rebate and reliefs (sections 156 to 160), surcharge and cess, and credit for tax deducted or collected at source and advance tax.

slides.title: 3. Deemed Income
slides.html: Deemed income is an amount that the law treats as income, or as income of a particular person or year, by a legal fiction. The main groups are these.
slides.plain: 3. Deemed Income Deemed income is an amount that the law treats as income, or as income of a particular person or year, by a legal fiction. The main groups are these.

slides.title: 3.1 Deemed receipt and accrual
slides.html: Section 7 deems certain amounts received in a tax year, and section 9 deems certain incomes to accrue in India (Unit III).
slides.plain: 3.1 Deemed receipt and accrual Section 7 deems certain amounts received in a tax year, and section 9 deems certain incomes to accrue in India (Unit III).

slides.title: 3.2 Clubbing of income
slides.html:
1. Section 96: income arising to a person under a transfer of income without transfer of the asset is taxed as the transferor’s income, whether the transfer is revocable or not.
  2. Section 97: income from a revocable transfer of assets is taxed as the transferor’s income. This does not apply to a trust not revocable during the lifetime of the beneficiary (or another transfer not revocable during the transferee’s lifetime) if the transferor derives no benefit, but the income becomes his when the power to revoke arises.
  3. Section 99(1)(a)(i): the spouse’s salary, commission, fees or other remuneration from a concern in which the individual has a substantial interest (at least 20%) is included in the individual’s income, unless it is solely attributable to the spouse’s technical or professional knowledge, experience and qualification. Under section 99(5)(a), such income is included in the hands of the spouse whose total income before the inclusion is greater, and once included it is not shifted to the other spouse in later years unless the Assessing Officer is satisfied after hearing that spouse.
  4. Section 99(1)(a)(ii) and (b): income from assets transferred without adequate consideration to the spouse (except under an agreement to live apart), or to the son’s wife (on or after 1 June 1973), is included in the transferor’s income.
  5. Section 99(1)(c): a minor child’s income is included, except income from his own work, from activities involving his skill, talent, specialised knowledge or experience, or of a minor with a disability specified in section 154. Up to Rs. 1,500 per child of such income is excluded (Schedule III, Sl. No. 17).
  6. Section 99(3): income from separate property converted into the property of the individual’s Hindu undivided family without adequate consideration remains his income.

slides.title: 3.3 Unexplained income
slides.html:
1. Section 102 (unexplained credits): a sum credited in the books, whose nature and source the assessee does not satisfactorily explain, is taxed as his income. For loans, the creditor must also explain the source satisfactorily (section 102(2)); for share capital and premium of a company in which the public are not substantially interested, the resident shareholder must do so (section 102(3)); these rules do not apply to venture capital funds and companies (section 102(4)).
  2. Sections 103 to 105: unrecorded investments, unrecorded assets (including money, bullion, jewellery and virtual digital assets) and expenditure whose source is not satisfactorily explained are deemed income; deemed unexplained expenditure is not deductible.
  3. Section 106: amounts borrowed or repaid on a hundi or through a negotiable instrument other than an account payee cheque are deemed income.
  4. Rate: section 195, as amended by the Finance Act, 2026, taxes such income at 30% (earlier 60%), with no deduction or set off against it. The separate penalty in section 443 has been omitted.

Kale Khan Mohammad Hanif v. CIT [1963] 50 ITR 1 (SC)

The burden is on the assessee to prove the source of a cash credit; if he fails, the amount may be treated as his income.

CIT v. Durga Prasad More [1971] 82 ITR 540 (SC)

What is apparent is ordinarily real, but the authorities may look at surrounding circumstances to find the reality and need not accept a self serving explanation.

Sumati Dayal v. CIT 1995 Supp (2) SCC 453; [1995] 214 ITR 801 (SC)

A claim that large sums were winnings from horse races failed the test of human probabilities and was rightly taxed as unexplained cash credits.

slides.title: 4.1 Section 15
slides.html:
The following is chargeable under the head “Salaries”:

  1. salary due from an employer (including a former employer) in the tax year, whether paid or not;
  2. salary paid or allowed in the tax year, though not due or before it became due (advance salary); and
  3. arrears of salary paid or allowed in the tax year, if not taxed earlier.

Salary taxed in advance is not taxed again when due (section 15(3)). Salary is therefore taxed on the due or receipt basis, whichever is earlier; the method of accounting under section 276 does not apply to it. Remuneration of a partner from his firm is not salary (section 15(4)).
slides.plain: 4.1 Section 15 The following is chargeable under the head “Salaries”: salary due from an employer (including a former employer) in the tax year, whether paid or not; salary paid or allowed in the tax year, though not due or before it became due (advance salary); and arrears of salary paid or allowed in the tax year, if not taxed earlier. Salary taxed in advance is not taxed again when due (section 15(3)). Salary is therefore taxed on the due or receipt basis, whichever is earlier; the method of accounting under section 276 does not apply to it. Remuneration of a partner from his firm is not salary (section 15(4)).

slides.title: 4.2 Section 16
slides.html: “Salary” includes wages; annuity or pension; gratuity; fees or commission; perquisites; profits in lieu of or in addition to salary; advance of salary; leave encashment; the taxable accretion and transferred balance in a recognised provident fund; the employer’s contribution to the pension scheme under section 124; and the Central Government’s contribution to the Agniveer Corpus Fund.

slides.title: 4.3 The employer and employee relationship
slides.html:
Salary arises only from a contract of service, in which the employer controls how the work is done. Payments under a contract for services give business or professional income.

Ram Prashad v. CIT AIR 1973 SC 637; (1972) 2 SCC 696; [1972] 86 ITR 122 (SC)

Whether a managing director is an employee or an agent depends on the terms of his appointment and the articles of the company. A rough and ready test is whether the company exercises supervisory control over his work. On the facts, the managing director was held to be an employee, so his remuneration was salary.

CIT v. R.M. Chidambaram Pillai (1977) 1 SCC 431; [1977] 106 ITR 292 (SC)

Salary paid by a firm to a partner is not salary, because a partner cannot be an employee of himself and his co partners. It is a share of profit, now taxed as business income under section 26(2)(g) to the extent allowed to the firm under section 35(e).

Further points:

  1. An individual may earn salary from more than one employer in a year.
  2. Family pension received by members of a deceased employee’s family is not salary; it is income from other sources (see section 157(1)(d), which refers to its definition in section 93(1)(d)).
  3. A director’s remuneration is salary only if he is an employee.
  4. Daily and constituency allowances of members of Parliament and State Legislatures are excluded by Schedule III, Sl. Nos. 5 to 7.

slides.title: 4.4 Place of accrual, waiver and relief
slides.html: Salary for services rendered in India is deemed to accrue in India wherever it is paid; salary paid by the Government to an Indian citizen for services outside India is also deemed to accrue in India, but allowances and perquisites paid to him outside India by the Government are excluded (section 9(3); Schedule III, Sl. No. 9). Salary waived before it accrues is not taxable, but salary given up after it accrues is an application of income. Where arrears or advance salary, or profits in lieu of salary, push income into a higher rate, relief is available on application under section 157, except for amounts claimed as voluntary retirement compensation under section 19 (section 157(2)).
slides.plain: 4.4 Place of accrual, waiver and relief Salary for services rendered in India is deemed to accrue in India wherever it is paid; salary paid by the Government to an Indian citizen for services outside India is also deemed to accrue in India, but allowances and perquisites paid to him outside India by the Government are excluded (section 9(3); Schedule III, Sl. No. 9). Salary waived before it accrues is not taxable, but salary given up after it accrues is an application of income. Where arrears or advance salary, or profits in lieu of salary, push income into a higher rate, relief is available on application under section 157, except for amounts claimed as voluntary retirement compensation under section 19 (section 157(2)).

slides.title: 5. Perquisites
slides.html:
Section 17(1) says that “perquisite” includes:

(a) the value of rent free accommodation, and (b) the value of accommodation at a concessional rate to the extent it exceeds the rent recoverable from the employee, both computed as prescribed;

(c) the value of benefits provided free or at a concessional rate by a company to a director or employee with a substantial interest, or by any employer to an employee whose monetary salary exceeds the prescribed amount;

(d) the value of specified securities or sweat equity shares allotted free or at a concession, being the fair market value on the date of exercise less the amount paid (section 17(4)(h));

(e) other prescribed benefits;

(f) any obligation of the employee paid by the employer, such as his income tax or his children’s school fees;

(g) premiums paid by the employer for life assurance or an annuity for the employee, other than through a recognised provident fund, approved superannuation fund or deposit linked insurance fund; and

(h) the employer’s contributions to the employee’s recognised provident fund, pension scheme (section 124(1)) and approved superannuation fund in excess of Rs. 7,50,000 in a year, and (i) the accretion on such excess.

Not perquisites (section 17(2)). Medical treatment in the employer’s hospital; reimbursement of treatment in government or approved hospitals (or for prescribed diseases in approved hospitals); approved health insurance premiums paid or reimbursed by the employer; transport between residence and office; and medical treatment abroad, within the limits permitted by the Reserve Bank of India, with travel costs excluded only where the employee’s gross total income is within the prescribed amount (section 17(3)). Valuation of perquisites is laid down in the Rules.

Section 2(49)(g) also taxes benefits obtained from a company by a director or a person with a substantial interest, or their relatives, whether or not they are employees.

Arun Kumar v. Union of India (2007) 1 SCC 732; [2006] 286 ITR 89 (SC)

The valuation rule for accommodation was upheld, but the Court explained that the perquisite lies in the concession, that is, the benefit of accommodation at less than its value. Section 17(1)(b) now builds this in by taxing only the excess of the prescribed value over the rent recoverable.

CIT v. Infosys Technologies Ltd. (2008) 2 SCC 272; [2008] 297 ITR 167 (SC)

Under the law then in force, the benefit of stock options subject to a lock in period was notional and not a taxable perquisite at the time of exercise. Section 17(1)(d) now taxes it specifically on the date of exercise.

CIT v. L.W. Russel AIR 1965 SC 49; [1964] 53 ITR 91 (SC)

An employer’s contribution to a superannuation scheme in which the employee had no vested right was not a perquisite. Section 17(1)(h) now taxes contributions above Rs. 7,50,000 a year.

slides.title: 6. Profits in Lieu of Salary
slides.html:
Section 18(1) includes in “profits in lieu of salary”:

  1. compensation from an employer or former employer in connection with the termination of employment or the modification of its terms;
  2. any amount received from a person before joining or after leaving employment with him; and
  3. payments from an employer or from a provident or other fund (other than the employee’s own contributions and interest on them), and sums under a Keyman insurance policy.

Section 18(2) excludes exempt payments from statutory and recognised provident funds and approved superannuation funds, and exempt house rent allowance. Compensation connected with termination of employment that is not salary is taxed as income from other sources (section 92(2)(j)).

Compensation connected with termination of employment that is not salary is taxed as income from other sources (section 92(2)(j)).

slides.title: 7. Allowances and Exemptions
slides.html: Every allowance is part of salary unless a Schedule entry or rule excludes it; dearness allowance, for example, is fully taxable.
slides.plain: 7. Allowances and Exemptions Every allowance is part of salary unless a Schedule entry or rule excludes it; dearness allowance, for example, is fully taxable.

slides.title: 7.1 House rent allowance (Schedule III, Sl. No. 11)
slides.html:
The allowance is excluded to the prescribed extent if it is specifically granted for rent of accommodation occupied by the employee, the accommodation is not owned by him, and he actually pays rent. Under Rule 279 of the 2026 Rules (formerly Rule 2A), the exempt amount is the least of:

  1. the allowance actually received;
  2. rent paid in excess of 10% of salary; and
  3. 50% of salary in Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune, Ahmedabad or Bengaluru, and 40% elsewhere.

Hyderabad, Pune, Ahmedabad and Bengaluru were added to the 50% category from 1 April 2026. “Salary” for this purpose is defined in Rule 279; under the 1962 Rules it meant basic salary, dearness allowance forming part of retirement benefits and commission at a fixed percentage of turnover, and the current definition should be confirmed. The exemption is not available under the new regime. An employee without house rent allowance may claim the deduction for rent paid under section 134, outside the new regime.

slides.title: 7.2 Other exclusions
slides.html:
1. Leave travel concession (Schedule III, Sl. No. 8): travel in India on leave or after retirement, subject to prescribed conditions and limited to actual expenditure; not available under the new regime.
  2. Special allowances (Schedule III, Sl. Nos. 12 and 13): allowances for expenses wholly, necessarily and exclusively incurred in performing duties, to the extent actually spent, and prescribed allowances for personal expenses or cost of living; under the new regime only specifically prescribed allowances qualify.
  3. Employer paid tax on non monetary perquisites (Schedule III, Sl. No. 10) and Government allowances abroad for Indian citizens (Sl. No. 9).
  4. Gallantry pensions and related family pensions (Sl. Nos. 14 to 16).
  5. Provident fund and pension payouts: payments from statutory provident funds (Schedule II, Sl. No. 3, with interest on employee contributions above Rs. 2,50,000 a year, or Rs. 5,00,000 where the employer does not contribute, made on or after 1 April 2021 not excluded), the exempt part of a recognised provident fund balance (Sl. No. 4), and National Pension System payments on closure up to 60% (Sl. No. 6).

slides.title: 8. Deductions from Salaries: Section 19
slides.html:
The Table in section 19(1) contains deductions that were partly deductions and partly exemptions under the 1961 Act (sections 16, 10(10), 10(10A), 10(10AA), 10(10B) and 10(10C)).

  1. Tax on employment (Sl. No. 1): the entire amount paid under Article 276(2); not available under the new regime.
  2. Standard deduction (Sl. No. 2): Rs. 75,000 or the salary, whichever is less, under the new regime; Rs. 50,000 or the salary, whichever is less, otherwise.
  3. Gratuity of Government and local authority employees, and defence services (Sl. Nos. 3 and 4): entire amount.
  4. Gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (Sl. No. 5): up to the amount computed under section 4(2) and (3) of that Act, that is, fifteen days’ wages at the last drawn rate for each completed year of service (or part above six months), subject to the ceiling notified under that Act.
  5. Other gratuity (Sl. No. 6): the least of the actual gratuity, the limit notified by the Central Government, and half a month’s average salary (average of the ten months before the month of retirement) for each completed year of service. The total for all years and employers cannot exceed the notified limit (section 19(2)(a)), and “salary” includes dearness allowance if the terms of employment so provide but excludes other allowances and perquisites (section 19(2)(b)).
  6. Commuted pension (Sl. Nos. 7 to 9): entire amount for Government, local authority and statutory corporation employees and from funds in Schedule VII, Sl. No. 3; for other employees, the commuted value of one third of the pension if gratuity is also received, and of one half otherwise. Uncommuted (periodical) pension is fully taxable.
  7. Retrenchment compensation (Sl. Nos. 10 and 11): the least of the compensation received, the amount under section 25F(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and the notified amount (not less than Rs. 50,000); the entire amount under a scheme approved by the Central Government.
  8. Voluntary retirement compensation (Sl. No. 12): the compensation or Rs. 5,00,000, whichever is less, under a scheme of an employer listed in section 19(2)(h) that follows the prescribed guidelines; allowed only once in a lifetime, and not if relief under section 157 has been claimed for it (section 19(2)(e)).
  9. Leave encashment on retirement (Sl. Nos. 13 and 14): entire amount for Central and State Government employees; for others, the least of the cash equivalent of earned leave (counting not more than thirty days per year of service), ten months’ average salary, the notified amount, and the amount received. Leave encashment during service is fully taxable.

Under the 1961 regime, the notified limits were Rs. 20,00,000 for gratuity and Rs. 25,00,000 for leave encashment. Notifications continue under section 536(2)(j) unless replaced, but confirm the current figures before using them.

Exam focus. Under the 2025 Act, gratuity, commuted pension, retrenchment and voluntary retirement compensation and leave encashment are deductions in computing salary under section 19, not exemptions. Because section 202(2) withdraws only Sl. No. 1 (tax on employment), they remain available under the new regime.

slides.part: 9. The New Tax Regime and an Illustration
slides.title: 9. The New Tax Regime and an Illustration
slides.html:
Section 202 is the default regime. A person without business income may opt out each year when filing the return (section 202(4)(b)); a person with business income opts out by the due date, the choice continues for later years, and it can be withdrawn only once (section 202(4)(a)). Under the new regime, a salaried employee gets the Rs. 75,000 standard deduction and the section 19 retirement deductions, but loses the deduction for tax on employment, house rent allowance, leave travel concession, most special allowances, interest on a self occupied house, and most Chapter VIII deductions; a house property loss cannot be set off against other heads.

Illustration. Meera works for a private company in Pune for the tax year beginning 1 April 2026. Basic salary is Rs. 9,00,000, dearness allowance forming part of retirement benefits is Rs. 1,00,000, house rent allowance is Rs. 3,00,000, rent paid is Rs. 3,60,000 and tax on employment is Rs. 2,500. Assume that salary for house rent allowance is basic plus dearness allowance, Rs. 10,00,000.

  1. Opting out of the new regime. Exempt house rent allowance is the least of Rs. 3,00,000; Rs. 3,60,000 less 10% of salary (Rs. 1,00,000), which is Rs. 2,60,000; and 50% of salary, Rs. 5,00,000. So Rs. 2,60,000 is exempt and Rs. 40,000 taxable. Gross salary is Rs. 10,40,000; less standard deduction of Rs. 50,000 and tax on employment of Rs. 2,500, income from salary is Rs. 9,87,500. Tax then follows the Finance Act rates after any Chapter VIII deductions.
  2. Under the new regime. The whole allowance is taxable, so gross salary is Rs. 13,00,000; less standard deduction of Rs. 75,000, total income is Rs. 12,25,000. Tax under section 202(1) is Rs. 20,000 (5% of Rs. 4,00,000) plus Rs. 40,000 (10% of Rs. 4,00,000) plus Rs. 3,750 (15% of Rs. 25,000), totalling Rs. 63,750. Marginal relief under section 156(2)(b) limits the tax to the income above Rs. 12,00,000, that is Rs. 25,000, so the rebate is Rs. 38,750 and tax is Rs. 25,000, plus cess under the Finance Act.

slides.title: 1. Rationale of the Charge
slides.html:
The charge under this head is on the annual value of property, that is, the amount the property can reasonably be expected to fetch if let from year to year, or the actual rent if higher. It is not a tax on rent as such. The reasons are:

  1. ownership of a building is itself a source with an inherent capacity to yield income;
  2. a notional charge treats owners who let their property and owners who do not more equally; and
  3. annual value is easy to estimate, and a flat 30% deduction replaces verification of actual repair costs.

The law softens the notional charge: up to two houses occupied by the owner, or which he cannot occupy for any reason, have a nil annual value (section 21(6) and (7)), and unlet property held as stock in trade has a nil annual value for up to two years after completion (section 21(5)).

slides.part: 2. The Charge, the Owner and the Deemed Owner
slides.title: 2.1 Section 20
slides.html:
The annual value of property consisting of buildings or lands appurtenant to them, of which the assessee is the owner, is chargeable under this head (section 20(1)), except the portions he occupies for his own business or profession whose profits are taxable (section 20(2)). Three conditions therefore apply:

  1. the property is a building (any structure with walls and a roof, such as a house, flat, shop or godown) or land appurtenant to it (such as a courtyard or garage); income from letting vacant land not attached to a building falls under other sources or business;
  2. the assessee is the owner; and
  3. the property is not used for the assessee’s own taxable business or profession.
slides.plain: 2.1 Section 20 The annual value of property consisting of buildings or lands appurtenant to them, of which the assessee is the owner, is chargeable under this head (section 20(1)), except the portions he occupies for his own business or profession whose profits are taxable (section 20(2)). Three conditions therefore apply: the property is a building (any structure with walls and a roof, such as a house, flat, shop or godown) or land appurtenant to it (such as a courtyard or garage); income from letting vacant land not attached to a building falls under other sources or business; the assessee is the owner; and the property is not used for the assessee’s own taxable business or profession.

slides.part: 2. The Charge, the Owner and the Deemed Owner
slides.title: 2.2 Who is the owner
slides.html:
R.B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala v. CIT (1971) 3 SCC 369; [1971] 82 ITR 570 (SC)

The owner is the person entitled to receive the income from the property in his own right. Property that had vested in the Custodian of Evacuee Property in Pakistan was not the assessee’s for this purpose.

CIT v. Podar Cement (P) Ltd. (1997) 5 SCC 482; [1997] 226 ITR 625 (SC)

A person who has paid for a property, is in possession and receives the rent in his own right is the owner, even if the sale deed has not been registered.

slides.part: 2. The Charge, the Owner and the Deemed Owner
slides.title: 2.3 Deemed owners: section 25
slides.html:
“Owner” includes:

(a) an individual who transfers property without adequate consideration to his or her spouse (except under an agreement to live apart) or to a minor child (other than a married daughter);

(b) the holder of an impartible estate;

(c) a member of a cooperative society, company or association to whom a building is allotted or leased under a house building scheme;

(d) a person in possession under part performance of a contract under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; and

(e) a person who acquires rights in a building (other than a monthly lease or a lease of up to one year) by sale, exchange or a lease of at least twelve years, or through membership, shares or any arrangement that enables enjoyment of the property.

slides.part: 2. The Charge, the Owner and the Deemed Owner
slides.title: 2.4 House property or business income
slides.html:
Sultan Brothers (P) Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1964 SC 1389; [1964] 51 ITR 353 (SC)

Where a building is let together with furniture or machinery and the two lettings are inseparable, the income is not house property income; it is income from other sources or business income. This rule is now in section 92(2)(g).

Chennai Properties and Investments Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 373 ITR 673 (SC)

Where letting of property was the main object of the company and its whole business, the rent was business income. The same view was taken in Rayala Corporation (P) Ltd. v. Assistant CIT [2016] 386 ITR 500 (SC).

New rule. Section 26(4) now provides that income from letting out a residential house, or part of it, by the owner is chargeable only as income from house property. For residential property, therefore, the Chennai Properties approach no longer applies; it may still matter for commercial property let as a business.

Further points: a resident and ordinarily resident owner is taxed on foreign property too; a tenant who sub lets is not the owner, so his income is not house property income.

slides.title: 3.1 The basic rule
slides.html:
The annual value is the higher of (a) the sum for which the property might reasonably be expected to let from year to year, and (b) the actual rent received or receivable, if the property or part of it is let (section 21(1)). In practice the expected rent is estimated from the municipal valuation and the fair rent of similar property, limited by the standard rent where a rent control law applies.

Mrs. Sheila Kaushish v. CIT (1981) 4 SCC 121; [1981] 131 ITR 435 (SC)

Where a rent control law applies, the annual value cannot exceed the standard rent determinable under that law, even if no standard rent has actually been fixed. This followed Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee (1980) 1 SCC 685; [1980] 122 ITR 700 (SC), on rateable value for municipal tax.
slides.plain: 3.1 The basic rule The annual value is the higher of (a) the sum for which the property might reasonably be expected to let from year to year, and (b) the actual rent received or receivable, if the property or part of it is let (section 21(1)). In practice the expected rent is estimated from the municipal valuation and the fair rent of similar property, limited by the standard rent where a rent control law applies. Mrs. Sheila Kaushish v. CIT (1981) 4 SCC 121; [1981] 131 ITR 435 (SC) Where a rent control law applies, the annual value cannot exceed the standard rent determinable under that law, even if no standard rent has actually been fixed. This followed Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee (1980) 1 SCC 685; [1980] 122 ITR 700 (SC), on rateable value for municipal tax.

slides.title: 3.2 Adjustments
slides.html:
1. Vacancy: if the property is let but vacant for the whole or part of the year, and because of the vacancy the actual rent is less than the expected rent, the actual rent is the annual value (section 21(2)).
  2. Municipal taxes: taxes levied by a local authority and actually paid by the owner during the year reduce the annual value, whatever year they relate to (section 21(3)).
  3. Unrealised rent is excluded from actual rent, subject to rules (section 21(4)). Under the 1962 Rules (Rule 4) the conditions were a bona fide tenancy, the defaulting tenant having vacated or steps taken to evict him, the tenant not occupying any other property of the owner, and reasonable steps, including legal proceedings, taken to recover the rent; check the corresponding 2026 Rule.
  4. Stock in trade: unlet property held as stock in trade has a nil annual value up to two years from the end of the financial year in which the completion certificate is obtained (section 21(5), as amended).
  5. Self occupied houses: the annual value is nil if the owner occupies the house for his own residence or cannot actually occupy it due to any reason (section 21(6)). This is wider than the 1961 Act, which required residence elsewhere because of employment, business or profession. The benefit is limited to two houses chosen by the owner, and is lost if the house is let at any time in the year or the owner derives any other benefit from it (section 21(7)).

slides.title: 4. Deductions: Section 22
slides.html:
(a) Standard deduction: 30% of the annual value, whatever the actual expenditure. No other repair or maintenance deduction is allowed.

(b) Interest payable on capital borrowed to acquire, construct, repair, renew or reconstruct the property, on an accrual basis.

(c) Pre construction interest: interest for the period before the tax year in which the property is acquired or constructed, allowed in five equal instalments from that year (reduced by any interest allowed elsewhere, section 22(3)).

For self occupied houses, the total of (b) and (c) is limited to Rs. 2,00,000 if the property was acquired or constructed with a loan for that purpose, completed within five years from the end of the year of borrowing, and the lender’s certificate is furnished; otherwise Rs. 30,000 (section 22(2) and (4)). The combined limit for all self occupied houses is Rs. 2,00,000 (section 22(5)). Under the new regime, no interest deduction is allowed on a self occupied house. For let out houses, section 22 sets no limit on interest. Interest payable outside India is not deductible if tax has not been deducted or paid on it and there is no agent in India (section 22(6)).

slides.part: 5. Arrears, Unrealised Rent, Co Owners and Losses
slides.title: 5. Arrears, Unrealised Rent, Co Owners and Losses
slides.html:
1. Arrears and unrealised rent received later are income of the year of receipt, even if the assessee is no longer the owner, and 30% of the amount is deducted (section 23).
  2. Co owners with definite and ascertainable shares are not assessed as an association of persons; each is taxed on his share, and each gets the self occupied benefit individually (section 24).
  3. Losses: a house property loss can be set off against other house property income (section 108), and against other heads up to Rs. 2,00,000 a year (section 109(1)(b)); the balance is carried forward for up to eight tax years against house property income only (section 110). Under the new regime it cannot be set off against other heads.
slides.plain: 5. Arrears, Unrealised Rent, Co Owners and Losses Arrears and unrealised rent received later are income of the year of receipt, even if the assessee is no longer the owner, and 30% of the amount is deducted (section 23). Under the new regime it cannot be set off against other heads.

slides.title: 6. Illustrations
slides.html:
Let out property. Anil’s flat is let for the whole year. Expected rent is Rs. 3,00,000, actual rent Rs. 3,60,000, municipal taxes paid Rs. 20,000 and loan interest Rs. 1,50,000. Annual value is Rs. 3,60,000 less Rs. 20,000, that is Rs. 3,40,000. Less 30% (Rs. 1,02,000) and interest (Rs. 1,50,000), income from house property is Rs. 88,000.

Self occupied property. Sunita lives in her own house, bought with a loan in 2023 and completed within five years, with interest of Rs. 2,40,000 for the year and the lender’s certificate. Outside the new regime, the annual value is nil and the interest deduction is limited to Rs. 2,00,000, giving a loss of Rs. 2,00,000 that can be set off against her salary. Under the new regime, there is no interest deduction and the income from the house is nil.

slides.title: 1. Charge and Scope: Section 26
slides.html:
“Business” includes any trade, commerce or manufacture, or any adventure or concern in the nature of trade, commerce or manufacture (section 2(20)). “Profession” includes vocation (section 2(86)). Section 26(2) makes the following chargeable under this head:

(a) profits and gains of any business or profession carried on during the tax year;

(b) compensation received by a person managing an Indian company, holding an agency in India or holding a business contract, in connection with the termination or modification of the management, agency or contract (reversing, for these cases, the capital receipt view in Kettlewell Bullen);

(c) compensation for the vesting of the management of any property or business in the Government;

(d) income of a trade, professional or similar association from specific services to members;

(e) export incentives, such as profit on sale of import licences, cash assistance and duty drawback;

(f) the value of any benefit or perquisite arising from business, whether or not convertible into money;

(g) interest, salary, bonus, commission or remuneration received by a partner from his firm, to the extent allowed to the firm under section 35(e);

(h) sums received for not carrying on an activity in relation to a business (non compete fees) or for not sharing know how, patents, trademarks and similar rights, except a transfer of the right to manufacture or carry on business taxable as capital gains;

(i) sums received under a Keyman insurance policy;

(j) the fair market value of inventory converted into a capital asset; and

(k) sums received on the transfer or destruction of an asset whose entire cost was deducted under section 46.

A speculation business is treated as distinct from any other business (section 26(3)); a speculative transaction is one settled otherwise than by actual delivery, subject to exceptions such as hedging and eligible derivative transactions (section 66(31) and (33)). Income from letting a residential house by its owner is house property income, not business income (section 26(4)). Business income is computed under sections 28 to 60, except section 58, which has its own presumptive scheme (section 27).

slides.part: 2. Basic Principles for Arriving at Business Income
slides.title: 2.1 What amounts to business
slides.html:
Narain Swadeshi Weaving Mills v. Commissioner of Excess Profits Tax AIR 1955 SC 176; [1954] 26 ITR 765 (SC)

“Business” connotes a real, substantial and systematic or organised course of activity with a set purpose.

G. Venkataswami Naidu and Co. v. CIT AIR 1959 SC 359; [1959] 35 ITR 594 (SC)

A single, isolated transaction can be an adventure in the nature of trade. The indicators include an intention to resell at a profit when buying, the nature and quantity of the commodity, any work done to improve or market it, and how it was financed. No single factor is decisive.

slides.part: 2. Basic Principles for Arriving at Business Income
slides.title: 2.2 Illegal business
slides.html: Profits of an illegal business are taxable (CIT v. S.C. Kothari [1971] 82 ITR 794 (SC)). A loss incidental to such a business may be allowed: in CIT v. Piara Singh [1980] 124 ITR 40 (SC), currency carried by a smuggler and confiscated was allowed as a business loss. But a penalty for breaking the law is not deductible (Haji Aziz and Abdul Shakoor Bros. v. CIT, AIR 1961 SC 1265; [1961] 41 ITR 350 (SC)), and section 34(2)(a) and (3) now disallow any expenditure for a purpose that is an offence or prohibited by law.

slides.part: 2. Basic Principles for Arriving at Business Income
slides.title: 2.3 Commercial principles
slides.html: Business income is computed on ordinary commercial principles as modified by the Act, aiming at real profit, but specific statutory provisions prevail. A loss arising in the ordinary course of business, such as embezzlement by an employee, is allowed as a trading loss (Badridas Daga v. CIT, AIR 1958 SC 783; [1958] 34 ITR 10 (SC)). Each tax year is separate and res judicata does not strictly apply, but a position accepted for years on unchanged facts should not be reopened without good reason (Radhasoami Satsang v. CIT (1992) 1 SCC 659; [1992] 193 ITR 321 (SC)). Income and expenditure are recognised under the cash or mercantile system regularly employed, subject to the notified Income Computation and Disclosure Standards (section 276).

slides.part: 2. Basic Principles for Arriving at Business Income
slides.title: 2.4 Capital and revenue expenditure
slides.html:
Capital expenditure is not deductible under section 34, though it may attract depreciation or a specific deduction.

British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. v. Atherton [1926] AC 205

Expenditure made once and for all to bring into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade is ordinarily capital (the enduring benefit test).

Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1955 SC 89; [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC)

Payments for a lease of limestone quarries and for protection against competition during the lease were capital, because they secured an enduring advantage. Fixed capital earns profit by being kept; circulating capital by being parted with.

Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1980) 4 SCC 25; [1980] 124 ITR 1 (SC)

A payment to buy loom hours (the right to work more looms under an industry agreement) was revenue. The enduring benefit test is not conclusive; an advantage that only makes the existing business run more efficiently, without adding to the capital structure, is revenue.

Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1989) 3 SCC 329; [1989] 177 ITR 377 (SC)

Payment for technical know how to improve production of an existing product was revenue. No single test decides the question.

In short, expenditure to acquire, extend or improve the profit making structure is generally capital; expenditure to run the business or keep the existing structure working is generally revenue.

slides.title: 3. Scheme of Business Deductions
slides.html:
1. Specific deductions: section 28 (rent, rates, taxes, repairs, insurance), 29 (employee welfare), 30 (insurance premia), 31 (bad debts), 32 (other items) and 33 (depreciation).
  2. Special deductions: sections 44 to 52, such as preliminary expenses (section 44), scientific research (section 45), capital expenditure of specified businesses (section 46), and development accounts and funds (sections 48 and 49).
  3. General deduction: section 34.
  4. Disallowances and timing rules: sections 35 and 36, and section 37 (deduction only on actual payment).
  5. Deemed profits: section 38.
  6. Computation rules: actual cost (section 39) and written down value (section 41).
  7. Presumptive taxation, books and audit: sections 58, 61, 62 and 63.

slides.title: 4. The General Deduction: Section 34
slides.html:
Any expenditure is deductible if it is not covered by sections 28 to 33, 44 to 49, 51 and 52, is not capital expenditure or personal expenditure, and is laid out wholly and exclusively for the business or profession (section 34(1)).

Sassoon J. David and Co. (P) Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 118 ITR 261 (SC)

“Wholly and exclusively” does not mean “necessarily”. Expenditure incurred voluntarily, without legal necessity, is deductible if incurred for the business.

CIT v. Malayalam Plantations Ltd. AIR 1964 SC 1734; [1964] 53 ITR 140 (SC)

“For the purpose of the business” is wider than “for earning profits” and includes carrying on, preserving and protecting the business. Estate duty paid by the company in respect of deceased shareholders’ shares was, however, not for the purpose of the business.

S.A. Builders Ltd. v. CIT (Appeals) (2007) 1 SCC 781; [2007] 288 ITR 1 (SC)

Interest on borrowed money lent interest free to a sister concern was deductible because the loan was made for commercial expediency. The Revenue cannot put itself in the businessman’s armchair. Earlier decisions such as Eastern Investments Ltd. v. CIT, AIR 1951 SC 278, and CIT v. Walchand and Co. [1967] 65 ITR 381 (SC) had likewise held that commercial expediency and reasonableness are judged from the businessman’s point of view.

Never “wholly and exclusively” for business (section 34(2) and (3)). Expenditure for any purpose that is an offence or prohibited by any law in or outside India; benefits or perquisites to a person whose acceptance of them violates the law, rules or guidelines governing his conduct; compounding an offence; settling notified contravention proceedings; corporate social responsibility expenditure under section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013; and advertisement in political party publications.

Apex Laboratories (P) Ltd. v. Deputy CIT (Supreme Court, 2022)

Freebies given by a pharmaceutical company to doctors, whose acceptance was prohibited by their professional conduct regulations, were not deductible. Section 34(3)(b) now states this rule expressly.

slides.title: 5. Specific Deductions
slides.html:
1. Section 28: for premises, machinery, plant and furniture used for the business: insurance premium, land revenue and municipal taxes, rent paid by a tenant, and current repairs (not capital), with only a fair proportion allowed where use is partly for business.
  2. Section 29 (employee welfare): employer’s contributions to recognised provident funds and approved superannuation funds within prescribed limits; contributions to the pension scheme under section 124 up to 14% of salary; contributions to an approved gratuity fund; provisions for such contributions or for gratuity payable in the year (no other gratuity provision is allowed); and employees’ own contributions to provident fund and welfare funds, if credited to their accounts by the due date for filing the return (section 29(1)(e)). No other contribution to funds or trusts is deductible unless required by law (section 29(3)).
  3. Section 30: insurance premia on stocks and stores, on cattle of members of primary milk societies (by a federal milk cooperative), and on employees’ health (paid other than in cash).
  4. Section 32: bonus or commission to employees (if not a substitute for profits or dividend); interest on capital borrowed for business, excluding interest for the period before an asset acquired with it is first put to use; transfers by specified financial entities to special reserves (up to 20% of eligible profits, within twice the paid up capital and general reserves); family planning expenditure by a company (capital expenditure over five years); loss on animals that die or become useless; securities and commodities transaction tax; and other specified items.
  5. Section 44: an Indian company, or a resident other than a company, may deduct one fifth of specified preliminary expenses, incurred before commencement of business or for an extension or new unit, in each of five successive tax years.
  6. Section 50: trade, professional and similar associations may deduct the shortfall between receipts from members and expenditure for their common interest, up to 50% of total income.

The change in section 29(1)(e). In Checkmate Services (P) Ltd. v. CIT (Supreme Court, 2022), the Supreme Court held that employees’ contributions are their own money held in trust and are deductible only if deposited by the due date under the relevant fund law. The 2025 Act originally followed this, but the Finance Act, 2026 substituted section 29(1)(e) so that the deduction is now available if the amount is credited by the due date of the return. Section 37(6) confirms that the actual payment rule does not apply to these contributions.

slides.title: 6.1 Conditions
slides.html:
Depreciation is allowed if:

  1. the asset is a tangible asset (buildings, machinery, plant or furniture) or an intangible asset acquired on or after 1 April 1998 (know how, patents, copyrights, trademarks, licences, franchises or similar business or commercial rights), but not goodwill;
  2. the asset is owned, wholly or partly, by the assessee; and
  3. it is used wholly and exclusively for the business or profession, with only a fair proportion allowed for partial business use (section 33(3)(b)).

“Plant” includes ships, vehicles, books, scientific apparatus and surgical equipment, but not tea bushes, livestock, buildings, or furniture and fittings (section 66(17)). Improvements to a leased building made by the tenant for his business are treated as a building owned by him (section 33(6)).

Improvements to a leased building made by the tenant for his business are treated as a building owned by him (section 33(6)).

slides.title: 6.2 Block of assets and written down value
slides.html: Depreciation is charged at the prescribed rate on the written down value of each block of assets, that is, a class of assets carrying the same rate (sections 2(17) and 33(3)(a)). Under section 41(1)(c), the written down value of a block is the previous year’s figure less the depreciation allowed for that year, plus the actual cost of assets added during the year, less the sale price and scrap value of assets of the block sold, discarded or destroyed (not exceeding the amount so far computed). Actual cost is reduced by subsidies, GST input credit and similar amounts, and cash payments above Rs. 10,000 a day are excluded from it (section 39). Rates are in the Rules; under the 1962 Rules, general plant and machinery carried 15%, computers 40%, furniture 10% and intangible assets 25%. Confirm the 2026 rates before use.

slides.title: 6.3 Special rules
slides.html:
1. Half rate: only 50% of the rate is allowed if the asset is acquired and used for less than 180 days in the year (section 33(4)).
  2. Compulsory: depreciation applies whether or not claimed (section 33(7)). This reverses CIT v. Mahendra Mills (2000) 3 SCC 615; [2000] 243 ITR 56 (SC), which had treated depreciation as optional under the earlier law.
  3. Additional depreciation: 20% of the actual cost of new plant or machinery (other than ships and aircraft) acquired and installed by a manufacturer or power undertaking, or 10% in the first year and 10% in the next if used for less than 180 days; not for second hand assets, office or residential installations, office appliances, road vehicles or assets fully deducted otherwise (section 33(8) and (9)).
  4. Power undertakings may claim depreciation on actual cost (section 33(2)), with a terminal deduction for loss on sale (section 33(10)) and a balancing charge on gain (section 38(1)(b)).
  5. Unabsorbed depreciation: depreciation exceeding the profits of the year is carried forward and added to the next year’s allowance, without time limit (section 33(11)).

slides.title: 6.4 Leading cases
slides.html:
1. CIT v. Taj Mahal Hotel (1971) 3 SCC 550; [1971] 82 ITR 44 (SC): sanitary fittings in a hotel are plant; “plant” includes any apparatus used to carry on the business, other than stock in trade.
  2. Scientific Engineering House (P) Ltd. v. CIT (1986) 1 SCC 11; [1986] 157 ITR 86 (SC): technical drawings and designs used as tools of the trade are plant.
  3. Mysore Minerals Ltd. v. CIT (1999) 7 SCC 106; [1999] 239 ITR 775 (SC): “owned” includes a person who has dominion over and uses the asset in his own right, though legal title has not passed.
  4. CIT v. Smifs Securities Ltd. (2012) 13 SCC 488; [2012] 348 ITR 302 (SC): goodwill was held depreciable under the earlier law; the 2025 Act expressly excludes goodwill (sections 2(17)(b) and 33(1)(b)).

slides.title: 7. Bad Debts: Section 31
slides.html:
A bad debt, or part of it, is deductible in the year in which it is written off as irrecoverable in the accounts, if it was taken into account in computing income of that or an earlier year, or it represents money lent in the ordinary course of a banking or money lending business (section 31(2)). If less is finally recovered than the amount not deducted, the shortfall is deductible in the year of recovery. A provision for bad and doubtful debts is not a write off (section 31(3)(a)). Banks may deduct a provision up to 8.5% of total income plus 10% of average rural advances, and foreign banks, public financial institutions and non banking financial companies up to 5% of total income (section 31(1)); their write offs are then allowed only to the extent they exceed the provision. A later recovery in excess of the amount not allowed is taxable (section 38(1)(d)).

TRF Ltd. v. CIT [2010] 323 ITR 397 (SC)

After the 1989 amendment of the 1961 Act, the assessee need not prove that a debt has actually become irrecoverable; writing it off in the accounts is enough. Section 31(2) keeps this requirement.

Vijaya Bank v. CIT (2010) 5 SCC 416; [2010] 323 ITR 166 (SC)

Debiting bad debts to the profit and loss account and reducing the loans and advances in the balance sheet accordingly is a valid write off, even without closing each debtor’s account.

Southern Technologies Ltd. v. Joint CIT (2010) 2 SCC 548; [2010] 320 ITR 577 (SC)

A provision for non performing assets made under Reserve Bank directions is not a write off and is not deductible as a bad debt.

slides.part: 8. Disallowances, Actual Payment and Deemed Profits
slides.title: 8.1 Section 35: amounts not deductible
slides.html:
1. Income tax, including surcharge and cess, tax paid by an employer on employees’ non monetary perquisites, and foreign tax for which relief is available.
  2. Failure to deduct tax at source: 30% of a sum payable to a resident is disallowed if tax was deductible but not deducted, or not paid by the due date of the return; it is allowed in the year the tax is paid. For interest, royalty, technical fees or other sums payable outside India or to non residents, the whole amount is disallowed on the same basis.
  3. Salary payable outside India or to a non resident without deduction of tax.
  4. Levies by a State exclusively on a State Government undertaking.
  5. Payments by a firm to partners: remuneration to non working partners; remuneration or interest not authorised by the partnership deed or relating to a period before it; remuneration to working partners above the limit (on the first Rs. 6,00,000 of book profit or in case of loss, Rs. 3,00,000 or 90% of book profit, whichever is higher, and 60% of the balance); and interest above 12% simple a year.
  6. Payments by an association of persons or body of individuals to its members.

Palam Gas Service v. CIT (2017) 7 SCC 613; [2017] 394 ITR 300 (SC)

The disallowance for failure to deduct tax applies to amounts paid during the year as well as amounts payable at the year end.

slides.part: 8. Disallowances, Actual Payment and Deemed Profits
slides.title: 8.2 Section 36: excessive and cash payments
slides.html:
1. Excessive or unreasonable payments to specified persons (relatives, directors, partners, members and persons with a substantial interest of at least 20%) are disallowed to the extent of the excess, judged by market value, business needs and benefit (section 36(2) and (3)).
  2. Expenditure paid to a person in a day above Rs. 10,000 (Rs. 35,000 for goods carriages) otherwise than by an account payee cheque or draft, electronic clearing or other prescribed electronic mode is disallowed; a later cash payment of a liability deducted earlier is deemed income (section 36(4) to (8); section 66(32)).
  3. Marked to market losses are not deductible except as allowed under the notified standards (section 36(9)).

Attar Singh Gurmukh Singh v. Income Tax Officer (1991) 4 SCC 385; [1991] 191 ITR 667 (SC)

The disallowance of cash payments was upheld as constitutional. It aims to check unaccounted money, and exceptions for genuine cases make it reasonable.

slides.part: 8. Disallowances, Actual Payment and Deemed Profits
slides.title: 8.3 Section 37: deduction only on actual payment
slides.html:
Taxes, duties, cess and fees; employer’s contributions to provident, gratuity and welfare funds; leave encashment; bonus or commission to employees; interest to specified financial entities; amounts payable to the Indian Railways; and amounts payable to micro and small enterprises beyond the time allowed under section 15 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 are deductible only when actually paid (section 37(1) and (2)). If paid after the year ends but by the due date of the return, they are allowed for the year of the liability, except payments to micro and small enterprises (section 37(3)). Interest converted into a loan or debenture is not treated as paid (section 37(4)).

Allied Motors (P) Ltd. v. CIT (1997) 3 SCC 472; [1997] 224 ITR 677 (SC) and CIT v. Alom Extrusions Ltd. (2010) 1 SCC 489; [2009] 319 ITR 306 (SC)

The provisions allowing payment up to the due date of the return were held to be curative and retrospective, both for taxes (Allied Motors) and for employers’ contributions to welfare funds (Alom Extrusions).

slides.part: 8. Disallowances, Actual Payment and Deemed Profits
slides.title: 8.4 Section 38: deemed profits
slides.html:
The following are taxed as business income of the year in which they arise:

(a) the benefit of remission or cessation of a trading liability for which a deduction was allowed, including a unilateral write off in the assessee’s own accounts, and any later recovery of a loss or expenditure allowed earlier;

(b) a balancing charge on sale of assets of a power undertaking;

(c) the excess on sale of a scientific research asset;

(d) recovery of a bad debt in excess of the amount not allowed; and

(e) withdrawals from a special reserve under section 32(e).

These apply even if the business has ceased (section 38(5)), and a successor in business is taxed on benefits it receives (section 38(4)).

CIT v. T.V. Sundaram Iyengar and Sons Ltd. [1996] 222 ITR 344 (SC)

Trade deposits that remained unclaimed and were transferred to the profit and loss account became the assessee’s own money and were taxable as trading receipts.

CIT v. Sugauli Sugar Works (P) Ltd. [1999] 236 ITR 518 (SC)

A remission can be granted only by the creditor, and a cessation occurs only by operation of law or a bilateral act, so the debtor’s own write back of a liability did not attract the provision then in force. Parliament reversed this by Explanation 1 to section 41(1) of the 1961 Act from the assessment year 1997 to 1998, and section 38(1)(a)(i) now expressly covers a unilateral write off.

CIT v. Mahindra and Mahindra Ltd. (Supreme Court, 2018)

Waiver of a loan taken to buy capital assets was not a business benefit (which must be in kind, not cash) and not a remission of a trading liability (no deduction had been claimed for it). Under the 2025 Act too, section 38(1)(a) applies only where a deduction was allowed.

slides.title: 9.1 Section 58
slides.html:
1. Small business: for an eligible assessee with turnover up to Rs. 2 crore, or up to Rs. 3 crore where cash receipts do not exceed 5%, income is deemed to be 6% of turnover received by banking or online modes (by the due date of the return) plus 8% of other turnover, or the actual profit if higher.
  2. Goods carriages: for an assessee owning not more than ten goods carriages, Rs. 1,000 per ton of gross vehicle weight per month for each heavy goods vehicle and Rs. 7,500 per month for each other vehicle, or the actual profit if higher.
  3. Professionals: for a specified profession with gross receipts up to Rs. 50 lakh, or Rs. 75 lakh where cash receipts do not exceed 5%, 50% of gross receipts, or the actual profit if higher.

No further deductions or losses are allowed against presumptive income, and depreciation is treated as allowed for computing written down value (section 58(4) and (6)). An assessee who declares lower profit and whose income exceeds the exemption limit must keep books and get them audited (section 58(3)). A small business that leaves the scheme within five years of opting for it cannot return for the next five years (section 58(7)). Under the corresponding 1961 provision (section 44AD), an eligible assessee was a resident individual, Hindu undivided family or partnership firm other than a limited liability partnership; check the definition in section 58. Section 61 has a separate presumptive scheme for certain activities of non residents.

slides.title: 9.2 Books of account: section 62
slides.html: Persons in specified professions (legal, medical, engineering, architecture, accountancy, technical consultancy, interior decoration, information technology, company secretary and notified professions) must keep books. Others must do so if business or professional income exceeds Rs. 1,20,000 or turnover exceeds Rs. 10 lakh in any of the three preceding years (Rs. 2,50,000 and Rs. 25 lakh for individuals and Hindu undivided families), or if they declare less than the presumptive income.

Others must do so if business or professional income exceeds Rs. 1,20,000 or turnover exceeds Rs. 10 lakh in any of the three preceding years (Rs. 2,50,000 and Rs. 25 lakh for individuals and Hindu undivided families), or if they declare less than the presumptive income.

slides.title: 9.3 Tax audit: section 63
slides.html: Audit is required where business turnover exceeds Rs. 1 crore (Rs. 10 crore if cash receipts and cash payments are each within 5%), where professional receipts exceed Rs. 50 lakh, or where a presumptive assessee declares lower profit. The report must be furnished one month before the due date of the return, and a cheque or draft that is not account payee counts as cash.

slides.title: 10. Worked Illustration
slides.html:
A trading company (not a bank) shows a net profit of Rs. 20,00,000 for the tax year beginning 1 April 2026, after debiting book depreciation of Rs. 3,00,000 (tax depreciation under section 33 is Rs. 3,60,000), income tax of Rs. 1,50,000, a cash payment of Rs. 50,000 to a supplier on one day, professional fees of Rs. 4,00,000 to a resident without deduction of tax, a provision for doubtful debts of Rs. 80,000, bonus of Rs. 2,00,000 (of which Rs. 50,000 was paid after the due date of the return) and CSR expenditure of Rs. 1,00,000. It also credited dividend income of Rs. 60,000.

  1. Net profit: Rs. 20,00,000.
  2. Add book depreciation Rs. 3,00,000; income tax Rs. 1,50,000 (section 35(a)); cash payment Rs. 50,000 (section 36(4)); 30% of professional fees Rs. 1,20,000 (section 35(b)(i)); provision for doubtful debts Rs. 80,000 (section 31(3)(a)); bonus paid late Rs. 50,000 (section 37); CSR Rs. 1,00,000 (section 34(2)(b)). Total additions: Rs. 8,50,000, giving Rs. 28,50,000.
  3. Less tax depreciation Rs. 3,60,000 and dividend Rs. 60,000 (taxable under other sources, section 92(2)(a)).
  4. Business income: Rs. 24,30,000. The disallowed fees and bonus will be allowed in the years in which the tax is paid and the bonus is paid.

slides.title: Practice Questions for Unit VI
slides.html:
1. What is “business”? When does an isolated transaction become an adventure in the nature of trade?

cases.name: IRC v. Duke of Westminster [1936] AC 1 (House of Lords)
cases.h: Payments to a gardener under a deed of covenant, instead of wages, were held deductible. Lord Tomlin’s speech is the source of the principle that a person may arrange his affairs so that the tax payable is less than it would otherwise be.
cases.plain: IRC v. Duke of Westminster [1936] AC 1 (House of Lords) Payments to a gardener under a deed of covenant, instead of wages, were held deductible. Lord Tomlin’s speech is the source of the principle that a person may arrange his affairs so that the tax payable is less than it would otherwise be.

cases.name: McDowell and Co. Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer (1985) 3 SCC 230
cases.h: Buyers paid excise duty on liquor directly to the excise authorities so that it would not form part of the seller’s turnover for sales tax. The Supreme Court rejected the device. Chinnappa Reddy J. said that colourable devices cannot be part of tax planning.
cases.plain: McDowell and Co. Ltd. v. The Supreme Court rejected the device. Chinnappa Reddy J. said that colourable devices cannot be part of tax planning.

cases.name: Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan (2004) 10 SCC 1
cases.h: A CBDT circular allowing Mauritius residents to claim treaty benefits was upheld. Treaty shopping is not illegal in itself, and legitimate tax planning is permissible.
cases.plain: Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan (2004) 10 SCC 1 A CBDT circular allowing Mauritius residents to claim treaty benefits was upheld. Treaty shopping is not illegal in itself, and legitimate tax planning is permissible.

cases.name: Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v. Union of India (2012) 6 SCC 613
cases.h: A sale between non residents of shares in a foreign company that indirectly held an Indian business was held not taxable under the 1961 Act as it then stood. The transaction must be looked at as a whole, and a structure can be disregarded only if it is a sham or colourable device.
cases.plain: Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v. Union of India (2012) 6 SCC 613 A sale between non residents of shares in a foreign company that indirectly held an Indian business was held not taxable under the 1961 Act as it then stood. The transaction must be looked at as a whole, and a structure can be disregarded only if it is a sham or colourable device.

cases.name: Kewal Krishan Puri v. State of Punjab (1980) 1 SCC 416
cases.h: A market fee must bear a close and reasonable relationship to services rendered to the payers, and a good and substantial portion of it must be shown to be spent for their special benefit.
cases.plain: Kewal Krishan Puri v. State of Punjab (1980) 1 SCC 416 A market fee must bear a close and reasonable relationship to services rendered to the payers, and a good and substantial portion of it must be shown to be spent for their special benefit.

cases.name: Sreenivasa General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1983) 4 SCC 353
cases.h: The correlation between a fee and the services need not be exact. A broad and general correlation is enough, and the services may benefit the payers as a class.
cases.plain: Sreenivasa General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1983) 4 SCC 353 The correlation between a fee and the services need not be exact. A broad and general correlation is enough, and the services may benefit the payers as a class.

cases.name: Corporation of Calcutta v. Liberty Cinema AIR 1965 SC 1107
cases.h: A levy called a “licence fee”, for which no service was rendered, was in substance a tax. The label does not decide the nature of a levy.
cases.plain: Corporation of Calcutta v. Liberty Cinema AIR 1965 SC 1107 A levy called a “licence fee”, for which no service was rendered, was in substance a tax. The label does not decide the nature of a levy.

cases.name: Hingir Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa AIR 1961 SC 459
cases.h: A cess on mine owners, credited to a fund for developing mining areas, was held to be a fee because it was linked to services that benefited the payers.
cases.plain: Hingir Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa AIR 1961 SC 459 A cess on mine owners, credited to a fund for developing mining areas, was held to be a fee because it was linked to services that benefited the payers.

cases.name: India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu (1990) 1 SCC 12 and Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India 2024 SCC OnLine SC 1796
cases.h: India Cement struck down a State cess on royalty and described royalty as a tax. On 25 July 2024, a nine judge bench in Mineral Area Development Authority held by 8 to 1 (Nagarathna J. dissenting) that royalty is not a tax but a contractual consideration, overruled India Cement on that point, and held that the States’ power to tax mineral rights under Entry 50 of List II is not taken away by the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.
cases.plain: India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu (1990) 1 SCC 12 and Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India 2024 SCC OnLine SC 1796 India Cement struck down a State cess on royalty and described royalty as a tax. On 25 July 2024, a nine judge bench in Mineral Area Development Authority held by 8 to 1 (Nagarathna J. dissenting) that royalty is not a tax but a contractual consideration, overruled India Cement on that point, and held that the States’ power to tax mineral rights under Entry 50 of List II is not taken away by the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.

cases.part: 1. Sources of the Power to Tax
cases.name: Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1971) 2 SCC 779
cases.h: Wealth tax on net wealth including agricultural land was upheld. It was not a tax on lands and buildings under Entry 49 of List II, so Parliament could levy it under its residuary power (Article 248 and Entry 97 of List I).
cases.plain: Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1971) 2 SCC 779 Wealth tax on net wealth including agricultural land was upheld. It was not a tax on lands and buildings under Entry 49 of List II, so Parliament could levy it under its residuary power (Article 248 and Entry 97 of List I).

cases.part: 2. Distribution of Revenues and Centre State Financial Relations
cases.name: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (Supreme Court, 19 May 2022)
cases.h: GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding, on Parliament and the State Legislatures, because Article 246A gives both simultaneous power. The Court described Indian federalism as a dialogue involving both cooperation and contestation.
cases.plain: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (Supreme Court, 19 May 2022) GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding, on Parliament and the State Legislatures, because Article 246A gives both simultaneous power. The Court described Indian federalism as a dialogue involving both cooperation and contestation.

cases.name: Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala AIR 1961 SC 552
cases.h: A flat rate of land tax on all lands, whether productive or barren, with no machinery for assessment or objections, treated unequals as equals and was struck down. It was also held confiscatory.
cases.plain: Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala AIR 1961 SC 552 A flat rate of land tax on all lands, whether productive or barren, with no machinery for assessment or objections, treated unequals as equals and was struck down. It was also held confiscatory.

cases.name: Suraj Mall Mohta and Co. v. A.V. Visvanatha Sastri AIR 1954 SC 545
cases.h: A harsher procedure under the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, for persons who could equally be dealt with under the normal procedure of the 1922 Act, was held discriminatory. Procedural provisions of tax laws are also tested under Article 14.
cases.plain: Suraj Mall Mohta and Co. v. A.V. Visvanatha Sastri AIR 1954 SC 545 A harsher procedure under the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, for persons who could equally be dealt with under the normal procedure of the 1922 Act, was held discriminatory. Procedural provisions of tax laws are also tested under Article 14.

cases.name: R.K. Garg v. Union of India (1981) 4 SCC 675
cases.h: The Special Bearer Bonds scheme, which gave immunity to persons investing unaccounted money, was upheld. Laws on economic activities are viewed with greater latitude than laws affecting civil rights.
cases.plain: R.K. Garg v. Union of India (1981) 4 SCC 675 The Special Bearer Bonds scheme, which gave immunity to persons investing unaccounted money, was upheld. Laws on economic activities are viewed with greater latitude than laws affecting civil rights.

cases.name: Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Association of India v. Union of India (1989) 3 SCC 634
cases.h: The Expenditure Tax Act, 1987, which taxed expenditure in certain hotels with high room charges, was upheld. The legislature has greater freedom of classification in taxation.
cases.plain: Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Association of India v. Union of India (1989) 3 SCC 634 The Expenditure Tax Act, 1987, which taxed expenditure in certain hotels with high room charges, was upheld. The legislature has greater freedom of classification in taxation.

cases.name: Kettlewell Bullen and Co. Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1965 SC 65; [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC)
cases.h: The assessee company, which held managing agencies of several companies, received compensation for surrendering the managing agency of Fort William Jute Co. The Supreme Court held it to be a capital receipt, because the agency was a capital asset forming part of the assessee’s business structure and was not given up in the ordinary course of business.
cases.plain: Kettlewell Bullen and Co. Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1965 SC 65; [1964] 53 ITR 261 (SC) The assessee company, which held managing agencies of several companies, received compensation for surrendering the managing agency of Fort William Jute Co. The Supreme Court held it to be a capital receipt, because the agency was a capital asset forming part of the assessee’s business structure and was not given up in the ordinary course of business.

cases.name: CIT v. Shoorji Vallabhdas and Co. AIR 1962 SC 1281; [1962] 46 ITR 144 (SC)
cases.h: Managing agents agreed, before the year ended, to accept a lower commission. Only the reduced commission was taxable. If income does not really result, there is no tax, even if a book entry shows hypothetical income.
cases.plain: CIT v. Shoorji Vallabhdas and Co. AIR 1962 SC 1281; [1962] 46 ITR 144 (SC) Managing agents agreed, before the year ended, to accept a lower commission. Only the reduced commission was taxable. If income does not really result, there is no tax, even if a book entry shows hypothetical income.

cases.name: State Bank of Travancore v. CIT (1986) 2 SCC 11; [1986] 158 ITR 102 (SC)
cases.h: Interest on doubtful loans that had accrued under the mercantile system was taxable even though credited to a suspense account. The real income theory cannot override the statutory scheme; the remedy is a bad debt deduction if the loan is later lost.
cases.plain: State Bank of Travancore v. CIT (1986) 2 SCC 11; [1986] 158 ITR 102 (SC) Interest on doubtful loans that had accrued under the mercantile system was taxable even though credited to a suspense account. The real income theory cannot override the statutory scheme; the remedy is a bad debt deduction if the loan is later lost.

cases.name: Godhra Electricity Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1997) 4 SCC 530; [1997] 225 ITR 746 (SC)
cases.h: Enhanced charges that consumers disputed and never paid were not real income of the company, even under the mercantile system.
cases.plain: Godhra Electricity Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1997) 4 SCC 530; [1997] 225 ITR 746 (SC) Enhanced charges that consumers disputed and never paid were not real income of the company, even under the mercantile system.

cases.name: Raja Bejoy Singh Dudhuria v. CIT (1933) 1 ITR 135 (PC)
cases.h: Maintenance payable to the assessee’s stepmother under a decree, and charged on his estate, was diverted at source and was not his income.
cases.plain: Raja Bejoy Singh Dudhuria v. CIT (1933) 1 ITR 135 (PC) Maintenance payable to the assessee’s stepmother under a decree, and charged on his estate, was diverted at source and was not his income.

cases.name: CIT v. Sitaldas Tirathdas AIR 1961 SC 728; [1961] 41 ITR 367 (SC)
