cases.h: Maintenance payable to the assessee’s wife and children under a decree, but not charged on his income or property, was an application of income. The true test is whether the amount, in truth, never reached the assessee as his income.
cases.plain: CIT v. Sitaldas Tirathdas AIR 1961 SC 728; [1961] 41 ITR 367 (SC) Maintenance payable to the assessee’s wife and children under a decree, but not charged on his income or property, was an application of income. The true test is whether the amount, in truth, never reached the assessee as his income.

cases.name: CIT v. Sunil J. Kinariwala (2003) 1 SCC 660; [2003] 259 ITR 10 (SC)
cases.h: A partner assigned part of his share of the firm’s profits to a trust. The share first became his income and was then applied, so the whole share was taxable in his hands.
cases.plain: CIT v. Sunil J. Kinariwala (2003) 1 SCC 660; [2003] 259 ITR 10 (SC) A partner assigned part of his share of the firm’s profits to a trust. The share first became his income and was then applied, so the whole share was taxable in his hands.

cases.name: Bangalore Club v. CIT (2013) 5 SCC 509; [2013] 350 ITR 509 (SC)
cases.h: The Supreme Court laid down three conditions: complete identity between contributors and participants; actions of the contributors and participants in furtherance of the mandate of the association; and no scope for profiteering by contributors from a fund that can only be spent on or returned to them. Interest earned by the club on deposits with banks that were its corporate members was held taxable, because the money went out of the closed circle of members into commercial lending.
cases.plain: Bangalore Club v. CIT (2013) 5 SCC 509; [2013] 350 ITR 509 (SC) The Supreme Court laid down three conditions: complete identity between contributors and participants; actions of the contributors and participants in furtherance of the mandate of the association; and no scope for profiteering by contributors from a fund that can only be spent on or returned to them. Interest earned by the club on deposits with banks that were its corporate members was held taxable, because the money went out of the closed circle of members into commercial lending.

cases.name: CIT v. Royal Western India Turf Club Ltd. AIR 1954 SC 85; [1953] 24 ITR 551 (SC)
cases.h: A club that carried on the business of conducting races and served members and non members alike could not claim mutuality.
cases.plain: CIT v. Royal Western India Turf Club Ltd. AIR 1954 SC 85; [1953] 24 ITR 551 (SC) A club that carried on the business of conducting races and served members and non members alike could not claim mutuality.

cases.name: Chelmsford Club v. CIT (2000) 3 SCC 214; [2000] 243 ITR 89 (SC)
cases.h: A club providing facilities only to its members, with any surplus usable only for them, was entitled to the benefit of mutuality.
cases.plain: Chelmsford Club v. CIT (2000) 3 SCC 214; [2000] 243 ITR 89 (SC) A club providing facilities only to its members, with any surplus usable only for them, was entitled to the benefit of mutuality.

cases.name: E.D. Sassoon and Co. Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1954 SC 470; [1954] 26 ITR 27 (SC)
cases.h: Managing agents transferred their agencies during the year, and their commission was payable only at the end of the year. The Supreme Court held that income accrues when the assessee acquires a right to receive it, so that it becomes a debt due to him. No commission had accrued to the transferors before the transfer. “Accrue” and “arise” are used in contrast to “receive”: income is received when it reaches the assessee, and accrues when the right to it vests in him.
cases.plain: E.D. Sassoon and Co. Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1954 SC 470; [1954] 26 ITR 27 (SC) Managing agents transferred their agencies during the year, and their commission was payable only at the end of the year. The Supreme Court held that income accrues when the assessee acquires a right to receive it, so that it becomes a debt due to him. No commission had accrued to the transferors before the transfer. “Accrue” and “arise” are used in contrast to “receive”: income is received when it reaches the assessee, and accrues when the right to it vests in him.

cases.name: CIT v. Toshoku Ltd. [1980] 125 ITR 525 (SC)
cases.h: Commission earned by a non resident for services outside India and credited in the books of an Indian company was neither received in India (a book credit is not receipt) nor accrued in India.
cases.plain: CIT v. Toshoku Ltd. [1980] 125 ITR 525 (SC) Commission earned by a non resident for services outside India and credited in the books of an Indian company was neither received in India (a book credit is not receipt) nor accrued in India.

cases.name: CIT v. R.D. Aggarwal and Co. AIR 1965 SC 1526; [1965] 56 ITR 20 (SC)
cases.h: A business connection requires a real and intimate relation between the non resident’s activity outside India and an activity in India that contributes to earning the income, with an element of continuity. A stray or isolated transaction is not normally a business connection.
cases.plain: CIT v. R.D. Aggarwal and Co. AIR 1965 SC 1526; [1965] 56 ITR 20 (SC) A business connection requires a real and intimate relation between the non resident’s activity outside India and an activity in India that contributes to earning the income, with an element of continuity. A stray or isolated transaction is not normally a business connection.

cases.name: Ishikawajima Harima Heavy Industries Ltd. v. Director of Income Tax (2007) 3 SCC 481
cases.h: Income from offshore supply of equipment for an Indian project, with title passing outside India, was not taxable in India, and fees for services rendered outside India needed a sufficient territorial nexus. Parliament responded with the rule now in section 9(11).
cases.plain: Ishikawajima Harima Heavy Industries Ltd. v. Director of Income Tax (2007) 3 SCC 481 Income from offshore supply of equipment for an Indian project, with title passing outside India, was not taxable in India, and fees for services rendered outside India needed a sufficient territorial nexus. Parliament responded with the rule now in section 9(11).

cases.name: CIT v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy AIR 1957 SC 768; [1957] 32 ITR 466 (SC)
cases.h: “Agriculture” requires basic operations on the land itself, such as tilling, sowing and planting, involving human skill and labour. Subsequent operations (weeding, pruning, protection) count only when they follow basic operations. Income from a forest of spontaneous growth was therefore not agricultural income. On the same reasoning, dairy and poultry farming are generally not agriculture.
cases.plain: CIT v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy AIR 1957 SC 768; [1957] 32 ITR 466 (SC) “Agriculture” requires basic operations on the land itself, such as tilling, sowing and planting, involving human skill and labour. Subsequent operations (weeding, pruning, protection) count only when they follow basic operations. Income from a forest of spontaneous growth was therefore not agricultural income. On the same reasoning, dairy and poultry farming are generally not agriculture.

cases.name: Mrs. Bacha F. Guzdar v. CIT AIR 1955 SC 74; [1955] 27 ITR 1 (SC)
cases.h: Dividends from a company owning tea estates are not agricultural income in the shareholder’s hands. Income “derived from” land requires a direct and immediate relation with the land.
cases.plain: Mrs. Bacha F. Guzdar v. CIT AIR 1955 SC 74; [1955] 27 ITR 1 (SC) Dividends from a company owning tea estates are not agricultural income in the shareholder’s hands. Income “derived from” land requires a direct and immediate relation with the land.

cases.name: V.V.R.N.M. Subbayya Chettiar v. CIT AIR 1951 SC 101; [1951] 19 ITR 168 (SC)
cases.h: “Control and management” means the controlling and directive power, “the head and brain” as it is sometimes called, and “situated” implies that this power functions at a place with some degree of permanence. On the facts, the family had not shown that its control and management was wholly outside India, so it was held resident.
cases.plain: V.V.R.N.M. Subbayya Chettiar v. CIT AIR 1951 SC 101; [1951] 19 ITR 168 (SC) “Control and management” means the controlling and directive power, “the head and brain” as it is sometimes called, and “situated” implies that this power functions at a place with some degree of permanence. On the facts, the family had not shown that its control and management was wholly outside India, so it was held resident.

cases.name: CIT v. Nandlal Gandalal [1960] 3 SCR 620
cases.h: Control and management means de facto control and management, not merely the legal right to control or manage.
cases.plain: CIT v. Nandlal Gandalal [1960] 3 SCR 620 Control and management means de facto control and management, not merely the legal right to control or manage.

cases.name: United Commercial Bank Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1957 SC 918; [1957] 32 ITR 688 (SC)
cases.h: Interest on securities held by a bank as part of its business had to be computed under the specific head then provided for interest on securities, not as business income. Each head deals with a particular source.
cases.plain: United Commercial Bank Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1957 SC 918; [1957] 32 ITR 688 (SC) Interest on securities held by a bank as part of its business had to be computed under the specific head then provided for interest on securities, not as business income. Each head deals with a particular source.

cases.name: East India Housing and Land Development Trust Ltd. v. CIT [1961] 42 ITR 49 (SC)
cases.h: Rent from shops and stalls built by a company dealing in land was taxable under the property head, whatever the object of the company.
cases.plain: East India Housing and Land Development Trust Ltd. v. CIT [1961] 42 ITR 49 (SC) Rent from shops and stalls built by a company dealing in land was taxable under the property head, whatever the object of the company.

cases.name: Kale Khan Mohammad Hanif v. CIT [1963] 50 ITR 1 (SC)
cases.h: The burden is on the assessee to prove the source of a cash credit; if he fails, the amount may be treated as his income.
cases.plain: Kale Khan Mohammad Hanif v. CIT [1963] 50 ITR 1 (SC) The burden is on the assessee to prove the source of a cash credit; if he fails, the amount may be treated as his income.

cases.name: CIT v. Durga Prasad More [1971] 82 ITR 540 (SC)
cases.h: What is apparent is ordinarily real, but the authorities may look at surrounding circumstances to find the reality and need not accept a self serving explanation.
cases.plain: CIT v. Durga Prasad More [1971] 82 ITR 540 (SC) What is apparent is ordinarily real, but the authorities may look at surrounding circumstances to find the reality and need not accept a self serving explanation.

cases.name: Sumati Dayal v. CIT 1995 Supp (2) SCC 453; [1995] 214 ITR 801 (SC)
cases.h: A claim that large sums were winnings from horse races failed the test of human probabilities and was rightly taxed as unexplained cash credits.
cases.plain: Sumati Dayal v. CIT 1995 Supp (2) SCC 453; [1995] 214 ITR 801 (SC) A claim that large sums were winnings from horse races failed the test of human probabilities and was rightly taxed as unexplained cash credits.

cases.name: Ram Prashad v. CIT AIR 1973 SC 637; (1972) 2 SCC 696; [1972] 86 ITR 122 (SC)
cases.h: Whether a managing director is an employee or an agent depends on the terms of his appointment and the articles of the company. A rough and ready test is whether the company exercises supervisory control over his work. On the facts, the managing director was held to be an employee, so his remuneration was salary.
cases.plain: Ram Prashad v. CIT AIR 1973 SC 637; (1972) 2 SCC 696; [1972] 86 ITR 122 (SC) Whether a managing director is an employee or an agent depends on the terms of his appointment and the articles of the company. A rough and ready test is whether the company exercises supervisory control over his work. On the facts, the managing director was held to be an employee, so his remuneration was salary.

cases.name: CIT v. R.M. Chidambaram Pillai (1977) 1 SCC 431; [1977] 106 ITR 292 (SC)
cases.h: Salary paid by a firm to a partner is not salary, because a partner cannot be an employee of himself and his co partners. It is a share of profit, now taxed as business income under section 26(2)(g) to the extent allowed to the firm under section 35(e).
cases.plain: CIT v. R.M. Chidambaram Pillai (1977) 1 SCC 431; [1977] 106 ITR 292 (SC) Salary paid by a firm to a partner is not salary, because a partner cannot be an employee of himself and his co partners. It is a share of profit, now taxed as business income under section 26(2)(g) to the extent allowed to the firm under section 35(e).

cases.name: Arun Kumar v. Union of India (2007) 1 SCC 732; [2006] 286 ITR 89 (SC)
cases.h: The valuation rule for accommodation was upheld, but the Court explained that the perquisite lies in the concession, that is, the benefit of accommodation at less than its value. Section 17(1)(b) now builds this in by taxing only the excess of the prescribed value over the rent recoverable.
cases.plain: Arun Kumar v. Union of India (2007) 1 SCC 732; [2006] 286 ITR 89 (SC) The valuation rule for accommodation was upheld, but the Court explained that the perquisite lies in the concession, that is, the benefit of accommodation at less than its value. Section 17(1)(b) now builds this in by taxing only the excess of the prescribed value over the rent recoverable.

cases.name: CIT v. Infosys Technologies Ltd. (2008) 2 SCC 272; [2008] 297 ITR 167 (SC)
cases.h: Under the law then in force, the benefit of stock options subject to a lock in period was notional and not a taxable perquisite at the time of exercise. Section 17(1)(d) now taxes it specifically on the date of exercise.
cases.plain: CIT v. Infosys Technologies Ltd. (2008) 2 SCC 272; [2008] 297 ITR 167 (SC) Under the law then in force, the benefit of stock options subject to a lock in period was notional and not a taxable perquisite at the time of exercise. Section 17(1)(d) now taxes it specifically on the date of exercise.

cases.name: CIT v. L.W. Russel AIR 1965 SC 49; [1964] 53 ITR 91 (SC)
cases.h: An employer’s contribution to a superannuation scheme in which the employee had no vested right was not a perquisite. Section 17(1)(h) now taxes contributions above Rs. 7,50,000 a year.
cases.plain: CIT v. L.W. Russel AIR 1965 SC 49; [1964] 53 ITR 91 (SC) An employer’s contribution to a superannuation scheme in which the employee had no vested right was not a perquisite. Section 17(1)(h) now taxes contributions above Rs. 7,50,000 a year.

cases.part: 2. The Charge, the Owner and the Deemed Owner
cases.name: R.B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala v. CIT (1971) 3 SCC 369; [1971] 82 ITR 570 (SC)
cases.h: The owner is the person entitled to receive the income from the property in his own right. Property that had vested in the Custodian of Evacuee Property in Pakistan was not the assessee’s for this purpose.
cases.plain: R.B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala v. CIT (1971) 3 SCC 369; [1971] 82 ITR 570 (SC) The owner is the person entitled to receive the income from the property in his own right. Property that had vested in the Custodian of Evacuee Property in Pakistan was not the assessee’s for this purpose.

cases.part: 2. The Charge, the Owner and the Deemed Owner
cases.name: CIT v. Podar Cement (P) Ltd. (1997) 5 SCC 482; [1997] 226 ITR 625 (SC)
cases.h: A person who has paid for a property, is in possession and receives the rent in his own right is the owner, even if the sale deed has not been registered.
cases.plain: CIT v. Podar Cement (P) Ltd. (1997) 5 SCC 482; [1997] 226 ITR 625 (SC) A person who has paid for a property, is in possession and receives the rent in his own right is the owner, even if the sale deed has not been registered.

cases.part: 2. The Charge, the Owner and the Deemed Owner
cases.name: Sultan Brothers (P) Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1964 SC 1389; [1964] 51 ITR 353 (SC)
cases.h: Where a building is let together with furniture or machinery and the two lettings are inseparable, the income is not house property income; it is income from other sources or business income. This rule is now in section 92(2)(g).
cases.plain: Sultan Brothers (P) Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1964 SC 1389; [1964] 51 ITR 353 (SC) Where a building is let together with furniture or machinery and the two lettings are inseparable, the income is not house property income; it is income from other sources or business income. This rule is now in section 92(2)(g).

cases.part: 2. The Charge, the Owner and the Deemed Owner
cases.name: Chennai Properties and Investments Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 373 ITR 673 (SC)
cases.h: Where letting of property was the main object of the company and its whole business, the rent was business income. The same view was taken in Rayala Corporation (P) Ltd. v. Assistant CIT [2016] 386 ITR 500 (SC).
cases.plain: Chennai Properties and Investments Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 373 ITR 673 (SC) Where letting of property was the main object of the company and its whole business, the rent was business income. The same view was taken in Rayala Corporation (P) Ltd. v. Assistant CIT [2016] 386 ITR 500 (SC).

cases.name: Mrs. Sheila Kaushish v. CIT (1981) 4 SCC 121; [1981] 131 ITR 435 (SC)
cases.h: Where a rent control law applies, the annual value cannot exceed the standard rent determinable under that law, even if no standard rent has actually been fixed. This followed Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee (1980) 1 SCC 685; [1980] 122 ITR 700 (SC), on rateable value for municipal tax.
cases.plain: Mrs. Sheila Kaushish v. CIT (1981) 4 SCC 121; [1981] 131 ITR 435 (SC) Where a rent control law applies, the annual value cannot exceed the standard rent determinable under that law, even if no standard rent has actually been fixed. This followed Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee (1980) 1 SCC 685; [1980] 122 ITR 700 (SC), on rateable value for municipal tax.

cases.part: 2. Basic Principles for Arriving at Business Income
cases.name: Narain Swadeshi Weaving Mills v. Commissioner of Excess Profits Tax AIR 1955 SC 176; [1954] 26 ITR 765 (SC)
cases.h: “Business” connotes a real, substantial and systematic or organised course of activity with a set purpose.
cases.plain: Narain Swadeshi Weaving Mills v. Commissioner of Excess Profits Tax AIR 1955 SC 176; [1954] 26 ITR 765 (SC) “Business” connotes a real, substantial and systematic or organised course of activity with a set purpose.

cases.part: 2. Basic Principles for Arriving at Business Income
cases.name: G. Venkataswami Naidu and Co. v. CIT AIR 1959 SC 359; [1959] 35 ITR 594 (SC)
cases.h: A single, isolated transaction can be an adventure in the nature of trade. The indicators include an intention to resell at a profit when buying, the nature and quantity of the commodity, any work done to improve or market it, and how it was financed. No single factor is decisive.
cases.plain: G. Venkataswami Naidu and Co. v. CIT AIR 1959 SC 359; [1959] 35 ITR 594 (SC) A single, isolated transaction can be an adventure in the nature of trade. The indicators include an intention to resell at a profit when buying, the nature and quantity of the commodity, any work done to improve or market it, and how it was financed. No single factor is decisive.

cases.part: 2. Basic Principles for Arriving at Business Income
cases.name: British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. v. Atherton [1926] AC 205
cases.h: Expenditure made once and for all to bring into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade is ordinarily capital (the enduring benefit test).
cases.plain: British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. v. Atherton [1926] AC 205 Expenditure made once and for all to bring into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade is ordinarily capital (the enduring benefit test).

cases.part: 2. Basic Principles for Arriving at Business Income
cases.name: Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1955 SC 89; [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC)
cases.h: Payments for a lease of limestone quarries and for protection against competition during the lease were capital, because they secured an enduring advantage. Fixed capital earns profit by being kept; circulating capital by being parted with.
cases.plain: Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1955 SC 89; [1955] 27 ITR 34 (SC) Payments for a lease of limestone quarries and for protection against competition during the lease were capital, because they secured an enduring advantage. Fixed capital earns profit by being kept; circulating capital by being parted with.

cases.part: 2. Basic Principles for Arriving at Business Income
cases.name: Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1980) 4 SCC 25; [1980] 124 ITR 1 (SC)
cases.h: A payment to buy loom hours (the right to work more looms under an industry agreement) was revenue. The enduring benefit test is not conclusive; an advantage that only makes the existing business run more efficiently, without adding to the capital structure, is revenue.
cases.plain: Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1980) 4 SCC 25; [1980] 124 ITR 1 (SC) A payment to buy loom hours (the right to work more looms under an industry agreement) was revenue. The enduring benefit test is not conclusive; an advantage that only makes the existing business run more efficiently, without adding to the capital structure, is revenue.

cases.part: 2. Basic Principles for Arriving at Business Income
cases.name: Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1989) 3 SCC 329; [1989] 177 ITR 377 (SC)
cases.h: Payment for technical know how to improve production of an existing product was revenue. No single test decides the question.
cases.plain: Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1989) 3 SCC 329; [1989] 177 ITR 377 (SC) Payment for technical know how to improve production of an existing product was revenue. No single test decides the question.

cases.name: Sassoon J. David and Co. (P) Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 118 ITR 261 (SC)
cases.h: “Wholly and exclusively” does not mean “necessarily”. Expenditure incurred voluntarily, without legal necessity, is deductible if incurred for the business.
cases.plain: Sassoon J. David and Co. (P) Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 118 ITR 261 (SC) “Wholly and exclusively” does not mean “necessarily”. Expenditure incurred voluntarily, without legal necessity, is deductible if incurred for the business.

cases.name: CIT v. Malayalam Plantations Ltd. AIR 1964 SC 1734; [1964] 53 ITR 140 (SC)
cases.h: “For the purpose of the business” is wider than “for earning profits” and includes carrying on, preserving and protecting the business. Estate duty paid by the company in respect of deceased shareholders’ shares was, however, not for the purpose of the business.
cases.plain: CIT v. Malayalam Plantations Ltd. AIR 1964 SC 1734; [1964] 53 ITR 140 (SC) “For the purpose of the business” is wider than “for earning profits” and includes carrying on, preserving and protecting the business. Estate duty paid by the company in respect of deceased shareholders’ shares was, however, not for the purpose of the business.

cases.name: S.A. Builders Ltd. v. CIT (Appeals) (2007) 1 SCC 781; [2007] 288 ITR 1 (SC)
cases.h: Interest on borrowed money lent interest free to a sister concern was deductible because the loan was made for commercial expediency. The Revenue cannot put itself in the businessman’s armchair. Earlier decisions such as Eastern Investments Ltd. v. CIT, AIR 1951 SC 278, and CIT v. Walchand and Co. [1967] 65 ITR 381 (SC) had likewise held that commercial expediency and reasonableness are judged from the businessman’s point of view.
cases.plain: S.A. Builders Ltd. v. CIT (Appeals) (2007) 1 SCC 781; [2007] 288 ITR 1 (SC) Interest on borrowed money lent interest free to a sister concern was deductible because the loan was made for commercial expediency. The Revenue cannot put itself in the businessman’s armchair. Earlier decisions such as Eastern Investments Ltd. v. CIT , AIR 1951 SC 278, and CIT v. Walchand and Co. [1967] 65 ITR 381 (SC) had likewise held that commercial expediency and reasonableness are judged from the businessman’s point of view.

cases.name: Apex Laboratories (P) Ltd. v. Deputy CIT (Supreme Court, 2022)
cases.h: Freebies given by a pharmaceutical company to doctors, whose acceptance was prohibited by their professional conduct regulations, were not deductible. Section 34(3)(b) now states this rule expressly.
cases.plain: Apex Laboratories (P) Ltd. v. Deputy CIT (Supreme Court, 2022) Freebies given by a pharmaceutical company to doctors, whose acceptance was prohibited by their professional conduct regulations, were not deductible. Section 34(3)(b) now states this rule expressly.

cases.name: TRF Ltd. v. CIT [2010] 323 ITR 397 (SC)
cases.h: After the 1989 amendment of the 1961 Act, the assessee need not prove that a debt has actually become irrecoverable; writing it off in the accounts is enough. Section 31(2) keeps this requirement.
cases.plain: TRF Ltd. v. CIT [2010] 323 ITR 397 (SC) After the 1989 amendment of the 1961 Act, the assessee need not prove that a debt has actually become irrecoverable; writing it off in the accounts is enough. Section 31(2) keeps this requirement.

cases.name: Vijaya Bank v. CIT (2010) 5 SCC 416; [2010] 323 ITR 166 (SC)
cases.h: Debiting bad debts to the profit and loss account and reducing the loans and advances in the balance sheet accordingly is a valid write off, even without closing each debtor’s account.
cases.plain: Vijaya Bank v. CIT (2010) 5 SCC 416; [2010] 323 ITR 166 (SC) Debiting bad debts to the profit and loss account and reducing the loans and advances in the balance sheet accordingly is a valid write off, even without closing each debtor’s account.

cases.name: Southern Technologies Ltd. v. Joint CIT (2010) 2 SCC 548; [2010] 320 ITR 577 (SC)
cases.h: A provision for non performing assets made under Reserve Bank directions is not a write off and is not deductible as a bad debt.
cases.plain: Southern Technologies Ltd. v. Joint CIT (2010) 2 SCC 548; [2010] 320 ITR 577 (SC) A provision for non performing assets made under Reserve Bank directions is not a write off and is not deductible as a bad debt.

cases.part: 8. Disallowances, Actual Payment and Deemed Profits
cases.name: Palam Gas Service v. CIT (2017) 7 SCC 613; [2017] 394 ITR 300 (SC)
cases.h: The disallowance for failure to deduct tax applies to amounts paid during the year as well as amounts payable at the year end.
cases.plain: Palam Gas Service v. CIT (2017) 7 SCC 613; [2017] 394 ITR 300 (SC) The disallowance for failure to deduct tax applies to amounts paid during the year as well as amounts payable at the year end.

cases.part: 8. Disallowances, Actual Payment and Deemed Profits
cases.name: Attar Singh Gurmukh Singh v. Income Tax Officer (1991) 4 SCC 385; [1991] 191 ITR 667 (SC)
cases.h: The disallowance of cash payments was upheld as constitutional. It aims to check unaccounted money, and exceptions for genuine cases make it reasonable.
cases.plain: Attar Singh Gurmukh Singh v. Income Tax Officer (1991) 4 SCC 385; [1991] 191 ITR 667 (SC) The disallowance of cash payments was upheld as constitutional. It aims to check unaccounted money, and exceptions for genuine cases make it reasonable.

cases.part: 8. Disallowances, Actual Payment and Deemed Profits
cases.name: Allied Motors (P) Ltd. v. CIT (1997) 3 SCC 472; [1997] 224 ITR 677 (SC) and CIT v. Alom Extrusions Ltd. (2010) 1 SCC 489; [2009] 319 ITR 306 (SC)
cases.h: The provisions allowing payment up to the due date of the return were held to be curative and retrospective, both for taxes (Allied Motors) and for employers’ contributions to welfare funds (Alom Extrusions).
cases.plain: Allied Motors (P) Ltd. v. CIT (1997) 3 SCC 472; [1997] 224 ITR 677 (SC) and CIT v. Alom Extrusions Ltd. (2010) 1 SCC 489; [2009] 319 ITR 306 (SC) The provisions allowing payment up to the due date of the return were held to be curative and retrospective, both for taxes (Allied Motors) and for employers’ contributions to welfare funds (Alom Extrusions).

cases.part: 8. Disallowances, Actual Payment and Deemed Profits
cases.name: CIT v. T.V. Sundaram Iyengar and Sons Ltd. [1996] 222 ITR 344 (SC)
cases.h: Trade deposits that remained unclaimed and were transferred to the profit and loss account became the assessee’s own money and were taxable as trading receipts.
cases.plain: CIT v. T.V. Sundaram Iyengar and Sons Ltd. [1996] 222 ITR 344 (SC) Trade deposits that remained unclaimed and were transferred to the profit and loss account became the assessee’s own money and were taxable as trading receipts.

cases.part: 8. Disallowances, Actual Payment and Deemed Profits
cases.name: CIT v. Sugauli Sugar Works (P) Ltd. [1999] 236 ITR 518 (SC)
cases.h: A remission can be granted only by the creditor, and a cessation occurs only by operation of law or a bilateral act, so the debtor’s own write back of a liability did not attract the provision then in force. Parliament reversed this by Explanation 1 to section 41(1) of the 1961 Act from the assessment year 1997 to 1998, and section 38(1)(a)(i) now expressly covers a unilateral write off.
cases.plain: CIT v. Sugauli Sugar Works (P) Ltd. [1999] 236 ITR 518 (SC) A remission can be granted only by the creditor, and a cessation occurs only by operation of law or a bilateral act, so the debtor’s own write back of a liability did not attract the provision then in force. Parliament reversed this by Explanation 1 to section 41(1) of the 1961 Act from the assessment year 1997 to 1998, and section 38(1)(a)(i) now expressly covers a unilateral write off.

cases.part: 8. Disallowances, Actual Payment and Deemed Profits
cases.name: CIT v. Mahindra and Mahindra Ltd. (Supreme Court, 2018)
cases.h: Waiver of a loan taken to buy capital assets was not a business benefit (which must be in kind, not cash) and not a remission of a trading liability (no deduction had been claimed for it). Under the 2025 Act too, section 38(1)(a) applies only where a deduction was allowed.
cases.plain: CIT v. Mahindra and Mahindra Ltd. (Supreme Court, 2018) Waiver of a loan taken to buy capital assets was not a business benefit (which must be in kind, not cash) and not a remission of a trading liability (no deduction had been claimed for it). Under the 2025 Act too, section 38(1)(a) applies only where a deduction was allowed.

quiz.concept: No quid pro quo marks a tax
quiz.q: A State Act imposes a compulsory annual levy on all residents. The money goes into the Consolidated Fund and is spent on general administration; payers receive nothing specific in return. A resident says the levy is defective because he gets no service for it. Is he right?
quiz.ok: No. A tax never promises a specific return; that is a defining feature, not a defect.
no: Yes. A compulsory levy should give each payer a service roughly proportionate to what he pays.
Yes. Money paid into the Consolidated Fund must be matched by a direct benefit to each payer.
No, but mainly because the State has chosen to call the levy a tax rather than a fee.
quiz.why: A tax is a compulsory exaction for public purposes, enforceable by law, and not a payment for services rendered. The absence of a quid pro quo is what separates a tax from a fee, so the payer cannot demand a special service in return. Relying on the State’s choice of label reaches the right result for the wrong reason, because a label never decides the character of a levy. Authority: Shirur Mutt (adopting Matthews v. Chicory Marketing Board).

quiz.concept: Uncertain component defeats the levy
quiz.q: A State Act imposes a tax of 2% of the price on “every transfer of a motor vehicle”, but nowhere says, expressly or by necessary implication, whether the transferor or the transferee must pay it. What is the consequence?
quiz.ok: The levy fails, because the person liable, an essential component, is left uncertain.
no: The levy stands, and the Revenue may recover the tax from whichever party it chooses.
The levy stands, and the court will place liability on whichever party benefits more.
The levy stands, because only the taxable event and the rate are essential to a valid tax.
quiz.why: Every tax has four components: the taxable event, the person liable, the rate, and the measure to which the rate applies. If any of them is uncertain, the levy fails. Here the event, rate and measure are fixed but the person liable is not, and neither the Revenue nor the court can supply that by choice or inference. Authority: Govind Saran Ganga Saran v. Commissioner of Sales Tax.

quiz.concept: Taxable event versus measure
quiz.q: In income tax, how does the taxable event differ from the measure of the tax?
quiz.ok: The event is earning total income in a tax year; the measure is that income computed under the Act.
no: The event is filing the return of income; the measure is the income declared in that return.
The event is the Finance Act fixing the year’s rates; the measure is the tax payable at those rates.
The event is the making of an assessment order; the measure is the income the assessing officer determines.
quiz.why: The taxable event is what attracts the charge: earning total income in a tax year. The measure is the value to which the rate applies: total income computed under the Act. Filing a return and making an assessment are machinery for quantifying and collecting a liability the event has already created, and the Finance Act supplies the rate, which is a separate component. Authority: Govind Saran Ganga Saran; sections 4 and 5 of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Moderation in ancient tax thought
quiz.q: The Manusmriti asks the king to collect his revenue as the leech, the calf and the bee take their food. Which idea does this image best express?
quiz.ok: Taxes should be light and gradual, so that the payer’s capacity to produce survives.
no: Taxes should be heavy enough to discourage the subjects from harmful habits of consumption.
Each subject should pay in proportion to the benefit he receives from the king.
Taxes should be collected in one annual instalment, to keep the cost of collection low.
quiz.why: The leech, the calf and the bee take their food little by little without destroying its source. The lesson is moderation: tax should not cripple the payer’s productive capacity, an idea that survives in the canon of economy. The image says nothing about discouraging consumption, the benefit theory or the timing of collection. Authority: Manusmriti, Chapter VII.

quiz.concept: Taxation for the subjects’ welfare
quiz.q: Kalidasa compares King Dilipa’s taxation to the sun, which draws up water from the earth only to return it a thousandfold as rain. Which feature of a tax does the image stress?
quiz.ok: Its proceeds serve public purposes and return to the people as public benefit.
no: Each payer is entitled to a specific return worth more than what he has paid in.
Collections should rise in years of plenty and fall in years of scarcity.
Taxes may be raised only with the prior consent of the people’s representatives.
quiz.why: The image is about the purpose of revenue: it is collected for the welfare of the subjects as a whole and comes back to them as public benefit, the “public purposes” element of a tax. It does not promise each payer a return of his own, which would be closer to the quid pro quo of a fee. Nor does it speak to elasticity or to legislative consent. Authority: Kalidasa, Raghuvamsha.

quiz.concept: Regressive effect of a uniform tax
quiz.q: The Government levies a uniform tax of Rs. 10 on every kilogram of salt. A labourer and a wealthy businessman buy the same quantity each month. Judged by its burden relative to income, how is the tax best classified?
quiz.ok: Regressive, because the same amount takes a larger share of the poorer buyer’s income.
no: Proportional, because each buyer pays exactly the same amount on each kilogram he buys.
Progressive, because households that buy more salt end up paying more tax in total.
Degressive, because the tax stops rising once a household’s need for salt is met.
quiz.why: Progression is judged by tax as a share of income. A uniform tax on a necessity takes the same rupee amount from rich and poor, which is a far larger share of a poor person’s income, so it is regressive. It looks proportional only because the charge per kilogram is uniform; relative to income, the burden falls as income rises.

quiz.concept: Direct and indirect taxes
quiz.q: A manufacturer pays GST on its supplies and raises its prices by the full amount of the tax. A salaried employee pays income tax, partly deducted at source by her employer, and cannot pass it on. Which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: GST is indirect, as its burden can be passed on through prices; income tax is direct, as the payer bears it.
no: GST is direct, as the manufacturer pays it to the Government; income tax is indirect, as the employer deducts it.
Both are direct taxes, because in each case a person pays money straight to the Government.
GST is indirect, as both the Union and the States levy it; income tax is direct, as the Union levies it.
quiz.why: A tax is direct when the person on whom it is imposed also bears it, and indirect when its burden can be shifted to others, usually through prices. Deduction at source is only a collection mechanism: the employee still bears the tax, so income tax remains direct. Whether the Union, the States or both levy a tax is a different classification, by level of government.

quiz.concept: Proportional is not progressive
quiz.q: Unexplained income is taxed at a flat 30%, whatever its amount. A student calls this progressive, because a person with Rs. 10 lakh of unexplained income pays more than one with Rs. 1 lakh. What is wrong with the reasoning?
quiz.ok: Progression needs a rising rate; a flat 30% on every rupee makes the tax proportional.
no: Nothing; a tax under which richer people pay more rupees is, for that reason, progressive.
The tax is really regressive, because a flat rate always burdens poorer people more.
The tax is really degressive, because the rate rises to 30% and then stays flat.
quiz.why: A progressive tax takes a rising share as income rises, as the slabs that charge nil up to Rs. 4,00,000 and then 5% to 30% do. A proportional tax applies one rate whatever the size of the base, so the rupee amount grows with income but the share does not. A degressive tax rises up to a point and then stays flat, whereas this rate is flat from the first rupee. Authority: sections 195 and 202(1) of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Formalisation as a purpose of tax
quiz.q: The 2025 Act disallows large cash payments as business expenses, offers a lower presumptive rate on digital receipts and requires tax to be deducted at source. Which purpose of taxation do these measures chiefly share?
quiz.ok: Formalisation: moving transactions into recorded channels the tax system can see.
no: Redistribution: shifting more of the burden of tax from poorer to richer taxpayers.
Stabilisation: raising overall demand in the economy during a slowdown in growth.
Regulation: discouraging harmful consumption, in the way high taxes on tobacco do.
quiz.why: Formalisation is one of the purposes of modern taxation. Disallowing large cash payments, rewarding digital receipts with a lower presumptive rate and collecting tax at source all push economic activity into channels that leave a record. They are not aimed at who bears the burden (redistribution), at the level of demand (stabilisation) or at harmful consumption. Authority: sections 36(4), 58, 392 and 393 of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Regulating behaviour through tax
quiz.q: The Government sharply raises the tax on cigarettes and, in the same Budget, allows a deduction for health insurance premiums. Beyond their effect on revenue, what common purpose do the two measures serve?
quiz.ok: Regulation: discouraging harmful consumption and rewarding desirable choices.
no: Redistribution: taking a larger share of income from the richest taxpayers.
Formalisation: moving cash transactions into banking channels that can be traced.
Stabilisation: restraining overall demand when the economy begins to overheat.
quiz.why: Taxation also steers conduct. A high tax on tobacco discourages its use, while deductions for things such as donations and health insurance encourage choices the State wants to promote. Neither measure is aimed at income inequality, at cash transactions or at the business cycle as such. Authority: sections 126 and 133 of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Redistribution and the Directive Principles
quiz.q: A Finance Bill raises the rate on the highest income slab and leaves the lower slabs unchanged. Which purpose of taxation does this chiefly serve, and what constitutional support does it have?
quiz.ok: Redistribution, backed by the Directive Principles against inequality and concentrated wealth.
no: Regulation of behaviour, supported by the freedom to carry on a trade or business.
Formalisation, supported by the rule that a tax needs the authority of a law.
Stabilisation, supported by the statutory path laid down for reducing the fiscal deficit.
quiz.why: Progressive rates redistribute income by taking a larger share from those who have more. The Directive Principles ask the State to minimise inequalities in income and to prevent the concentration of wealth, which gives redistribution constitutional support. The authority-of-law rule governs how a tax is imposed, not why. Authority: Article 38(2) and Article 39(b) and (c).

quiz.concept: Canon of certainty
quiz.q: A taxpayer cannot tell from the law when his tax falls due or how it is to be computed, because both depend on unpublished departmental instructions. Which of Adam Smith’s canons is most clearly offended?
quiz.ok: Certainty: the amount, time and manner of payment should be clear to the taxpayer.
no: Convenience: tax should be collected at the time and in the manner that suit the payer.
Economy: the cost of collecting the tax should be kept as low as possible.
Equality: each person should contribute in proportion to his ability to pay.
quiz.why: Certainty requires that the amount, time and manner of payment be clear, which is impossible when they turn on unpublished instructions. Convenience is the tempting answer, but it asks whether the time and manner of collection suit the payer, not whether they can be known at all. The single “tax year” and the Tables of the 2025 Act are meant to serve certainty. Authority: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations.

quiz.concept: Benefit theory versus ability to pay
quiz.q: A critic argues that a poor family that uses public hospitals heavily should pay more income tax than a rich family that uses only private hospitals. Which theory is the critic relying on, and which does income tax mainly rest on?
quiz.ok: The critic relies on the benefit theory; income tax rests mainly on ability to pay.
no: The critic relies on ability to pay; income tax rests mainly on the benefit theory.
The critic relies on minimum sacrifice; income tax rests mainly on the benefit theory.
The critic relies on the canon of equality; income tax rests mainly on the canon of economy.
quiz.why: The benefit theory says people should pay according to the benefit they receive from the State; ability to pay says they should pay according to their capacity, and income tax, with its progressive slabs, rests mainly on it. Sacrifice theories explain ability to pay, and minimum sacrifice supports steep progression, the opposite of the critic’s view. The canon of equality is itself about contribution in proportion to ability.

quiz.concept: Canon of economy
quiz.q: A proposed tax would cost almost as much to administer as it raises, and would discourage people from working extra hours. Which canon does it most clearly fail?
quiz.ok: Economy: a tax should cost little to collect and do minimal harm to productive activity.
no: Certainty: the amount, time and manner of payment should be clear to the payer.
Convenience: the tax should be collected at the time and in the manner that suit the payer.
Equality: the burden should be shared in proportion to each person’s ability.
quiz.why: The canon of economy has two parts: a low cost of collection and minimal harm to productive activity. A tax that nearly consumes its own yield in administration and discourages work fails on both counts. Nothing in the facts suggests that the tax is unclear, badly timed or unequal. Authority: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations.

quiz.concept: Evasion, planning and avoidance
quiz.q: Classify each: (1) a trader keeps part of his sales off the books; (2) a salaried person invests in a scheme for which the Act offers a deduction; (3) a company routes a deal through artificial entities with no business purpose, satisfying the letter of the Act but defeating its purpose.
quiz.ok: (1) evasion; (2) tax planning; (3) avoidance.
no: (1) avoidance; (2) tax planning; (3) evasion.
(1) evasion; (2) avoidance; (3) tax planning.
(1) evasion; (2) avoidance; (3) avoidance.
quiz.why: Evasion is illegal non-payment through concealment or fraud, and it attracts penalty and prosecution. Planning arranges one’s affairs within the law and its purpose, such as claiming a deduction the law offers. Avoidance uses the letter of the law to defeat its purpose, often through artificial arrangements, and is now met by the General Anti-Avoidance Rule. Authority: Chapter XI of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Genuine arrangements may lower tax
quiz.q: A family converts its business into a company because companies may opt for a lower rate of tax. The conversion is real: the company owns the assets, keeps its own accounts and runs the business. The Revenue says the conversion should be ignored because it was made to save tax. Which principle supports the family?
quiz.ok: A person may arrange his affairs so that the tax payable is less than it would otherwise be.
no: A taxpayer may adopt any device, however artificial, so long as it meets the letter of the law.
Tax is payable on the economic substance of a business, whatever legal form the owners adopt.
An arrangement made mainly to save tax should be disregarded as a colourable device.
quiz.why: A genuine arrangement that is actually carried out is taxed by its real legal effect, even if it was chosen to save tax. That does not protect any device that merely meets the letter of the law: colourable devices are rejected, and arrangements lacking commercial substance now face the General Anti-Avoidance Rule. The substance and colourable-device options would support the Revenue, not the family. Authority: IRC v. Duke of Westminster; McDowell and Co. v. CTO.

quiz.concept: Genuine arrangement versus colourable device
quiz.q: Arrangement A: an employer pays a gardener under a binding deed of covenant instead of wages, so that the payments are deductible; the deed is genuine and acted on. Arrangement B: buyers pay excise duty directly to the authorities instead of to the seller, solely so that it is left out of the seller’s turnover for sales tax. Why is A respected and B rejected?
quiz.ok: A is a genuine arrangement; B is a colourable device whose only object is to escape tax.
no: A concerns income tax and B sales tax, and sales tax laws are construed much more strictly.
A was made for a genuine business reason, while B was made only to save tax.
B was unlawful evasion of the tax, whereas A kept within the letter of the law.
quiz.why: Both arrangements were made to reduce tax, so motive alone cannot separate them. The deed of covenant was a genuine legal arrangement that was actually carried out, and a person may arrange his affairs to pay less tax; the duty-payment scheme was a colourable device, and colourable devices cannot be part of tax planning. The scheme was rejected as a device, not as concealment or fraud, so calling it evasion misdescribes it. Authority: IRC v. Duke of Westminster; McDowell and Co. v. CTO.

quiz.concept: Treaty shopping is not illegal per se
quiz.q: A student argues: “The courts have held that colourable devices cannot be part of tax planning. So any arrangement that reduces tax is illegitimate, and investing in India through a country with a favourable tax treaty, to claim its benefits, is unlawful.” What is the main flaw in the argument?
quiz.ok: Genuine planning remains lawful, and treaty shopping is not illegal in itself.
no: There is no flaw; every arrangement made to reduce tax is now unlawful in India.
The premise is wrong: that view has been overruled, so colourable devices are now lawful.
Only the scale is wrong: an arrangement is lawful so long as the tax it saves is modest.
quiz.why: Rejecting colourable devices did not outlaw tax planning: arranging one’s affairs within the law and its purpose remains legitimate. The Supreme Court later upheld a CBDT circular allowing Mauritius residents to claim treaty benefits, holding that treaty shopping is not illegal in itself. The claim that colourable devices are now lawful overcorrects, and the size of the saving does not decide legitimacy. Authority: McDowell and Co. v. CTO; Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan.

quiz.concept: When a structure may be disregarded
quiz.q: A foreign company indirectly owns an Indian business through a chain of subsidiaries, and its shares are sold between two non-residents. Apart from any specific statutory rule, when may a court disregard the holding structure and treat the sale as a transfer of the Indian business?
quiz.ok: Only if it is a sham or colourable device, looking at the transaction as a whole.
no: Whenever the structure yields less Indian tax than a direct sale of the business would.
Whenever any company in the chain is resident in a country with low tax rates.
When the Indian business makes up most of the value of the foreign company’s shares.
quiz.why: The transaction must be looked at as a whole, and a structure can be disregarded only if it is a sham or colourable device; on that basis an offshore share sale was held not taxable under the 1961 Act as it then stood. A lower tax bill, a low-tax jurisdiction or the weight of the Indian business is not enough without a statutory rule, and Parliament has since enacted an indirect-transfer rule and the General Anti-Avoidance Rule. Authority: Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v. Union of India.

quiz.concept: What GAAR adds beyond the sham test
quiz.q: After the courts held that a structure could be disregarded only if it was a sham or colourable device, Parliament enacted a General Anti-Avoidance Rule. What does such a rule add?
quiz.ok: A statutory test reaching avoidance arrangements that lack commercial substance, not just shams.
no: A statutory restatement of the sham test, so that only sham arrangements can be disregarded.
A rule that makes all tax planning unlawful, including the claiming of deductions the Act offers.
A rule taxing sales of shares in foreign companies that derive their value from Indian assets.
quiz.why: The General Anti-Avoidance Rule describes an impermissible avoidance arrangement, explains when an arrangement lacks commercial substance and sets out the consequences, so the Revenue need not show a sham. It does not outlaw ordinary planning, such as claiming a deduction the Act offers. Taxing offshore share sales that derive value from India is a separate, specific rule on indirect transfers. Authority: sections 178 to 184 and 9(10) of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Taxing the profits of illegal business
quiz.q: A person runs an illegal betting business. He argues that (a) its profits cannot be taxed because the business is unlawful, and (b) in any case he may deduct a bribe paid to an official to avoid a raid. How does the law respond?
quiz.ok: Profits are taxable like any income, but a bribe, being for an offence, is not deductible.
no: The profits are not taxable, because the law will not recognise income from an unlawful source.
The profits are taxable, and the bribe is deductible as an expense incurred in earning them.
The profits become taxable only once he is convicted, and the bribe is deductible until then.
quiz.why: Tax law does not ask whether income was lawfully earned: the profits of an illegal business are taxable, and its losses can be set off against its profits. But expenditure for a purpose that is an offence or is prohibited by law is not deductible, and a bribe falls squarely in that category. Taxability does not wait for a conviction. Authority: CIT v. S.C. Kothari; section 34(2)(a) and (3) of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Why retrospective tax troubles fairness
quiz.q: After a court held an offshore share sale not taxable, the law was amended retrospectively to tax such sales. Years later, Parliament provided that no demand would be raised for earlier transfers, and such transfers are now taxed only prospectively. Which concern does this history best illustrate?
quiz.ok: It defeats reliance on the law as it stood, undermining certainty and fairness.
no: Retrospective tax is always void, as the Constitution forbids laws reaching into the past.
Retrospective tax is harmless, because it merely clarifies what the law was meant to say.
It shows that India has no power to tax indirect transfers of Indian assets at all.
quiz.why: People arrange their affairs on the law as it then stood, so a later charge on past transactions undermines certainty and fairness; that is the moral objection. In constitutional terms a tax law may be retrospective, since the bar is on retrospective criminal laws, so the claim that it is always void is wrong. Nor did the later relief deny the power to tax indirect transfers: they are now taxed prospectively. Authority: Finance Act, 2012; Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021; section 9(10) of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Impact and incidence in GST
quiz.q: A shopkeeper collects GST from his customers as part of the price and deposits it with the Government. Where do the impact and the incidence of the tax usually fall?
quiz.ok: Impact on the shopkeeper, who pays the Government; incidence on the customer, who bears it.
no: Impact on the customer, who pays first; incidence on the shopkeeper, who deposits the tax.
Both on the shopkeeper, because the law makes him the person liable to deposit the tax.
Both on the customer, because the customer is the person liable to the Government in law.
quiz.why: Impact is the immediate burden on the person who pays the tax to the Government; incidence is its final resting place, on the person who cannot pass it on. In an indirect tax such as GST, the supplier bears the impact and the consumer the incidence. Legal liability to deposit fixes the impact, not the incidence.

quiz.concept: Elasticity and the burden of tax
quiz.q: A tax is levied on a life-saving drug for which patients have no substitute, so demand barely responds to price. Manufacturers can easily switch their plants to other drugs. Who is likely to bear most of the tax?
quiz.ok: Patients, because the more inelastic side of the market bears more of a tax.
no: Manufacturers, because the law imposes the tax on them and they must pay it.
Manufacturers, because the side with more alternatives cannot pass the tax on.
Buyers and sellers equally, because a tax is always split evenly between them.
quiz.why: The more inelastic side of the market bears more of the tax. Patients cannot cut back or switch, so demand is inelastic; manufacturers can move their capacity elsewhere, so supply is elastic, and the tax is shifted forward through higher prices. Legal liability determines the impact, not the incidence, and saying that the side with more alternatives cannot pass the tax on turns the elasticity rule upside down.

quiz.concept: Time and the shifting of tax
quiz.q: A new tax is imposed on a crop that has already been harvested and must be sold this season. Over the next few seasons, farmers are free to plant less. How is the burden likely to change over time?
quiz.ok: Farmers bear most of it at first, but more passes to buyers as supply adjusts later.
no: Buyers bear most of it at first, but more passes back to farmers in later seasons.
The burden stays wherever it first falls, because shifting does not depend on time.
The burden passes wholly to buyers at once, as sellers simply add the tax to the price.
quiz.why: Shifting is easier in the long run, when supply can adjust. With a harvested crop, supply is fixed for the season, so farmers cannot hold back output and must absorb most of the tax; once they can plant less, supply responds and more of the burden moves forward to buyers through prices. The idea that sellers simply add the tax to the price ignores both elasticity and time.

quiz.concept: Coverage of close substitutes
quiz.q: A State taxes one brand of bottled water but not the many rival brands of similar quality. Compared with a tax on all bottled water, what is likely?
quiz.ok: The taxed brand will struggle to pass it on, since buyers can switch to untaxed rivals.
no: The taxed brand will pass the tax on more easily, because fewer sellers share the burden.
Nothing changes, because only the rate of tax, not its coverage, decides who bears it.
Buyers will bear most of it, because bottled water is a necessity with few substitutes.
quiz.why: A tax on all close substitutes is harder to escape than a tax on one product. When only one brand is taxed, buyers can move to untaxed rivals, so the seller cannot raise its price without losing custom and must absorb more of the tax. Coverage works alongside elasticity, market power and time.

quiz.concept: Employer-borne tax: perquisite versus salary
quiz.q: Employer X chooses to pay the tax on a non-monetary perquisite it gives an employee. Employer Y agrees to pay the tax on its employee’s salary. How is the tax paid by each employer treated in the employee’s hands?
quiz.ok: X’s payment is excluded from the employee’s income, while Y’s payment is part of it.
no: Both payments are part of the employee’s income, because each is a benefit from the employment.
Both payments are excluded from the employee’s income, as the employer bears the tax in both.
X’s payment forms part of the employee’s income, while Y’s payment is excluded from it.
quiz.why: In both cases the employer, not the employee, bears the incidence, but the law treats the two differently. Tax paid by the employer on a non-monetary perquisite is excluded from the employee’s income (and is not deductible for the employer), whereas tax paid by the employer on the employee’s salary is itself the employee’s income. Authority: Schedule III, Sl. No. 10; section 35(a)(ii); Emil Webber v. CIT; section 17(1)(f).

quiz.concept: Permanent Act and annual Finance Act
quiz.q: Why does a person’s income tax for a year depend on both the 2025 Act and that year’s Finance Act?
quiz.ok: The Act is the permanent law of charge and computation; the Finance Act supplies the rates.
no: The 2025 Act applies only to individuals, while the Finance Act applies to companies and firms.
The 2025 Act lapses each year unless the Finance Act re-enacts the whole of it.
The Finance Act decides who is liable to pay, while the 2025 Act fixes the year’s rates.
quiz.why: The 2025 Act is the permanent law: it charges total income and lays down how it is computed. The rates for the year come mainly from the annual Finance Act, although some, such as the slabs in section 202(1), are set in the Act itself. The Act does not lapse, and it is the Act that identifies the person liable (“every person”). Authority: section 4(1) of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Money Bills and the Rajya Sabha
quiz.q: A Bill that deals only with the imposition and computation of income tax is introduced in Parliament. What role does the Rajya Sabha have?
quiz.ok: As a Money Bill, it starts in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes.
no: It is an ordinary Bill, so the Rajya Sabha may reject it outright and block the law.
As a Money Bill, it may be introduced in either House and needs both Houses to pass it.
As a Money Bill, it goes straight to the President without passing through the Rajya Sabha.
quiz.why: A Bill dealing only with taxation is a Money Bill. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations, within fourteen days, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject. The Income Tax (No. 2) Bill, 2025 was passed as a Money Bill. Authority: Articles 109 and 110 of the Constitution.

quiz.concept: No tax without legislative authority
quiz.q: Facing a revenue shortfall, the Government issues an executive order imposing a new levy on online purchases, planning to seek legislation later. What is the constitutional objection?
quiz.ok: A tax needs the authority of law, and a mere executive order is not law.
no: None, because the executive may always impose taxes in an emergency and seek approval later.
Mainly that the proceeds have not been shared with the States through the divisible pool.
Mainly that the levy was not first recommended by the GST Council to the Union.
quiz.why: No tax may be levied or collected except by authority of law, an idea carried forward from the English Bill of Rights, 1689, which forbade levying money for the Crown without the grant of Parliament. An executive order is not such a law, and money collected without authority of law can be recovered. Revenue sharing and the GST Council’s role are secondary questions that arise only once there is a valid levy. Authority: Article 265.

quiz.concept: Progressive tax as automatic stabiliser
quiz.q: In a boom, income tax collections rise sharply; in a slowdown, they fall, all without any change in the law. What is this an example of?
quiz.ok: An automatic stabiliser, restraining demand in booms and cushioning it in slowdowns.
no: Discretionary demand management, with Parliament changing tax rates by fresh legislation.
Fiscal discipline imposed by the statutory path for reducing the fiscal deficit year by year.
The canon of convenience, since tax is collected when people can best afford to pay.
quiz.why: Because rates rise with income, a progressive income tax collects more in booms and less in slowdowns without new legislation, taking spending power out of an overheating economy and leaving more with people when it slows. Discretionary demand management needs a deliberate change in the law, and the deficit-reduction law sets a fiscal path rather than responding automatically. Convenience concerns the time and manner of payment, not how the yield moves with the economy.

quiz.concept: Tax incentives for investment
quiz.q: During a slowdown, the Government wants firms to expand their productive capacity, without cutting the general rate of tax. Which tool fits that aim best?
quiz.ok: Additional depreciation, which lowers the tax of firms that buy new plant and machinery.
no: A new cess on corporate income, credited to a special fund for promoting industrial growth.
A ban on business deductions for large cash payments made by firms to their suppliers.
A higher rate of tax deducted at source on interest that firms earn on their deposits.
quiz.why: Investment incentives target the behaviour the Government wants: additional depreciation on new plant and machinery reduces the tax of firms that invest, without a general rate cut. A new cess adds to the burden even if its proceeds are earmarked, and cash-payment restrictions and tax deducted at source serve formalisation rather than investment. Authority: section 33(8) of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Compulsory fee credited to Consolidated Fund
quiz.q: A State charges every operator of a tourist boat on a lake Rs. 500 a month. A good and substantial part of the collections is spent on jetties, buoys and rescue services for the operators, and the money is credited to the State’s Consolidated Fund. The operators say the levy must be a tax, because payment is compulsory and the money goes into the Consolidated Fund. Are they right?
quiz.ok: No. A fee may be compulsory, and all revenues must go to the Consolidated Fund anyway.
no: Yes. A fee must be voluntary, paid only by those who choose to use the services.
Yes. A fee must be credited to a separate fund, not to the State’s general revenue.
No, but only because a levy for a specific purpose is a cess, and a cess is never a tax.
quiz.why: A fee is levied in consideration of a special service that individuals accept willingly or unwillingly, so compulsion does not make it a tax. Separate earmarking is only a relevant sign, not an absolute condition, because all revenues must be credited to the Consolidated Fund. A cess, for its part, is normally a tax, though it can be a fee if it has a fee’s character. Authority: Shirur Mutt; Article 266.

quiz.concept: Broad correlation suffices for a fee
quiz.q: A market committee spends most of its market fee on roads, storage and drainage in the market area. These benefit traders as a class, but no trader can show that he personally received services equal to the fee he paid. Is the fee valid?
quiz.ok: Yes. A broad correlation is enough, and the services may benefit payers as a class.
no: No. Each trader must be shown to receive services equal in value to the fee he pays.
No. A fee is valid only if the whole of the collection is spent on services to the payers.
Yes, because a market fee is a regulatory fee and so needs no link with any services.
quiz.why: A fee must bear a close and reasonable relationship to the services, with a good and substantial portion spent for the payers’ special benefit, but the correlation need not be exact: a broad and general correlation is enough, and the benefit may go to the payers as a class. Calling the fee regulatory does not help, because this fee is charged for services and is tested by correlation. Authority: Kewal Krishan Puri v. State of Punjab; Sreenivasa General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh.

quiz.concept: Regulatory fees need no strict quid pro quo
quiz.q: A State requires every private security agency to hold a licence and charges an annual licence fee. The money is used mainly to inspect and supervise the agencies, not to provide services that benefit them. Does the lack of any special benefit to the agencies make the levy a tax?
quiz.ok: No. A fee charged to regulate a trade does not need a strict quid pro quo.
no: Yes. Every fee must confer a special benefit on those who pay it, or it is a tax.
Yes, unless the State shows that the agencies benefit as a class from the inspections.
No, because a levy that the legislature calls a “fee” is treated as a fee.
quiz.why: Fees charged for services need a broad correlation with those services, but a regulatory fee, charged to regulate a trade, does not need a strict quid pro quo, so the State need not show any benefit to the payers. The label still does not decide the matter: a so-called licence fee that neither regulates nor pays for any service may be a tax in substance, which is why an answer resting on the label alone is wrong. Authority: Corporation of Calcutta v. Liberty Cinema (on labels).

quiz.concept: Substance, not label, decides
quiz.q: A municipal law calls a levy on cinema shows a “licence fee”. The municipality renders no service to the cinema owners, and the levy is not used to regulate them. How will a court characterise it?
quiz.ok: As a tax in substance, because a label never decides the true nature of a levy.
no: As a fee, because the legislature has expressly called it a licence fee.
As a fee, because all charges on licensed businesses are fees by definition.
As a cess, because it is levied on one class of businesses for a specific purpose.
quiz.why: A levy is classified by its substance, not its name. A “licence fee” for which no service is rendered, and which is not a regulatory fee, is in substance a tax. Both “fee” options rely on the label, which is exactly what the courts refuse to do. Authority: Corporation of Calcutta v. Liberty Cinema.

quiz.concept: A cess can be a fee
quiz.q: A State levies a “cess” on mine owners, credits it to a fund for developing the mining areas, and spends it on works that benefit the mine owners. How is the levy best characterised?
quiz.ok: As a fee, because it is linked to services that benefit the mine owners.
no: As a tax, because a levy described as a cess is always a tax, whatever its use.
As a royalty, because it is paid by mine owners in respect of minerals.
As a surcharge, because it is added on top of an existing levy for a purpose.
quiz.why: A cess is a levy for a specific purpose. It is normally a tax, but it can be a fee if it has the character of one, as where it is credited to a fund used for services that benefit the payers. Royalty is different: it is a contractual consideration for the right to extract minerals. Authority: Hingir Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa.

quiz.concept: Royalty is not a tax
quiz.q: A mining lessee pays the State a royalty under the lease, in return for the right to extract minerals. Applying the features of a tax, how is royalty best characterised?
quiz.ok: As contractual consideration paid for the right to extract minerals, not a tax.
no: As a tax, because it is a compulsory payment made to a public authority.
As a fee, because the State renders the lessee a special service in return.
As a cess, because it is levied for the specific purpose of mineral development.
quiz.why: A tax is a compulsory exaction for public purposes, not a payment in return for something. Royalty is paid under a lease as the price of the right to extract minerals, so it is contractual consideration; a nine-judge bench so held in 2024, also holding that the States’ power to tax mineral rights is not taken away by the central mining law. Authority: Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India (overruling India Cement on this point).

quiz.concept: Cess on income tax not deductible
quiz.q: A company pays income tax together with the Health and Education Cess levied on it. It claims the cess as a business expense, arguing that the cess is not itself income tax. Is the claim sound under the 2025 Act?
quiz.ok: No. A cess on income tax counts as part of the tax, so no business deduction is allowed.
no: Yes. The cess is a fee for health and education services, so it is a business expense.
Yes. Only the basic income tax is disallowed, not cesses or surcharges added to it.
No, but because the cess is levied by the States rather than by the Union.
quiz.why: For business deductions, the 2025 Act treats a cess on income tax as part of the tax: it denies a deduction for income tax, including any surcharge or cess. A cess for a specific purpose is normally a tax, not a fee, and the Health and Education Cess is levied by the Union through the Finance Acts. Contrast revenue-sharing, where a specific-purpose cess is kept outside the pool shared with the States. Authority: section 35(a) of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Fee Bills are not Money Bills
quiz.q: A Bill provides only for fees for licences and for services rendered. A member insists it must be passed as a Money Bill, because it brings money to the Government. Is he right?
quiz.ok: No. Providing for fees does not by itself make a Bill a Money Bill.
no: Yes. A Bill under which money is paid to the Government is a Money Bill.
Yes. Fees are a kind of tax, so a Bill providing for them is a Money Bill.
No, because fees can be imposed only by the States, never by Parliament.
quiz.why: A Bill imposing a tax is a Money Bill, but the Constitution expressly provides that a Bill is not one merely because it provides for fees for licences or for services. Fees are distinct from taxes and have their own legislative entries in each List, so Parliament too can provide for fees. Authority: Article 110(2); Entry 96 of List I, Entry 66 of List II and Entry 47 of List III.

quiz.concept: Linking land revenue to productive capacity
quiz.q: Under Akbar, Raja Todar Mal based land revenue on the measurement of land and its average produce. Compare a levy of the same flat amount on every acre, fertile or barren. What does the older system do that the flat levy does not?
quiz.ok: It links the burden on each holding to what that land can actually produce.
no: It charges a higher rate on larger holdings, which makes the land revenue progressive.
It replaces land revenue with a tax on each cultivator’s income from all sources.
It lets each cultivator declare his own produce, so no official assessment is needed.
quiz.why: Basing revenue on measured land and its average produce relates the demand to what each holding can yield, an early form of the idea that tax should follow ability. A flat amount per acre treats fertile and barren land alike, the defect for which a modern flat land tax was struck down. The older system rested on official measurement, not self-declaration, and did not raise the rate with the size of a holding. Authority: Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala (on flat land taxes).

quiz.concept: Why the States tax agricultural income
quiz.q: The Government of India Act, 1935 gave the Centre taxes on income other than agricultural income and left agricultural income to the provinces. How does the Constitution treat this division?
quiz.ok: It keeps it: Parliament taxes non-agricultural income, and the States tax agricultural income.
no: It ends it: Parliament now taxes all income, including agricultural income, under one entry.
It reverses it: the States tax non-agricultural income, and Parliament taxes agricultural income.
It ends it: agricultural income may now be taxed by neither Parliament nor the States.
quiz.why: The Constitution carried the 1935 division forward: taxes on income other than agricultural income are in the Union List, and taxes on agricultural income are in the State List. That is why the Union’s income tax law leaves agricultural income out of its charge while the States may tax it. Authority: Government of India Act, 1935 (Entry 54, Federal List); Entry 82 of List I; Entry 46 of List II.

quiz.concept: India’s first income tax met a revenue need
quiz.q: India’s first income tax was introduced in 1860, when the Government faced severe financial strain after the revolt of 1857. Which purpose of taxation did it chiefly serve?
quiz.ok: Revenue: raising money to meet the Government’s pressing public expenditure.
no: Redistribution: narrowing inequality between rich and poor through progressive rates.
Regulation: discouraging forms of consumption that the Government thought harmful.
Formalisation: drawing trade into recorded channels that tax officials could trace.
quiz.why: The tax was introduced to meet the financial strain after the revolt, which is the revenue purpose: finding money for public expenditure such as administration and defence. Redistribution, regulation of behaviour and formalisation are purposes that tax systems also pursue, but nothing in the circumstances of 1860 points to them. The Income Tax Act, 1886 later gave the tax a lasting form.

quiz.concept: Raising taxes to curb inflation
quiz.q: Prices are rising fast because total demand in the economy exceeds what can be produced. Using tax policy alone, what is the standard demand-management response?
quiz.ok: Raise taxes, so that people and firms have less to spend and demand cools.
no: Cut taxes, so that firms produce more and the extra supply brings prices down.
Leave taxes alone, because only the central bank can influence the level of prices.
Raise taxes only on imported goods, so that demand shifts to domestic products.
quiz.why: Demand management uses taxes to influence total spending: lower taxes raise demand, and higher taxes help control inflation by leaving people and firms with less to spend. A tax cut would add to demand, the opposite of what is needed here. Monetary policy matters too, but tax policy is itself a tool of demand management, and a tax on imports alone shifts demand rather than reducing it.

quiz.concept: Fiscal discipline limits discretionary tax cuts
quiz.q: During a slowdown, the Government wants to cut income tax sharply to raise demand. A statute, however, binds it to a path for reducing the fiscal deficit. What does this illustrate?
quiz.ok: Fiscal discipline limits demand management, because a tax cut widens the deficit.
no: An automatic stabiliser, since the deficit statute adjusts tax rates without fresh laws.
Formalisation, because the statute moves Government accounts into recorded channels.
No real conflict, because a tax cut always pays for itself through faster growth.
quiz.why: Cutting taxes to raise demand is discretionary demand management, but lower taxes without matching spending cuts widen the fiscal deficit. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 sets a path for reducing that deficit, so the two goals pull in different directions and the Government must balance them. The deficit law does not change tax rates by itself, so it is not an automatic stabiliser. Authority: Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003.

quiz.concept: Fairness and good use aid compliance
quiz.q: Two countries have similar tax rates and similar enforcement. In Country A, people see revenue spent visibly on schools, roads and courts, and the law treats like cases alike; in Country B, revenue is widely thought to be wasted and the rich to escape. Where is voluntary compliance likely to be higher, and why?
quiz.ok: In A, as people comply more readily when the system seems fair and the money well used.
no: In B, because distrust makes people more careful to pay exactly what the law demands.
In neither, because compliance depends only on rates and enforcement, which are the same.
In A, but only because fair systems always have lower rates of tax than others.
quiz.why: Taxation is usually justified as the price of an organised society; in Holmes J.’s words, taxes are what we pay for civilized society. Voluntary compliance improves when people see the system as fair and the money as well used, so with rates and enforcement held equal, legitimacy makes the difference. Lower rates cannot explain it, since the rates are similar. Authority: Compania General de Tabacos de Filipinas v. Collector of Internal Revenue (Holmes J., dissenting).

quiz.concept: Every exemption shifts the burden to others
quiz.q: A critic accepts that the exemption for agricultural income helps small farmers, but still calls it unfair. Which argument best supports the critic?
quiz.ok: It shifts more of the burden onto other taxpayers, and shelters rich farmers and disguised income.
no: It is unconstitutional, because tax laws may not treat farmers differently from other earners.
It is regressive, because it takes a larger share of the income of poorer farmers than richer ones.
It means agricultural income can then be taxed by no government in India at all.
quiz.why: Every exemption shifts the burden onto others, since what one group does not pay must be met by the rest. The agricultural income exemption protects small farmers but also benefits wealthy agriculturists and can be misused to disguise other income. The exemption mirrors the Constitution’s allocation of agricultural income to the States, which may tax it, so such income is not beyond all tax; and reasonable classification in tax laws is permitted. Authority: Schedule II, Sl. No. 1 of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Delegated legislation cannot create a charge
quiz.q: The 2025 Act empowers the making of rules to carry out its provisions. A rule made under that power imposes a levy on a class of receipts that the Act itself does not charge. Is the rule valid?
quiz.ok: No. A rule cannot go beyond its parent Act, so it cannot create a new charge.
no: Yes. Rules made under the Act have the force of the Act, whatever they provide.
