Yes, provided the rule is laid before Parliament and is not annulled there.
No, because rules may never deal with any matter connected with taxation.
quiz.why: Only the legislature can impose a tax, and rules made under an Act are valid only within the limits the parent Act sets, so a rule cannot create a charge the Act does not impose. Laying the rule before Parliament does not turn it into the Act. Saying that rules can never touch taxation overstates the point, since rules may validly deal with details and procedure within the Act. Authority: Article 265; section 533 of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Valid law needed for levy and collection
quiz.q: A State collects a tax from traders under an Act that the courts later hold to be beyond the State’s legislative competence. What follows from the rule that no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law?
quiz.ok: Only a valid law counts, so the collection lacked authority and the tax can be recovered.
no: The collection stands, because the Act was on the statute book when the tax was collected.
The collection stands, because the rule covers the levy of a tax but not its collection.
The collection stands, because the State has already spent the money for public purposes.
quiz.why: “Law” in this rule means a valid law, made by a competent legislature and consistent with fundamental rights and other constitutional limits. An Act beyond the State’s competence is no authority for either the levy or the collection, both of which need legal authority, and money collected without authority of law can be recovered. Authority: Article 265.

quiz.concept: Authority of law: constitutional, not fundamental, right
quiz.q: A company says tax is being collected from it without authority of law, and wants to go to court on that ground alone. Which remedy is usually appropriate, and why?
quiz.ok: A High Court writ petition, as the guarantee is constitutional but not a fundamental right.
no: A petition directly to the Supreme Court, because the guarantee is one of the fundamental rights.
No court remedy at all, because only the tax department may decide whether a levy is lawful.
A reference to the Finance Commission, which decides disputes about the levy of taxes.
quiz.why: The rule that no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law sits in Part XII of the Constitution, not in Part III. It is therefore a constitutional right but not a fundamental right, so a violation on that ground alone is usually challenged in the High Court’s writ jurisdiction rather than by a petition to the Supreme Court for enforcing fundamental rights. Authority: Articles 265 and 226.

quiz.concept: Taxing entries are separate from general entries
quiz.q: A State Legislature legislates on a subject under a general entry in the State List. No entry in the State List or the Concurrent List permits a tax on that subject, but the State imposes one, relying on the general entry. Is the tax valid?
quiz.ok: No. A general entry never carries a power to tax, as taxing entries are separate.
no: Yes. The power to regulate a subject necessarily includes the power to tax it.
Yes. A State may tax any subject that is not expressly reserved to the Union.
Yes, provided Parliament has not already imposed a tax on the same subject.
quiz.why: The Seventh Schedule separates taxing entries from general entries, and a power to legislate on a subject does not include a power to tax it unless there is a taxing entry. A State has no residuary taxing power either: any tax not mentioned in the State or Concurrent List falls to Parliament. The State could, however, levy a genuine fee under its fee entry. Authority: M.P.V. Sundararamier and Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh; Entry 97 of List I.

quiz.concept: Parliament’s residuary taxing power
quiz.q: Parliament levies a tax on the net wealth of individuals and includes agricultural land among the assets counted. A State argues that only it may tax agricultural land. On what basis can Parliament’s levy be upheld?
quiz.ok: A net wealth tax is not a tax on lands and buildings, so Parliament’s residuary power supports it.
no: Parliament’s power to tax income also covers agricultural income, and so agricultural land.
The Finance Commission recommended including agricultural land, and its advice binds the States.
Parliament may tax agricultural land under its simultaneous GST power shared with the States.
quiz.why: A tax on net wealth falls on the total value of a person’s assets, not on lands and buildings as such, so it is not the State tax on lands and buildings. Any tax not mentioned in the State or Concurrent List falls within Parliament’s residuary power, and the levy was upheld on that basis. Authority: Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon; Article 248; Entry 97 of List I; Entry 49 of List II.

quiz.concept: Who defines agricultural income
quiz.q: The Constitution gives “agricultural income” the meaning it has under the Indian income tax law. Suppose the income-tax definition were narrowed, so that some income now treated as agricultural no longer is. What would be the constitutional consequence?
quiz.ok: The Union’s field would widen and the States’ power over agricultural income would shrink.
no: Nothing, because the Constitution’s own fixed meaning of agricultural income would apply.
Only the Union’s field would change; the States would still tax the same income as before.
The States would lose their power to tax agricultural income from then on.
quiz.why: Because the Constitution borrows the income-tax definition, that definition (now section 2(5) of the 2025 Act) decides both what the Union cannot tax and what the States may tax as agricultural income. Changing it moves the boundary between the two fields. That is why a Bill varying the meaning of agricultural income for income-tax purposes needs the President’s recommendation: it touches the States’ interests. Authority: Articles 366(1) and 274; Entry 82 of List I; Entry 46 of List II.

quiz.concept: Extra-territorial laws need a nexus
quiz.q: Parliament deems income to accrue in India where a non-resident has a significant economic presence in India. The non-resident argues that Parliament cannot make laws operating outside India. Which view is correct?
quiz.ok: Valid, as Parliament may legislate on extra-territorial matters with a nexus to India.
no: Void, because Parliament can never tax persons or transactions located outside India.
Valid, and it would remain valid even for matters having no connection with India.
Valid, provided the foreign country agrees to India taxing the income concerned.
quiz.why: A law of Parliament is not invalid because it operates outside India, but Parliament may legislate on extra-territorial matters only where they have a nexus with India, not on matters with no such nexus. The deemed-accrual rules on business connection, significant economic presence and indirect transfers rest on such a nexus. A treaty may allocate taxing rights, but the power to legislate does not depend on foreign consent. Authority: Article 245(2); GVK Industries Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer; section 9.

quiz.concept: Union tax on a State’s business
quiz.q: A State runs a commercial bus service as a business. The Union seeks to tax the income of that business, and the State claims that its income is immune from Union taxation. Who is right?
quiz.ok: The Union: a State’s income is generally exempt, but its trade or business is taxable.
no: The State: a State’s income is immune from Union taxes, whatever its source.
The State: Union taxes cannot apply to a State’s activities without its consent.
The Union: a State’s income is taxable by the Union in every case, like anyone else’s.
quiz.why: The Constitution exempts the property and income of a State from Union taxes, but lets the Union tax a trade or business carried on by a State. The reverse immunity also exists: Union property is exempt from State taxes unless Parliament provides otherwise. Saying the Union may tax a State’s income in every case overstates its power, since a State’s non-business income and property remain exempt. Authority: Articles 285 and 289.

quiz.concept: Surcharges stay with the Union
quiz.q: The Union levies a surcharge on income tax for Union purposes. A State claims a share of the surcharge collections, arguing that a surcharge is simply part of income tax. For the purpose of sharing revenue, is the State right?
quiz.ok: No. Surcharges belong wholly to the Union and stay outside the divisible pool.
no: Yes. A surcharge is part of income tax, so it is shared exactly like the basic tax.
Yes, but only if the Finance Commission recommends that the surcharge be shared.
No, because income tax itself is no longer shared with the States.
quiz.why: Taxes in the Union List are shared with the States, but surcharges for Union purposes and cesses for specific purposes are excluded and belong wholly to the Union. The argument that a surcharge is simply part of income tax confuses two contexts: for denying a business deduction the 2025 Act treats a surcharge as part of income tax, but for revenue sharing the Constitution keeps it out of the pool. Income tax and corporation tax themselves are shared. Authority: Articles 270 and 271.

quiz.concept: A single divisible pool
quiz.q: The Union raises basic customs duty, and collections rise sharply. Under the present scheme for sharing Union taxes, do the States gain from the increase?
quiz.ok: Yes. All Union List taxes, save stated exclusions such as surcharges, form one pool.
no: No. Only income tax and corporation tax are shared; other Union taxes stay with the Union.
No. Customs duties are collected and kept wholly by the Union under the Constitution.
Yes, but only if Parliament passes a separate law each year to share customs duty.
quiz.why: Originally only income tax had to be shared, and Union excise duties could be shared by law. The Eightieth Amendment (2000) replaced that scheme with a single divisible pool of all Union List taxes, subject to the stated exceptions, following the Tenth Finance Commission’s alternative scheme of devolution. So a rise in basic customs duty enlarges the pool, whereas a rise in a surcharge or a specific-purpose cess would not. Authority: Article 270; Constitution (Eightieth Amendment) Act, 2000.

quiz.concept: Vertical and horizontal imbalance
quiz.q: Consider two problems: (1) the States together carry heavy spending duties in health, police and education, while the Union controls the most productive taxes; (2) a poor, populous State raises far less of its own revenue than a rich one. How are they described?
quiz.ok: (1) is vertical imbalance and (2) is horizontal imbalance.
no: (1) is horizontal imbalance and (2) is vertical imbalance.
Both are vertical imbalance, as both concern State revenues.
Both are horizontal imbalance, as both concern capacity.
quiz.why: Vertical imbalance is the mismatch between the Union, which controls the most productive taxes, and the States, which carry heavy spending responsibilities. Horizontal imbalance is the difference among States in their capacity to raise revenue. The Constitution corrects both through tax devolution, grants in aid and borrowing within limits. Authority: Articles 270, 275, 282 and 293.

quiz.concept: Cesses shrink the States’ effective share
quiz.q: The Finance Commission keeps the States’ share of the divisible pool unchanged. Over the next few years, the Union raises a growing part of its revenue through cesses and surcharges. What happens to the States’ position?
quiz.ok: Their share of total Union revenue falls, though their percentage of the pool is unchanged.
no: Nothing changes, because their percentage share of the divisible pool stays exactly the same.
Their share rises, because cesses and surcharges are added to the divisible pool each year.
Their share rises, because cesses must be spent within the States that pay them.
quiz.why: Cesses for specific purposes and surcharges are outside the divisible pool. When the Union relies more on them, the pool becomes a smaller part of total Union revenue, so the States receive a smaller share of the whole even though their percentage of the pool has not changed. This is a recurring source of tension between the Union and the States. Authority: Articles 270(1) and 271.

quiz.concept: GST Council recommendations are persuasive
quiz.q: The GST Council recommends a particular treatment for a supply. A State Legislature, after considering it, legislates differently. A taxpayer argues that the State law is void merely because it departs from the Council’s recommendation. Which view is better?
quiz.ok: It fails: the Council’s recommendations persuade but do not bind, as GST power is shared.
no: It succeeds: the Council’s recommendations bind Parliament and the State Legislatures alike.
It succeeds: only Parliament may legislate on GST, so the State had no power at all.
It succeeds unless Parliament later passes a law ratifying the State’s departure from them.
quiz.why: The One Hundred and First Amendment gave Parliament and the State Legislatures simultaneous power to make laws on GST. Because the power is shared, the Council’s recommendations are persuasive, not binding: treating them as binding would subordinate the legislatures to the Council. The Court described Indian federalism as a dialogue involving both cooperation and contestation. Authority: Articles 246A and 279A; Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd.

quiz.concept: Reasonable classification in tax laws
quiz.q: A tax law charges expenditure in hotels whose room charges exceed a stated level, but not in cheaper hotels. A hotel in the taxed class says this discriminates against it. How will a court approach the challenge?
quiz.ok: Uphold it if the class rests on an intelligible differentia linked to the law’s object.
no: Strike it down, because equality requires all hotels to be taxed alike, whatever they charge.
Refuse to examine it, because taxing laws are wholly outside the fundamental rights.
Uphold it only if the State proves that no other classification was possible at all.
quiz.why: Classification is permitted if it rests on an intelligible differentia with a rational relation to the object of the law. Courts allow the legislature greater freedom of classification in taxation, and an expenditure tax on hotels with high room charges was upheld on that basis. Taxing laws remain subject to Part III, so a court will not refuse to examine the challenge. Authority: Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar; Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Association of India v. Union of India.

quiz.concept: Treating unequals as equals
quiz.q: A State levies the same flat amount per acre on all land, fertile or barren, with no procedure for assessment or objections. On what ground is the levy most vulnerable?
quiz.ok: It treats unequals as equals, and may be confiscatory for owners of barren land.
no: It charges owners of larger holdings more in total than others, which is discriminatory.
It is a proportional tax, and the Constitution forbids proportional taxes on land altogether.
It is in truth a tax on agricultural income, which only Parliament may levy.
quiz.why: Equality does not mean uniformity. A flat rate on all lands, productive or barren, with no machinery for assessment or objections, treated unequals as equals and was struck down; it was also held confiscatory. Calling it a tax on agricultural income that only Parliament may levy is wrong twice over: it is a land tax, and agricultural income is in any case a State subject. Authority: Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala.

quiz.concept: Procedural discrimination in tax laws
quiz.q: A law lets the Government send some suspected evaders to a special body with a harsher procedure, although they could equally be dealt with under the normal procedure, and gives no basis for choosing between them. What is the likely result?
quiz.ok: It is discriminatory, as procedural provisions of tax laws are also tested for equality.
no: It is valid, because equality applies only to the rates of tax, not to the procedure used.
It is valid, because suspected evaders form a reasonable class by their very nature.
It is valid, because a harsher procedure for evaders is proportionate to the wrong.
quiz.why: Equality applies to the procedural provisions of tax laws as well as to the charge. Subjecting some persons to a harsher procedure, when they could equally be dealt with under the normal procedure at the Government’s unguided choice, was held discriminatory. The class-based argument fails because the same persons fall within both procedures. Authority: Suraj Mall Mohta and Co. v. A.V. Visvanatha Sastri.

quiz.concept: Latitude for economic legislation
quiz.q: A scheme allows people to invest unaccounted money in special bonds, with immunity from inquiry into its source. Honest taxpayers argue that it rewards evaders and violates equality. How is a court likely to respond?
quiz.ok: Uphold it, since economic laws get greater latitude than laws affecting civil rights.
no: Strike it down, because a law that benefits wrongdoers can never satisfy equality.
Strike it down, because an amnesty for evaders has no rational link to any lawful object.
Refuse to hear the challenge, because economic laws are immune from review.
quiz.why: Courts give the legislature greater latitude in economic matters, which involve complex choices, than in laws affecting civil rights. A scheme granting immunity to persons who invested unaccounted money in special bearer bonds was upheld on that basis, its aim of drawing such money into the open being a legitimate object. Latitude is not immunity, though: economic and tax laws remain open to challenge under Part III. Authority: R.K. Garg v. Union of India.

quiz.concept: Tax and freedom of the press
quiz.q: A tax on newsprint is set so high that many newspapers must print far fewer copies or close down. The Government says newspapers, like any business, can be taxed. What is the correct position?
quiz.ok: Newspapers can be taxed, but a tax heavy enough to curtail circulation can violate press freedom.
no: Newspapers are immune from taxation altogether, because of the guarantee of freedom of the press.
The tax is valid, because press freedom does not extend to the business side of a newspaper.
The tax is valid, because a tax can be challenged only under the freedom of trade.
quiz.why: A tax is not normally an unreasonable restriction on trade, and becomes open to challenge only if it is confiscatory or prohibitive. Newspapers are not immune from taxation, but a tax heavy enough to curtail circulation can violate the freedom of speech and expression, of which press freedom is part. Authority: Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India; Article 19(1)(a) and (g).

quiz.concept: Retrospective tax versus retrospective offence
quiz.q: A Finance Act (a) imposes a tax on a class of receipts with effect from two years earlier, and (b) makes it a criminal offence, punishable with imprisonment, not to have paid that tax during those two years. Which part does the Constitution forbid from operating retrospectively?
quiz.ok: Part (b): criminal liability cannot be retrospective, though a tax law can be.
no: Part (a), because the Constitution forbids every tax law with retrospective effect.
Both parts, because neither a tax nor an offence can ever be made retrospective.
Neither part, because Parliament may give any law it passes retrospective effect.
quiz.why: The constitutional bar is on retrospective criminal laws: no one may be convicted for an act that was not an offence when it was done, or given a heavier penalty than the law then allowed. A tax law may be retrospective, though the length and effect of the retrospective period can be relevant when its reasonableness is tested. So part (b) cannot reach back, while part (a) is valid in principle. Authority: Article 20(1); Rai Ramkrishna v. State of Bihar.

quiz.concept: Privacy limits on tax data
quiz.q: A taxpayer argues that the compulsory linking of PAN with Aadhaar violates his fundamental right to privacy, so the requirement must fall. What is the best response?
quiz.ok: The argument fails: tax laws must respect privacy, and the linking has been upheld as doing so.
no: The argument succeeds, because any collection of personal data for tax purposes violates privacy.
The argument fails, because privacy is not recognised as a fundamental right in India.
The argument fails, because taxing laws are wholly outside the reach of fundamental rights.
quiz.why: Privacy is a fundamental right, and tax laws that collect personal information must satisfy its requirements. Linking PAN with Aadhaar has been upheld as meeting them, and the 2025 Act continues the requirement, levying a fee for default in intimating the Aadhaar number. Answers saying the argument fails because privacy is unrecognised, or because tax laws are outside fundamental rights, reach the right result for the wrong reason. Authority: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India; the Aadhaar judgment; section 430 of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Discretionary power and fair procedure
quiz.q: A tax law empowers a high authority to transfer an assessee’s case from one officer to another. The assessee says the power itself is arbitrary and void. What is the likely result?
quiz.ok: Valid, since it must be used reasonably, though an arbitrary transfer may still be challenged.
no: Void, because a discretionary power in a tax law necessarily violates the guarantee of equality.
Valid, and no individual transfer made under it can ever be questioned in a court of law.
Valid, but only if the assessee consents to each transfer made under it.
quiz.why: A power to transfer cases was upheld because it was given to a high authority and had to be exercised reasonably. Its validity does not shield its misuse: an arbitrary transfer in a particular case can still be challenged. The corresponding power is now in the 2025 Act. Authority: Pannalal Binjraj v. Union of India; section 243 of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Non-discriminatory taxes and free trade
quiz.q: A State, acting within its taxing power, levies a tax on goods carried by road at the same rate whether the goods come from within the State or from other States. A trader says this violates the freedom of trade throughout India. What is the result under the current approach?
quiz.ok: It stands, because a non-discriminatory tax does not offend the freedom of trade.
no: It falls unless the State proves the tax is compensatory, paying for trading facilities.
It falls, because a tax on the movement of goods directly restricts trade and commerce.
It stands only if the State shows the tax is regulatory rather than revenue-raising.
quiz.why: Earlier cases held that a tax directly restricting the movement of trade was hit by the freedom of trade, while excluding regulatory measures and compensatory taxes. A nine-judge bench later held that non-discriminatory taxes do not offend that freedom at all and rejected the compensatory-tax test; what remains barred is discrimination against goods from other States. Authority: Atiabari Tea Co. v. State of Assam; Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan; Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana; Articles 301 and 304(a).

quiz.concept: Horizontal devolution among States
quiz.q: A Finance Commission increases the weight given to forest and ecology in its formula, leaving the States’ overall share of the divisible pool unchanged. What does the change directly affect?
quiz.ok: Horizontal devolution: how the States’ share is divided among the individual States.
no: Vertical devolution: the share of the divisible pool that goes to the States together.
The rates of income tax that Parliament may levy during the award period.
The funds that NITI Aayog allocates to individual States for development projects.
quiz.why: The Finance Commission recommends both the distribution of the net proceeds of shareable taxes between the Union and the States (vertical devolution) and their allocation among the States (horizontal devolution). Changing the weight of a criterion such as forest and ecology, while the overall share stays fixed, redistributes among States only. NITI Aayog transfers no funds. Authority: Article 280(3); Fifteenth Finance Commission criteria.

quiz.concept: Finance Commission advice is not binding
quiz.q: The Union decides not to implement one of the Finance Commission’s recommendations on grants in aid. What does the Constitution require?
quiz.ok: Lay it before Parliament with a memorandum of the action taken; the advice is not binding.
no: Implement it anyway, because the Commission’s recommendations bind the Union Government.
Refer the disagreement to the Supreme Court, which decides such Union–State disputes finally.
Nothing, because the Commission’s recommendations are never placed before Parliament.
quiz.why: The Commission’s recommendations are advisory, though those on tax devolution have in practice been accepted. Accountability comes through Parliament: the President lays every recommendation before it with an explanatory memorandum of the action taken. Treating the advice as binding confuses that practice with a legal duty, and no reference to a court is provided for. Authority: Articles 280 and 281.

quiz.concept: Finance Commission and local bodies
quiz.q: Panchayats and municipalities in a State are short of resources. What can the Finance Commission do about it?
quiz.ok: Recommend measures to augment the State’s Consolidated Fund to support local bodies.
no: Transfer Union funds directly to each Panchayat and Municipality according to its needs.
Fix the rates of property tax that Panchayats and Municipalities may levy.
Approve the annual budgets of Panchayats and Municipalities before they are passed.
quiz.why: Since the Seventy-Third and Seventy-Fourth Amendments, the Finance Commission recommends measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of its Panchayats and Municipalities. It works through the State’s finances and only makes recommendations; it does not fund, tax or supervise local bodies directly. Authority: Article 280(3).

quiz.concept: Union territories fall outside the States’ share
quiz.q: A Finance Commission had given the States 42% of the divisible pool. After one State was reorganised into Union territories, the next Commission cut the States’ share to 41%. What explains the cut?
quiz.ok: Union territories are funded by the Union, not out of the share given to the States.
no: The divisible pool itself shrank, because the reorganised State’s taxes were abolished.
Union territories receive their share of Union taxes through the GST Council instead.
The cut penalised the States for failing to raise enough revenue of their own.
quiz.why: Devolution under a Finance Commission award goes to the States. When Jammu and Kashmir became Union territories, their needs fell on the Union, so the States’ collective share was cut from 42% to 41%, a vertical adjustment that leaves the Union a larger part of the pool. A change in the percentage says nothing about the size of the pool, and the GST Council does not distribute Union taxes. Authority: Fifteenth Finance Commission; Article 280(3).

quiz.concept: Finance Commission versus NITI Aayog
quiz.q: A State wants a bigger formula-based slice of the money the Union collects in taxes over the next five years. To which body’s recommendations should it look, and why?
quiz.ok: The Finance Commission, the constitutional body that recommends how Union taxes are shared.
no: NITI Aayog, because it replaced the Planning Commission and took over its role of funding States.
NITI Aayog, because its Governing Council includes the Chief Ministers of the States.
The GST Council, because it decides how Union taxes are divided among the States.
quiz.why: The Finance Commission is a constitutional body that recommends the sharing of taxes and grants for an award period, usually five years. NITI Aayog, set up by a Cabinet resolution, is neither constitutional nor statutory; it advises on policy and promotes cooperative federalism but, unlike the Planning Commission, does not allocate funds. The GST Council deals with GST, not with the sharing of all Union taxes. Authority: Article 280.

quiz.concept: No tax by inference or analogy
quiz.q: A charging provision taxes “the sale of motor cars”. The Revenue argues that motorcycles should also be taxed, because they serve the same purpose and the legislature must have meant to include them. How should the court respond?
quiz.ok: Reject it, because no tax can be imposed by inference or analogy from the words.
no: Accept it, because a taxing statute should be read to give effect to its spirit.
Accept it, because a doubt in a charging provision is resolved in favour of the Revenue.
Accept it, because words in a charging provision bear their widest possible meaning.
quiz.why: In a taxing Act one looks only at what is clearly said: there is no equity about a tax, and nothing is read in or implied. A person within the letter is taxed however great the hardship, and a person outside it is free however much he seems within its spirit. Any genuine doubt in a charge favours the assessee, not the Revenue. Authority: Partington v. Attorney General; Cape Brandy Syndicate v. IRC; A.V. Fernandez v. State of Kerala.

quiz.concept: Benefit of doubt needs genuine ambiguity
quiz.q: An assessee constructs an ingenious alternative reading of a charging provision whose meaning, on a fair reading, is clear. He claims the benefit of doubt. Will he succeed?
quiz.ok: No. Only a genuine ambiguity, with two reasonable constructions, gives the assessee the benefit.
no: Yes. Any arguable alternative reading of a charging provision must be adopted in his favour.
Yes. Charging provisions are construed in the assessee’s favour, however clear their words may be.
No. Doubts in charging provisions are resolved in favour of the Revenue, not the assessee.
quiz.why: If a charging provision is reasonably capable of two constructions, the one favouring the assessee is adopted. But the rule applies only to genuine ambiguity; it does not let an assessee manufacture doubt where the meaning is clear. Saying that doubts favour the Revenue reverses the rule: real doubt in a charge benefits the assessee, and it is ambiguity in an exemption that benefits the Revenue. Authority: CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd.

quiz.concept: Courts cannot complete a charge
quiz.q: A municipal Act imposes a tax on buildings but provides no workable method for determining the annual value on which it is charged. The municipality asks the court to supply a reasonable method. What should the court do?
quiz.ok: Decline, because the Act must clearly fix the measure, and courts cannot fill gaps in a charge.
no: Supply a reasonable method, because courts must keep taxing statutes workable for the Revenue.
Adopt the method used in a neighbouring municipality’s Act, applying it by analogy.
Allow a provisional levy now, until the legislature fills the gap at a later date.
quiz.why: The charging provision must clearly identify the subject, the person, the rate and the measure, and courts cannot fill gaps in it. Supplying a method, borrowing one by analogy or allowing a provisional levy would all amount to the court completing a tax the legislature has left incomplete. Authority: Mathuram Agrawal v. State of Madhya Pradesh; Govind Saran Ganga Saran (Unit I).

quiz.concept: Charge and computation form one code
quiz.q: An Act charges gains on the transfer of capital assets, computed as sale price minus cost of acquisition. It has no rule for an asset, such as self-generated goodwill, that has no ascertainable cost, and deems no cost for it. Which principle decides whether the gain is taxed?
quiz.ok: Charge and computation form one code, so if the computation cannot apply, the charge fails.
no: The charge prevails over the computation, so the officer must estimate a reasonable cost.
The gain is taxed as ordinary business income instead, since it cannot be a capital gain.
The court fills the gap by applying the computation rule for a similar asset.
quiz.why: The charging section and the computation provisions are an integrated code: if the computation provisions cannot be applied to a transaction, the charge fails, so gains on self-generated goodwill could not be taxed. Neither the officer nor the court can supply a cost, and the gain does not move to another head. Parliament later supplied a rule deeming the cost of such goodwill to be nil, so the gain became taxable by statute rather than by a court filling the gap. Authority: CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty.

quiz.concept: Ambiguity in exemptions favours the Revenue
quiz.q: An importer claims that an exemption notification covers his goods. The wording is genuinely ambiguous: one reading covers the goods, the other does not. How is the ambiguity resolved?
quiz.ok: In favour of the Revenue, as exemptions are read strictly and the claimant bears the burden.
no: In favour of the importer, because every ambiguity in a tax law benefits the taxpayer.
In favour of the importer, because exemptions are beneficial provisions that are read liberally.
By granting part of the exemption, so as to give some effect to each of the two readings.
quiz.why: Exemptions are construed strictly: the person claiming one must show he falls clearly within it, and ambiguity in an exemption benefits the Revenue. This is the reverse of the rule for charging provisions, where genuine ambiguity benefits the assessee; confusing the two rules is the commonest mistake here. Authority: Commissioner of Customs (Import), Mumbai v. Dilip Kumar and Co.

quiz.concept: Incentives read liberally once eligible
quiz.q: A company clearly qualifies for an incentive deduction meant to promote new industrial undertakings. The Revenue then reads the provision’s operative terms narrowly to cut down the benefit. Which approach is correct?
quiz.ok: Once eligibility is clear, the provision is construed liberally to advance its object.
no: The narrow reading prevails, because ambiguity in a tax concession is resolved in favour of the Revenue.
The narrow reading prevails, because incentives are exemptions read strictly at every stage.
The company must also show that the legislature specifically intended to benefit companies like it.
quiz.why: Whether a person falls within an exemption or incentive is decided strictly, but once he does, the provision is applied fairly, and an incentive provision meant to promote growth is construed liberally to advance its object. The Revenue’s approach wrongly carries the strictness of the eligibility stage into the application stage. Authority: Bajaj Tempo Ltd. v. CIT; Dilip Kumar and Co.

quiz.concept: Purposive reading to avoid absurdity
quiz.q: A provision aimed at understatement of sale prices would, read literally, tax honest sellers on market value they never received, even where the agreed price was genuine and fully disclosed. How should a court read it?
quiz.ok: Purposively, confining it to cases where the consideration was actually understated.
no: Literally, because there is no equity about a tax and hardship is irrelevant.
As void for uncertainty, because it fails to define what consideration means.
Literally, though honest sellers may later reclaim the tax on value they never received.
quiz.why: Strict construction is the starting point, but it does not require a court to give a provision a meaning that defeats its own purpose and produces absurd results. A literal reading of the old capital gains provision would have taxed honest sellers on notional consideration; the Court read it as applying only where consideration was understated, relying on its purpose and the Finance Minister’s speech. Authority: K.P. Varghese v. Income Tax Officer.

quiz.concept: New burdens are presumed prospective
quiz.q: An amendment imposes a new burden on assessees but says nothing about past years. The Revenue applies it to earlier years, calling it clarificatory, although it plainly changes the law. What is the correct view?
quiz.ok: Prospective, since a new burden applies to past years only if the law expressly or impliedly says so.
no: Retrospective, because a tax amendment automatically applies to the years that are still pending.
Retrospective, because the Revenue has described the amendment as merely clarificatory of the law.
Prospective, because Parliament can never make a tax law reach back to past years.
quiz.why: A provision imposing a new burden is presumed to be prospective unless it is made retrospective expressly or by necessary implication. A truly clarificatory or curative provision may operate retrospectively, but calling a change “clarificatory” does not make it one. Parliament can expressly make a tax retrospective, so the claim that tax laws can never reach back is wrong, even though it points to the right result here. Authority: CIT v. Vatika Township (P) Ltd.; Rai Ramkrishna v. State of Bihar.

quiz.concept: Circulars do not bind the assessee
quiz.q: A CBDT circular interprets a provision against assessees. An assessee argues that the circular misreads the Act. Is he bound to accept it?
quiz.ok: No. A circular binds the department, not the assessee or the courts, who apply the Act itself.
no: Yes. Circulars bind everyone, including assessees and the courts, until the Board withdraws them.
Yes, unless he first obtains a contrary circular from the Board in his favour.
No, but only because all circulars issued under the 1961 Act lapsed on its repeal.
quiz.why: A CBDT circular binds the income tax authorities, but it does not bind the assessee or the courts, and a circular contrary to the statute cannot prevail over it. The assessee may therefore contest the circular’s reading of the Act. Circulars issued under the 1961 Act did not lapse; they continue so far as they are consistent with the 2025 Act. Authority: UCO Bank v. CIT; Commissioner of Central Excise v. Ratan Melting and Wire Industries; section 536(2)(j) of the 2025 Act.

quiz.concept: Beneficial treaty provisions prevail
quiz.q: A notified double taxation agreement taxes a non-resident’s interest income at a lower rate than the 2025 Act does. Which rate applies?
quiz.ok: The treaty rate, since a notified treaty more favourable to the assessee can prevail.
no: The Act’s rate, because a treaty can never override a law that Parliament has made.
The higher of the two, because the Revenue may pick the rate that yields more tax.
The Act’s rate, unless the non-resident first pays tax on the interest in his own country.
quiz.why: The 2025 Act itself provides for double taxation agreements, and a notified treaty provision that is more beneficial to the assessee can prevail over the Act, so applying the treaty rate gives effect to Parliament’s scheme rather than defying it. Using treaty benefits is legitimate tax planning, since treaty shopping is not illegal in itself. Authority: section 159 of the 2025 Act; Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan.

quiz.concept: Old precedents under the new Act
quiz.q: One provision of the 2025 Act repeats the words of a 1961 Act provision substantially unchanged. Another restates an old rule in materially different words. How should decisions under the 1961 Act be used?
quiz.ok: They guide the unchanged provision, but the reworded one’s new words must be given effect.
no: They have no value now, because the 1961 Act has been repealed in full.
They bind for both provisions, because the 2025 Act merely restates the old law in new form.
They apply only to the reworded provision, because unchanged words need no fresh interpretation.
quiz.why: The 2025 Act is a consolidating and amending Act. Where its words are substantially the same as the old ones, decisions under the 1961 Act remain good guidance; where the words have changed, the change must be given effect rather than read away by old precedent.

quiz.concept: Pending proceedings survive repeal
quiz.q: An assessment for a year governed by the 1961 Act is pending when the 2025 Act comes into force. The assessee argues that, with the 1961 Act repealed, the proceeding lapses. Is he right?
quiz.ok: No. The savings provision keeps pending proceedings and accrued liabilities alive.
no: Yes. A repealed Act is treated as if it had never existed, so the proceeding ends.
Yes, unless the Revenue starts a fresh proceeding under the 2025 Act for that year.
No, because the 2025 Act applies retrospectively to the years governed by the 1961 Act.
quiz.why: The 2025 Act’s repeal and savings provision preserves the previous operation of the 1961 Act, accrued rights and liabilities, and pending proceedings, and it applies the general savings rule of the General Clauses Act to the repeal. Repeal therefore does not wipe out what was done or pending under the old law. Authority: section 536(2) and (4) of the 2025 Act; section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.

quiz.concept: Union property is immune from State taxes
quiz.q: A State introduces a new tax on buildings and applies it to an office building owned by the Union Government. Parliament has made no law allowing this. The State says its taxing entry on lands and buildings covers every building in the State. Is the levy valid?
quiz.ok: No. Union property is exempt from State taxes unless Parliament provides otherwise.
no: Yes. The State’s entry on lands and buildings reaches every building in its territory.
Yes, provided the State shares a fair part of the proceeds of the tax with the Union.
No, because a State may tax buildings only when they are used for trade or business.
quiz.why: The property of the Union is exempt from all taxes imposed by a State or by any authority within it, save so far as Parliament by law provides otherwise. A general taxing entry does not override that specific immunity, and sharing the proceeds cannot cure it. The trade-or-business idea belongs to the reverse rule, under which the Union may tax a trade or business carried on by a State. Authority: Articles 285 and 289.

quiz.concept: Aim of the 2025 Act
quiz.q: A classmate says the Income Tax Act, 2025 was enacted chiefly to overhaul India’s income tax policy. Which statement best describes the Act’s main aim?
quiz.ok: To simplify the law’s language and structure, consolidating it without fundamentally changing policy
no: To overhaul tax policy fundamentally, with new heads of income and wholly new classes of taxable persons
To codify every earlier judicial decision, so that case law under the 1961 Act ceases to matter
To transfer the power to tax agricultural income from the States to Parliament for uniformity
quiz.why: After six decades of amendments, provisos and Explanations, the 1961 Act had become hard to read. The 2025 Act, described in its long title as an Act to consolidate and amend the law, aims mainly at simpler language and structure, such as one tax year, exemptions in Schedules, and Tables and formulae, rather than new policy. It codifies only some positions, so decisions under the 1961 Act still guide where the words are substantially the same. Authority: the long title of the Income Tax Act, 2025.

quiz.concept: Transition: procedure for earlier years
quiz.q: The 2025 Act came into force on 1 April 2026. Income earned between 1 April 2025 and 31 March 2026 is taken up for assessment in 2027. Which Act’s procedure governs that assessment?
quiz.ok: The 1961 Act’s: proceedings for earlier tax years continue under it, even if started later
no: The 2025 Act’s: the 1961 Act had already been repealed before these proceedings began
The 2025 Act’s, because a new procedure always governs proceedings that start after it commences
Whichever Act the assessee elects, because the savings clause leaves the choice of procedure to him
quiz.why: The repeal is subject to a savings clause: proceedings for any tax year beginning before 1 April 2026, whether pending or started later, continue under the procedure of the 1961 Act. Income of 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 is the previous year 2025 to 2026 under the old Act. The repeal therefore does not move those years to the new procedure, and the assessee has no choice in the matter. Authority: section 536(2)(c) and (3).

quiz.concept: Transition: brought forward losses
quiz.q: A business has a loss under the 1961 Act that it could not fully set off before the 2025 Act came into force on 1 April 2026. What happens to the unabsorbed loss?
quiz.ok: It carries over, because the savings clause preserves accrued rights, including brought forward losses
no: It lapses, because the right to carry it forward existed only under the Act that has now been repealed
It carries over only after it is recomputed afresh under the heads of income of the 2025 Act
It can be set off only against income assessed under the 1961 Act, and never against later income
quiz.why: The savings clause preserves the previous operation of the 1961 Act and the rights and liabilities accrued under it, and it expressly carries brought forward losses over to the new Act. The tempting view that the right died with the repealed Act ignores this: a repeal subject to savings does not wipe out rights that had already accrued. Authority: section 536(2)(a), (b), (m) and (n).

quiz.concept: Retirement benefits: deduction, not exemption
quiz.q: Under the 2025 Act, relief for gratuity, commuted pension and leave encashment sits in the Table of deductions for salaries, not among the exemptions. What does this mean for the computation?
quiz.ok: The amounts are included in salary first, and the qualifying part is subtracted within that head
no: The amounts never enter the computation of total income at all, exactly as under the old 1961 Act
The amounts reduce the tax payable rather than the income, in the same way as a rebate
The amounts are deducted from gross total income, along with all the other Chapter VIII deductions
quiz.why: An exemption keeps income out of total income altogether, while a deduction is subtracted while computing income, here under the head Salaries through the Table in section 19. Moving retirement benefits from exemptions to deductions changes where the relief sits in the computation. A rebate reduces tax rather than income, and Chapter VIII deductions come off gross total income, not within a head. Authority: section 19.

quiz.concept: Inclusive definition of income
quiz.q: A receipt is not mentioned anywhere in the list in the statutory definition of “income”, but it has every feature of income in the ordinary sense. How is it treated?
quiz.ok: As income, because an inclusive definition adds to the ordinary meaning without cutting it down
no: As not income, because the items listed in the definition form a complete and exhaustive catalogue
As income only if a court has already treated that same kind of receipt as income in an earlier case
As not income unless the Rules separately notify it as a taxable kind of receipt
quiz.why: The definition says income “includes” the listed items, so it enlarges the natural meaning rather than restricting it. Anything that is income in the ordinary sense is income even if unlisted, and the listed items are income even if they would not otherwise be. On this reasoning a prize won in a motor rally was held to be income. Authority: section 2(49); CIT v. G.R. Karthikeyan.

quiz.concept: Tax paid by employer is employee’s income
quiz.q: An employer agrees to bear the income tax on an employee’s salary and pays it directly to the government. The employee never handles that money. Is the tax so paid the employee’s income?
quiz.ok: Yes, because paying his tax discharges his own liability, which benefits him just as cash would
no: No, because the employee never actually received the amount, either in his hands or in his account
No, because a payment made to the government can never be the income of any person
Yes, but only if the employer first deducts the amount of the tax from the employee’s gross salary
quiz.why: Income is not limited to cash in hand: money applied to discharge a person’s own obligation benefits him as surely as a payment to him. The Supreme Court held that tax paid by an employer on an employee’s salary is the employee’s income. That the money went straight to the government does not change whose liability was met. Authority: Emil Webber v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Receipts that are not income
quiz.q: Asha receives four sums in a tax year. Assume gifts of money are taxed only when their total in the year exceeds Rs. 50,000. Which sum is income?
quiz.ok: Rs. 40,000 won as a prize on a lottery ticket she bought
no: Rs. 5,00,000 borrowed from a bank, repayable over five years
Rs. 20,000 from a friend as a birthday gift, her only gift that year
Rs. 40,000 refunded by her employer for official travel she paid for
quiz.why: A loan is not a gain, because it carries an equal obligation to repay; a reimbursement only makes good money spent on official duties; and a single small gift falls below the stated threshold for the gift charge. Winnings from lotteries, by contrast, are expressly listed in the inclusive definition of income. Authority: section 2(49); section 92(2)(m).

quiz.concept: Loans versus unexplained credits
quiz.q: A trader’s books show a large cash credit entered as a loan from a friend, but he cannot identify the friend or explain where the money came from. Can the credit be taxed, given that loans are not income?
quiz.ok: Yes: calling a credit a loan does not protect it when its nature and source are not explained
no: No: a sum recorded in the books as a loan is a capital receipt, so it can never be taxed as income
Yes, but only as a gift, and only to the extent that his gifts for the year exceed the gift threshold
Yes, because every loan is income when it is received and is deducted later, when it is repaid
quiz.why: Borrowed money is not income, because it carries an obligation to repay. But the Act allows an unexplained credit in the books to be taxed, so calling an entry a loan does not protect it when its nature and source are not explained. The charge does not depend on treating the sum as a gift. Authority: section 102.

quiz.concept: Capital or revenue: the source test
quiz.q: Which question best helps decide whether compensation received by a business is a capital or a revenue receipt?
quiz.ok: Does it replace a lost source of income or only income from a source that continues?
no: Is the amount large when compared with the profits the assessee usually earns in a year?
Was the amount received as a single lump sum rather than in a series of instalments?
Has the payer treated the payment as a deductible business expense in its own accounts?
quiz.why: No single test decides the question, but the courts ask whether the receipt relates to the fixed capital, the profit making structure, or to circulating capital, and whether it compensates for the loss of a source of income or only for income lost from a source that continues. The size of the amount, the mode of payment and the payer’s treatment do not decide it. Authority: Kettlewell Bullen and Co. Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Agency compensation under the 2025 Act
quiz.q: A company holding several agencies receives compensation when one agency contract is terminated. Under the source test alone, the receipt might be capital. How does the 2025 Act treat it?
quiz.ok: As business income, because the Act now specifically taxes compensation for ending a business contract
no: As a capital receipt outside income, because the agency formed part of the company’s profit making structure
As income from other sources, because the compensation is not a receipt from the company’s trading in goods
As exempt income, because compensation for losing a source of income is listed in a Schedule
quiz.why: Capital receipts are outside income unless a provision taxes them. The source test would treat compensation for surrendering an agency that formed part of the business structure as capital, but the Act now taxes compensation connected with the termination or modification of a management, agency or business contract as business income. The old decision therefore matters today mainly for its test. Authority: section 26(2)(b); Kettlewell Bullen and Co. Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Subsidies and the purpose test
quiz.q: Earlier, a government subsidy was capital or revenue depending on its purpose. Why does that purpose test now play only a narrow role?
quiz.ok: The definition of income now covers most government subsidies and grants, with only limited exclusions
no: The Supreme Court has since held that every government subsidy, whatever its purpose, is a capital receipt
Subsidies of every kind are now listed as exempt income in the Schedules, so their purpose no longer matters
Subsidies are now taxed only when they are spent on the day to day running of a business
quiz.why: Under the purpose test, a subsidy to run a business was revenue, while one to repay loans taken for expansion was capital. The inclusive definition now treats any subsidy, grant, incentive, duty drawback, waiver or reimbursement from a government or authority as income, except a subsidy that reduces the actual cost of an asset and a Central Government corpus grant to a government trust or institution. Authority: section 2(49)(w); Sahney Steel and Press Works Ltd. v. CIT; CIT v. Ponni Sugars and Chemicals Ltd.

quiz.concept: Real income: commission given up
quiz.q: Before the year ends, a managing agent agrees with the company to accept a lower commission than its contract allows. On what amount is the agent taxable?
quiz.ok: Only the reduced commission, since tax falls on real income and the part given up never arose
no: The full commission, because giving up part of it is merely an application of its own income
The full commission, because a book entry for the full amount fixes the income for the year
Nothing at all, because the revised agreement makes the whole of the commission for the year uncertain
quiz.why: Income tax is levied on real, not hypothetical, income. Because the agent gave up part of the commission before the year ended, that part never became its income, so there was nothing to apply; only the reduced commission was taxable, whatever the books showed. Application of income, by contrast, presupposes that the income first became the assessee’s. Authority: CIT v. Shoorji Vallabhdas and Co.

quiz.concept: Limits of the real income theory
quiz.q: A moneylender on the mercantile system credits interest on doubtful loans to a suspense account. A power company bills enhanced charges that consumers dispute and never pay. Assuming no special timing rule applies, which statement best reconciles the tax treatment of the two?
quiz.ok: Accrued interest is taxed, with bad debt relief if the loan fails; disputed, unpaid charges were never real income
no: Both are taxable, because under the mercantile system whatever is billed or has accrued is always income
Neither is taxable, because the real income theory overrides accrual whenever recovery of the amount is uncertain
The interest is taxable only when it is actually received, while the enhanced charges are taxable as soon as billed
quiz.why: Real income theory prevents tax on income that never really results, such as enhanced charges that consumers disputed and never paid. It cannot, however, override the statutory scheme: interest that has accrued under the mercantile system is taxable though credited to a suspense account, the remedy being a bad debt deduction if the loan is later lost. Doubtful recovery alone does not undo accrual. Authority: State Bank of Travancore v. CIT; Godhra Electricity Co. Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Diversion by overriding title
quiz.q: A court decree makes maintenance for the assessee’s stepmother a charge on the estate that produces his income. Is the maintenance amount taxable in his hands?
quiz.ok: No, because the charge on the estate diverts that part of the income at its source
no: Yes, because he first receives the estate’s income and only then pays the maintenance out of it
Yes, because maintenance paid to a relative is a personal expense, which is never deductible
No, because every payment made under a court decree falls outside the payer’s income
quiz.why: Where an overriding legal obligation attaches to the source, the income it covers is diverted before it becomes the assessee’s, so it is not his income. The decisive feature was the charge on the estate, not the decree as such; a decree that is not charged on the income or property leaves only an application of income. Authority: Raja Bejoy Singh Dudhuria v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Application of income under a decree
quiz.q: A court decree obliges the assessee to pay maintenance to his wife and children, but the amount is not charged on his income or on any property. How is the maintenance treated?
quiz.ok: As an application of his income, because the income reaches him first and he then pays it away
no: As a diversion by overriding title, because the decree gives his wife and children a binding right to it
As outside his income, because a payment he is legally compelled to make cannot be his income
As partly diverted and partly applied, the children’s share being diverted at source and the wife’s applied
quiz.why: The test is whether the amount, in truth, never reached the assessee as his income. A personal obligation, even under a decree, that is not charged on the source leaves the income his, so paying it is an application of his own income. The decree alone does not create diversion; a charge on the source does. Authority: CIT v. Sitaldas Tirathdas.

quiz.concept: Assignment of a partner’s profit share
quiz.q: A partner executes a deed assigning part of his share in the firm’s profits to a trust for his relatives. Applying the diversion test, how is the assignment characterised?
quiz.ok: As an application, because the share first becomes his income and he then parts with a portion
no: As a diversion, because the deed gives the trust an enforceable legal title to the assigned share
As a diversion, because the trust, not the partner, receives the assigned portion straight from the firm
As a transfer of part of his interest in the firm, so that the assigned portion is the trust’s income
quiz.why: An assignment of part of a profit share operates only after the share has become the partner’s income, so the assigned part is an application of his income, not a diversion at source. An enforceable right in the trust, payment straight to it, or calling the deed a transfer of part of his interest does not change that. Whether the share is taxed in his hands today is a separate question, since the Schedules now exempt a partner’s share of firm profits; the case is authority for the diversion test. Authority: CIT v. Sunil J. Kinariwala.

quiz.concept: Revocable transfer of assets
quiz.q: A mother transfers her shares to a trust for her adult daughter but keeps a power to take the shares back whenever she wishes. The company pays the dividends to the trust. In whose hands are the dividends taxed?
quiz.ok: The mother’s, because income from a revocable transfer of assets is taxed in the transferor’s hands
no: The trust’s, because the shares themselves were transferred, so the dividends are diverted at source
The daughter’s, because she is the person for whose benefit the trust receives and holds the dividends
The mother’s, but only for a year in which she actually uses her power to take the shares back
quiz.why: The Act prevents diversion by arrangement. Here the shares themselves were transferred, unlike a mere transfer of income, but because the mother can take them back, the transfer is revocable and the income from them is taxed in her hands. What matters is that she holds the power, not whether she uses it. Authority: section 97.

quiz.concept: Income transferred without the asset
quiz.q: A father keeps ownership of his building but directs the tenant to pay the rent straight to his adult son. In whose hands is the rent taxable?
quiz.ok: The father’s, because income transferred without the asset producing it remains the transferor’s
no: The son’s, because the father’s direction diverts the rent at its source, before it ever reaches him
The son’s, because he is the person who actually receives and enjoys the rent each month
Nobody’s, because rent passed on to a relative is a gift, and gifts within a family are not income
quiz.why: The Act prevents diversion by mere arrangement: where income is transferred without transferring the asset that produces it, the income remains the transferor’s. The father still owns the building, so his direction is only a way of applying his own income, and the son’s receipt and enjoyment of the rent do not make it the son’s. Authority: section 96.

quiz.concept: Why mutual surpluses are not income
quiz.q: A club open only to its members collects subscriptions, spends them on members’ facilities, and can use or return any surplus only to members. Why is the surplus not taxed?
quiz.ok: Because a person cannot make a profit out of himself, and it is the members’ own money
no: Because clubs are among the persons listed as exempt from tax on their whole income
Because any surplus collected from members is treated as a capital receipt of the club
Because such a surplus is exempt, as long as the club spends all of it within the same tax year
quiz.why: Under the doctrine of mutuality, where the contributors and the participants are the same and the fund can only be spent on or returned to them, a surplus is not income at all. The club is not exempt as a person; it simply has no income from dealing with itself. Authority: Chelmsford Club v. CIT; New York Life Insurance Co. v. Styles.

quiz.concept: Mutuality broken: deposits with member banks
quiz.q: A club open only to its members deposits its surplus funds with banks that happen to be corporate members of the club, and earns interest. Does mutuality protect the interest?
quiz.ok: No, because the money left the closed circle of members and went into the banks’ commercial lending
no: Yes, because the banks are themselves members, so the interest comes from within the membership
Yes, because the interest earned will be spent only on the facilities that the club provides for members
No, because a club loses mutuality altogether once it holds any surplus funds at all
quiz.why: Mutuality needs complete identity between contributors and participants, action in furtherance of the association’s mandate, and no scope for profiteering. The deposits went out of the closed circle into the banks’ commercial lending, so the interest arose from dealings outside the membership. That the banks were members, or that the interest would be spent on members, does not restore that identity. Authority: Bangalore Club v. CIT.

quiz.concept: No mutuality when trading with outsiders
quiz.q: A club carries on the business of conducting horse races, admitting members and the public alike on payment. How should its surplus from these activities be treated?
quiz.ok: As taxable, because contributors and participants are not identical once it trades with the public
no: As taxable, because mutuality never applies to a club that ends its year with any surplus at all
As mutual, because it is registered as a club and applies its whole surplus for club purposes
As mutual, provided that members rather than the public contribute the larger part of its racing receipts
quiz.why: Mutuality requires complete identity between those who contribute and those who participate. A club that conducts races as a business for members and non members alike is trading with outsiders, not managing its members’ common fund, so it cannot claim mutuality. It is these dealings with the public that defeat mutuality, not the club label or the mere existence of a surplus. Authority: CIT v. Royal Western India Turf Club Ltd.; contrast Chelmsford Club v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Statutory limits on mutuality
quiz.q: Each of these bodies earns a surplus from dealings with its own members. Which surplus is taxable despite the doctrine of mutuality?
quiz.ok: A trade association’s fees from members for specific services it performs for them
no: A club’s surplus from subscriptions that it can only spend on or return to its members
A housing society’s surplus from members’ maintenance contributions, usable only for them
A dining club’s surplus from meals served only to members, refundable to them on dissolution
quiz.why: Mutuality is a general principle that Parliament can displace. The Act taxes the income of trade, professional and similar associations from specific services performed for members, and the definition of income includes profits of mutual insurance companies, cooperative insurance and banking by cooperative societies with their members. A fund that can only be spent on or returned to the members otherwise stays outside income. Authority: section 26(2)(d); section 2(49)(l) and (m).

quiz.concept: Accrual: the right to receive
quiz.q: Managing agents are entitled to a commission that is computed and payable only at the end of the company’s year. They transfer the agency midway through the year. Has any commission accrued to them?
quiz.ok: No, because they never acquired a right to receive it, so no debt became due to them
no: Yes, a proportionate share, because they had done the work for part of the year
Yes, the full commission, because it was earned under the terms of their agency agreement
No, because commission can accrue only at the moment it is actually paid to the agent
quiz.why: Income accrues when the assessee acquires a right to receive it, so that it becomes a debt due to him; doing part of the work is not enough if the right arises only later. Since the commission became payable only at the end of the year, nothing had accrued to the transferors before the transfer. Tying accrual to payment confuses it with receipt, which happens when the income reaches the assessee. Authority: E.D. Sassoon and Co. Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Accrual and receipt: no double charge
quiz.q: A lawyer on the mercantile system is taxed on fees that accrued to her in one tax year. She actually receives them in the following tax year. Are they taxed again on receipt?
quiz.ok: No: accrual and receipt are alternative points of charge, not two separate incomes
no: Yes: receipt is a separate event that attracts the charge independently of accrual
Yes, but she can claim a credit for the tax already paid on the earlier accrual
No, but only if she switches to the cash system before the fees are received
quiz.why: Accrual and receipt are alternative points at which the same income is caught, not two separate incomes. Once income has been taxed on accrual, the Act prevents it from being taxed again on receipt. The method she regularly follows governs timing; it does not create a second charge. Authority: section 5(4).

quiz.concept: A book credit is not receipt
quiz.q: A non resident acts abroad as selling agent for an Indian exporter, procuring orders from foreign buyers. The exporter credits the commission to the agent’s account in its books in India. Assuming the commission is not a fee for technical services, is it taxable in India?
quiz.ok: No: a book credit is not receipt, and commission for selling abroad does not accrue in India
no: Yes: crediting the commission in books kept in India amounts to receiving it in India
Yes, because a payer resident in India by itself gives the commission a source in India
No, because commission earned by a non resident can never be taxed in India in any circumstances
quiz.why: A non resident is taxed only on income received or deemed received in India, or accruing or deemed to accrue in India. A mere credit in the payer’s books is not receipt, and commission earned for services rendered abroad did not accrue in India; an Indian payer does not by itself give such commission an Indian source. Authority: CIT v. Toshoku Ltd.; section 5(2).

quiz.concept: Salary for services rendered in India
quiz.q: A non resident engineer employed by a foreign company works on a project in India for four months. His salary for that period is paid into his bank account abroad. Is it taxable in India?
quiz.ok: Yes, because salary for services rendered in India is deemed to accrue here, wherever it is paid
no: No, because the salary was neither received in India nor paid by an employer based in India
No, because a non resident is taxed only on income that he actually receives in India during the year
Yes, but only if his stay in India is long enough to make him resident in India for the year
quiz.why: The place where services are rendered, not the place of payment, fixes the source of salary: salary for services rendered in India, including related rest or leave periods, is deemed to accrue in India. A non resident is taxed on income deemed to accrue in India as well as on income received here, so residence is not needed. Authority: section 9(3); section 5(2).

quiz.concept: Government salary for service abroad
quiz.q: An Indian citizen posted at an Indian embassy abroad is paid by the Government of India for services rendered entirely outside India. Is the salary deemed to accrue in India?
quiz.ok: Yes: this is a specific exception to the rule that salary accrues where the services are rendered
no: No: services rendered outside India always give salary a source outside India, whoever pays
No, unless the salary is credited to a bank account that he maintains in India throughout that year
Yes, but only if he is also resident in India for the year in which it is paid
quiz.why: Salary ordinarily accrues where the services are rendered, but the Act makes a specific exception: salary paid by the Government to an Indian citizen for services outside India is deemed to accrue in India. Where it is credited and how long he stays in India do not matter for this rule. Authority: section 9(3).

quiz.concept: Interest paid by a resident: the exception
quiz.q: A resident Indian company borrows from a foreign bank and uses the whole loan in a business it carries on outside India. Is the interest it pays deemed to accrue in India?
quiz.ok: No, because interest payable by a resident is excluded where the loan is used for business abroad
no: Yes, because interest paid by any resident always has its source in India, whatever the loan is used for
Yes, because the lender is a non resident, so all of its interest income from India is taxable here
No, because interest is deemed to accrue in India only when the Government is the payer
quiz.why: Interest, royalty and fees for technical services are deemed to accrue in India if payable by the Government, by a resident (unless used for a business or for earning income outside India), or by a non resident where used for a business or income in India. Here the resident payer used the borrowing for a business outside India, so the exception applies. Authority: section 9(5) to (7).

quiz.concept: Technical fees without territorial nexus
quiz.q: A non resident consultant with no office or business connection in India provides technical services from abroad to an Indian company for its Indian factory. Can the fees be taxed in India?
quiz.ok: Yes: such fees payable by a resident are taxable whether or not the services were rendered here
no: No: services rendered wholly outside India lack a sufficient territorial nexus with India
No, because a non resident with no business connection in India can never be taxed on such fees
Yes, but only if the consultant visits India at least once to deliver part of the services
quiz.why: Fees for technical services payable by a resident are deemed to accrue in India unless used for a business or income outside India. After the Supreme Court required a sufficient territorial nexus for services rendered outside India, Parliament provided that such fees are taxable whether or not the non resident has a residence, place of business or business connection in India, and whether or not the services were rendered in India. Authority: section 9(11); Ishikawajima Harima Heavy Industries Ltd. v. Director of Income Tax.

quiz.concept: Business connection: the dependent agent
quiz.q: A foreign company deals with India in one of the following ways. In which situation does it most clearly have a business connection in India?
quiz.ok: An agent in India who works only for it habitually concludes contracts on its behalf
no: An independent broker in India places some of its goods in the ordinary course of his own business
Its operations in India are confined to buying goods here for export to its overseas customers
It made one isolated sale to an Indian buyer through correspondence sent from abroad
quiz.why: A business connection includes business through a dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts, keeps stock for delivery or secures orders for the non resident. Business through an independent agent and purchases of goods in India for export are excluded, and a stray or isolated transaction is not normally enough, because the relation must be real and intimate with an element of continuity. Authority: section 9(9); CIT v. R.D. Aggarwal and Co.

quiz.concept: Significant economic presence
quiz.q: A foreign online platform has no office, staff or agent in India, but interacts systematically with more users in India than the prescribed number. Can it have a business connection in India?
quiz.ok: Yes: a significant economic presence can be a business connection without any physical presence
no: No: a business connection always requires an office, a branch or a dependent agent in India
No, because its income from users in India is received outside India and so escapes Indian tax altogether
Yes, but only if its servers or other equipment are physically located somewhere in India
quiz.why: A business connection traditionally required some presence in India, such as a dependent agent. The Act now also treats a significant economic presence, meaning transactions above a prescribed amount or systematic interaction with a prescribed number of users in India, as a business connection, so physical presence is not required. Authority: section 9(9).

quiz.concept: Indirect transfer of Indian assets
quiz.q: Assume shares of a foreign company are deemed situated in India if its Indian assets exceed Rs. 10 crore and are at least 50% of its total assets, except for holders of 5% or less without management rights. A non resident sells abroad a 30% stake in a foreign company whose Indian assets, worth Rs. 500 crore, are 80% of its total assets. Is the gain taxable in India?
quiz.ok: Yes: shares deriving their value substantially from Indian assets are deemed situated in India
no: No: the shares are those of a foreign company, and the transfer took place wholly outside India
No, because a 30% stake gives the seller no control over the company’s assets in India
Yes, but only if the buyer of the shares is a person who is resident in India for that tax year
quiz.why: Income from the transfer of a capital asset situated in India is deemed to accrue in India, and shares of a foreign company are deemed situated in India where their value is derived substantially from Indian assets, as here. Neither the place of transfer nor the company’s foreign incorporation saves the gain, and a 30% holder is well outside the small shareholder exclusion, whether or not he controls the company. Authority: section 9(2) and (10).

quiz.concept: Deemed receipt
quiz.q: The taxable accretion to an employee’s recognised provident fund is taxed in the tax year, although he cannot yet withdraw it. Which idea explains this?
quiz.ok: The Act deems such amounts received in the year, so receipt in hand is not needed
no: Provident fund accretions belong to the employer, who is therefore taxed on the employee’s behalf
Every amount credited to any account kept in a person’s name is an actual receipt by him
Income is always taxed when earned, so receipt never matters under any head of income
quiz.why: The Act charges income received or deemed received, as well as income that accrues. For some items it fixes the time of receipt by deeming: the taxable accretion and transferred balance in a recognised provident fund, and the employer’s contribution to the pension scheme, are deemed received in the tax year. A mere book credit is not otherwise receipt. Authority: section 5; section 7(1).

quiz.concept: Timing of salary income
quiz.q: An employee keeps her personal accounts on the cash basis. Salary that fell due to her in one tax year is paid only in the next. In which year is it taxed?
quiz.ok: In the year it fell due, since salary is taxed on due or receipt, whichever is earlier
no: In the year it is paid, because she regularly follows the cash system for her accounts
In both years, once when it fell due and again when it was actually paid to her
In whichever of the two years she chooses, provided she discloses that choice in her return
quiz.why: The cash or mercantile system regularly employed by the assessee governs business income and income from other sources. Salary has its own timing rule, due or receipt, whichever is earlier, so the employee’s method of keeping accounts does not matter. Authority: section 15; section 276(1).

quiz.concept: Tax year replaces previous and assessment years
quiz.q: Which statement best captures how the 2025 Act changed the timing framework of the 1961 Act?
quiz.ok: Income of a tax year is charged for that same year, replacing the previous year and assessment year
no: Income is now taxed in the year after it is earned, at the rates fixed for that later year
The tax year now follows the calendar year, so it runs from 1 January to 31 December
Each source of income now has its own twelve month year, which the assessee chooses for that source
quiz.why: Under the 1961 Act, income of the previous year was assessed in the following assessment year at that year’s rates. The 2025 Act charges tax for each tax year, the financial year beginning on 1 April, at Finance Act rates on the total income of that same tax year. Only a new business or source starts part way through, and its first tax year still ends with that financial year. Authority: sections 3 and 4.

quiz.concept: First tax year of a new business
quiz.q: A consultancy business is set up on 1 December 2026. Applying the rule for a newly set up business, what is its first tax year?
quiz.ok: 1 December 2026 to 31 March 2027, running from setting up to the end of that financial year
no: 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, because the tax year is always the full financial year
1 December 2026 to 30 November 2027, because a tax year is always twelve months long
1 April 2027 to 31 March 2028, because the first full financial year after setting up is taken
quiz.why: The tax year is normally the financial year beginning on 1 April. For a business or profession newly set up, or a new source of income, it begins on the date of setting up and ends with that financial year, so a first tax year can be shorter than twelve months. Authority: section 3(2).

quiz.concept: Commencement and the first tax year
quiz.q: The 2025 Act received assent in August 2025 and came into force on 1 April 2026. A lawyer earns fees in February 2026 and more fees in May 2026. Which law governs each amount?
quiz.ok: The February fees fall under the 1961 Act, and the May fees under the 2025 Act
no: Both fall under the 2025 Act, which governs all income earned after it received assent
