Both fall under the 1961 Act, since the first tax year under the 2025 Act begins in April 2027
Both fall under the 1961 Act, because its savings clause keeps it alive for the whole of 2026
quiz.why: An Act operates from its commencement, not from assent. Income earned from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 is the previous year 2025 to 2026 under the 1961 Act, while the first tax year under the 2025 Act runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, so the May fees fall in it. The savings clause preserves the 1961 Act only for years beginning before 1 April 2026, not for the calendar year 2026. Authority: section 1(3); sections 3 and 536.

quiz.concept: Why the definition matters constitutionally
quiz.q: Why does the definition of “agricultural income” in the Income Tax Act matter beyond the Act itself?
quiz.ok: It marks where Parliament’s taxing power ends and the States’ power over agricultural income begins
no: It decides which agricultural income Parliament may tax, at concessional rates, under the Act itself
It lets each State decide for itself what is to count as agricultural income within its own territory
It applies only for income tax purposes and has no constitutional significance at all
quiz.why: Parliament taxes income other than agricultural income, the States tax agricultural income, and the Constitution adopts the income tax definition of agricultural income. The statutory definition therefore fixes where Union taxing power ends and State taxing power begins, which is why the Act excludes agricultural income from total income without conditions. Authority: Entry 82, List I; Entry 46, List II; Article 366(1); section 2(5).

quiz.concept: Basic operations test for agriculture
quiz.q: An estate owner earns income from a forest of spontaneous growth. He never planted it, but he regularly employs workers to weed, prune and protect the trees. Is the income agricultural income?
quiz.ok: No: such operations count only when they follow basic operations like tilling, sowing or planting
no: Yes, because weeding, pruning and protecting the trees all involve human skill and labour on the land
Yes, because all income derived from land situated in India counts as agricultural income
No: income from trees is never agricultural income, whatever operations are carried out
quiz.why: Agriculture requires basic operations on the land itself, such as tilling, sowing and planting, involving human skill and labour. Subsequent operations such as weeding and pruning qualify only when they follow those basic operations, so on a forest of spontaneous growth they do not make the income agricultural. The difficulty is the missing basic operations, not the fact that the produce comes from trees. Authority: CIT v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy.

quiz.concept: Derived from land: a direct relation
quiz.q: A shareholder receives a dividend from a company whose entire income comes from growing tea on its own estates. Is the dividend agricultural income in the shareholder’s hands?
quiz.ok: No: it derives from his shares, not directly and immediately from land
no: Yes, because the company’s own income comes entirely from agricultural land
Yes, to the extent that the company’s income from the tea is agricultural income
No: a dividend is always exempt in the shareholder’s hands, whatever its source
quiz.why: Income “derived from” land requires a direct and immediate relation with the land. The shareholder’s income comes from his shares in the company; the tea estates are only a remote source, so the dividend is not agricultural income even though the company’s profits came from land. It remains income like any other dividend; it simply does not take on the character of agricultural income. Authority: Mrs. Bacha F. Guzdar v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Composite income: growing and processing
quiz.q: A company grows tea on its own estates and manufactures it in its own factory before selling it. How is its income from the tea treated?
quiz.ok: Split by the Rules: a fixed portion is taxable business income and the rest agricultural income
no: Wholly agricultural income, because all of the tea sold was grown on the company’s own land
Wholly business income, because manufacturing goes beyond what a cultivator does to market produce
Split equally: half business income and half agricultural income, whatever the crop
quiz.why: Where the same person grows and processes a crop, the income is partly agricultural and partly business. The Rules split it by fixed percentages that differ from crop to crop; for tea grown and manufactured, a stated portion is business income and the rest is agricultural income. It is treated neither wholly as one nor wholly as the other. Authority: Rule 271 of the Income Tax Rules, 2026.

quiz.concept: Partial integration
quiz.q: Where partial integration applies, how can exempt agricultural income still raise the tax of an individual who also has non agricultural income above the exemption limit?
quiz.ok: It is counted only to set the rate on the non agricultural income, pushing it into higher slabs
no: Agricultural income above a set amount is taxed, but only at half the rates that apply to other income
Agricultural income above a set amount stops being exempt and becomes part of total income
The States collect their agricultural income tax through the same return and simply add it to his tax
quiz.why: Partial integration does not tax agricultural income; it uses it only to set the rate on the non agricultural income. Under the Finance Acts of the 1961 regime, tax was computed on the two incomes together, then on agricultural income plus the exemption limit, and the difference was payable. The method is laid down in each year’s Finance Act, so it must be confirmed for the current year. Authority: section 405(2); the Finance Act of the year.

quiz.concept: Farm building let for other purposes
quiz.q: A farmer lets out the farmhouse on his agricultural land to a city family as a weekend holiday home. Is the rent agricultural income?
quiz.ok: No: income from a farm building used for another purpose, such as letting for residence, is excluded
no: Yes, because the building stands on agricultural land that the farmer himself owns and cultivates
Yes, because any rent derived from land that is used for agricultural purposes is agricultural income
No: a farm building can never produce agricultural income, whatever it is used for
quiz.why: Income from a farm building qualifies only where the cultivator or receiver of rent needs it, because of his connection with the land, as a dwelling house, store house or out building. Income from such a building used for any other purpose, including letting for residence or business, is excluded. So farm buildings can produce agricultural income, but not when let out like this. Authority: section 2(5)(c).

quiz.concept: Applying the definition to four incomes
quiz.q: Assume agricultural land is a capital asset if it lies within a municipality with a population of at least 10,000. Which one of these is agricultural income?
quiz.ok: Income from selling saplings grown in a nursery
no: Income from selling timber from a forest of spontaneous growth
A dividend from a company that owns and runs tea estates
Gain on selling farmland inside the limits of a city of 20 lakh people
quiz.why: The definition expressly includes income derived from saplings or seedlings grown in a nursery. A forest of spontaneous growth involves no basic operations; a dividend has no direct and immediate relation with the land; and income from transferring urban agricultural land is excluded from agricultural income and taxed as a capital gain. Authority: section 2(5); CIT v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy; Mrs. Bacha F. Guzdar v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Rural agricultural land is not a capital asset
quiz.q: Assume agricultural land is a capital asset only if it lies within a municipality of at least 10,000 people or within 2, 6 or 8 kilometres of its limits, depending on population. A farmer sells agricultural land in a village 40 kilometres from any municipality, at a large profit. Is the gain taxable?
quiz.ok: No, because rural agricultural land is not a capital asset, so no taxable capital gain arises
no: Yes, as capital gains, because every transfer of land at a profit produces a taxable capital gain
Yes, as business income, because any large profit made on land is always treated as a trading profit
No, because gains made by a farmer are exempt, whatever kind of land or other asset he sells
quiz.why: Capital gains arise only on the transfer of a capital asset, and agricultural land outside the urban areas described in the Act is not a capital asset. Land 40 kilometres from any town is outside every urban zone, so its sale gives no taxable capital gain. Urban agricultural land, by contrast, is a capital asset, and income from its transfer is not agricultural income. Authority: section 2(22)(iii); section 2(5).

quiz.concept: Land must be situated in India
quiz.q: A resident and ordinarily resident individual receives rent from agricultural land he owns in Nepal, where his tenants grow rice. Is the rent agricultural income excluded from his total income?
quiz.ok: No: agricultural income needs land situated in India, so this rent is taxable foreign income
no: Yes, because it is rent derived from land that is used for agricultural purposes
Yes, but only on condition that he does not bring any of the rent into India during the year
No: rent can never be agricultural income, since only income from growing crops can be
quiz.why: The definition covers rent or revenue derived from land situated in India and used for agricultural purposes. Rent from land abroad falls outside it, and a resident and ordinarily resident individual is taxed on income accruing outside India as well as in India. Authority: section 2(5)(a); section 5.

quiz.concept: One charge, collected during the year
quiz.q: Tax is deducted at source from an employee’s salary every month, and she also pays advance tax. How do these payments relate to the charge of income tax?
quiz.ok: They simply collect the one charge on her total income for the tax year
no: Each monthly deduction is a separate charge of tax on that month’s salary alone
They are an additional tax payable on top of the income tax charged for the year
They finally settle her liability, so her total income for the year need never be computed
quiz.why: Income tax is charged for each tax year, at the rates enacted by the Finance Act, on the total income of that tax year of every person. Deduction or collection at source and advance tax are the machinery for collecting that one charge during the year, not separate taxes. Authority: section 4(1), (2) and (5).

quiz.concept: Rebate only for resident individuals
quiz.q: Assume new regime slabs of nil up to Rs. 4,00,000, 5% from Rs. 4,00,001 to Rs. 8,00,000 and 10% from Rs. 8,00,001 to Rs. 12,00,000, and a rebate of the full tax up to Rs. 60,000 for a resident individual with total income up to Rs. 12,00,000. A non resident individual has total income of Rs. 10,00,000. What is the tax before cess?
quiz.ok: Rs. 40,000, because only a resident individual gets the rebate
no: Nil, because the full tax falls within the Rs. 60,000 rebate limit
Rs. 20,000, because only the income above Rs. 8,00,000 is taxed
Rs. 1,00,000, because 10% applies to the whole of the income
quiz.why: Tax is 5% of Rs. 4,00,000 (Rs. 20,000) plus 10% of Rs. 2,00,000 (Rs. 20,000), or Rs. 40,000, because each rate applies only to its own band. The rebate that would wipe this out is given only to a resident individual, so the non resident pays it in full. Authority: section 156; section 202(1).

quiz.concept: Individual residence: the two tests
quiz.q: Assume an individual is resident if in India for 182 days or more in the tax year, or for 60 days or more in the year and 365 days or more in the four preceding years. A foreign national spends 100 days in India this year and 400 days in the four preceding years. Is he resident in India for the year?
quiz.ok: Yes, because 100 days this year with 400 earlier days satisfies the second test
no: No, because he was in India for fewer than 182 days during the tax year itself
No, because only Indian citizens are allowed to rely on the 60 day condition
Yes, but only if he also spent 182 days in India in one of the four earlier years
quiz.why: An individual is resident if either test is met: 182 days in the year, or 60 days in the year plus 365 days in the four preceding years. Nationality does not matter for the second test, which is displaced only for certain Indian citizens and persons of Indian origin, and no earlier year needs 182 days. Whether he is also ordinarily resident is a separate question. Authority: section 6(2).

quiz.concept: Citizen leaving India for employment
quiz.q: Assume the general tests are 182 days in the year, or 60 days in the year plus 365 days in the four preceding years. An Indian citizen leaves India during the year for a job abroad, having spent 150 days in India that year and 1,200 days in the four preceding years. What is his status?
quiz.ok: Non resident: the 60 day test is unavailable to a citizen leaving India for employment abroad
no: Resident, because he satisfies both the 60 day condition and the 365 day condition for the year
Resident but not ordinarily resident, because he left India part way through the tax year
Non resident: no individual can be resident in the year in which he leaves India
quiz.why: For an Indian citizen who leaves India in the year for employment abroad, or as a crew member of an Indian ship, the 60 day condition does not apply, so he is resident only if he is in India for 182 days or more. With 150 days he is non resident, however long his earlier stays were; had he stayed 182 days, he would have been resident even in the year he left. Authority: section 6(2) and (3).

quiz.concept: Visiting citizens and the 120 day rule
quiz.q: Assume the general tests are 182 days, or 60 days plus 365 days in the four preceding years, and that a visiting citizen with income other than from foreign sources above Rs. 15,00,000 faces 120 days in place of 60. Two Indian citizens working abroad each visit India for 150 days, with 400 days in the four preceding years. Such income is Rs. 10,00,000 for A and Rs. 20,00,000 for B. What is their status?
quiz.ok: A is non resident; B is resident but not ordinarily resident
no: Both are resident and ordinarily resident, as both meet 60 days plus 365 days
A is non resident; B is resident and ordinarily resident
Both are non resident, as neither stayed in India for 182 days
quiz.why: For a visiting citizen the 60 day condition does not apply, so A, below the threshold, is resident only at 182 days and is therefore non resident. For B, above the threshold, the condition applies with 120 days, so 150 days plus 400 earlier days makes him resident; because his stay was 120 days or more but less than 182, he is not ordinarily resident. Authority: section 6(4), (5) and (13).

quiz.concept: Deemed residence of citizens taxed nowhere
quiz.q: Assume a Rs. 15,00,000 threshold for income other than from foreign sources. An Indian citizen living abroad spends 20 days in India, is not liable to tax in any country by reason of domicile or residence, and has such income of Rs. 25,00,000. What is his status?
quiz.ok: Deemed resident but not ordinarily resident, as a citizen taxed in no other country
no: Non resident, as he was in India for fewer than 60 days during the tax year
Resident and ordinarily resident, as he is not liable to tax in any other country
Non resident, as a citizen living abroad who visited India only briefly
quiz.why: An Indian citizen who is not liable to tax in any other country because of domicile or residence, and whose income other than from foreign sources exceeds the threshold, is deemed resident whatever his days of stay. A deemed resident citizen is, however, not ordinarily resident, so his foreign income is taxed only if derived from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India. Authority: section 6(7), (8) and (13).

quiz.concept: Scope of income: not ordinarily resident
quiz.q: Assume a resident is not ordinarily resident if he was non resident in nine of the ten preceding years. Returning after twelve years abroad, Vikram becomes resident this year. He earns salary in India and rent from a London flat, received in London. What is taxable in India?
quiz.ok: Only the salary: as a not ordinarily resident, he is not taxed on foreign rent received abroad
no: Both incomes, because every person who is resident is taxed on his income from all over the world
Both incomes, because being resident for one source of income makes him resident for every source
Neither income: a returning Indian is treated as non resident in his first year back
quiz.why: A resident who was non resident in nine of the ten preceding years is not ordinarily resident. He is taxed on income received or accruing in India, but on foreign income only if it is derived from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India. Being resident for all sources fixes his status, not the scope of the charge. Authority: section 6(13); section 5(1)(c).

quiz.concept: Scope of income: non resident
quiz.q: A non resident has (i) salary for services rendered in India, paid abroad; (ii) interest on a deposit with a Singapore bank, credited in Singapore; and (iii) fees for advice given abroad, paid by a foreign client directly into his bank account in India. Which are taxable in India?
quiz.ok: The salary and the fees, but not the Singapore interest
no: The salary only, not the fees or the Singapore interest
The fees only, not the salary or the Singapore interest
All three: the salary, the fees and the Singapore interest
quiz.why: A non resident is taxed only on income received or deemed received in India, and income accruing or deemed to accrue in India. Salary for services rendered in India is deemed to accrue in India wherever it is paid, and fees first received in India are caught on receipt even though the work was done abroad. Interest that accrues and is received abroad is outside the charge. Authority: section 5(2); section 9(3).

quiz.concept: Partial control in India: family resident
quiz.q: A Hindu undivided family’s karta lives abroad and takes most decisions there, but some of the family’s key policy decisions are in fact taken by an adult coparcener in India. Is the family resident in India?
quiz.ok: Yes: its control and management is not wholly outside India
no: No, because the karta, who manages the family’s affairs, lives and decides abroad
No: most of its control and management is exercised abroad
Yes, but only for the income of the business that is managed from India
quiz.why: A Hindu undivided family, firm or association of persons is resident unless the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly outside India. Because real control is partly exercised in India, the family is resident, even though most decisions are taken abroad. Residence is a status for all sources, so it cannot be resident for one business only. Authority: section 6(9) and (12).

quiz.concept: De facto, not legal, control
quiz.q: A firm’s deed gives a partner living in India full power to manage its affairs, but he never uses it; every decision is in fact taken by the other partners abroad. Is the firm resident in India?
quiz.ok: No: control and management means actual control, and all of it is exercised outside India
no: Yes, because a partner living in India holds the legal right to control and manage the firm
Yes, because a firm is resident in India unless every one of its partners lives outside India
No: a firm is resident in India only if most of its partners live in India
quiz.why: Control and management means de facto control and management, the controlling power as actually exercised, not merely the legal right to control or manage. Since every decision is in fact taken abroad, control and management is wholly outside India and the firm is non resident. Where the partners live does not decide it. Authority: CIT v. Nandlal Gandalal; V.V.R.N.M. Subbayya Chettiar v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Company residence: place of effective management
quiz.q: A company incorporated abroad holds its formal board meetings overseas, but its key management and commercial decisions are in substance made by executives working in Mumbai. Is it resident in India?
quiz.ok: Yes: its place of effective management, where decisions are in substance made, is in India
no: No: it is incorporated abroad, and its board of directors formally meets outside India
No, because only a company that is formed and registered in India can ever be resident in India
Yes, but only if most of its shareholders are also persons resident in India
quiz.why: A company is resident if it is an Indian company or if its place of effective management is in India, meaning the place where key management and commercial decisions for the business as a whole are in substance made. Substance prevails over form, so formal board meetings abroad do not decide the question. The test draws on the English central management and control test. Authority: section 6(10); De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd. v. Howe.

quiz.concept: Co owners are not an association
quiz.q: Two sisters inherit a building in definite equal shares and receive its rent jointly, without carrying on any joint venture. How are they assessed on the rent?
quiz.ok: As individuals, each on her own share, since joint receipt alone does not create an association
no: As an association of persons, because they receive the rent jointly from the same building every month
As a firm, because two people who share the income of a common property are partners
As a Hindu undivided family, because the building came to both of them by inheritance
quiz.why: Co owners of a building with definite shares are not assessed as an association of persons; each is assessed on her own share. An association needs persons who join in a common purpose or common action, and merely receiving income jointly from a common property is not enough. Authority: section 24(1); CIT v. Indira Balkrishna.

quiz.concept: Association of persons or body of individuals
quiz.q: A company and two individuals pool resources to run a joint venture for profit, without forming a firm or a company. Which category of person fits best?
quiz.ok: An association of persons, since a body of individuals can consist of individuals only
no: A body of individuals, since most of the members of the venture are individuals
An artificial juridical person, since the venture is a residual body with no natural personality
No separate person at all; each member is simply taxed on its own share of the profit
quiz.why: An association of persons arises when two or more persons, who may include companies, join in a common purpose or common action, as these three have by running the venture together. A body of individuals consists of individuals only, so the company’s participation rules it out. An association of persons is itself a person under the Act, separate from its members. Authority: section 2(77); CIT v. Indira Balkrishna.

quiz.concept: Family with a sole male coparcener
quiz.q: After the other coparceners die, a sole surviving male coparcener holds the ancestral property while living with his mother and wife. Can its income be assessed as that of a Hindu undivided family?
quiz.ok: Yes: it remains joint family property, and the family is a person separate from its members
no: No: a Hindu undivided family needs at least two male coparceners in order to exist
No, because the property becomes his own separate property once he is the sole surviving coparcener
Yes, but only if the women of the family are first made coparceners by a deed
quiz.why: A Hindu undivided family carries its Hindu law meaning and is a person separate from its members. Joint family property remains such even when held for the time being by a sole male coparcener with female members, so the family can still be assessed as such. Authority: Gowli Buddanna v. CIT; N.V. Narendranath v. Commissioner of Wealth Tax.

quiz.concept: Separate property thrown into the family
quiz.q: An individual throws his self acquired house into the common stock of his Hindu undivided family without receiving any consideration. In whose hands is the rent from the house taxed?
quiz.ok: The individual’s, because the Act taxes income from such converted property in his hands
no: The family’s, because the house has now become joint family property held by the family as a whole
All the members’, shared equally, because each member now has an interest in the converted house
Nobody’s, because a transfer to one’s own family is not treated as a transfer for any tax purpose
quiz.why: A Hindu undivided family is a person separate from its members, so converting separate property into family property could shift income to another taxpayer. The Act counters this by taxing income from separate property converted into family property without adequate consideration in the individual’s hands. Authority: section 99(3).

quiz.concept: Person versus assessee
quiz.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between a “person” and an “assessee”?
quiz.ok: Every assessee is a person, but a person is an assessee only through liability, proceedings or deeming
no: Every person automatically becomes an assessee from the moment he earns any income at all
An assessee is simply any person who has filed a return of income for some tax year
Only individuals can be assessees, while companies and other persons are merely taxable entities under the Act
quiz.why: An assessee is a person by whom tax or any other sum is payable, and includes every person in respect of whom proceedings are taken to assess his own or another person’s income, loss or refund, deemed assessees and assessees in default. So the category turns on liability, proceedings or deeming, not merely on being a person or earning income. Authority: section 2(11).

quiz.concept: Assessee in default
quiz.q: An employer fails to deduct tax at source from his employees’ salaries. The salaries are the employees’ income, not his. How does the Act treat the employer?
quiz.ok: As an assessee in default, since the Act deems such a payer an assessee
no: As a person with no liability at all, since the salaries are the income of the employees alone
As a representative assessee who is taxed on the whole of each employee’s salary income
As an assessee only if he also has taxable income of his own for that same tax year
quiz.why: The definition of assessee is wider than persons taxed on their own income: it includes every person deemed to be an assessee in default. A payer who fails to deduct tax at source or to pay it over is so deemed, so the employer is an assessee even though the salaries are not his income. He is not a representative assessee taxed on the employees’ income. Authority: section 2(11); section 398(2).

quiz.concept: Exemption, deduction and rebate
quiz.q: Which pairing correctly matches each form of relief with what it reduces?
quiz.ok: Exemption: keeps income out of total income; deduction: reduces income; rebate: reduces the tax itself
no: Exemption: reduces the tax itself; deduction: keeps income out; rebate: reduces gross total income
Exemption: reduces income under a head; deduction: reduces the tax; rebate: keeps income out
Exemption, deduction and rebate all reduce gross total income, only at different stages of the computation
quiz.why: An exemption keeps the income out of total income altogether. A deduction is subtracted while computing income, either under a head or from gross total income under Chapter VIII. A rebate or relief, such as the rebate for incomes up to a stated limit or relief for arrears of salary, reduces the tax computed on total income. Authority: sections 11, 122, 156 and 157.

quiz.concept: Chapter VIII deductions capped at gross total income
quiz.q: An individual’s gross total income is Rs. 3,00,000, and her eligible Chapter VIII deductions add up to Rs. 3,50,000. What is the result?
quiz.ok: The deductions are limited to Rs. 3,00,000, so total income is nil and no loss arises
no: Total income becomes a loss of Rs. 50,000, which she can carry forward to later years
All of the deductions are disallowed because together they exceed gross total income
The excess of Rs. 50,000 is refunded to her as a credit against tax already paid
quiz.why: Chapter VIII deductions are allowed from gross total income, which is total income before these deductions, and cannot exceed it. They can bring total income down to nil, but they cannot create a loss to carry forward or a refund. Authority: section 122(1), (2) and (10).

quiz.concept: Conditional exemptions are construed strictly
quiz.q: A taxpayer meets most of the conditions attached to an exemption in a Schedule but fails one of its substantive eligibility conditions. He argues that his case is within the spirit of the exemption. How is the claim decided?
quiz.ok: It fails, because exemptions are construed strictly and unmet conditions leave the income taxed
no: He gets the exemption in proportion to the number of the conditions that he has actually satisfied
He gets the full exemption, because any ambiguity in a taxing statute favours the taxpayer
He gets the full exemption, because exemptions are construed liberally to advance their object
quiz.why: Incomes in the Schedules are excluded only subject to their conditions; if the conditions are not met, the income is taxed. Whether a person falls within an exemption is decided strictly, with the burden on him and any ambiguity benefiting the Revenue; liberal construction is for incentive provisions once a person is within them, not for the question of eligibility. Authority: section 11(1) and (2); Unit II, Part 5.4.

quiz.concept: Disallowance without exempt income
quiz.q: A company incurs expenditure in connection with investments whose income, when earned, is exempt. This year the investments yield nothing, and it argues that no disallowance can arise. Is it right?
quiz.ok: No, because expenditure relating to exempt income is disallowed even in a year when none is earned
no: Yes, because the disallowance applies only in a year in which exempt income is actually earned
Yes, because expenditure on investments is always allowed in full against the company’s business income
No, but only if the investments go on to yield exempt income in some later year
quiz.why: No deduction is allowed for expenditure incurred in relation to income that does not form part of total income, and the Act now states expressly that this applies even if no exempt income is earned in the year. If the Assessing Officer is not satisfied with the assessee’s own figure, he determines the amount by the prescribed method. Authority: section 14(1) to (3).

quiz.concept: Dominant purpose does not avoid disallowance
quiz.q: An assessee holds shares as stock in trade, mainly to trade in them, but the shares also yield some income that is exempt. It argues that its dominant trading purpose rules out any disallowance. What is the correct view?
quiz.ok: Expenditure is disallowed to the extent it relates to the exempt income, whatever the dominant purpose
no: Nothing is disallowed, because the dominant purpose of holding the shares is to trade in them for profit
All expenditure on the shares is disallowed, because the shares yield some exempt income
Nothing is disallowed, because shares held as stock in trade cannot yield exempt income
quiz.why: The disallowance applies to expenditure incurred in relation to exempt income. The Supreme Court held that the dominant purpose of holding shares does not avoid it, even for shares held as stock in trade, but only expenditure relating to the exempt income is disallowed, not all expenditure on the shares. Authority: section 14; Maxopp Investment Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Exempt incomes versus exempt persons
quiz.q: How does relief for a person listed in Schedule VII differ from relief for an item of income listed in Schedules II to VI?
quiz.ok: The person is not chargeable on its total income at all, while a listed income is excluded only as that item
no: The listed person gets a deduction from its gross total income, while a listed income attracts a rebate of tax
There is no real difference, since both simply exclude particular items of income for anyone who receives them
The listed person is taxed at a concessional rate, while a listed item of income is taxed at a nil rate
quiz.why: Section 11 works in two ways. Incomes in Schedules II to VI are excluded from total income item by item, subject to their conditions, while persons in Schedule VII are not chargeable on their total income at all while they meet the conditions. In either case, if the conditions are not met, the relief is lost. Authority: section 11(1) to (4).

quiz.concept: New regime withdraws most reliefs
quiz.q: A salaried individual is taxed under the new regime because she has not opted out. She claims house rent allowance exemption, leave travel concession and interest on her self occupied house. What is the position?
quiz.ok: None is available, because the new regime withdraws most exemptions and deductions, including these
no: All are available, because the new regime changes only the slab rates and leaves every relief untouched
Only the house rent allowance, because it is an exemption rather than a deduction
Only the interest on her house, because it is a deduction under a head of income
quiz.why: The new regime, which applies unless the person opts out, applies its own slab rates but withdraws most exemptions and deductions, among them house rent allowance, leave travel concession, tax on employment, interest on a self occupied house and most Chapter VIII deductions. Whether a relief is an exemption or a deduction does not save it. Authority: section 202(1) and (2).

quiz.concept: Rebate reduces tax, not total income
quiz.q: Priya, a resident individual under the new regime, has total income of Rs. 11,00,000, and the tax computed on it at the slab rates is Rs. 50,000. Assume a rebate of the full tax up to Rs. 60,000 for a resident individual with total income up to Rs. 12,00,000. Which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: Her total income stays Rs. 11,00,000, and the rebate cancels the Rs. 50,000 of tax computed on it
no: Her income is exempt up to the rebate limit, so her total income is nil and no tax is computed
The Rs. 60,000 rebate is deducted from her income, so tax is computed on Rs. 10,40,000
She must first pay the Rs. 50,000 of tax in full, and the rebate is then refunded to her
quiz.why: A rebate is a reduction of the tax itself: tax is computed on total income at the slab rates, and the rebate then cancels it up to the limit. Nothing is exempt and nothing is deducted in computing income, so her total income remains Rs. 11,00,000, and there is no tax to pay first and reclaim. Authority: section 156; section 202(1).

quiz.concept: Charge on every person; residence fixes scope
quiz.q: A non resident earns rent from a flat he owns in Mumbai. He argues that the charging section applies only to residents, so a non resident cannot be charged to income tax at all. Is he right?
quiz.ok: No: tax is charged on the total income of every person, and residence only decides what it includes
no: Yes: a non resident is outside the charge, and pays tax in India only where a tax treaty allows it
No, but he can be charged only on income that he actually brings into India during the tax year
Yes, unless he chooses to be treated as a resident by filing a return of income in India that year
quiz.why: Section 4 charges income tax on the total income of every person for the tax year, resident or not. Residence matters at the next step, because it fixes the scope of total income: a non resident’s total income includes income accruing in India, such as rent from property in India, whether or not it is brought into India. Authority: section 4(1); section 5(2).

quiz.concept: Assessee through refund proceedings
quiz.q: Tax was deducted at source from a student’s fees for freelance work, but her income is so low that no tax is payable by her. She files a return claiming a refund, and the Assessing Officer takes up the claim. Is she an assessee?
quiz.ok: Yes: the proceedings taken on her own refund claim are enough to make her an assessee
no: No: only a person by whom some tax or other sum is payable under the Act can be an assessee
No: she becomes an assessee only if the claim is rejected and a demand is raised against her
Yes, but only from the date on which the refund is actually paid to her by the Department
quiz.why: The definition is not limited to persons by whom tax is payable. It includes every person in respect of whom proceedings have been taken for assessing his own income, loss or refund, so the proceedings on her refund claim make her an assessee though she owes nothing. Authority: section 2(11).

quiz.concept: Legal representative as an assessee
quiz.q: A trader dies in October. The Department takes proceedings against his son, as his legal representative, to assess the father’s income for the tax year up to his death. Is the son an assessee for this purpose?
quiz.ok: Yes: proceedings taken against him for another person’s income make him an assessee
no: No: an assessee must be the person whose own income is assessed in the proceedings
No: the father’s liability ended with his death, so no one can now be assessed on it
Yes, but only after he has first been held to be an assessee in default for the tax
quiz.why: An assessee includes every person in respect of whom proceedings have been taken to assess the income of another person, and every person deemed to be an assessee. Death does not end the liability: the deceased’s income is assessed in the hands of his legal representative, who is treated as an assessee for that purpose. Authority: section 2(11); section 302.

quiz.concept: Heads of income are mutually exclusive
quiz.q: A bank holds government securities as part of its banking business. At the time, the Act had a separate head for interest on securities, but the bank wanted the interest computed as business income. What principle decides the head?
quiz.ok: Income covered by a specific head must be computed under that head, even if it arises in the course of business
no: Income earned in the course of business is always business income, because the business head is the widest of all the heads
The assessee may choose between overlapping heads, because each head merely offers a method of computation
The head follows the way the bank records the interest in its own books of account
quiz.why: The heads of income are mutually exclusive: each deals with a particular source and has its own computation rules. Income that a specific head covers must be computed under it, so the bank could not pull the interest into the business head merely because the securities were held in its business. Authority: section 13; United Commercial Bank Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Residuary head: income from other sources
quiz.q: An item of income is not excluded from total income, but it does not fit within salaries, house property, business or profession, or capital gains. How is it treated?
quiz.ok: It is income from other sources, the residuary head for taxable income not chargeable under any other head
no: It escapes tax altogether, because income must fall within one of the specific heads before any charge can arise
It is taxed as business income, because that head is wide enough to absorb any receipt that no other head covers
It is taxed under whichever specific head the Assessing Officer considers closest to its nature
quiz.why: Income from other sources is the residuary head: it covers income of every kind, not excluded from total income, that is not chargeable under the other four heads. So nothing taxable escapes merely because it lacks a specific head, and business income is a specific head with its own conditions, not a catch all. Authority: section 92(1).

quiz.concept: Rent from buildings: property head prevails
quiz.q: A company whose business is buying, developing and selling land builds shops and stalls on part of its land and lets them out. It argues that the rent is business income because dealing in land is its trade. Under which head is the rent taxed?
quiz.ok: House property, because the rent comes from buildings it owns, whatever its trade in land
no: Business income, because the company’s objects include dealing in land and the shops and stalls are part of its trading activity
Capital gains, because the shops are built on land that the company holds for eventual sale
Income from other sources, because the company let shops and stalls rather than residential houses
quiz.why: Each head deals with a particular source. Rent from shops and stalls built by a land dealing company was held taxable under the property head: the source is the ownership and letting of buildings, and the company’s trade in land does not change that. Contrast the later cases in Unit V, where letting itself was the company’s main object and whole business. Authority: East India Housing and Land Development Trust Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Stage for Chapter VIII deductions
quiz.q: In computing total income, at which stage are the Chapter VIII deductions subtracted?
quiz.ok: From gross total income, after income under each head is computed and losses are set off
no: Before income under the heads is computed, by subtraction from the assessee’s gross receipts of the year
After tax is computed at the applicable rates, as a direct reduction of the tax payable, like the rebate
Before clubbed income is added, so that only the assessee’s own income is reduced by these deductions
quiz.why: The sequence is: leave out exempt income, compute each head with its own deductions, add clubbed income and set off losses to reach gross total income, and only then subtract Chapter VIII deductions (unless the new regime bars them) to reach total income. Reductions of tax, such as the rebate, come only after the rates are applied. Authority: section 2(108) and the computation steps in the notes.

quiz.concept: Credits against tax versus deductions from income
quiz.q: Which of the following reduces the tax payable after tax has been computed, rather than reducing income?
quiz.ok: Credit for tax deducted at source from the assessee’s salary during the year
no: The standard deduction allowed in computing income under the head Salaries
Set off of a loss brought forward from an earlier year against the income of this year
A deduction subtracted from gross total income to arrive at the total income of the year
quiz.why: Deductions under each head, set off of losses and deductions from gross total income all reduce income. Tax is then computed at the rates, adjusted for rebate, reliefs, surcharge and cess, and finally reduced by credit for tax deducted or collected at source and advance tax. So tax deducted at source is a credit against the tax, not a deduction from income. Authority: computation steps for total income.

quiz.concept: Transfer of income without the asset
quiz.q: Vikram keeps ownership of his shares but irrevocably assigns to his brother the right to receive the dividends on them for five years. Whose income are the dividends?
quiz.ok: Vikram’s, because income transferred without the asset stays the transferor’s, revocable or not
no: The brother’s, because the assignment is irrevocable, so Vikram can never take the dividend income back
The brother’s, because he is the one who actually receives the dividends each year
Shared equally, because both brothers now hold an interest in the same shares
quiz.why: Where a person transfers only the income and keeps the asset, the income is taxed as his, whether the transfer is revocable or not. Irrevocability can matter where the asset itself is transferred, but not where only the income is passed on. Authority: section 96.

quiz.concept: Spouse’s remuneration: professional skill exception
quiz.q: Arjun has a substantial interest in a company. His wife, a qualified chartered accountant with long experience, is employed as its finance head, and her salary is paid purely for her professional work. Is her salary included in Arjun’s income?
quiz.ok: No, because her remuneration is attributable to her own professional knowledge, experience and qualification
no: Yes, because Arjun has a substantial interest in the company that employs and pays her
Yes, because a spouse’s salary from a concern linked to the family is always clubbed
Only partly, because the part of her salary above a fair market salary must be clubbed
quiz.why: A spouse’s remuneration from a concern in which the individual has a substantial interest is normally included in the individual’s income. The rule does not apply where the remuneration is solely attributable to the spouse’s technical or professional knowledge, experience and qualification. Arjun’s substantial interest triggers the rule, but it does not defeat the exception. Authority: section 99(1)(a)(i).

quiz.concept: Minor child’s income: skill exception
quiz.q: Tara, aged 14, earns fees from her performances as a classical dancer. She also earns interest on a fixed deposit that her father gifted to her. How is her income treated?
quiz.ok: Only the interest is clubbed, not the dance fees, because they come from her own skill and talent
no: Both are included in the parent’s income, because all income of a minor child is treated as the parent’s income
Neither is included, because both the deposit and the performances belong to Tara herself
The dance fees are clubbed but the interest is not, because the gifted deposit now stands in Tara’s own name
quiz.why: A minor child’s income is included in the parent’s income, except income from the child’s own work or from activities involving skill, talent, specialised knowledge or experience, and income of a minor with a specified disability. Interest on a gifted deposit involves no skill, so it is clubbed (subject to a small exclusion per child), while the dance fees are not. Authority: section 99(1)(c).

quiz.concept: Unexplained cash credit: burden and probabilities
quiz.q: A credit of Rs. 40,00,000 appears in Sohan’s books. He says it is winnings from horse races and produces betting tickets, but the story is hard to believe. How may the Assessing Officer approach it?
quiz.ok: Test it against surrounding circumstances and human probabilities, because the burden of explaining it is on Sohan
no: Accept the explanation, because documents that look genuine are conclusive and cannot be looked behind
Tax the credit only after the officer proves its actual source, because the burden of proof lies on the department alone
Ignore the credit, because a sum recorded in the assessee’s own books cannot be his income
quiz.why: The assessee must satisfactorily explain the nature and source of a credit in his books; if he fails, it may be taxed as his income. What is apparent is ordinarily real, but the authorities may look at the surrounding circumstances and need not accept a self serving explanation, and a claim of large race winnings has failed the test of human probabilities. Authority: section 102; Kale Khan Mohammad Hanif v. CIT; CIT v. Durga Prasad More; Sumati Dayal v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Deemed unexplained income: no set off
quiz.q: Sanjay has a business loss for the year. The Assessing Officer also finds an investment whose source Sanjay cannot satisfactorily explain, which is deemed to be his income. Can the business loss be set off against the deemed income?
quiz.ok: No, because deemed unexplained income allows no deduction or set off against it
no: Yes, because all income of the year, from whatever source, is pooled before the losses of the year are set off
Yes, but only a loss of the same year, because a brought forward loss cannot be used against it
Yes, after which any balance of the deemed income is taxed at the normal slab rates, not a special rate
quiz.why: Unrecorded investments whose source is not satisfactorily explained are deemed income. The law taxes such income at a special flat rate and allows no deduction or set off against it, so it cannot be sheltered by losses. Ordinary income is pooled before losses are set off, but that pooling is expressly excluded here. Authority: sections 103 and 195.

quiz.concept: Salary: due or receipt, whichever is earlier
quiz.q: Neha’s salary falls due on the last day of each month. Her salary for March, the last month of this tax year, is paid late, in May; her salary for April, the first month of the next tax year, is paid early, in March. In which tax year is each taxed?
quiz.ok: Both in this tax year, because salary is taxed when due or when received, whichever is earlier
no: March salary next year, when paid, and April salary this year, when paid, because only receipt counts
March salary this year, when due, and April salary next year, when due, because only the due date counts
Both next year, because the late salary is taxed when paid and the early salary when it falls due
quiz.why: Salary is taxed on the due or receipt basis, whichever is earlier. The March salary fell due this year, so it is taxed now though paid later; the April salary was received this year before it fell due, so it is taxed now as advance salary and not again when due. The method of accounting does not apply to salary. Authority: section 15(1) and (3).

quiz.concept: Arrears of salary and relief for bunching
quiz.q: A pay revision in the current year gives Ravi arrears for the two previous years, paid now and not taxed earlier. The lump sum pushes him into a higher rate. How is it treated?
quiz.ok: It is taxed this year, because arrears are taxed when paid, and he may apply for relief for bunching
no: It is taxed in the two earlier years, by reopening them, because that is when the services were actually rendered
It is not taxed at all, because it was not taxed in the years to which it relates
It is taxed in the current year with no relief at all, because arrears are simply ordinary salary of that year
quiz.why: Arrears of salary paid in the tax year are chargeable in that year if not taxed earlier. Because bunching several years’ salary into one year can push income into a higher rate, relief is available on application. The relief has to be claimed; it is not given automatically. Authority: sections 15 and 157.

quiz.concept: Contract of service versus contract for services
quiz.q: A company pays two people regularly. Anjali, a consultant, is engaged to deliver reports and chooses her own methods and hours. Dev, an analyst, works under the company’s directions on how the work is to be done. Whose payment is salary?
quiz.ok: Only Dev’s, because salary arises from a contract of service, where the employer controls how work is done
no: Both, because each of them is paid regularly by the same company for work done for the purposes of its business
Only Anjali’s, because her fee is fixed in advance under a formal written contract with the company
Neither, because a payment counts as salary only if tax is deducted from it at source
quiz.why: Salary arises only from a contract of service, in which the employer controls how the work is done. A contract for services, where the worker decides how to do the job, produces business or professional income however regular the payments. Authority: notes on the employer and employee relationship; Ram Prashad v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Managing director: employee or agent
quiz.q: A company’s managing director is paid a fixed monthly sum and a commission. Under his terms of appointment and the articles, the board supervises and controls how he does his work. Is his remuneration salary, and on what basis?
quiz.ok: Yes, because the company’s supervisory control over his work makes him an employee, not an agent
no: No, because a managing director acts for the company as its agent, so he cannot also be its employee
No, because a commission on profits shows that he shares in the business like a partner, not an employee
Yes, because a director’s remuneration is salary simply because he holds that office in the company
quiz.why: Whether a managing director is an employee or an agent depends on the terms of his appointment and the articles. A rough and ready test is whether the company exercises supervisory control over his work; if it does, he is an employee and his remuneration is salary. Holding the office of director is not enough on its own, and a commission does not make him a partner. Authority: Ram Prashad v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Partner’s remuneration is not salary
quiz.q: A firm describes the monthly payment to its working partner as “salary”, issues pay slips and deducts tax as it would for an employee. How is the payment taxed?
quiz.ok: As business income, because a partner cannot be an employee of himself and his co partners
no: As salary, because the firm describes the payment as salary and treats it that way in its records
As salary, because he works full time in the firm and is paid a fixed monthly amount
As income from other sources, because it is neither a share of profit nor true salary
quiz.why: Remuneration of a partner from his firm is not salary. A partner cannot be an employee of himself and his co partners, so there is no contract of service; the payment is a share of profit taxed as business income, to the extent allowed to the firm. Labels and pay slips do not change its character. Authority: section 15(4); CIT v. R.M. Chidambaram Pillai.

quiz.concept: Pension versus family pension
quiz.q: Mr. Iyer, a retired employee, received a monthly pension from his former employer. After his death, his widow receives a family pension from the same employer. How are the two taxed?
quiz.ok: His pension was salary, but her family pension is income from other sources, because she was never the employee
no: Both are salary, because both are paid by the same employer under the same pension scheme for the same service
Both are income from other sources, because neither payment is made for any services currently being rendered
His pension was exempt and her family pension is salary, because it replaces his income
quiz.why: Pension is part of salary because it comes from the pensioner’s own former employment, and salary includes amounts due from a former employer. Family pension goes to members of a deceased employee’s family, who never had a contract of service with the payer, so it is income from other sources. Authority: section 16; notes on family pension.

quiz.concept: Waiver of salary before and after accrual
quiz.q: Two employees give up salary. Asha, before the year begins, waives her right to the coming year’s salary. Ben, after his salary for the year has accrued, gives it up in favour of his employer. Who is taxable on the salary given up?
quiz.ok: Only Ben, because salary given up after it accrues is an application of income already his
no: Both, because salary is taxed as soon as the employment contract creates the right to receive it
Neither, because neither of them actually received the money from the employer
Only Asha, because a voluntary waiver in advance is treated as a gift to the employer
quiz.why: Salary waived before it accrues never becomes the employee’s income, so there is nothing to tax. Once salary has accrued it is his income, and giving it up is merely an application of that income, which remains taxable. Actual receipt is irrelevant, since salary is taxed when due even if unpaid. Authority: section 15; notes on waiver of salary.

quiz.concept: Place of accrual of salary
quiz.q: Leena works in Bengaluru throughout the year for a company based in the United States, which credits her salary to her bank account in New York. Where does the salary accrue?
quiz.ok: In India, because salary for services rendered here accrues here wherever paid
no: Outside India, because the salary is paid by the employer into a bank account outside India
Outside India, because the employer is a foreign company that has no office or business in India
In India only if it is later brought into India, because accrual of salary follows its remittance
quiz.why: Salary for services rendered in India is deemed to accrue in India wherever it is paid. The place of payment and the nationality of the employer do not matter; what matters is where the services are rendered. Authority: section 9(3).

quiz.concept: Accommodation perquisite lies in the concession
quiz.q: Kiran’s employer provides her a flat. The prescribed value of the accommodation for the year is Rs. 3,00,000, and Rs. 1,00,000 rent is recoverable from her. What is the perquisite?
quiz.ok: Rs. 2,00,000, because the perquisite is the concession, the value in excess of the rent recoverable
no: Rs. 3,00,000, because the prescribed value of the accommodation is the whole of her benefit
Rs. 1,00,000, because the rent recoverable from her measures the value of what she receives
Nil, because accommodation for which rent is recoverable from the employee is not a perquisite
quiz.why: The perquisite lies in the concession, that is, the benefit of accommodation at less than its value. For concessional accommodation the law taxes only the excess of the prescribed value over the rent recoverable from the employee, here Rs. 2,00,000. Authority: section 17(1)(b); Arun Kumar v. Union of India.

quiz.concept: Stock options taxed on exercise
quiz.q: Rohan exercises stock options, paying Rs. 100 a share when the fair market value on the date of exercise is Rs. 500. The shares are under a two year lock in, and he sells them later at Rs. 800. What is the perquisite?
quiz.ok: Rs. 400 a share on exercise, because the perquisite is the fair market value then less the amount paid
no: Nothing until sale, because the lock in makes the benefit on exercise merely notional and not yet taxable
Rs. 700 a share on sale, because the benefit is realised only when the locked in shares are finally sold
Rs. 500 a share on exercise, because the full market value of the shares is the benefit
quiz.why: The value of specified securities allotted free or at a concession is a perquisite, measured as fair market value on the date of exercise less the amount paid. Under the earlier law a lock in made the benefit notional and not taxable on exercise, but the Act now taxes it specifically on the date of exercise. Authority: section 17(1)(d) and (4)(h); CIT v. Infosys Technologies Ltd.

quiz.concept: Employee’s obligation versus tax on perquisites
quiz.q: Priya’s employer (i) pays the school fees of her children directly to the school and (ii) bears the income tax on the value of her non monetary perquisites. How are these treated?
quiz.ok: (i) is a perquisite, as her obligation met by the employer, but (ii) is specifically excluded
no: Neither is a perquisite, because no money is paid into the employee’s own hands
Both are perquisites, because each one discharges an obligation that the employee would otherwise have to bear herself
(i) is exempt as an education allowance, while (ii) is a perquisite as tax paid for her
quiz.why: Any obligation of the employee paid by the employer, such as school fees or the employee’s income tax, is a perquisite. But tax paid by the employer on non monetary perquisites is specifically excluded, so (ii) is not taxed even though it would otherwise fall within the obligation rule. Authority: section 17(1)(f); Schedule III, Sl. No. 10.

quiz.concept: Benefits taxed only for specified employees
quiz.q: A company gives the same free service to two employees, Ali and Bina, neither of whom is a director or shareholder. Ali’s monetary salary exceeds the prescribed amount; Bina’s does not. Assume the benefit is caught only by the rule on benefits provided free or at a concessional rate. For whom is it a perquisite?
quiz.ok: Only Ali, because that rule reaches employees whose monetary salary exceeds the prescribed amount
no: Both, because the rule on free or concessional benefits looks at the benefit, not the employee’s salary
Neither, because a free service puts no money into the employee’s hands, so nothing is received
Only Bina, because a free service is worth more to an employee whose monetary salary is below the prescribed amount
quiz.why: Some benefits are perquisites only for particular employees: benefits provided free or at a concession by a company to a director or an employee with a substantial interest, or by any employer to an employee whose monetary salary exceeds the prescribed amount. Bina is in none of these groups, so the same benefit is not her perquisite. Other perquisites, such as rent free accommodation, apply to all employees. Authority: section 17(1)(c).

quiz.concept: Medical benefits excluded from perquisites
quiz.q: An employer reimburses the cost of Farhan’s treatment in a government hospital and also pays the premium on an approved health insurance policy for him. How are these treated?
quiz.ok: Neither is a perquisite, because both fall within the specific exclusions for medical benefits
no: Both are perquisites, because each meets a personal obligation that Farhan would otherwise bear
Only the premium is a perquisite, because it is paid to an insurer rather than to Farhan
Only the reimbursement is a perquisite, because it puts cash into Farhan’s hands
quiz.why: An obligation of the employee met by the employer is generally a perquisite, but the Act specifically declares certain medical benefits not to be perquisites: treatment in the employer’s hospital, reimbursement of treatment in government or approved hospitals, and approved health insurance premiums paid or reimbursed by the employer. The specific exclusion prevails over the general rule. Authority: section 17(2).

quiz.concept: Contribution without a vested right
quiz.q: Under an old superannuation scheme, the employer contributed for an employee who had no vested right in the contributions and might never receive anything from them. Why was the contribution held not to be his perquisite?
quiz.ok: Because nothing had vested in him when the contribution was made, so it was not yet his income
no: Because contributions to a retirement scheme are capital receipts, which can never be income of the employee
Because only benefits paid to the employee in cash, and not contributions to a fund, can be perquisites
Because the employer could deduct the contribution as its own business expense
quiz.why: A perquisite must be a benefit to the employee. Where he has no vested right in a superannuation contribution, nothing accrues to him when it is made, so it is not his perquisite. The Act now taxes employer contributions to such funds above an annual limit in aggregate, together with the accretion on the excess. Authority: CIT v. L.W. Russel; section 17(1)(h) and (i).

quiz.concept: Amount received before joining employment
quiz.q: Two weeks before joining a new employer, Rhea receives Rs. 3,00,000 from it as an inducement to accept the job. She argues that it is not taxable as salary because she was not yet an employee. Is she right?
quiz.ok: No, because amounts received from a person before joining employment with him are profits in lieu of salary
no: Yes, because no employer and employee relationship yet existed between them on the date she received the money
Yes, because a one time inducement to change jobs is a capital receipt, not income
Partly, because only the part relating to the period after she joins can be salary
quiz.why: Profits in lieu of salary expressly include any amount received from a person before joining, or after leaving, employment with him. The link to the employment is enough, even though there was no contract of service on the date of receipt. Authority: section 18(1).

quiz.concept: Compensation for modifying employment terms
quiz.q: An employer pays its staff a lump sum for agreeing to reduced future benefits under their contracts. The staff remain employed. How is the lump sum taxed?
quiz.ok: As profits in lieu of salary, because it is compensation for modifying the terms of employment
no: As a capital receipt, because it compensates the staff for the loss of a source of future income
Not at all, because the payment is not made for any service actually rendered by the staff
As salary only when the employment eventually ends, because no termination has yet occurred
quiz.why: Profits in lieu of salary include compensation from an employer or former employer in connection with the termination of employment or the modification of its terms. A payment for accepting changed terms is therefore taxed under the head Salaries even though no service is rendered for it and the employment continues. Authority: section 18(1).

quiz.concept: Termination compensation from a non employer
quiz.q: A rival firm, which has never employed Raj and which he does not join, pays him a sum for resigning from his employer. How is the sum taxed?
quiz.ok: As income from other sources, because it is connected with termination of employment but is not salary
no: As profits in lieu of salary, because it is connected with the end of his employment
Not at all, because a payment from someone who is not his employer cannot be income
As a capital gain, because he has surrendered his rights under the employment contract
quiz.why: Profits in lieu of salary cover payments from an employer or former employer, or from a person before joining or after leaving employment with him. A payment from a stranger to the employment falls outside the head Salaries, but compensation connected with termination of employment that is not salary is taxed as income from other sources. Authority: sections 18(1) and 92(2)(j).

quiz.concept: Every allowance taxable unless excluded
quiz.q: An employee argues that his dearness allowance is not income because it merely compensates him for rising prices. How is the allowance treated?
quiz.ok: It is fully taxable, because every allowance is part of salary unless a specific entry or rule excludes it
no: It is exempt, because an allowance that merely offsets rising prices leaves the employee no richer than before
It is taxable only above the rise in prices, because the rest merely restores his real salary
It is exempt whenever it forms part of retirement benefits, because it is then treated as pay deferred to retirement
quiz.why: Every allowance is part of salary unless a Schedule entry or rule excludes it, and nothing excludes dearness allowance, so it is fully taxable. Whether it forms part of retirement benefits matters only for computing other limits, such as the salary base for house rent allowance under the old Rules, not for whether it is taxed. Authority: notes on allowances.

quiz.concept: House rent allowance needs rent actually paid
quiz.q: Kavya receives a house rent allowance but lives in a flat she owns and pays no rent. She has opted out of the new regime. How much of the allowance is exempt?
quiz.ok: None, because the exemption requires rent actually paid for accommodation that the employee does not own
no: All of it, because the allowance was specifically granted to her for housing
Up to the rent her flat could fetch, because she forgoes that rent by living there
Up to her home loan instalments, because for an owner occupier they take the place of the rent a tenant pays
quiz.why: The exemption applies only if the allowance is specifically granted for rent of accommodation occupied by the employee, the accommodation is not owned by the employee, and rent is actually paid. Kavya owns her flat and pays no rent, so the whole allowance is taxable; notional rent and loan instalments are not rent paid. Authority: Schedule III, Sl. No. 11.

quiz.concept: House rent allowance: least of three limits
quiz.q: Ajay, outside the new regime, receives house rent allowance of Rs. 2,40,000 and pays rent of Rs. 1,80,000. His salary for this purpose is Rs. 6,00,000, and the cap in his city is 40% of salary. The exempt amount is the least of the allowance received, rent paid in excess of 10% of salary, and the city cap. How much is exempt?
quiz.ok: Rs. 1,20,000, because rent paid in excess of 10% of salary is the lowest limit
no: Rs. 1,80,000, because the whole rent he actually pays is the true measure of his housing burden
Rs. 2,40,000, because the allowance received does not exceed the cap of 40% of his salary
Rs. 60,000, because only 10% of his salary is treated as spent on rent for this purpose
quiz.why: The limits are: allowance received, Rs. 2,40,000; rent paid less 10% of salary, Rs. 1,80,000 minus Rs. 60,000, that is Rs. 1,20,000; and 40% of salary, Rs. 2,40,000. The least, Rs. 1,20,000, is exempt, and the other Rs. 1,20,000 is taxable. The 10% limb means that only rent beyond a basic share of salary is relieved. Authority: Schedule III, Sl. No. 11; Rule 279.

quiz.concept: Duty allowance exempt only to extent spent
quiz.q: Outside the new regime, Imran receives a travel allowance of Rs. 60,000 for official tours and spends Rs. 45,000 on those tours during the year. How is the allowance treated?
quiz.ok: Rs. 45,000 is excluded and Rs. 15,000 taxed, because the exclusion covers only amounts actually spent
no: All Rs. 60,000 is excluded, because the whole allowance was granted for official duties
All Rs. 60,000 is taxable, because every allowance is part of salary without exception
Rs. 30,000 is excluded, because half of a duty allowance is presumed to be spent on duties
quiz.why: Allowances for expenses wholly, necessarily and exclusively incurred in performing duties are excluded only to the extent actually spent for that purpose. The unspent Rs. 15,000 is a gain rather than a reimbursement, so it is taxed as salary. Under the new regime only specifically prescribed allowances qualify. Authority: Schedule III, Sl. Nos. 12 and 13.

quiz.concept: Leave travel concession covers travel in India
quiz.q: Outside the new regime, Arun uses his leave travel concession for a family holiday in Singapore. How much of the concession is excluded from his income?
quiz.ok: None, because the exclusion covers only travel in India, subject to the prescribed conditions
no: All of it, because the concession was granted to him for travel while on leave, wherever he goes
All of it, because the concession is limited only by the actual expenditure that he incurred on the trip
Half of it, because a foreign trip combines leave travel with a personal holiday
quiz.why: The leave travel concession is excluded only for travel in India on leave or after retirement, subject to prescribed conditions and limited to actual expenditure. A foreign holiday is outside the exclusion, so the concession is taxable. The exclusion is not available at all under the new regime. Authority: Schedule III, Sl. No. 8.

quiz.concept: Retirement benefits are deductions, not exemptions
quiz.q: Under the 2025 Act, how is gratuity received on retirement by a private sector employee treated?
quiz.ok: It is part of salary, and a deduction within prescribed limits is allowed in computing salary income
no: It is exempt income, because retirement benefits are left out before the income under any head is computed
It is a capital receipt that falls outside the head Salaries altogether, being paid only once
It is fully taxable, because retirement benefits no longer receive any relief under the Act
quiz.why: Gratuity is part of salary by definition. Under the 1961 Act such retirement benefits were partly exemptions, but the 2025 Act treats gratuity, commuted pension, retrenchment and voluntary retirement compensation and leave encashment as deductions in computing salary, within limits. Authority: sections 16 and 19.

quiz.concept: Standard deduction cannot exceed salary
quiz.q: Sneha works part time and earns a salary of Rs. 40,000 in the year under the new regime, where the standard deduction is Rs. 75,000 or the salary, whichever is less. What standard deduction is allowed, and with what result?
quiz.ok: Rs. 40,000, so her salary income is nil, since the deduction cannot exceed the salary
no: Rs. 75,000, giving a salary loss of Rs. 35,000 that she can set off against her other income
Rs. 75,000, with the unused Rs. 35,000 of the deduction carried forward to the next year
No deduction at all, because the standard deduction is meant only for full time employees
quiz.why: The standard deduction is a flat amount allowed without proof of expenses, but it is capped at the salary itself. It can therefore reduce salary income to nil, but it can never create a loss under the head or be carried forward. Authority: section 19.

quiz.concept: Gratuity limit covers all employers and years
quiz.q: Ramesh, a private sector employee not covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act, claimed a gratuity deduction of Rs. 8,00,000 when he left his first employer. On retiring from his second employer he receives gratuity of Rs. 15,00,000. Assume the notified limit is Rs. 20,00,000 and his other limits exceed Rs. 15,00,000. What deduction is available now?
quiz.ok: Rs. 12,00,000, because the notified limit covers the gratuity deducted for all years and employers together
no: Rs. 15,00,000, because the notified limit applies separately to the gratuity from each employer
Nil, because a gratuity deduction, like voluntary retirement compensation, is allowed only once in a lifetime
Rs. 7,00,000, because the earlier deduction is set against the gratuity received now
quiz.why: For gratuity not covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act, the deduction is the least of the actual gratuity, the notified limit and half a month’s average salary for each completed year of service. The notified limit is an aggregate for all years and employers, so the Rs. 8,00,000 already deducted leaves room for only Rs. 12,00,000. Authority: section 19(2)(a).

quiz.concept: Commuted versus uncommuted pension
quiz.q: Sunil, a retired private sector employee, commutes part of his pension for a lump sum and receives the rest as a monthly pension. Which part can qualify for a deduction?
quiz.ok: Only the commuted lump sum, within a permitted fraction, because uncommuted pension is fully taxable
no: Both parts, because pension of either kind is a retirement benefit that is deductible in full from salary
Only the monthly pension, because a commuted lump sum is a capital receipt that falls outside salary
Neither part, because pension is not salary once the employment has ended
quiz.why: Pension is part of salary. A deduction is allowed for commuted pension: the entire amount for Government and similar employees, and for others the commuted value of a fraction of the pension, a smaller fraction where gratuity is also received. Uncommuted, periodical pension gets no deduction and is fully taxable. Authority: section 19.

quiz.concept: Voluntary retirement: deduction or relief, not both
quiz.q: Meena receives compensation under a qualifying voluntary retirement scheme, and it pushes her into a higher rate. She wants both the deduction for voluntary retirement compensation and relief for the higher rate caused by the lump sum. What is the position?
quiz.ok: She must choose one, because the law bars claiming both the deduction and the relief for the same compensation
no: She gets both, because the deduction reduces her income while the relief reduces only her tax, so they do not overlap
She gets only the relief, because voluntary retirement compensation is never deductible from salary
She gets both, provided neither benefit has been claimed at any earlier time in her life
quiz.why: The voluntary retirement deduction is allowed only once in a lifetime and not if relief for bunching has been claimed for the compensation; correspondingly, the relief is not available for amounts claimed under this deduction. The law prevents a double benefit on the same receipt. Authority: sections 19(2)(e) and 157(2).

quiz.concept: Leave encashment: in service or on retirement
quiz.q: Nisha, a private sector employee, encashes some earned leave while in service, and receives leave encashment again when she retires. Which of the two amounts can qualify for a deduction?
quiz.ok: Only the retirement encashment, because the deduction covers only leave encashed on retirement
no: Both qualify for the deduction, because each is payment for earned leave that was not taken
Neither qualifies, because leave encashment is part of salary and is fully taxable in every case
Only the encashment during service qualifies, because it is paid while she is still employed
quiz.why: Leave encashment is part of salary. A deduction is allowed only for leave encashment on retirement, in full for Central and State Government employees and within limits for others. Encashment during service gets no deduction and is fully taxable. Authority: section 19.

quiz.concept: New regime keeps retirement deductions
quiz.q: A student argues: “Under the new regime an employee loses every deduction from salary except the standard deduction, so gratuity received on retirement is fully taxable.” What is wrong with this reasoning?
quiz.ok: Only the deduction for tax on employment is withdrawn, so retirement benefit deductions remain available
no: Nothing, because the new regime allows only the standard deduction against salary income
Gratuity is exempt income under both regimes, so salary deductions are irrelevant to it
Gratuity is deductible under the new regime only for Government employees, because private limits are withdrawn
quiz.why: Under the 2025 Act, gratuity, commuted pension, retrenchment and voluntary retirement compensation and leave encashment are deductions in the salary Table. The new regime withdraws only the entry for tax on employment, so these deductions, along with the larger standard deduction, remain available. What the employee loses are items such as the house rent allowance exemption and the leave travel concession. Authority: sections 19 and 202(2).

quiz.concept: Opting out: salaried versus business income
quiz.q: Priya, a salaried employee with no business income, opted out of the new regime last year. This year she would like to be taxed under the new regime. Can she?
quiz.ok: Yes, because a person without business income may choose afresh each year when filing the return
no: No, because once a person opts out of the new regime, that choice binds her for all the later years
Yes, but only once in her lifetime, because a withdrawal of the choice is allowed only a single time
Only with the Assessing Officer’s approval, because the new regime is the default regime
quiz.why: The new regime is the default. A person without business income can opt out, or not, each year when filing the return. The rule that the choice continues for later years and can be withdrawn only once applies to a person with business income. Authority: section 202(4).

quiz.concept: Why gross salary rises under the new regime
quiz.q: Meera receives house rent allowance and pays rent. On the same pay, her gross salary is Rs. 10,40,000 outside the new regime but Rs. 13,00,000 under it. What explains the difference?
quiz.ok: The house rent allowance exemption is unavailable under the new regime, so the whole allowance is taxed
no: Dearness allowance becomes taxable only under the new regime, so it is added to gross salary
The standard deduction is added back under the new regime before gross salary is found
Tax on employment is added back to salary under the new regime, because it is no longer deductible there
