quiz.why: Outside the new regime, Rs. 2,60,000 of Meera’s Rs. 3,00,000 allowance is exempt, so only Rs. 40,000 enters gross salary. Under the new regime the exemption is withdrawn, so the full allowance is included and gross salary rises by Rs. 2,60,000. The larger standard deduction under the new regime comes after gross salary is found. Authority: section 202; illustration in the notes.

quiz.concept: Marginal relief at the rebate threshold
quiz.q: Under the new regime, a rebate wipes out the tax where total income does not exceed Rs. 12,00,000; above that, marginal relief limits the tax to the income above Rs. 12,00,000. Meera’s total income is Rs. 12,25,000 and her tax at the rates is Rs. 63,750. What tax does she pay, before cess?
quiz.ok: Rs. 25,000, because the tax is capped at the income above the threshold
no: Rs. 63,750, because the rebate is lost entirely once income crosses the threshold, however slightly
Nil, because her income exceeds the threshold by only a small amount, so the full rebate applies
Rs. 38,750, because the income above the threshold is deducted from the tax at the rates
quiz.why: Without marginal relief, earning Rs. 25,000 above the threshold would cost Rs. 63,750 in tax, leaving Meera worse off than someone exactly at the threshold. Marginal relief limits the tax to Rs. 25,000, the income above the threshold, so the rebate works out to Rs. 38,750. Authority: section 156(2)(b).

quiz.concept: Special rate applies only to its income
quiz.q: Vinod’s total income of Rs. 15,00,000 includes Rs. 2,00,000 of unexplained cash credits, which the Act taxes at a special flat rate. How is the tax on his total income worked out?
quiz.ok: The special rate applies to the Rs. 2,00,000, and the normal rates to the other Rs. 13,00,000
no: The normal rates apply to all Rs. 15,00,000, and the special rate only adds a surcharge on top
The special rate applies to all Rs. 15,00,000, because the unexplained credits taint the whole income
The Rs. 2,00,000 is kept out of total income altogether, and only the rest is taxed at normal rates
quiz.why: The unexplained credits form part of total income, but the rates are applied in parts: the special rate on that income and the normal rates on the rest of the total income. The special rate does not spread to the other income, and the credits are not left out of total income. Authority: section 195(1); computation steps for total income.

quiz.concept: Trust irrevocable for the beneficiary’s lifetime
quiz.q: Rohit settles shares on a trust for his adult niece. The deed bars him from revoking it during her lifetime, although he may revoke it after her death, and he derives no benefit from the income. How are the dividends treated while the niece is alive?
quiz.ok: They are not Rohit’s income, because the trust cannot be revoked during the beneficiary’s lifetime
no: They are Rohit’s income, because a power to revoke after her death makes the transfer revocable now
They are Rohit’s income, because he settled the shares on the trust without any consideration
They are Rohit’s income, because a transfer of shares to a trust is treated as a transfer of income only
quiz.why: Income from a revocable transfer of assets is the transferor’s, but the rule does not apply to a trust not revocable during the beneficiary’s lifetime where the transferor derives no benefit. A power that can arise only after her death does not change that while she lives; the income becomes Rohit’s only when the power to revoke arises. Authority: section 97(2) and (3).

quiz.concept: Government allowances abroad are excluded
quiz.q: Salary paid by the Government of India to an Indian citizen for service outside India is deemed to accrue in India. Ritu, an Indian citizen posted at an Indian embassy abroad, also receives a foreign allowance that the Government pays her there. How is the allowance treated?
quiz.ok: It is excluded from her income, though her salary for the same service is deemed to accrue in India
no: It is taxable with her salary, because both are paid by the Government for the same service abroad
It is taxable, because every allowance is part of salary unless it is spent on official duties
It is excluded only to the extent that she spends it on her official duties abroad
quiz.why: Salary for services rendered outside India would normally accrue outside India, but Government salary paid to an Indian citizen for such service is specifically deemed to accrue in India. Allowances and perquisites that the Government pays such a citizen outside India are excluded altogether, whether or not spent. The rule for duty allowances, excluded only to the extent spent, does not apply. Authority: section 9(3); Schedule III, Sl. No. 9.

quiz.concept: Voluntary retirement deduction: once in a lifetime
quiz.q: Years ago, Kunal was allowed the deduction for voluntary retirement compensation when he left his first employer under a qualifying scheme. He now receives compensation under a qualifying scheme of his second employer. Can he claim the deduction again?
quiz.ok: No, because the deduction is allowed only once in a lifetime, whichever employer pays
no: Yes, because the limit applies afresh to each employer’s scheme, like a new contract of employment
Yes, up to the unused part of the limit, as with the gratuity limit across employers
Yes, provided he gives up relief for the higher rate on the earlier compensation
quiz.why: Once the voluntary retirement deduction has been allowed for any tax year, it cannot be allowed for any other year, so a second scheme brings no fresh deduction. Unlike gratuity, where an aggregate limit leaves room for later amounts, this deduction is a single lifetime benefit. Authority: section 19(2)(e).

quiz.concept: Charge on annual value, not rent
quiz.q: A student argues: “The house property head is simply a tax on rent, so an owner is never taxed on more than the rent he actually receives.” What is wrong with this reasoning?
quiz.ok: The charge is on annual value, which exceeds the rent received when a house is let below expected rent
no: Nothing, because annual value is defined as the rent actually received during the year
The charge is on the market value of the building, so rent is irrelevant to it
The charge is on the municipal valuation alone, because the local authority fixes the annual value of every house
quiz.why: The charge under this head is on annual value: the amount the property can reasonably be expected to fetch if let from year to year, or the actual rent if higher. It is not a tax on rent as such, so an owner who lets below the expected rent is taxed on the higher expected rent. Municipal valuation is only one guide to the expected rent. Authority: sections 20 and 21(1).

quiz.concept: Why the law imposes a notional charge
quiz.q: Which statement best explains why the law charges the annual value of a building rather than only the rent actually received?
quiz.ok: A building is itself a source of income, and a notional charge treats letting and non letting owners more equally
no: Owners who do not let their buildings are presumed to receive rent secretly, so a notional charge prevents evasion
The charge is really a wealth tax on buildings, so it must be measured by their capital value
A notional charge penalises owners who keep housing idle, so as to increase the supply of rented homes
quiz.why: The notes give three reasons: ownership of a building is itself a source with an inherent capacity to yield income; a notional charge treats owners who let and owners who do not more equally; and annual value is easy to estimate, with a flat deduction in place of verifying repairs. The law then softens the charge, for example by giving self occupied houses a nil annual value. Authority: rationale of the charge in the notes.

quiz.concept: Building or appurtenant land, not vacant land
quiz.q: Mohan lets out two things: a vacant plot, not attached to any building, to a car parking operator; and the garage attached to his house, to a neighbour. Which rent is house property income?
quiz.ok: Only the garage rent, because the head covers buildings and appurtenant land, not vacant land
no: Both, because each is immovable property that Mohan owns and lets out to another person for rent
Neither, because the head covers only buildings that are used as dwelling houses by their occupants
Only the plot rent, because a garage is not a building in its own right
quiz.why: The head covers buildings and lands appurtenant to them, such as a courtyard or garage. Income from letting vacant land not attached to a building falls under other sources or business, not house property. A building need not be a dwelling; shops and godowns also qualify. Authority: section 20.

quiz.concept: Property used for own business excluded
quiz.q: Dr. Rao owns a two storey building. She runs her clinic on the ground floor, and her professional profits are taxed. She lets the first floor. What is chargeable under house property?
quiz.ok: Only the first floor, because the clinic portion is used for her own taxable profession
no: Both floors’ annual value, because she owns the whole building and the charge follows ownership
Neither floor, because a building used partly for a profession becomes a business asset as a whole
Both floors, but the clinic at a reduced value, because she does not pay herself any rent
quiz.why: The annual value of property owned by the assessee is charged, except the portions he occupies for his own business or profession whose profits are taxable. The clinic’s use is reflected in her taxable professional profits, so only the let portion is charged under this head. Authority: section 20(2).

quiz.concept: Owner means entitled to the income
quiz.q: Property registered in Harish’s name has vested by law in a custodian, who manages it and keeps the rent; Harish can claim none of it. Is Harish the owner for the house property head?
quiz.ok: No, because the owner is the person entitled to the property’s income in his own right
no: Yes, because he still holds the registered title to the property in his own name
Yes, because the custodian merely collects the rent on his behalf as his agent
He is a deemed owner, because a statutory authority holds and manages the property for him
quiz.why: The owner for this head is the person entitled to receive the income from the property in his own right. Where property had vested in a custodian and the registered holder had no right to its income, he was not the owner for this purpose, whatever the title records show. Authority: R.B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Unregistered buyer in possession is owner
quiz.q: Kiran has paid the full price for a flat, taken possession and let it, collecting the rent herself. The sale deed has not yet been registered. Who is chargeable on the house property income?
quiz.ok: Kiran, because the test is entitlement to the rent in her own right, not registered title
no: The seller, because legal title to the flat passes to Kiran only when the sale deed is registered
No one, because ownership of the flat is in suspense until the sale deed is registered
Kiran and the seller equally, because until registration each holds part of the owner’s rights
quiz.why: A person who has paid for a property, is in possession and receives the rent in his own right is the owner for this head, even if the sale deed has not been registered. The test is entitlement to the income in one’s own right, not formal title. The Act also treats a person in possession under part performance of a contract as a deemed owner. Authority: CIT v. Podar Cement (P) Ltd.; section 25(d).

quiz.concept: Deemed owner: gift to spouse
quiz.q: Ravi gifts a flat to his wife, with whom he lives. She lets it and keeps the rent. Who is chargeable on the house property income?
quiz.ok: Ravi, as deemed owner, because he transferred the flat to his spouse without adequate consideration
no: His wife, because after the gift she is the legal owner of the flat and receives all of the rent herself
Both of them equally, because spouses who live together share the income of one household between them
Ravi, but only if his wife has no other income of her own
quiz.why: An individual who transfers property without adequate consideration to his or her spouse, except under an agreement to live apart, is deemed to be its owner. So Ravi is taxed on the flat’s income although his wife holds the title and collects the rent. This mirrors the clubbing rule for assets transferred to a spouse. Authority: section 25(a).

quiz.concept: Long lease deemed owner versus sub letting tenant
quiz.q: Anu, who holds an eleven month lease of a flat, sub lets it. Bina, who acquired rights in a flat under a fifteen year lease, also sub lets. The Act treats a person acquiring rights under a lease of at least twelve years as a deemed owner. Whose income is house property income?
quiz.ok: Only Bina’s, because she is a deemed owner while Anu is merely a tenant
no: Both, because each of them receives rent from a building that she lets to another person
Neither, because only the freehold owner of a building can ever have house property income
Neither yet, because a lessee becomes a deemed owner only after holding the lease for twelve years
quiz.why: A tenant who sub lets is not the owner, so the sub letting income is not house property income. But a person who acquires rights in a building under a lease of at least twelve years (monthly leases and leases of up to one year are excluded) is a deemed owner, taxed under this head. Authority: section 25(e); notes on sub letting.

quiz.concept: Inseparable letting with plant or furniture
quiz.q: A company lets its factory building together with the plant installed in it. The tenant cannot use one without the other, and the company would not let them separately. How is the rent taxed?
quiz.ok: Not house property, because an inseparable letting of building and plant is business or other sources income
no: As house property income, because a building forms part of what is let, and the head always follows the building
Split between heads, because the building’s share must be taxed under house property
As capital gains, because the plant let with the building is a capital asset
quiz.why: Where a building is let together with furniture or machinery and the two lettings are inseparable, the income is not house property income; it is business income or income from other sources. The rent cannot be split, because the letting is one composite transaction. Authority: Sultan Brothers (P) Ltd. v. CIT; section 92(2)(g).

quiz.concept: Residential letting: house property only
quiz.q: A company whose sole business and main object is letting property owns a commercial complex and a block of residential apartments, and lets both. How is the rent taxed?
quiz.ok: Residential rent goes to house property under a specific rule, while commercial rent may still be business income
no: Both are business income, because letting is the company’s main object and its whole business
Both are house property income, because the specific rule for residential letting extends to commercial property too
Residential rent is business income for such a company, while commercial rent stays under house property
quiz.why: Where letting was a company’s main object and whole business, the rent was held to be business income. The Act now provides that income from letting a residential house, or part of it, by the owner is chargeable only as house property income, so that approach no longer applies to residential property. It may still matter for commercial property let as a business. Authority: section 26(4); Chennai Properties and Investments Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Higher of expected and actual rent
quiz.q: Ajit lets his flat to a friend for Rs. 1,20,000 a year, although similar flats fetch Rs. 2,40,000. No rent control law applies, and the flat was let all year. What is the annual value, before municipal taxes?
quiz.ok: Rs. 2,40,000, because annual value is the higher of expected and actual rent
no: Rs. 1,20,000, because only the rent actually received from the tenant can be taxed
Rs. 1,80,000, because the expected and actual rents are averaged where they differ
Nil, because a letting to a friend at a concession is not a commercial letting at all
quiz.why: Annual value is the higher of the sum for which the property might reasonably be expected to let from year to year and the actual rent received or receivable. Letting below market rent does not reduce the charge, because the head taxes what the property could fetch, not merely what the owner chooses to charge. Authority: section 21(1).

quiz.concept: Rent control caps the expected rent
quiz.q: A flat is subject to a rent control law. The fair rent of similar flats is Rs. 4,80,000, the municipal valuation is Rs. 2,60,000, and the standard rent determinable under the law is Rs. 2,00,000, though no authority has fixed it. Actual rent is Rs. 1,80,000. What is the annual value, before municipal taxes?
quiz.ok: Rs. 2,00,000, because expected rent is capped at the standard rent determinable, which exceeds the actual rent
no: Rs. 4,80,000, because the cap applies only once a standard rent has actually been fixed
Rs. 2,60,000, because the municipal valuation alone decides expected rent, whatever the standard rent may be
Rs. 1,80,000, because only the actual rent counts where a rent control law applies
quiz.why: Expected rent is estimated from the municipal valuation and the fair rent of similar property, but where a rent control law applies it cannot exceed the standard rent determinable under that law, even if none has actually been fixed. The capped expected rent of Rs. 2,00,000 exceeds the actual rent, so it is the annual value. Authority: Mrs. Sheila Kaushish v. CIT; section 21(1).

quiz.concept: Vacancy: actual rent becomes annual value
quiz.q: The expected rent of Sameer’s flat is Rs. 3,00,000. He lets it at Rs. 30,000 a month, but it stays vacant for three months, so he receives Rs. 2,70,000. What is the annual value, before municipal taxes?
quiz.ok: Rs. 2,70,000, because when vacancy pulls actual rent below expected rent, actual rent is the annual value
no: Rs. 3,00,000, because annual value is the higher of expected and actual rent, vacant or not
Rs. 3,60,000, because rent for the full year is taken as if the flat had never been vacant
Rs. 2,25,000, because the expected rent is reduced in proportion to the three vacant months
quiz.why: Ordinarily annual value is the higher of expected and actual rent. But if a let property is vacant for the whole or part of the year and, because of the vacancy, actual rent is less than expected rent, the actual rent is the annual value. Here the shortfall below Rs. 3,00,000 is caused by the vacancy, so Rs. 2,70,000 is taken. Authority: section 21(2).

quiz.concept: Municipal taxes: actually paid by the owner
quiz.q: During the year, Sohan pays municipal tax on his let out flat: Rs. 15,000 for the current year and Rs. 10,000 of arrears for an earlier year. Another Rs. 8,000 levied for the current year remains unpaid at the year end. How much reduces the annual value this year?
quiz.ok: Rs. 25,000, because taxes actually paid by the owner in the year count, whatever year they relate to
no: Rs. 23,000, because only the taxes levied for the current year count, whether or not they have been paid
Rs. 15,000, because only the current year’s taxes that are also paid within that same year can count
Rs. 33,000, because all taxes paid or payable by the owner, of any year, count
quiz.why: Taxes levied by a local authority reduce annual value only when actually paid by the owner during the year, and then whatever year they relate to. So the arrears paid this year count, while the unpaid Rs. 8,000 will count in the year it is paid. Authority: section 21(3).

quiz.concept: Unrealised rent: when it is excluded
quiz.q: Rent that the owner cannot realise may be left out of actual rent, subject to conditions in the Rules aimed at genuine defaults that the owner actively pursues. Which situation best supports leaving the unpaid rent out?
quiz.ok: A genuine tenant defaulted and vacated, and the owner took legal proceedings to recover the rent
no: The tenant is a close relative, and the owner has decided not to press for the unpaid rent this year
The defaulting tenant has moved into another property of the same owner, where he lives, and still owes the rent
The tenant is still in occupation, and the owner expects to be paid next year without taking any action at all
quiz.why: Unrealised rent is excluded from actual rent subject to rules. Under the old Rule 4 the conditions were a bona fide tenancy, the defaulting tenant having vacated or steps taken to evict him, the tenant not occupying any other property of the owner, and reasonable steps, including legal proceedings, to recover the rent; the 2026 Rule should be checked. Only the tenant who vacated and was sued for the rent shows a genuine default that the owner is actively pursuing. Authority: section 21(4).

quiz.concept: Nil annual value: cannot occupy for any reason
quiz.q: Arjun owns one house, in Kochi, which is not let. He cannot live in it because he must stay in Delhi to care for his parents, not for any job or business. What is the Kochi house’s annual value?
quiz.ok: Nil, because the benefit covers an owner who cannot occupy the house for any reason
no: Its expected rent, because he does not live elsewhere for employment, business or profession
Its expected rent, because a house that the owner does not occupy is treated as let
Nil, but only if he pays rent for the house in which he lives in Delhi
quiz.why: Annual value is nil if the owner occupies the house for his own residence or cannot actually occupy it due to any reason. This is wider than the 1961 Act, which required the owner to reside elsewhere because of employment, business or profession. Authority: section 21(6).

quiz.concept: Self occupied benefit lost if let
quiz.q: Sara lives in her only house for ten months of the year and lets it for the other two months while she is abroad. Does she keep the nil annual value?
quiz.ok: No, because the benefit is lost if the house is let at any time during the year
no: Partly, because annual value is nil for ten months and expected rent for the two months
Yes, because she lived in the house for most of the year as her residence
Yes, and the two months’ rent is taxed separately as income from other sources
quiz.why: The nil annual value for a self occupied house is lost if the house is let at any time in the year or the owner derives any other benefit from it. The annual value for that year is then found under the normal rules, without splitting the year into occupied and let months. Authority: section 21(7).

quiz.concept: Limit on houses with nil annual value
quiz.q: Vivek owns three houses, none of them let. He lives in one and cannot occupy the other two. The nil annual value is available for up to two houses chosen by the owner. What is the position?
quiz.ok: Two houses of his choice have nil annual value, but the third is charged on its annual value though unlet
no: All three have nil annual value, because none of the three houses is let out to anyone at any time in the year
Only the house he actually lives in has nil annual value, because the other two are not occupied by him at all
The Assessing Officer, not Vivek, picks which two houses get the nil annual value
quiz.why: The nil annual value applies to houses the owner occupies or cannot occupy for any reason, but only for up to two houses chosen by him. Any further house is charged on its annual value, which for an unlet house is its expected rent. Authority: section 21(6) and (7).

quiz.concept: Unlet stock in trade: limited nil period
quiz.q: A builder holds unsold, unlet flats as stock in trade. Such flats have a nil annual value only for a limited period after construction is completed, and that period has now ended. What follows?
quiz.ok: Their annual value is now chargeable under house property, though they remain unlet
no: They stay at nil, because stock in trade is taxed only as business income when it is sold
Nothing is charged, because only property that is actually let can have an annual value
Their expected rent is added to the builder’s business profits instead, as trading stock
quiz.why: Unlet property held as stock in trade gets a nil annual value only for a limited period after completion. Once that period ends, the ordinary notional charge applies: ownership of a building is a source of income, so annual value is charged even though the flats are unlet. Authority: section 21(5).

quiz.concept: Flat 30% deduction replaces actual repairs
quiz.q: The Act allows a deduction of 30% of the annual value of a let out house. Leela spends an amount equal to 45% of her let out flat’s annual value on repairs during the year. Her neighbour, with an identical let out flat, spends nothing. What deduction for repairs does each get?
quiz.ok: Each gets the same 30% of annual value, because actual repair costs are neither verified nor allowed
no: Leela gets her actual 45% and the neighbour nothing, because only real spending is deductible
Leela gets 45% and the neighbour 30%, because the flat rate is only a minimum allowance
Each gets actual repairs up to 30%, so Leela gets 30% and the neighbour gets nothing
quiz.why: The standard deduction is 30% of the annual value, whatever the actual expenditure, and no other repair or maintenance deduction is allowed. The flat rate replaces verification of actual repair costs, so both owners get the same 30%. Authority: section 22.

quiz.concept: Interest deductible on accrual basis
quiz.q: Interest of Rs. 1,20,000 accrues for the year on the loan Prakash took to buy his let out flat, but he pays only Rs. 80,000 by the year end. How much interest is deductible this year?
quiz.ok: Rs. 1,20,000, because interest on borrowed capital is deductible on an accrual basis
no: Rs. 80,000, because only interest actually paid during the year is deductible
Rs. 40,000, being the unpaid interest, because it remains an outstanding liability at the year end
Nil, because no interest is deductible until the full year’s interest is paid
quiz.why: Interest payable on capital borrowed to acquire, construct, repair, renew or reconstruct the property is deductible on an accrual basis, so the full Rs. 1,20,000 payable for the year counts whether or not it has been paid. For a let out house the Act sets no limit on interest. Authority: section 22.

quiz.concept: Pre construction interest: period and instalments
quiz.q: Pooja borrowed in June 2023 to build a house, which was completed during the tax year beginning 1 April 2026. Pre construction interest is allowed in five equal instalments. Which interest is pre construction interest, and when do the instalments begin?
quiz.ok: Interest from June 2023 to 31 March 2026, with instalments beginning in the tax year of completion
no: Interest up to the date of completion, deducted in full in the tax year of completion
Interest from June 2023 to 31 March 2026, with instalments beginning only in the year after completion
Interest from June 2023 to 31 March 2026, which is never deductible because no house existed then at all
quiz.why: Pre construction interest is interest for the period before the tax year in which the property is acquired or constructed. It is deducted in five equal instalments starting from that tax year, while interest for the year of completion itself is deducted as ordinary interest. Authority: section 22(3).

quiz.concept: Self occupied interest cap: repair loan
quiz.q: Nikhil, outside the new regime, bought his self occupied house years ago with his own money. This year he pays interest of Rs. 80,000 on a loan taken to repair it. For self occupied houses interest is capped at Rs. 2,00,000 or Rs. 30,000, depending on the conditions met. Which cap applies?
quiz.ok: Rs. 30,000, because the higher cap is only for acquisition or construction loans
no: Rs. 2,00,000, because any housing loan qualifies once the lender’s certificate is furnished
No cap at all, because loans for repair are treated in the same way as loans for a let out house
Neither cap, because interest on a loan taken for repairs is not deductible at all
quiz.why: Interest on capital borrowed for repair is deductible, but for a self occupied house the higher cap applies only where the property was acquired or constructed with a loan for that purpose, completed within five years, with the lender’s certificate. Every other case, including a repair loan, gets the lower cap. Authority: section 22(2) and (4).

quiz.concept: Combined interest cap for self occupied houses
quiz.q: Outside the new regime, Lata has two self occupied houses, each bought with a qualifying loan, and interest of Rs. 1,50,000 on each. The cap for qualifying self occupied houses is Rs. 2,00,000. How much interest is deductible in all?
quiz.ok: Rs. 2,00,000, because the cap is one combined limit for all self occupied houses together
no: Rs. 3,00,000, because each self occupied house carries its own separate cap of Rs. 2,00,000
Rs. 1,50,000, because interest is allowed for only one of the self occupied houses
Nil, because owning two self occupied houses withdraws the interest deduction altogether
quiz.why: Each house’s interest is within the cap on its own, but the Act fixes a combined limit for all self occupied houses, so Lata’s total deduction is Rs. 2,00,000. The nil annual value can extend to two houses, but the interest relief is shared between them. Authority: section 22(5).

quiz.concept: Interest payable outside India
quiz.q: Gopal pays interest on the loan for his let out flat to a lender outside India who has no agent in India. He has neither deducted nor paid tax on the interest. Is the interest deductible?
quiz.ok: No, because without tax deducted or paid, or an agent in India, interest payable abroad is disallowed
no: Yes, because the Act sets no limit on the interest deductible for a let out house
Yes, because the foreign lender will in any case be taxed on the interest in its own country of residence
Yes, because tax need be deducted on such interest only where the lender has an agent in India
quiz.why: Interest payable outside India is not deductible if tax has not been deducted or paid on it and there is no agent in India. The absence of a cap on interest for let out houses does not override this condition. Authority: section 22(6).

quiz.concept: Arrears of rent received after sale
quiz.q: Rekha sold her let out flat last year. This year she recovers arrears of rent from the former tenant. How are the arrears treated?
quiz.ok: Taxed this year under house property, because arrears are taxed in the year of receipt
no: Not taxed at all, because she was no longer the owner of the flat on the date she received the arrears
Taxed in the earlier years when the rent fell due, because that is when the rent was actually earned
Taxed as capital gains, because the arrears are part of the price of the flat sold
quiz.why: Arrears of rent, and unrealised rent received later, are income of the year of receipt, even if the assessee is no longer the owner, and 30% of the amount is deducted. The charge follows receipt, not current ownership. Authority: section 23.

quiz.concept: Co owners with definite shares
quiz.q: Two brothers co own a house in equal, definite shares, and both live in it with their families. How are they assessed?
quiz.ok: Each on his own share, with his own self occupied benefit, because their shares are definite
no: As an association of persons, because they own the house jointly, so the benefit is given once
The elder brother alone, as head of the household, because co owned property is taxed in one hand
Neither can claim the self occupied benefit, because the house is not owned by one person
quiz.why: Co owners whose shares are definite and ascertainable are not assessed as an association of persons. Each is taxed on his own share, and each gets the self occupied benefit individually. Authority: section 24.

quiz.concept: House property loss: set off and carry forward
quiz.q: Rahul, outside the new regime, has a house property loss of Rs. 3,50,000 from interest on a let out flat, and salary income of Rs. 12,00,000. A house property loss may be set off against other heads up to Rs. 2,00,000 a year. What happens to the loss?
quiz.ok: Rs. 2,00,000 is set off against salary, and Rs. 1,50,000 is carried forward against house property income only
no: The full Rs. 3,50,000 is set off against salary, because a let out house has no limit on the interest deductible
Rs. 2,00,000 is set off against salary, and the balance of Rs. 1,50,000 lapses at once
Rs. 2,00,000 is set off against salary, and Rs. 1,50,000 is carried forward against any income
quiz.why: A house property loss can be set off against other house property income and against other heads up to the annual limit. The balance is carried forward for a limited number of years, against house property income only. A let out house has no cap on interest, but the set off limit contains the resulting loss, and under the new regime no set off against other heads is allowed. Authority: sections 108 to 110.

quiz.concept: Order of computation for let out property
quiz.q: Anil’s flat is let all year. Expected rent is Rs. 3,00,000, actual rent Rs. 3,60,000, municipal taxes paid Rs. 20,000, and loan interest Rs. 1,50,000. In what order are these used to reach his income from house property?
quiz.ok: Take the higher rent, subtract municipal taxes to get annual value, deduct 30% of that, then deduct interest
no: Take the higher rent, deduct 30% of it, then deduct the municipal taxes and the interest
Take the expected rent, deduct 30% of it, then deduct the municipal taxes and the interest
Take the actual rent, deduct the interest, then deduct 30% of the balance and the municipal taxes
quiz.why: Municipal taxes paid reduce the annual value itself, and the 30% is a percentage of that annual value: Rs. 3,60,000 less Rs. 20,000 gives Rs. 3,40,000, and 30% of it is Rs. 1,02,000. Interest of Rs. 1,50,000 is then deducted, leaving Rs. 88,000. Applying 30% to the gross rent would overstate the deduction. Authority: sections 21 and 22; illustration in the notes.

quiz.concept: Self occupied house with a loan, both regimes
quiz.q: Sunita, a salaried employee, lives in her own house, bought with a qualifying loan. Interest for the year is Rs. 2,40,000. Outside the new regime the interest cap is Rs. 2,00,000, and a house property loss can be set off against other heads up to Rs. 2,00,000. What is her income from the house outside the new regime, and under it?
quiz.ok: A loss of Rs. 2,00,000 outside the new regime, set off against her salary, and nil under the new regime
no: A loss of Rs. 2,40,000 outside the new regime, and a capped loss of Rs. 2,00,000 under the new regime
A loss of Rs. 2,00,000 under both regimes, because the interest cap is exactly the same in each regime
Nil under both regimes, because a self occupied house always has a nil annual value
quiz.why: Outside the new regime the annual value is nil, so the 30% deduction is also nil, and interest is capped at Rs. 2,00,000, giving a loss of Rs. 2,00,000 that can be set off against salary. Under the new regime no interest deduction is allowed for a self occupied house, so the income is simply nil. Authority: sections 21(6), 22 and 202; illustration in the notes.

quiz.concept: Letting and non letting owners treated alike
quiz.q: Asha and Bina own identical shops in the same market, each able to fetch Rs. 3,00,000 a year. Asha lets hers at that rent. Bina, who carries on no business, keeps hers locked all year and makes no attempt to let it. How are the two shops charged under house property, before municipal taxes?
quiz.ok: Both on an annual value of Rs. 3,00,000, because owning the building, not letting it, is the source taxed
no: Only Asha’s, on Rs. 3,00,000, because Bina receives no rent and the head taxes only rent received
Asha’s on Rs. 3,00,000 and Bina’s at nil, because property its owner leaves unused has a nil annual value
Both, but Bina’s at a higher value, because the notional charge is meant to penalise owners who keep property idle
quiz.why: The charge is on annual value, the sum a property can reasonably be expected to fetch, not on rent received, because owning a building is itself a source capable of yielding income. A notional charge therefore treats an owner who lets and one who does not alike. The nil annual value is only for a house that the owner occupies or cannot occupy, not for an unused shop. Authority: sections 20 and 21(1).

quiz.concept: Pre construction interest in a let out computation
quiz.q: Meena’s flat was completed at the start of this tax year and let for the whole year; its annual value is Rs. 3,00,000. Interest on her construction loan is Rs. 1,00,000 for this year and Rs. 2,50,000 for the years before completion. The deduction is 30% of annual value, and pre construction interest is allowed in five equal instalments. What is her income from house property this year?
quiz.ok: Rs. 60,000, after 30%, this year’s interest and one fifth of the pre construction interest
no: A loss of Rs. 1,40,000, because all the pre construction interest is deducted in the year of completion
Rs. 1,10,000, because interest for the years before completion relates to no income and is disallowed
Rs. 2,10,000, because the flat 30% deduction also stands in for the interest on the loan
quiz.why: Annual value of Rs. 3,00,000 less 30% (Rs. 90,000) and this year’s interest (Rs. 1,00,000) leaves Rs. 1,10,000. The Rs. 2,50,000 of pre construction interest is deducted in five equal instalments starting in the year of completion, so Rs. 50,000 comes off now, leaving Rs. 60,000. Deducting it all at once, or not at all, misstates the income, and the 30% covers repairs, not interest. Authority: section 22(1).

quiz.concept: Self occupied house: no 30% deduction
quiz.q: Outside the new regime, Sunita lives in her own house, so its annual value is nil. During the year she spends Rs. 60,000 on repairs, and she also pays interest on a qualifying home loan. The Act allows 30% of annual value as a deduction. What deduction does she get for the repairs?
quiz.ok: None, because 30% of a nil annual value is nil, and actual repair costs are not deductible
no: 30% of the house’s expected rent, because the flat deduction covers repairs whether or not the house is let
The actual Rs. 60,000, because with a nil annual value there is no 30% figure to replace actual repairs
Rs. 60,000, but added to her interest and limited by the same cap that applies to interest
quiz.why: The 30% deduction is computed on annual value, so where annual value is nil it is nil too, and no other repair or maintenance deduction is allowed. Her only deduction is interest within the cap, which is why a self occupied house can show a loss but never a repairs deduction. Authority: sections 21(6) and 22; illustration in the notes.

quiz.concept: New regime: no set off against other heads
quiz.q: Under the new regime, Kabir has a salary of Rs. 15,00,000 and a loss of Rs. 1,20,000 from his let out flat, because the interest on his loan exceeds the flat’s income. Outside the new regime, up to Rs. 2,00,000 of such a loss could reduce his other income. How is the loss treated this year?
quiz.ok: It cannot reduce his salary, because the new regime bars set off of a house property loss against other heads
no: It reduces his salary in full, because the loss is within the Rs. 2,00,000 limit for other heads
It reduces his salary, because the new regime denies interest only on a self occupied house
No loss arises at all, because under the new regime interest on every house is disallowed
quiz.why: Under the new regime interest on a let out house is still deductible, so a loss can arise, but it cannot be set off against salary or any other head. The Rs. 2,00,000 set off against other heads is available only outside the new regime, and denying interest on a self occupied house is a separate restriction. Authority: sections 22, 109 and 202.

quiz.concept: Compensation on termination of an agency
quiz.q: An Indian company has been the sole selling agent in India of a foreign manufacturer for twelve years. The manufacturer ends the agency early and pays the company a lump sum as compensation. How is the lump sum treated?
quiz.ok: Business income, because the Act expressly charges compensation for ending an agency
no: A capital receipt outside the charge, because it compensates for the loss of a source of income
Taxable only to the extent it replaces the commission the agent would have earned this year
Capital gains, because the agency was a capital asset that the agent has given back to the manufacturer
quiz.why: Under general principles, compensation for losing an agency that forms part of the structure of the recipient’s business is a capital receipt; that was the view in Kettlewell Bullen. The Act overrides this for compensation received on the termination or modification of a management, agency or business contract and charges it as business income. So the ‘loss of a source’ answer states the old test, not the present law. Authority: section 26(2)(b); Kettlewell Bullen and Co. Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Non compete fee versus right to manufacture
quiz.q: On selling her business, a manufacturer receives two sums from the buyer: one for transferring to it her right to manufacture a product, and another for promising not to carry on a competing business for five years. How is each sum taxed?
quiz.ok: The non compete sum is business income; the sum for the right to manufacture is taxed as capital gains
no: Both are capital receipts outside the charge, since both compensate her for giving up her business for good
Both are business income, since both are paid to her under the agreement for the sale of her business
The non compete sum is a capital receipt; the sum for the right to manufacture is taxed as business income
quiz.why: The Act charges as business income any sum received for agreeing not to carry on an activity in relation to a business, but carves out a sum received for transferring the right to manufacture or carry on business, which is taxed as capital gains. The line is between accepting a restraint and parting with a right. Treating both sums alike misses that carve out. Authority: section 26(2)(h).

quiz.concept: Inventory converted into a capital asset
quiz.q: A builder holds flats as stock in trade. It converts one flat, which cost it Rs. 40 lakh and is now worth Rs. 60 lakh, into its own office. What is the tax consequence of the conversion?
quiz.ok: Its Rs. 60 lakh market value is treated as a business receipt, so the Rs. 20 lakh profit is taxed now
no: Nothing is taxed now; the whole gain is taxed as capital gains when the office is eventually sold
Nothing is taxed, because no one has paid the builder anything and only real income is taxed
The Rs. 20 lakh rise in value is taxed as capital gains at the date of conversion
quiz.why: When inventory is converted into a capital asset, the Act charges its fair market value as business income at the time of conversion; set against the flat’s cost, this taxes the Rs. 20 lakh profit that built up while it was trading stock. That profit cannot slip out of the business head merely because the flat changed character. The real income objection fails because the Act itself makes the value chargeable, and the charge does not wait for a later sale. Authority: section 26(2)(j).

quiz.concept: Hedging is not speculation
quiz.q: A copper wire manufacturer has contracts to supply wire at fixed prices. To guard against a rise in the price of the copper it needs for those contracts, it enters into forward contracts for copper, which it settles by paying or receiving the price difference without taking delivery. Are these speculative transactions?
quiz.ok: No; such hedging contracts are excluded, even though they are settled without delivery
no: Yes; every transaction settled otherwise than by actual delivery is speculative
Yes, but only the losses on them are speculative; any profits are ordinary business income
No; a transaction is speculative only if it is illegal or amounts to a wager
quiz.why: A speculative transaction is one settled otherwise than by actual delivery, and a speculation business is treated as distinct from any other business. The definition, however, excludes contracts for raw materials that a manufacturer makes to guard against price changes affecting its contracts to deliver its goods, so these hedges form part of its ordinary business. The ‘every non delivery contract’ answer ignores this exception. Authority: section 26(3); section 66(31).

quiz.concept: Isolated transaction as adventure in trade
quiz.q: A doctor who has never traded borrows heavily to buy 50 acres of farmland, divides it into plots, lays roads, advertises, and sells all the plots within a year. She argues that the profit cannot be business income because it came from a single transaction. Is she right?
quiz.ok: No; the borrowing, development and quick resale together show an adventure in the nature of trade
no: Yes; a single, isolated transaction can never amount to business, however profitable it turns out
Yes; land is by nature a capital asset, so any profit on it can only be a capital gain
No; but only because any profit on the resale of land is automatically business income
quiz.why: ‘Business’ includes an adventure in the nature of trade, so a single transaction can be business. The indicators are weighed together: an intention to resell at a profit when buying, the nature and quantity of the property, work done to improve or market it, and borrowed finance, and here all of them point to trade. The result is not automatic, though, because no single factor, such as the resale of land itself, is decisive. Authority: section 2(20); G. Venkataswami Naidu and Co. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: No single indicator is decisive
quiz.q: A salaried engineer buys a flat, partly with a bank loan, lives in it for six years, and then sells it at a profit. The Assessing Officer treats the profit as business income solely because the purchase was financed by borrowing. What is wrong with this reasoning?
quiz.ok: Borrowing is only one indicator, and the lack of any intention to resell outweighs it here
no: Nothing; borrowed finance on its own is enough to show that the flat was bought as stock in trade
A home can never be trading stock, so profit on selling one is always a capital gain
Only the period of ownership counts, and six years is long enough to rule out trade
quiz.why: Whether an isolated purchase and sale is an adventure in the nature of trade depends on all the indicators taken together: intention to resell at a profit when buying, the nature and quantity of the asset, work done to improve or market it, and financing. No single factor is decisive, so borrowing alone cannot turn a home bought to live in into trading stock. Equally, neither the kind of asset nor the period of holding settles the question on its own; a builder’s flats, for example, are trading stock. Authority: G. Venkataswami Naidu and Co. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Profits of an illegal business
quiz.q: A person carries on an unlicensed liquor trade, which is illegal. He argues that its profits cannot be taxed because the State cannot share in the proceeds of an unlawful activity. Which statement correctly states the law?
quiz.ok: The profits are taxable, but a penalty imposed for breaking the law is not deductible from them
no: The profits are not taxable, because the law cannot recognise or tax income from an unlawful source
The profits are taxable, and any penalties are deductible as a normal cost of carrying on that trade
The profits are taxable only because the trade is merely unlicensed; the profits of a crime would not be
quiz.why: Tax is charged on the profits of a business whether or not the business is lawful, so illegality of any kind does not take the profits out of the charge. But a penalty for breaking the law is not deductible, and expenditure for a purpose that is an offence or prohibited by law is expressly treated as not laid out for the business. Authority: CIT v. S.C. Kothari; Haji Aziz and Abdul Shakoor Bros. v. CIT; section 34(2)(a) and (3).

quiz.concept: Penalty versus contractual damages
quiz.q: A transport company pays (i) a fine imposed by the traffic authorities for overloading its trucks, and (ii) damages to a customer, under the terms of their contract, for delivering goods late. Which payment is deductible?
quiz.ok: Only the damages; a penalty for breaking the law is never a business expense
no: Both, because both were incurred in the course of running the transport business
Neither, because both are penalties that the company suffered for its own default in performance
Only the fine, because it is a statutory levy on the business, like a tax
quiz.why: A penalty for breaking the law is not deductible, and expenditure for a purpose that is an offence or prohibited by law is never treated as laid out for the business. Contractual damages are different: they are an ordinary commercial liability of carrying on the business and pass the general deduction test. The ‘both’ answer overlooks that breaking the law is not a business purpose. Authority: Haji Aziz and Abdul Shakoor Bros. v. CIT; section 34(2) and (3).

quiz.concept: Loss incidental to carrying on business
quiz.q: A firm’s cashier absconds with Rs. 3 lakh of the day’s cash collections, and the money cannot be traced. The firm claims a deduction for the loss. What is the correct view?
quiz.ok: Allowable as a trading loss, since handling cash through employees is part of the business
no: Allowable only as a capital loss, to be set off against the firm’s capital gains
Not allowable, because the firm did not voluntarily lay out the money as expenditure
Not allowable, because a loss caused by a crime can never be a business deduction
quiz.why: Business income is computed on commercial principles aimed at real profit, so a loss arising in the ordinary course of business, such as embezzlement by an employee, is allowed as a trading loss even though it is not expenditure laid out. The firm is the victim of the crime, not its author, so the rule against deducting penalties has no application. Authority: Badridas Daga v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Consistency across tax years
quiz.q: For ten years the tax department accepted that a society’s surplus was not business income. Nothing in its activities has changed, but a new officer now proposes to tax the surplus. Which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: Each year stands alone, but a long accepted position on unchanged facts needs good reason to disturb
no: The earlier assessments are res judicata, so the officer is absolutely barred from taking a different view
Each year is separate, so the officer is entirely free to change the position whenever he wishes to
The officer may change the position only after first reopening and revising all the earlier assessments
quiz.why: Res judicata does not strictly apply in tax, because each tax year is a separate unit of assessment. But consistency matters: where a position has been accepted for years and the facts are unchanged, it should not be reopened without good reason. Both ‘absolutely barred’ and ‘entirely free’ overstate the position. Authority: Radhasoami Satsang v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Enduring advantage makes expenditure capital
quiz.q: A cement company pays a lump sum for a twenty year lease of limestone quarries, and a further sum for the lessor’s promise not to let competitors quarry in the area during the lease. How are the two payments classified?
quiz.ok: Both are capital, because together they secure an enduring advantage for the business
no: Both are revenue, because limestone is the raw material consumed in making cement
The lease is capital, but the protection payment is revenue because it buys no physical asset
Both are revenue, because the advantage they secure ends when the lease expires
quiz.why: Expenditure made once and for all to bring into existence an asset or advantage of enduring benefit to the trade is ordinarily capital. A long quarry lease and protection from competition during it are part of the profit making structure, fixed capital kept to earn profit rather than raw material parted with. An advantage need not be physical or permanent to be enduring. Authority: Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT; British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. v. Atherton.

quiz.concept: Enduring benefit test is not conclusive
quiz.q: Under an industry agreement that fixes the hours for which each mill may work its looms, a jute mill buys some of another mill’s allotted loom hours, so that it can work more of the looms it already has. The benefit lasts for some years. Is the payment capital?
quiz.ok: No; it lets existing looms earn more without adding to the capital structure, so it is revenue
no: Yes; any advantage that lasts beyond the year is capital under the enduring benefit test
Yes; it buys a right from another mill, and the purchase of any right is capital
No; it is revenue only because every payment made to a competitor is an ordinary trading expense
quiz.why: The enduring benefit test is a guide, not a conclusive test. What matters is whether the advantage adds to the profit making structure or only lets the existing structure operate more efficiently or profitably; buying loom hours did the latter, so it was revenue although the benefit lasted. A payment to a competitor is not automatically revenue: protection against competition was capital where it secured an enduring advantage. Authority: Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Fixed and circulating capital
quiz.q: A car dealer and a taxi operator each buy ten new cars. Which statement best explains why the cost is revenue expenditure for the dealer but capital expenditure for the taxi operator?
quiz.ok: The dealer earns its profit by parting with the cars, the operator by keeping and using them
no: Cars are capital assets by nature, but the law gives car dealers a special concession for them
The dealer buys the cars with borrowed money, while the operator uses its own funds
Only traders may deduct the cost of goods; service businesses must always capitalise their purchases
quiz.why: The same asset can be circulating capital in one business and fixed capital in another. Circulating capital earns profit by being parted with, so the dealer’s cars are stock in trade and their cost is revenue; fixed capital earns profit by being kept, so the operator’s cars are part of its profit making structure and attract depreciation instead. Neither the source of funds nor the nature of the asset in the abstract decides. Authority: Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Know how for an existing product
quiz.q: A drug company pays for technical know how to improve production of an existing product. The Assessing Officer treats the payment as capital, reasoning that know how appears in the list of depreciable intangible assets. Is he right?
quiz.ok: No; it only helps the existing business run more efficiently, so the payment is revenue
no: Yes; anything that appears in the list of depreciable intangible assets must be capital expenditure
Yes; know how always brings an enduring benefit to the business, and that alone makes it capital
No; it is revenue only because know how can never be owned as an asset of the business
quiz.why: No single test decides whether expenditure is capital. Know how that only helps an existing business make an existing product more efficiently, without adding to the profit making structure, was held to be revenue. The depreciation list tells you how capital know how is relieved; it does not make every payment for know how capital. Authority: Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Residuary role of the general deduction
quiz.q: Which statement best describes how the general deduction fits into the scheme of business deductions?
quiz.ok: It is residuary: it covers revenue, non personal business expenditure not dealt with by the specific provisions
no: It is the primary provision, and the specific deductions merely illustrate what it already allows
It allows any expense debited in the profit and loss account, unless a specific disallowance applies to it
It also covers capital expenditure, provided it is laid out wholly and exclusively for the business
quiz.why: The Act first gives specific deductions, such as rent, repairs, employee welfare, bad debts and depreciation, and special deductions such as preliminary expenses. The general deduction then picks up other expenditure that is not covered by those provisions, is neither capital nor personal, and is laid out wholly and exclusively for the business, while the disallowances and timing rules apply across the whole scheme. An accounting debit is not enough, because every deduction must fit a provision and pass its tests. Authority: section 34(1); sections 35 to 37.

quiz.concept: Relief for capital and preliminary costs
quiz.q: Before starting business, a new Indian company incurs expenses of a kind specified as preliminary expenses, and also buys machinery. Which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: The machinery attracts depreciation, and the expenses are deducted in equal parts over a set period
no: Both are deducted in full under the general deduction, being laid out wholly for the business
Neither gets any relief, because capital expenditure can never be set against business income
The machinery is deducted in full when bought, and the preliminary expenses get no relief at all
quiz.why: Capital expenditure is not deductible under the general deduction, but the scheme relieves it in other ways. Machinery is a depreciable asset, so its cost is recovered through depreciation, while specified preliminary expenses incurred before commencement (or for an extension or new unit) are deducted in fifths over five years. The ‘no relief at all’ answer overlooks these routes. Authority: sections 33, 34(1) and 44.

quiz.concept: Wholly and exclusively is not necessarily
quiz.q: A retailer learns that heaters it sold, made by a supplier, have damaged some customers’ homes. Although it has no legal liability, it voluntarily compensates those customers to protect its reputation. Is the payment deductible?
quiz.ok: Yes; voluntary spending to protect the business qualifies, though no law required it
no: Yes, but only up to the profit it made on those heaters, since the outlay must earn that profit
No; a payment made without any legal obligation cannot be expenditure for the business
No; it is a charitable gesture, not expenditure incurred in carrying on the business
quiz.why: The general deduction asks whether the expenditure was laid out wholly and exclusively for the business, not whether it was legally necessary, so voluntary spending to preserve the goodwill of the business qualifies. Nor need it be tied to earning a particular profit: ‘for the purpose of the business’ is wider than ‘for earning profits’ and includes preserving and protecting the business. Authority: Sassoon J. David and Co. (P) Ltd. v. CIT; CIT v. Malayalam Plantations Ltd.

quiz.concept: Limits of the business purpose test
quiz.q: A company pays the estate duty due on the shares of its deceased shareholders and claims it as business expenditure, relying on the rule that ‘for the purpose of the business’ is wider than ‘for earning profits’. Is the claim sound?
quiz.ok: No; the duty relates to the shareholders’ estates, not to the company’s own business
no: Yes; any payment that keeps the company’s shareholders satisfied helps to preserve its business
Yes; the wider test covers every payment that the company is called upon to make
No; estate duty is a tax, and taxes can never be deducted from business income
quiz.why: ‘For the purpose of the business’ is wider than earning profits and includes carrying on, preserving and protecting the business, but it still needs a link with the company’s own business. Estate duty in respect of deceased shareholders’ shares was held to lack that link. The ‘taxes are never deductible’ reasoning is wrong, since taxes such as municipal taxes on business premises are deductible. Authority: CIT v. Malayalam Plantations Ltd.

quiz.concept: Commercial expediency and the businessman’s view
quiz.q: A company borrows at interest and lends part of the money interest free to its subsidiary, whose timely completion of a plant is vital to the company’s own supplies. The Assessing Officer disallows the proportionate interest, saying the company could have charged interest. What is the correct view?
quiz.ok: Deductible if lent for commercial expediency; the officer cannot substitute his own business judgement
no: Not deductible, because the borrowed money was not used in the company’s own business
Deductible only to the extent that the subsidiary itself pays interest to the company
Disallowed as an excessive payment to a related person, since the subsidiary is a related concern
quiz.why: Money borrowed and lent onward for commercial expediency, such as securing the company’s supplies through its subsidiary, is used for the purposes of the business. Whether the expediency exists is judged from the businessman’s point of view, and the Revenue cannot put itself in the businessman’s armchair. The related person rule does not fit, because the interest is paid to the lender, not to the subsidiary. Authority: S.A. Builders Ltd. v. CIT (Appeals).

quiz.concept: Benefits whose acceptance breaches rules
quiz.q: A drug company gives doctors free foreign trips to promote its medicines. The doctors’ professional conduct regulations forbid them to accept such gifts, but no rule forbids the company from giving them. The company argues that only the doctors broke a rule, so its own spending is a legitimate sales expense. Is the argument sound?
quiz.ok: No; the bar covers benefits whose acceptance breaches the recipient’s own conduct rules
no: Yes; the bar applies only where the giver itself commits an offence by giving
Yes; the doctors’ regulations bind only the doctors and cannot affect how the company is taxed
No; sales promotion spending is always capital, because it builds lasting brand goodwill
quiz.why: The Act treats as never laid out wholly and exclusively for the business any benefit or perquisite given to a person whose acceptance of it violates the law, rules or guidelines governing his conduct. The giver loses the deduction even though only the recipient’s rules are broken; this is the result reached for freebies to doctors, now stated expressly. Authority: section 34(3)(b); Apex Laboratories (P) Ltd. v. Deputy CIT.

quiz.concept: Outlays deemed not for business
quiz.q: Which of these outlays by a company can qualify for deduction under the general deduction?
quiz.ok: An advertisement in a trade journal to promote its products
no: An advertisement in a souvenir published by a political party
An amount paid to compound an offence under a tax law
Spending required of it by the corporate social responsibility rules of company law
quiz.why: Certain outlays are declared never to be wholly and exclusively for the business, whatever the commercial motive: expenditure for an offence or prohibited purpose, compounding an offence, settling notified contravention proceedings, corporate social responsibility spending under company law, and advertisement in political party publications. Ordinary trade advertising falls outside these bars. Legal compulsion does not rescue corporate social responsibility spending, because the bar is statutory. Authority: section 34(2) and (3).

quiz.concept: Employees’ provident fund contributions
quiz.q: An employer deducts provident fund contributions from its employees’ March salaries. It credits them to the fund in July, after the due date under the provident fund law but before the due date for filing its return. Under the current law, what is the position?
quiz.ok: Deductible for that year, because crediting the contributions by the due date of the return is now enough
no: Never deductible, because the employees’ money held in trust was not deposited by the fund law due date
Deductible only in the next year, under the actual payment rule, as it was paid after 31 March
Deductible only if the employer also pays the interest due for the delay under the fund law
quiz.why: Employees’ own contributions are their money, held by the employer in trust, and the deduction depends on crediting them to the employees’ accounts in time. Checkmate Services had required deposit by the due date under the fund law, but the Finance Act, 2026 substituted the provision so that credit by the due date of the return now suffices. The actual payment rule expressly does not apply to these contributions. Authority: sections 29(1)(e) and 37(6).

quiz.concept: Contributions to unapproved funds
quiz.q: A company voluntarily contributes to a staff welfare trust that is not a recognised or approved fund, and no law requires the contribution. It argues that voluntary spending for the business is deductible under the general deduction. Is it right?
quiz.ok: No; contributions to other funds or trusts are barred unless required by law
no: Yes; ‘wholly and exclusively’ does not mean ‘necessarily’, so voluntary staff welfare spending qualifies in full
Yes, but only up to the limit that would have applied to an approved fund
No; all staff welfare spending is capital, because it builds an enduring workforce
quiz.why: The Act allows employer contributions to recognised provident funds, approved superannuation and gratuity funds and the pension scheme within limits, and then provides that no other contribution to a fund or trust is deductible unless required by law. Because a specific provision deals with the matter, the general deduction, which covers only expenditure not dealt with by the specific provisions, cannot be used to get round it. The voluntary spending principle is sound in general but yields to the specific bar. Authority: section 29(3); section 34(1).

quiz.concept: Interest before an asset is first used
quiz.q: A company borrows Rs. 1 crore in April to buy a machine for its business. The machine is first put to use in October. How is the year’s interest on the loan treated?
quiz.ok: Interest from October is deductible; interest for the period before first use is not
no: All the year’s interest is deductible, because the loan was taken for the business
None of the interest is deductible, because the loan financed a capital asset
Interest before first use is deductible; interest after it is added to the machine’s cost
quiz.why: Interest on capital borrowed for the business is deductible even when the borrowing finances a capital asset, so the capital nature of the machine does not taint the interest. But interest for the period before an asset acquired with the loan is first put to use is excluded, as until then it relates to acquiring the asset rather than running the business. Authority: section 32.

quiz.concept: Tenant’s improvements to leased premises
quiz.q: A tenant running a restaurant in rented premises spends heavily to add a mezzanine floor, a permanent structural addition to the building. How is this cost treated?
quiz.ok: Capital, not a current repair, but the tenant may depreciate it as a building owned by him
no: Deductible in full as a current repair, because a tenant can never own the building he occupies
Neither deductible nor depreciable, because the tenant does not own the building it is part of
Deductible in equal parts over five years, in the same way as preliminary expenses for an extension
quiz.why: Current repairs to business premises are deductible, but a structural addition creates a new asset of enduring benefit and is capital expenditure. Depreciation normally requires ownership, yet improvements made by a tenant to a leased building for his business are treated as a building owned by him, so he recovers the cost through depreciation. Authority: sections 28 and 33(6).

quiz.concept: Goodwill is not depreciable
quiz.q: On buying a running business, a company pays separately for the seller’s goodwill and for a registered trademark. Under the 2025 Act, on which can it claim depreciation?
quiz.ok: Only the trademark: it is a listed intangible asset, while goodwill is expressly excluded
no: Both, because the Supreme Court has held goodwill to be a depreciable intangible asset
Neither, because only tangible assets such as buildings and machinery are depreciable
Only the goodwill, because a trademark is a legal right rather than a business asset
quiz.why: Depreciation extends to intangible assets such as know how, patents, copyrights, trademarks, licences, franchises and similar commercial rights, but the 2025 Act expressly excludes goodwill. Smifs Securities held goodwill depreciable under the earlier law, so relying on it today is an error. Authority: sections 2(17)(b) and 33(1)(b); CIT v. Smifs Securities Ltd.

quiz.concept: Sale of an asset from a block
quiz.q: A company’s plant and machinery block has a written down value of Rs. 20 lakh at the start of the year. During the year it sells one machine, originally bought for Rs. 8 lakh, for Rs. 5 lakh, and buys nothing new. The block continues. How is the sale reflected?
quiz.ok: Rs. 5 lakh is deducted from the block, and depreciation runs on the remaining Rs. 15 lakh
no: Rs. 8 lakh, the original cost, is deducted from the block, leaving Rs. 12 lakh for depreciation
The gain or loss against the machine’s own written down value is taxed or allowed separately
The block stays at Rs. 20 lakh, and the Rs. 5 lakh is taxed as business income
quiz.why: Depreciation is charged on the written down value of the block as a whole, not asset by asset. When an asset of the block is sold, its sale price, not its cost or its own book value, is deducted from the block (but not beyond the block’s value), and depreciation runs on what remains. No separate gain or loss is worked out for the machine while the block continues. Authority: section 41(1)(c).

quiz.concept: Actual cost of a depreciable asset
quiz.q: A manufacturer buys a machine for Rs. 10,00,000 plus GST of Rs. 1,80,000, for which it takes full input tax credit. It also receives a government subsidy of Rs. 2,00,000 towards the cost of the machine. What is the machine’s actual cost for depreciation?
quiz.ok: Rs. 8,00,000: the price less the subsidy, without the GST for which credit was taken
no: Rs. 11,80,000: the full amount paid to the seller, including the GST charged on the invoice
Rs. 9,80,000: the full amount paid to the seller, including GST, less the subsidy received
Rs. 10,00,000: the price alone, because the subsidy is dealt with separately as income
quiz.why: Actual cost is the cost the assessee really bears, so it is reduced by subsidies and by GST for which input credit is taken; otherwise the same cost would be relieved twice. Here Rs. 10,00,000 less the Rs. 2,00,000 subsidy gives Rs. 8,00,000, and the credited GST never enters the cost. Authority: section 39.

quiz.concept: Half rate depends on days of use
quiz.q: A machine bought on 10 May is, because of installation delays, first put to use on 15 January, before the tax year ends on 31 March. Only half the normal rate is allowed for an asset acquired and used for less than 180 days in the year. What depreciation is allowed this year?
quiz.ok: Half the normal rate, as it was used under 180 days, however long it was owned
no: The full rate, because the machine was owned for more than 180 days of the year
Half the rate now, with the other half added to next year’s depreciation allowance for it
No depreciation at all this year, because the machine stood idle for most of the year
quiz.why: The half rate turns on the period of use in the year of acquisition, not the period of ownership, so a machine used for under 180 days gets half the rate even if it was bought early in the year. There is no rule carrying the unused half forward to the next year; that kind of split belongs to additional depreciation, not normal depreciation. Authority: section 33(4).

quiz.concept: Compulsory depreciation and unabsorbed carry forward
quiz.q: A company’s business profits for the year, before depreciation, are Rs. 2 lakh, and the depreciation due for the year is Rs. 5 lakh. It has no other income. It decides not to claim depreciation this year, so that it can claim all of it when profits rise. What is the effect?
quiz.ok: Rs. 2 lakh is deducted anyway, and the other Rs. 3 lakh is carried forward without time limit
no: Nothing is deducted now, and the full Rs. 5 lakh can be claimed in whichever later year it chooses
Rs. 2 lakh is deducted anyway, but the other Rs. 3 lakh is lost, as no profit is left to absorb it
Rs. 2 lakh is deducted anyway, and the other Rs. 3 lakh may be carried forward for a few years only
quiz.why: Depreciation applies whether or not the assessee claims it, reversing the earlier view in Mahendra Mills that it was optional, so the company cannot hold it back for a better year. Depreciation that exceeds the year’s profits is not lost either: the unabsorbed Rs. 3 lakh is added to the next year’s allowance and carried forward without time limit. Authority: section 33(7) and (11).

quiz.concept: Scope of additional depreciation
quiz.q: A manufacturer acquires four assets during the year, each put to use for more than 180 days. Which one qualifies for additional depreciation?
quiz.ok: A new machine installed on the factory floor to expand production
no: A second hand machine bought from a factory abroad that has closed down
A new delivery truck for carrying finished goods to customers
New computers and copiers installed in the head office
quiz.why: Additional depreciation rewards fresh investment in new plant and machinery by a manufacturer or power undertaking. It is not available for second hand assets, office or residential installations, office appliances, road vehicles, ships and aircraft, or assets whose cost is fully deducted otherwise, so only the new factory machine qualifies. Authority: section 33(8) and (9).

quiz.concept: Ownership without registered title
quiz.q: A company has paid the full price for a factory building, taken possession and used it in its business all year, but the sale deed has not yet been registered. Can it claim depreciation on the building?
quiz.ok: Yes; dominion and use in its own right are ownership for depreciation, though title has not passed
no: No; depreciation is allowed only to the person who holds the registered legal title to the building
Yes, but only at half the normal rate until the sale deed is finally registered
No; until registration it is merely a tenant, and a tenant may claim only current repairs
quiz.why: Depreciation requires that the assessee own the asset, wholly or partly. ‘Owned’ is read practically: a person who has dominion over the asset and uses it in his own right is its owner for this purpose, though legal title has not passed. The half rate rule concerns assets used for less than 180 days, not incomplete title. Authority: section 33; Mysore Minerals Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Which debts can be bad debts
quiz.q: A cloth trader, who is not a money lender, writes off two irrecoverable amounts: (i) the price of cloth sold on credit to a customer, and (ii) a loan he made to a friend’s firm. Which can he deduct as a bad debt?
quiz.ok: Only (i), because only the sale price was taken into account in computing his income
no: Both, because both have been written off in his accounts as irrecoverable
Only (ii), because a loan is a debt in the strict sense and a trade receivable is not
Neither, unless he first proves that each debtor has become insolvent
quiz.why: Writing off is necessary but not sufficient: the debt must also have been taken into account in computing income of that or an earlier year, or represent money lent in the ordinary course of a banking or money lending business. The credit sale entered his income; the loan to a friend’s firm did neither. Proof of insolvency is not required once the debt is written off. Authority: section 31(2); TRF Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Write off without proving irrecoverability
quiz.q: A manufacturing company writes off a customer’s debt as irrecoverable in its accounts. The Assessing Officer refuses the deduction because the company has not shown that it sued the customer or that recovery is impossible. Is he right?
quiz.ok: No; a write off in the accounts suffices, and actual irrecoverability need not be proved
no: Yes; a bad debt is allowed only after all recovery proceedings have been exhausted
Yes; the officer must be satisfied that the debt actually became bad during the year
No, but the deduction is limited to the provision for doubtful debts made in earlier years
quiz.why: Before the 1989 amendment of the earlier law, the assessee had to show that the debt had actually become bad; since then it is enough that the debt is written off as irrecoverable in the accounts, provided the income or money lending condition is met. The 2025 Act keeps this requirement, so the officer cannot demand proof of recovery steps. Authority: section 31(2); TRF Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Provision is not a write off
quiz.q: Following accounting standards, a trading company debits Rs. 5 lakh to its profit and loss account as a provision for doubtful debts, leaving the debtors’ balances unchanged in its balance sheet. Can it deduct the Rs. 5 lakh?
quiz.ok: No; a provision is not a write off, and only a debt actually written off is deductible
no: Yes; business income is computed on commercial principles, and prudent accounting requires this provision
Yes, up to a fixed percentage of its total income, like any provision for doubtful debts
No; a debt can be written off for tax only after the debtor has been declared insolvent
quiz.why: Commercial principles yield to specific statutory rules, and the Act allows a bad debt only when it is written off as irrecoverable, expressly stating that a provision for bad and doubtful debts is not a write off. A provision leaves the debts intact on the asset side, even when accounting standards or a regulator require it. Only specified banks and financial entities get a limited deduction for provisions. Authority: section 31; Southern Technologies Ltd. v. Joint CIT.

quiz.concept: What counts as writing off
quiz.q: A bank debits bad debts to its profit and loss account and reduces the ‘loans and advances’ figure in its balance sheet by the same amount, but keeps the individual borrowers’ ledger accounts open to pursue recovery. Has it written off the debts?
quiz.ok: Yes; the debts no longer stand as assets in its accounts, though the ledger accounts stay open
no: No; each individual borrower’s account must first be closed before a debt counts as written off
No; keeping the accounts open shows it is only a provision, as recovery is still hoped for
Yes, but only if the bank also proves that each of the borrowers was insolvent at the year end
quiz.why: The question is whether the debt has actually been written off in the accounts. Debiting the profit and loss account and correspondingly reducing loans and advances in the balance sheet does that, even if the bank keeps individual accounts open to pursue recovery. A provision, by contrast, leaves the debts undiminished on the asset side. Authority: Vijaya Bank v. CIT.
