quiz.concept: Recovery of a debt already allowed
quiz.q: A trader’s customer owed Rs. 1,00,000. The trader wrote off Rs. 60,000 as bad and was allowed that deduction. Two years later the customer pays Rs. 55,000 in full settlement. What is the tax effect in the year of recovery?
quiz.ok: Rs. 15,000 is taxed as business income: the recovery beyond the Rs. 40,000 never deducted
no: Rs. 55,000 is taxed, because the whole recovery is a business receipt of that year
Nothing is taxed now; instead the earlier year is reopened to cut the deduction to Rs. 45,000
Rs. 15,000 is taxed, but only if the trader still carries on the same business
quiz.why: Rs. 40,000 of the debt was never deducted, so recovering up to that amount is not income; only the further Rs. 15,000 reverses a deduction already allowed. That excess is deemed business income of the year of recovery, and the charge applies even if the business has ceased. Had the trader recovered less than Rs. 40,000, the shortfall would have been deductible in the year of recovery. Authority: sections 31(2) and 38(1)(d) and (5).

quiz.concept: Disallowance for failure to deduct tax
quiz.q: A company pays a resident consultant fees of Rs. 4,00,000 during the year without deducting the tax that was deductible. It makes good the default by paying the tax in the following year. The Act disallows 30% of such a sum. What is the treatment?
quiz.ok: Rs. 1,20,000 is disallowed now and allowed in the following year, when the tax is paid
no: Rs. 1,20,000 is disallowed for good, as a penalty for the company’s failure to deduct tax
The whole Rs. 4,00,000 is disallowed this year and allowed when the tax is paid
Nothing is disallowed, because the fees were fully paid during the year, not left payable
quiz.why: For a sum payable to a resident on which tax was deductible but not deducted, or not paid by the due date of the return, 30% is disallowed and then allowed in the year the tax is paid, so the rule defers rather than forfeits the deduction. It applies to amounts paid during the year as well as amounts outstanding at the year end. The whole amount is disallowed only for payments to non residents or outside India. Authority: section 35(b); Palam Gas Service v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Partner interest: firm and partner matched
quiz.q: A partnership deed authorises interest on partners’ capital at 18% a year, which the firm pays. A firm may deduct interest to partners only up to 12% simple a year. How are the firm and the partners taxed on this interest?
quiz.ok: The firm deducts interest up to 12%; each partner is taxed as business income only on that part
no: The firm deducts the full 18%, because the deed authorises it, and each partner is taxed on 18%
The firm deducts interest up to 12%, but each partner is still taxed on the full 18% received
The firm deducts nothing, because payments to partners are only drawings of their own money
quiz.why: The Act caps the firm’s deduction for interest to partners and taxes the partner as business income only to the extent the payment was allowed to the firm. The disallowed 6% stays in the firm’s taxable profit, so the same amount is not taxed twice. The ‘drawings’ view ignores that the Act expressly allows such payments within limits. Authority: sections 26(2)(g) and 35(e).

quiz.concept: Conditions for deducting partner remuneration
quiz.q: A firm’s partnership deed, executed on 1 October, authorises remuneration to working partners. The firm pays remuneration for the whole year from 1 April to all three partners, one of whom only contributed capital and takes no part in the business. What can the firm deduct, subject to the statutory limits?
quiz.ok: Remuneration to the two working partners for the period from 1 October only
no: Remuneration to all three partners for the whole year, since the deed authorises remuneration
Remuneration to the two working partners for the whole year, since the deed now covers them
Nothing, because remuneration paid to its own partners is never deductible by a firm
quiz.why: A firm may deduct remuneration only if it is paid to working partners, is authorised by the partnership deed and does not relate to a period before the deed, and then only within the statutory limits. Remuneration to the partner who merely contributed capital, and remuneration for April to September, fail these conditions. Authority: section 35(e).

quiz.concept: Excessive payments to related persons
quiz.q: A company pays a director’s son Rs. 15 lakh a year as marketing manager. Comparable managers earn about Rs. 6 lakh, and his work brings no special benefit to the business. The company argues that the Revenue cannot sit in the businessman’s armchair. What is the correct treatment?
quiz.ok: Rs. 9 lakh, the excess over a reasonable amount, is disallowed; the reasonable Rs. 6 lakh is deductible
no: The whole Rs. 15 lakh is disallowed, because payments to relatives of directors are not deductible
The whole Rs. 15 lakh is deductible, because business judgement on salaries cannot be questioned
The excess can be disallowed only if the officer first proves that the appointment itself is a sham
quiz.why: Commercial expediency is ordinarily judged from the businessman’s point of view, but the Act makes a specific exception for payments to relatives, directors, partners and other specified persons. Where such a payment is excessive or unreasonable, judged by market value, the needs of the business and the benefit derived, only the excess is disallowed. The armchair principle cannot override this specific rule, and the reasonable part stays deductible. Authority: section 36(2) and (3).

quiz.concept: Cash payments above the daily limit
quiz.q: A trader pays a supplier Rs. 50,000 for goods in one day by a bearer cheque. The Act disallows expenditure where payments to a person in a day exceed Rs. 10,000 and are not made through the specified banking or online modes. How much is disallowed?
quiz.ok: The whole Rs. 50,000, because a bearer cheque is not one of the specified modes
no: Nothing, because the payment was made by cheque and not in cash
Rs. 40,000, the amount by which the payment exceeds the daily limit
Rs. 50,000 this year, but it is allowed next year once the cheque has cleared
quiz.why: The rule disallows the whole expenditure, not just the excess, when more than the limit is paid to one person in a day otherwise than through the specified modes: an account payee cheque or draft, electronic clearing through a bank account or another prescribed electronic mode. A bearer cheque can be cashed by anyone, so it leaves no better trail than cash. The rule aims to check unaccounted money, which is why it was upheld as constitutional. Authority: sections 36(4) and 66(32); Attar Singh Gurmukh Singh v. Income Tax Officer.

quiz.concept: Later cash payment of a deducted liability
quiz.q: In year 1 a trader buys goods on credit and deducts their cost. In year 2 he settles the Rs. 60,000 due by paying the supplier in cash on a single day, above the daily limit for cash payments. Why does the Act treat the Rs. 60,000 as his income of year 2?
quiz.ok: Because otherwise the cash rule could be avoided by deducting on credit and paying in cash later
no: Because a purchase that is unpaid at the end of year 1 is never deductible in year 1
Because cash received by a supplier is presumed to be the buyer’s own unexplained income of that year
Because settling a trade debt in a later year counts as a remission of the liability
quiz.why: The cash rule disallows expenditure paid in cash above the daily limit. If the expense was deducted in an earlier year on accrual and the liability is later paid in cash above the limit, the Act deems the payment to be income of the year of payment, closing the obvious route around the rule. Authority: section 36(4) to (8).

quiz.concept: Actual payment and the return due date
quiz.q: A company’s bonus to employees for the year ending 31 March is Rs. 2,00,000. It pays Rs. 1,50,000 in June, before the due date for filing its return, and Rs. 50,000 the following January, after that date. How is the bonus deducted?
quiz.ok: Rs. 1,50,000 for the year of the liability, and Rs. 50,000 in the year of payment
no: The whole Rs. 2,00,000 for the year of the liability, because the bonus accrued under mercantile accounting
The whole Rs. 2,00,000 in the following year, since none of it was paid by 31 March
Rs. 1,50,000 for the year of the liability; the Rs. 50,000 paid late is lost for good
quiz.why: Bonus is deductible only on actual payment, overriding the mercantile system, but payment after the year ends and by the due date of the return counts for the year of the liability. So Rs. 1,50,000 is allowed for that year, while the Rs. 50,000 paid after the due date is not lost but allowed in the year of actual payment. Authority: section 37; Allied Motors (P) Ltd. v. CIT; CIT v. Alom Extrusions Ltd.

quiz.concept: Interest converted into a loan
quiz.q: A company owes a year’s interest to a lender that is a specified financial entity. Instead of paying, it agrees with the lender to convert the overdue interest into a new term loan. Can the company deduct the interest?
quiz.ok: Not yet; conversion only defers the liability, so the interest is allowed when actually paid
no: Yes; the conversion discharges the interest debt, so it counts as payment in substance
Yes; the actual payment rule covers only taxes and duties, not interest owed to lenders
Never; interest once converted into a loan becomes part of the capital and cannot be deducted
quiz.why: Interest payable to specified financial entities is deductible only on actual payment. Converting it into a loan, debenture or similar instrument merely replaces one liability with another and is expressly not treated as payment, so the deduction waits until the interest is actually paid. Authority: section 37(1) and (4).

quiz.concept: Late payments to micro and small enterprises
quiz.q: A company buys goods in February from a micro enterprise and pays in June, after the time allowed by the small enterprises law but before the due date of its return. In which year is the cost of the goods deductible?
quiz.ok: In the year of payment, as the return due date grace does not extend to such late dues
no: In the year of purchase, because it was paid before the due date of the return
Never, because a late payment to a micro enterprise is disallowed permanently as a penalty for the delay
In the year of purchase, because the cost of goods is outside the actual payment rule
quiz.why: Amounts payable to micro and small enterprises beyond the time allowed under the small enterprises law are deductible only on actual payment. Unlike taxes, bonus and similar items, they do not get the grace of payment by the due date of the return, so a late payment made after the year ends is allowed only in the year of payment. Authority: section 37(1) to (3).

quiz.concept: Remission rule needs an earlier deduction
quiz.q: During the year a company’s creditors waive two debts: Rs. 5 lakh owed to a supplier for raw materials, whose cost the company had deducted, and a Rs. 50 lakh loan it had taken to buy machinery. Which waiver does the deemed profit rule for the remission of a trading liability catch?
quiz.ok: Only the supplier’s, because a deduction had been allowed for that liability but not for the loan
no: Both, because each waiver releases the company from a liability that arose in its business
Neither, because a creditor’s waiver is a voluntary gift, and a gift is a capital receipt
Both, provided that each creditor has also written the debt off in its own accounts
quiz.why: The deemed profit rule claws back an earlier deduction, so it taxes the remission or cessation of a trading liability only where a deduction was allowed for it. The raw material cost had been deducted, but nothing had been deducted for the machinery loan, so its waiver falls outside the rule, as was held for a waived loan taken to buy capital assets. A waiver is itself the creditor’s act, and nothing more is needed from the creditor. Authority: section 38(1)(a) and (2)(a); CIT v. Mahindra and Mahindra Ltd.

quiz.concept: Unilateral write back of liabilities
quiz.q: A company transfers to its profit and loss account old balances owed to trade creditors for purchases it deducted years ago. The creditors have not waived the debts. It argues that only a creditor can remit a debt, so the write back is not taxable. Is it right?
quiz.ok: No; the Act now expressly treats a unilateral write off in its own accounts as taxable
no: Yes; remission needs an act by the creditor, and a debtor’s own book entry changes nothing
Yes, at least until the debts become time barred, when they are taxed as remitted
No, but only the balances outstanding for more than three years are taxable
quiz.why: Under the earlier law, Sugauli Sugar Works held that remission needs the creditor’s act and cessation needs operation of law or a bilateral act, so a debtor’s own write back was not caught. Parliament reversed this, and the 2025 Act expressly covers a unilateral write off of a trading liability in the assessee’s accounts, where a deduction was allowed for it. Authority: section 38(1)(a)(i); CIT v. Sugauli Sugar Works (P) Ltd.

quiz.concept: Unclaimed trade deposits as trading receipts
quiz.q: A dealer collected security deposits from customers in the course of its trade. Years later, as no one has claimed them, it transfers the deposits to its profit and loss account. No deduction was ever allowed for them. Are they taxable?
quiz.ok: Yes; received in trade and now the dealer’s own money, they are taxable as trading receipts
no: No; deposits are loans, and loans are capital receipts that can never later become income
No; the deemed profit rule applies only to liabilities for which a deduction was allowed
Yes, but only as income from other sources, because the deposits are not the proceeds of sales
quiz.why: Deposits received in the course of trade were held taxable as trading receipts once, unclaimed, they were transferred to the profit and loss account and became the assessee’s own money. This rests on the trading character of the receipt, not on the deemed profit rule, so the absence of an earlier deduction does not help the dealer. Authority: CIT v. T.V. Sundaram Iyengar and Sons Ltd.

quiz.concept: Small business presumptive income
quiz.q: An eligible trader opts for the presumptive scheme. His turnover is Rs. 1.5 crore: Rs. 1 crore received through bank transfers during the year and Rs. 50 lakh in cash. The scheme deems 6% of turnover received by banking or online modes and 8% of other turnover to be income. His books show a profit of Rs. 7,50,000. What income is taxed under the scheme?
quiz.ok: Rs. 10,00,000: 6% of the bank receipts plus 8% of the cash receipts
no: Rs. 7,50,000: his actual profit, because the lower of the two figures is taken
Rs. 12,00,000: 8% of the whole turnover, because part of it was received in cash
Rs. 9,00,000: 6% of the whole turnover, because most of it came through banks
quiz.why: The scheme deems income at 6% of turnover received through banking or online modes and 8% of the rest, so Rs. 6,00,000 plus Rs. 4,00,000. The deemed figure is a floor, not a ceiling: the trader may declare a higher profit, but one who declares less and whose income exceeds the exemption limit must keep books and get them audited. Authority: section 58(2) and (3).

quiz.concept: Declaring profit below the presumptive figure
quiz.q: Two years after opting for the small business scheme, a trader’s actual profit falls well below the presumptive figure, and his total income exceeds the exemption limit. If he declares the lower actual profit, he cannot return to the scheme for the next five years. What else follows?
quiz.ok: He must keep books of account and have them audited, whatever the size of his turnover
no: Nothing more; being shut out of the scheme is the only consequence of declaring less
He must keep books, but needs no audit while his turnover is below the general audit threshold
He must still pay tax on the presumptive figure, whatever his books of account may show
quiz.why: Presumptive income is a floor, and a trader who declares less than it must, if his income exceeds the exemption limit, keep books and get them audited. The general turnover threshold for audit does not protect him, because this requirement turns on declaring less than the deemed profit, not on the size of the business. Once he declares lower profit and supports it with audited books, he is taxed on that profit rather than the deemed figure. Authority: section 58(3), (7) and (8); sections 62 and 63.

quiz.concept: No further deductions against presumptive income
quiz.q: An architect, whose profession qualifies for the presumptive scheme for professionals, has gross receipts of Rs. 40 lakh. The scheme deems 50% of gross receipts to be income. She wants to deduct Rs. 3 lakh of depreciation on her equipment and Rs. 2 lakh of staff salaries from that figure. What is her income from the profession under the scheme?
quiz.ok: Rs. 20,00,000: the deemed figure stands, and no further deductions are allowed against it
no: Rs. 15,00,000: the deemed figure less both the depreciation and the salaries
Rs. 17,00,000: the deemed figure less depreciation, which applies whether or not claimed
Rs. 18,00,000: the deemed figure less the salaries, since staff costs are always deductible
quiz.why: Under the presumptive scheme the deemed income, here 50% of Rs. 40 lakh, is final: no further deductions or losses are allowed against it. Depreciation is treated as already allowed when computing written down value, so the ‘depreciation is compulsory’ argument gives no extra deduction. Authority: section 58(4) and (6).

quiz.concept: Written down value after leaving the scheme
quiz.q: A small trader who used the presumptive scheme for three years owns a delivery van. He now leaves the scheme and computes his profits from his books. What written down value does he use for the van?
quiz.ok: Its cost reduced as if depreciation had been allowed for each of the presumptive years
no: Its full original cost, because no depreciation was actually claimed in those years
Its market value on the day he leaves the scheme, as the scheme’s deemed starting point
Nil, because the presumptive income is deemed to have covered the van’s entire cost
quiz.why: No further deductions are allowed against presumptive income, but depreciation is treated as having been allowed for computing written down value. On leaving the scheme the trader therefore starts from the reduced value and cannot claim depreciation on the full cost again, since the presumptive income is taken to have absorbed it. Authority: section 58(4) and (6).

quiz.concept: Presumptive income of goods carriages
quiz.q: A transporter owns three goods carriages throughout the year: two heavy goods vehicles of 15 tons gross vehicle weight each and one light goods vehicle. Its freight receipts are Rs. 40 lakh. Under the scheme for goods carriages, income is Rs. 1,000 per ton of gross vehicle weight a month for each heavy goods vehicle and Rs. 7,500 a month for each other vehicle. What is the presumptive income?
quiz.ok: Rs. 4,50,000: presumed vehicle by vehicle for each month, whatever the freight earned
no: Rs. 3,20,000: 8% of the freight receipts, as for other small businesses
Rs. 2,70,000: Rs. 7,500 a month for each of the three vehicles
Rs. 3,60,000: the two heavy vehicles only, as light vehicles are outside the scheme
quiz.why: For an assessee owning not more than ten goods carriages, income is presumed per vehicle for each month: Rs. 1,000 per ton of gross vehicle weight for a heavy goods vehicle and Rs. 7,500 for any other. Here 2 × 15 × 1,000 × 12 = Rs. 3,60,000, plus 7,500 × 12 = Rs. 90,000, and the freight receipts do not enter the presumptive figure. Authority: section 58.

quiz.concept: Who must keep books of account
quiz.q: Which of these persons must maintain books of account even though their income is modest?
quiz.ok: A newly qualified architect in her first year of practice
no: A small grocer whose income and turnover have always stayed below the thresholds
A shopkeeper below the thresholds who declares the full presumptive income
A salaried employee who also earns a little interest on bank deposits
quiz.why: Persons in specified professions, such as legal, medical, engineering, architecture and accountancy, must keep books whatever their income. Others carrying on business or profession need to do so only if their income or turnover crossed the thresholds in any of the three preceding years, or if they declare less than the presumptive income. Only the architect falls within the first category, and none of the others meets the second. Authority: section 62.

quiz.concept: Cash test for the higher audit threshold
quiz.q: A business has a turnover of Rs. 6 crore. Audit is required above Rs. 1 crore of turnover, raised to Rs. 10 crore where cash receipts and cash payments are each within 5% of the total. Its cash payments are 2%. Its receipts in currency notes are 3%, and a further 4% came by bearer cheques. Is audit required?
quiz.ok: Yes; bearer cheques count as cash, making cash receipts 7%, so the Rs. 1 crore threshold applies
no: No; its receipts in currency notes are only 3%, so the higher Rs. 10 crore threshold applies
No; its cash payments are within 5%, and that alone is enough for the higher threshold
Yes; all cheque receipts count as cash for this test, so the ordinary threshold applies
quiz.why: The higher threshold is for businesses that are almost cashless, so cash receipts and cash payments must each stay within 5%. For this purpose a cheque or draft that is not account payee counts as cash, so receipts in cash are 7% and the ordinary Rs. 1 crore threshold applies. Authority: section 63.

quiz.concept: Permanent versus timing disallowances
quiz.q: In computing business income, a company adds back: income tax; a cash payment above the daily limit; 30% of fees paid to a resident without deducting tax; bonus paid after the due date of the return; and corporate social responsibility expenditure. Which two of these items will be allowed as deductions in a later year?
quiz.ok: The 30% of the fees, when the tax is paid, and the late bonus, when it is paid
no: The income tax and the corporate social responsibility expenditure, once each has been paid
The cash payment, once later payments are made by cheque, and the income tax
The late bonus, when it is paid, and the corporate social responsibility spending, once the project is complete
quiz.why: Some items added back are only timing differences: the disallowance for failure to deduct tax reverses in the year the tax is paid, and bonus paid after the due date of the return is allowed in the year of payment. Others are permanent: income tax is never deductible, the cash payment disallowance is not reversed, and corporate social responsibility spending is declared never to be for the business. Authority: sections 34(2), 35, 36(4) and 37; worked illustration.

quiz.concept: From accounting profit to business income
quiz.q: A trading company’s net profit of Rs. 15,00,000 is after debiting book depreciation of Rs. 2,00,000 and crediting dividend income of Rs. 50,000. Depreciation under the Act is Rs. 2,80,000. Ignoring other adjustments, what is its business income?
quiz.ok: Rs. 13,70,000: book depreciation added back, the Act’s depreciation deducted, and the dividend excluded
no: Rs. 14,20,000: depreciation adjusted, but the dividend kept because it was credited in the accounts
Rs. 15,00,000: the audited net profit, since book depreciation is a genuine business expense
Rs. 16,50,000: book depreciation added back and the dividend excluded, with no other depreciation
quiz.why: The Act substitutes its own depreciation, computed on the written down value of each block, for the accounting charge, so book depreciation is added back and tax depreciation deducted. Dividend is chargeable under income from other sources, not as business income, so it is taken out of the business computation. Rs. 15,00,000 + 2,00,000 − 2,80,000 − 50,000 = Rs. 13,70,000. Authority: worked illustration; section 92(2)(a).

quiz.concept: Owner’s residential letting is house property income
quiz.q: A company’s main business, under its objects, is building residential flats and letting them out on rent. It owns the flats it lets. Under which head is the rent taxed?
quiz.ok: House property, because letting a residential house by its owner is kept out of business income
no: Business income, because letting out the flats is the main business in the company’s objects
Whichever head the company chooses, since the income fits the description of both heads
Business income, because a company cannot have income under the house property head
quiz.why: The Act expressly provides that income from letting a residential house, or part of one, by its owner is not business income and is chargeable only as income from house property. So even where letting is the company’s main business, the rent from residential flats it owns falls under house property. The heads are not a matter of choice, and a company can have house property income like any other owner. Authority: section 26(4).

quiz.concept: Business benefits in kind are taxable
quiz.q: A car dealer reaches its annual sales target, and as a reward the manufacturer gives it a new car, which the dealer keeps for use by its staff. No money changes hands. Is the value of the car taxable as business income?
quiz.ok: Yes; the value of a benefit arising from the business is taxable, though it comes in kind
no: No; the dealer received no money, and only receipts in money can be business income
No; the car is a capital asset, so its value is taxed only when the dealer sells it
No; it is a gift from the manufacturer, which is a capital receipt outside the charge
quiz.why: The Act charges as business income the value of any benefit or perquisite arising from business, whether or not it is convertible into money. The car rewards the dealer’s trading performance, so it arises from the business, and its value is taxed when received rather than on a later sale. Calling it a gift does not change its character as an incentive earned in the course of trade. Authority: section 26(2)(f).

quiz.concept: Plant is judged by its function
quiz.q: A company that makes machine tools buys a set of technical drawings and designs, which its engineers use as working tools in manufacturing its products. The Assessing Officer refuses depreciation, saying that plant means machinery and apparatus with a mechanical function, not paper. Is he right?
quiz.ok: No; plant is judged by its function, and things used as tools to carry on the business qualify
no: Yes; plant is confined to machinery and apparatus that perform some mechanical operation
Yes; drawings and designs are mere records of information, which cannot be depreciated
No; but only because the Act lists drawings and designs among its examples of plant
quiz.why: ‘Plant’ is read by function: it includes any apparatus used to carry on the business, other than stock in trade, so technical drawings and designs used as tools of the trade were held to be plant. The Act’s list of examples, such as ships, vehicles, books and scientific apparatus, is inclusive and does not mention drawings, so it is the functional test that decides. Authority: section 66(17); Scientific Engineering House (P) Ltd. v. CIT.

quiz.concept: Partial business use allows a fair proportion
quiz.q: A doctor uses her car 70% of the time for visiting patients and 30% for family outings. How is depreciation on the car treated?
quiz.ok: Only a fair proportion is allowed, reflecting the share of the car’s use for her profession
no: None is allowed, because the car is not used wholly and exclusively for her profession
All of it is allowed, because the car is used in her profession and depreciation is compulsory
All of it is allowed, but the 30% private use is taxed as a perquisite of her profession
quiz.why: Depreciation requires use for the business or profession, but where an asset is used only partly for it, the Act restricts the deduction to a fair proportion determined having regard to that use. So the private use does not forfeit the whole deduction, and the compulsory nature of depreciation does not extend it to the private share. Authority: section 33(1) and (3)(b).

quiz.concept: Bonus paid in place of dividend
quiz.q: A private company whose employees are also its only shareholders pays them a large ‘bonus’ each year, fixed in proportion to their shareholdings, instead of declaring a dividend. Can the company deduct the bonus?
quiz.ok: No; a bonus that would otherwise have reached them as profits or dividend is not deductible
no: Yes; bonus paid to employees for their services is a deductible business expense
Yes, but only in the year in which it is actually paid, under the rule for employee bonus
No; payments to employees who are also shareholders can never be deducted by a company
quiz.why: Bonus or commission to employees is deductible only if it would not otherwise have been payable to them as profits or dividend. A ‘bonus’ fixed by shareholding and paid in place of a dividend is a distribution of profit in disguise, so it fails this test whatever it is called. Genuine bonus for services remains deductible even when the employee is also a shareholder. Authority: section 32(a).

quiz.concept: Bank write offs beyond the provision
quiz.q: A bank has been allowed deductions for its provision for bad and doubtful debts, and that provision account now has a credit balance of Rs. 50 lakh. This year it writes off irrecoverable loans of Rs. 80 lakh against the provision. How much can it deduct as bad debts this year?
quiz.ok: Rs. 30 lakh, the part of the write off that exceeds the provision already allowed
no: Rs. 80 lakh, because a write off is deductible in full whatever provision was made earlier
Nothing, because a bank’s bad debts are relieved only through its provision deduction
Rs. 50 lakh, the provision balance, with the remaining Rs. 30 lakh carried forward
quiz.why: Banks may deduct a provision for bad and doubtful debts within limits, so allowing their write offs in full as well would relieve the same loss twice. The Act therefore allows a write off only to the extent it exceeds the credit balance in the provision, here Rs. 80 lakh less Rs. 50 lakh. Ordinary traders get no deduction for a provision and deduct only what they write off. Authority: section 31(1) and (2).

cards.f: May a taxpayer arrange his affairs so as to pay less tax?
cards.b: Yes. A person may arrange his affairs so that the tax payable is less than it would otherwise be: payments to a gardener under a deed of covenant, instead of wages, were held deductible. The arrangement must be genuine and actually carried out. — IRC v. Duke of Westminster

cards.f: Does the freedom to plan one’s taxes cover a colourable device?
cards.b: No. Colourable devices cannot be part of tax planning. A scheme in which buyers paid excise duty directly to the authorities, only so that it would not form part of the seller’s turnover for sales tax, was rejected. — McDowell and Co. v. Commercial Tax Officer

cards.f: Is treaty shopping illegal in itself?
cards.b: No. Using a tax treaty as it stands is legitimate tax planning; a CBDT circular allowing Mauritius residents to claim treaty benefits was upheld. Colourable devices remain impermissible. — Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan

cards.f: When may the Revenue disregard a holding structure used for an offshore deal?
cards.b: Only if it is a sham or colourable device; the transaction is looked at as a whole. A sale between non-residents of shares in a foreign company holding an Indian business was not taxable under the old law as it then stood. Parliament responded, and GAAR now governs avoidance. — Vodafone International Holdings v. Union of India

cards.f: On the stricter view, what link must a fee have with the services it pays for?
cards.b: A close and reasonable relationship: a good and substantial portion of the fee must be shown to be spent for the special benefit of the payers. — Kewal Krishan Puri v. State of Punjab

cards.f: Must a fee match the cost of services exactly, or benefit each payer personally?
cards.b: Neither. A broad and general correlation between the fee and the services is enough, and the services may benefit the payers as a class. — Sreenivasa General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh

cards.f: Does calling a levy a “licence fee” make it a fee?
cards.b: No. The label does not decide the nature of a levy. A “licence fee” for which no service was rendered was, in substance, a tax. — Corporation of Calcutta v. Liberty Cinema

cards.f: Can a “cess” be a fee rather than a tax?
cards.b: Yes, if it has the character of a fee. A cess on mine owners, credited to a fund for developing the mining areas that benefited them, was held to be a fee. — Hingir Rampur Coal Co. v. State of Orissa

cards.f: Is royalty paid under a mining lease a tax?
cards.b: No. Royalty is contractual consideration for the right to extract minerals, not a tax. The earlier view that royalty is a tax was overruled on this point, and the States’ power to tax mineral rights is not taken away by the central mining law. — Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India (overruling India Cement)

cards.f: What makes a levy a tax rather than any other payment to the State?
cards.b: It is compulsory, imposed by law, raised for public purposes, carries no quid pro quo, and is enforceable through machinery to assess, collect and punish evasion. The absence of a direct return is what separates a tax from a fee or a price. (Shirur Mutt)

cards.f: Which four components must every tax have, and what if one is uncertain?
cards.b: The taxable event, the person liable, the rate and the measure to which the rate applies. If any is uncertain, the levy fails. In income tax: earning total income in a tax year; every person; rates from the Finance Act or the Act itself; total income computed under the Act. (Govind Saran Ganga Saran)

cards.f: Distinguish the impact, incidence and effects of a tax.
cards.b: Impact: the immediate burden on whoever pays the Government. Incidence: where the burden finally rests, on someone who cannot pass it on. Effects: wider consequences on prices, production, savings and distribution. In GST the supplier bears the impact and the consumer the incidence.

cards.f: What decides how far a tax can be shifted?
cards.b: Elasticity: the more inelastic side bears more. Market structure: market power affects how far a seller can pass the tax on. Time: shifting is easier in the long run, as supply adjusts. Coverage: a tax on all close substitutes is harder to escape. A tax on an asset may also be capitalised into a lower price.

cards.f: What makes a levy a fee rather than a tax?
cards.b: A fee pays for a special service to the payers, accepted willingly or unwillingly, and is meant to meet its cost. A broad correlation is enough; a regulatory fee needs no strict quid pro quo. Earmarking is a sign, not a condition, since all revenue goes to the Consolidated Fund. Substance, not label, decides.

cards.f: Is a cess a tax or a fee, and why does the answer matter?
cards.b: A cess is a levy for a specific purpose, usually added to an existing tax. It is normally a tax, but a fee if it has a fee’s character. A specific-purpose cess stays outside the pool shared with the States, and a cess on income tax counts as part of the tax, so it is not deductible.

cards.f: Evasion, avoidance and planning: where are the lines?
cards.b: Evasion: illegal non-payment by concealment or fraud, punished by penalty and prosecution. Planning: arranging affairs within the law and its purpose, such as claiming a deduction. Avoidance: using the letter of the law to defeat its purpose, often by artificial arrangements, now met by the General Anti-Avoidance Rule.

cards.f: What are Adam Smith’s four canons, and how does the 2025 Act reflect them?
cards.b: Equality: progressive slabs tax by ability. Certainty: a single tax year and Tables make the amount, time and manner clear. Convenience: tax is deducted from salary at source. Economy: collection should cost little and harm productive activity as little as possible.

cards.f: Benefit theory or ability to pay: on which does income tax rest?
cards.b: Ability to pay: people contribute according to their capacity, not according to the benefit they receive from the State (the benefit theory). Sacrifice theories (equal, proportional or minimum sacrifice) explain ability to pay; minimum sacrifice supports steep progression.

cards.f: Progressive, proportional, regressive or degressive: how do you tell them apart?
cards.b: Look at tax as a share of income. Progressive: the share rises with income, as under the slabs. Proportional: one rate, so the share stays constant. Regressive: the share falls as income rises, as with a uniform tax on necessities. Degressive: the rate rises up to a point, then stays flat.

cards.f: Does a power to legislate on a subject include a power to tax it?
cards.b: No. Taxing entries in the Seventh Schedule are separate from general entries, so a tax needs a taxing entry (or, for Parliament, the residuary power). A State cannot tax a subject merely because it may regulate it. — M.P.V. Sundararamier and Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh

cards.f: How could Parliament levy a wealth tax that counts agricultural land?
cards.b: A tax on net wealth is not a tax on lands and buildings, which is a State subject. As no other entry covered it, Parliament could levy it under its residuary power. — Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon

cards.f: Are GST Council recommendations binding on legislatures?
cards.b: No. They are persuasive, because Parliament and the State Legislatures have simultaneous power over GST. Indian federalism is a dialogue involving both cooperation and contestation. — Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd.

cards.f: Can a uniform tax violate equality?
cards.b: Yes, if it treats unequals as equals. A flat land tax on all lands, productive or barren, with no machinery for assessment or objections, was struck down and also held confiscatory. — Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala

cards.f: Are the procedural provisions of a tax law tested for equality?
cards.b: Yes. Subjecting some persons to a harsher procedure, when they could equally be dealt with under the normal procedure, is discriminatory. — Suraj Mall Mohta and Co. v. A.V. Visvanatha Sastri

cards.f: How closely do courts scrutinise economic legislation for equality?
cards.b: With greater latitude than laws affecting civil rights, because economic choices are complex. A scheme giving immunity to people who invested unaccounted money in special bearer bonds was upheld. — R.K. Garg v. Union of India

cards.f: May the legislature single out a class, such as expensive hotels, for a tax?
cards.b: Yes. The legislature has greater freedom of classification in taxation; a tax on expenditure in hotels with high room charges was upheld. — Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Association of India v. Union of India

cards.f: When may a court depart from the literal words of a taxing provision?
cards.b: When a literal reading would defeat the provision’s purpose and produce absurd results. An anti-understatement rule that would have taxed honest sellers on notional consideration was confined to cases of actual understatement, relying on its object and the Finance Minister’s speech. — K.P. Varghese v. Income Tax Officer

cards.f: What does the “authority of law” for a tax require?
cards.b: A valid law by a competent legislature, consistent with fundamental rights, for both the levy and the collection. Rules must stay within the parent Act, and money collected without authority can be recovered. It is a constitutional, not a fundamental, right, so it is usually enforced in the High Court. (Article 265)

cards.f: Why do the States worry when the Union raises more through cesses and surcharges?
cards.b: Union List taxes are shared through the divisible pool, except surcharges, cesses for specific purposes and certain assigned duties. More cesses and surcharges mean the States get a smaller share of total Union revenue, even if their percentage of the pool is unchanged. (Articles 270 and 271)

cards.f: What does the Finance Commission recommend, and is it binding?
cards.b: Vertical devolution (the States’ share of the pool), horizontal devolution (division among States), principles for grants in aid, measures to supplement Panchayats and Municipalities, and matters the President refers. Its advice is not binding but is laid before Parliament with a memorandum of action taken. (Articles 280 and 281)

cards.f: Finance Commission or NITI Aayog: which shapes the flow of tax money to States?
cards.b: The Finance Commission: a constitutional body recommending formula-based sharing of taxes and grants for an award period. NITI Aayog: an executive think tank set up by Cabinet resolution; it advises on policy, ranks States and promotes cooperative federalism, but transfers no funds.

cards.f: How is a charging provision read?
cards.b: Strictly: there is no equity about a tax, and no tax is imposed by inference or analogy. The charge must be complete; if the computation cannot work, the charge fails, and only the legislature can fill the gap, as it later did for self-generated goodwill. Only genuine ambiguity favours the assessee. (Cape Brandy; A.V. Fernandez; Srinivasa Setty; Vegetable Products)

cards.f: How are exemptions and incentive provisions read?
cards.b: Eligibility is tested strictly: the claimant bears the burden, and ambiguity in an exemption favours the Revenue (Dilip Kumar). Once he qualifies, the provision is applied fairly, and an incentive meant to promote growth is read liberally to advance its object (Bajaj Tempo).

cards.f: Can a tax law be retrospective, and when is it presumed to be?
cards.b: It can be: the Constitution bars only retrospective criminal laws, though a long or harsh retrospective period bears on reasonableness (Rai Ramkrishna). But a provision imposing a new burden is presumed prospective unless made retrospective expressly or by necessary implication; truly clarificatory or curative provisions may reach back (Vatika Township).

cards.f: “Parliament defines agricultural income, but the States tax it.” How does that work?
cards.b: The Constitution gives agricultural income the meaning it has under the Indian income-tax law. That definition fixes the boundary: the Union taxes other income, and the States tax agricultural income. Because changing the definition moves the boundary, a Bill varying it needs the President’s recommendation. (Articles 366(1) and 274; Entry 82 of List I; Entry 46 of List II)

cards.f: Can a tax on newspapers violate the freedom of the press?
cards.b: Yes, if it is heavy enough to curtail circulation. Newspapers are not immune from taxation, and a tax is not normally an unreasonable restriction, but one that cripples circulation can violate the freedom of speech and expression. — Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India

cards.f: Does a non-discriminatory State tax offend the freedom of trade throughout India?
cards.b: No. Non-discriminatory taxes do not offend the freedom of trade, and the compensatory-tax test was rejected. What remains barred is discrimination against goods from other States. — Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana

cards.f: Can Parliament make tax laws that operate outside India?
cards.b: Yes, for matters that have a nexus with India. A law is not invalid merely because it operates outside India, but Parliament cannot legislate on matters with no such nexus. This supports deemed-accrual rules such as business connection and significant economic presence. — GVK Industries Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer

cards.f: Cap on profession tax (Article 276)
cards.b: Rs. 2,500 a year per person.

cards.f: States’ share of the divisible pool (Sixteenth Finance Commission)
cards.b: 41% for 2026 to 2031, accepted by the Union.

cards.f: Fifteenth Finance Commission criteria for distribution among States
cards.b: Income distance 45%, population 15%, area 15%, forest and ecology 10%, demographic performance 12.5%, tax and fiscal efforts 2.5%.

cards.f: Does a receipt escape being income because the statutory definition of “income” does not list it?
cards.b: No. The definition says income “includes” the listed items, so it enlarges the ordinary meaning without cutting it down: anything that is income in the ordinary sense is income even if unlisted, as a prize won in a motor rally was. — CIT v. G.R. Karthikeyan

cards.f: How widely is the word “income” read in a legislative entry that empowers Parliament to tax it?
cards.b: In its widest sense. Words in a legislative entry are read broadly, so “income” there covers capital gains, and Parliament could tax them as income. — Navinchandra Mafatlal v. CIT

cards.f: When is compensation for giving up part of a business a capital receipt rather than a revenue receipt?
cards.b: When it replaces a source of income, such as a capital asset forming part of the profit making structure given up outside the ordinary course of business, rather than income from a source that continues. Agency termination compensation is now taxed by statute, but the test survives. — Kettlewell Bullen and Co. Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: An agent gives up part of its commission before the year ends. Is the part given up taxable, and on what principle?
cards.b: No. Income tax is levied on real, not hypothetical, income: if income does not really result, there is no tax, even if a book entry shows it. Only the reduced commission was taxable. — CIT v. Shoorji Vallabhdas and Co.

cards.f: Can the real income theory prevent tax on interest that has accrued but may never be recovered?
cards.b: No. The theory cannot override the statutory scheme: interest that had accrued to the bank under the mercantile system was taxable though credited to a suspense account, the remedy being a bad debt deduction if the loan is later lost. — State Bank of Travancore v. CIT

cards.f: Under the mercantile system, are charges that customers dispute and never pay real income?
cards.b: No. Enhanced charges that consumers disputed and never paid did not result in real income, even under the mercantile system. — Godhra Electricity Co. Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: Distinguish diversion by overriding title from application of income.
cards.b: Diversion: an obligation attaches to the source, so the amount never becomes the assessee’s income and is not taxed in his hands. Application: the income first becomes his and he is then obliged to pay it away, so it is taxed in his hands. Test: did it, in truth, ever reach him as his income?

cards.f: When does a maintenance obligation divert income at source, so that it is not the payer’s income?
cards.b: When it is charged on the source, as where a decree charged maintenance on the estate, so the amount never becomes the assessee’s income. — Raja Bejoy Singh Dudhuria v. CIT

cards.f: Does a court decree to pay maintenance, by itself, divert the payer’s income at source?
cards.b: No. If the obligation is not charged on his income or property, the income reaches him first and paying it is an application of income. The true test: did the amount, in truth, never reach him as his income? — CIT v. Sitaldas Tirathdas

cards.f: A partner assigns part of his share of the firm’s profits to a trust. Diversion or application, and why?
cards.b: Application. An assignment operates only after the share has become his income, so the assigned part remains his income and is not diverted to the trust at source. — CIT v. Sunil J. Kinariwala

cards.f: Why is a genuine mutual surplus not income, and where has the Act overridden that?
cards.b: A person cannot make a profit out of himself, so a surplus that can only be spent on or returned to the contributors is not income. But the Act taxes mutual and cooperative insurance profits, banking by cooperative societies with members, and trade or professional associations’ income from specific services to members.

cards.f: What three conditions must a body satisfy to claim mutuality?
cards.b: (1) Complete identity between contributors and participants; (2) actions in furtherance of the association’s mandate; (3) no scope for profiteering from a fund that can only be spent on or returned to them. Interest on deposits with member banks failed: the money left the closed circle. — Bangalore Club v. CIT

cards.f: Can a club that trades with the public claim mutuality for its surplus?
cards.b: No. A club conducting races as a business for members and non members alike lacks identity between contributors and participants, so it cannot claim mutuality. — CIT v. Royal Western India Turf Club Ltd.

cards.f: When is a club’s surplus outside income under the doctrine of mutuality?
cards.b: When the club provides facilities only to its members and any surplus can be used only for them: a person cannot make a profit out of himself. — Chelmsford Club v. CIT

cards.f: Distinguish income that “accrues” from income that is “received”. Can the same income be taxed on both?
cards.b: It accrues when the right to receive it vests, so a debt is due; it is received when it reaches the assessee. Income taxed on accrual is not taxed again on receipt, and income accruing abroad is not received in India merely because it appears in a balance sheet prepared here.

cards.f: When does income accrue, and when is it too early to say that it has?
cards.b: When the assessee acquires a right to receive it, so that it becomes a debt due to him. Commission payable only at the end of the year had not accrued to agents who transferred their agency during the year. — E.D. Sassoon and Co. Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: Is crediting a non resident’s commission in an Indian company’s books a receipt in India?
cards.b: No. A book credit is not receipt. Commission for services rendered outside India, credited in Indian books, was neither received nor accrued in India. — CIT v. Toshoku Ltd.

cards.f: When are interest, royalty and fees for technical services deemed to accrue in India?
cards.b: When payable by the Government; by a resident, unless used for business or income outside India; or by a non resident, where used for business or income in India. This applies whether or not the non resident has a business connection here or rendered the services in India.

cards.f: Why are fees for services rendered outside India now taxable without a territorial nexus?
cards.b: Because Parliament overrode the case, which had held offshore supplies (title passing abroad) not taxable and required a sufficient territorial nexus for services rendered abroad. Interest, royalty and technical fees deemed to accrue in India are now taxable whether or not the services were rendered here. — Ishikawajima Harima Heavy Industries Ltd. v. Director of Income Tax

cards.f: What creates a business connection in India for a non resident, and what does not?
cards.b: Creates one: business through a dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts, keeps stock for delivery or secures orders; or a significant economic presence. Does not: business through an independent agent, purchases of goods in India for export, or a stray, isolated transaction.

cards.f: What kind of relation with India does a non resident need for a business connection?
cards.b: A real and intimate relation between its activity outside India and an activity in India that contributes to earning the income, with an element of continuity. A stray or isolated transaction is not normally enough. — CIT v. R.D. Aggarwal and Co.

cards.f: What is a “tax year”, and how does it work for a business set up part way through the year?
cards.b: The financial year beginning on 1 April, replacing the previous year and assessment year of the 1961 Act. A new business, profession or source starts its first tax year on the date it is set up or comes into existence, ending with that financial year.

cards.f: What must be true of the land, and of the income, for income to be agricultural income?
cards.b: Rent or revenue from land in India used for agricultural purposes, or income derived from such land by agriculture, a cultivator’s ordinary marketing process or his sale of unprocessed produce; qualifying farm building income; and, expressly, nursery saplings and seedlings. Excluded: buildings or land used for other purposes, and transfers of urban agricultural land.

cards.f: What makes an activity “agriculture”, and why is income from a forest of spontaneous growth not agricultural?
cards.b: Agriculture needs basic operations on the land, such as tilling, sowing and planting, involving human skill and labour. Subsequent operations such as weeding and pruning count only after basic operations. A spontaneous forest has none; dairy and poultry are generally not agriculture either. — CIT v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy

cards.f: Is a dividend from a tea company agricultural income for the shareholder? Why?
cards.b: No. Income “derived from” land needs a direct and immediate relation with the land; the shareholder’s income comes from his shares, not from the estates. — Mrs. Bacha F. Guzdar v. CIT

cards.f: Agricultural income is exempt. How can it still affect the tax computation?
cards.b: Composite income: where the grower also processes the crop (rubber, coffee, tea), the Rules split it into a taxable business part and an agricultural part. Partial integration: where the year’s Finance Act applies it, exempt agricultural income of individuals and similar persons is counted to set the rate on their non agricultural income.

cards.f: How is an individual’s residence decided, and who gets different rules?
cards.b: Resident if in India 182 days in the year, or 60 days plus 365 days in four preceding years. Citizens leaving to work abroad, and visiting citizens or persons of Indian origin, lose the 60 day test; visitors with income other than from foreign sources above Rs. 15,00,000 face 120 days. Citizens with such income taxed nowhere are deemed resident.

cards.f: Who is “not ordinarily resident”, and why does the status matter?
cards.b: A resident who was non resident in nine of ten preceding years or in India 729 days or less in seven; a visitor with income other than from foreign sources above Rs. 15,00,000 staying 120 to 181 days; or a deemed resident citizen. Foreign income is taxed only if from a business controlled, or profession set up, in India.

cards.f: How is residence decided for a company, and for a Hindu undivided family, firm or association?
cards.b: Company: resident if it is an Indian company or its place of effective management, where key decisions are in substance made, is in India. Family, firm, association and others: resident unless control and management is wholly outside India, so even partial actual control in India makes them resident.

cards.f: What does “control and management” mean in the residence test for a family or firm?
cards.b: The controlling and directive power, the “head and brain”; and “situated” implies that it functions at a place with some permanence. The family had not shown that its control and management was wholly outside India, so it was resident. — V.V.R.N.M. Subbayya Chettiar v. CIT

cards.f: Does a legal right to control a firm from India make it resident if the right is never exercised?
cards.b: No. Control and management means de facto control and management, what is actually exercised, not merely the legal right to control or manage. — CIT v. Nandlal Gandalal

cards.f: What income does each residential status bring into the charge?
cards.b: Resident and ordinarily resident: worldwide income, whether received or accruing in India or abroad. Not ordinarily resident: income received or accruing in India, plus foreign income from a business controlled in, or profession set up in, India. Non resident: only income received or deemed received, or accruing or deemed to accrue, in India.

cards.f: Distinguish a “person” from an “assessee”.
cards.b: A person includes an individual, Hindu undivided family, company, firm, association of persons or body of individuals, local authority and any other artificial juridical person. A person becomes an assessee only when tax is payable by him, proceedings are taken for his own or another’s income, loss or refund, or the Act deems him one.

cards.f: When do persons who receive income together form an association of persons?
cards.b: Only when they join in a common purpose or common action; merely receiving income jointly, as co owners do, is not enough. — CIT v. Indira Balkrishna

cards.f: Exemption, deduction, rebate: what does each one reduce?
cards.b: Exemption: the income never enters total income. Deduction: subtracted while computing income, under a head or from gross total income (Chapter VIII deductions cannot exceed gross total income). Rebate or relief: reduces the tax itself.

cards.f: Does a dominant trading purpose in holding shares avoid the disallowance of expenditure relating to exempt income?
cards.b: No. Even for shares held as stock in trade, expenditure is disallowed to the extent it relates to exempt income, whatever the dominant purpose of holding them. — Maxopp Investment Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: Is tax that an employer pays on an employee’s salary the employee’s income?
cards.b: Yes. Paying the employee’s tax discharges his own liability, which benefits him as surely as cash paid to him, so the amount is his income though it went straight to the government. — Emil Webber v. CIT

cards.f: How was a subsidy classed as capital or revenue, and why does that test matter less now?
cards.b: By its purpose: a subsidy to run the business is revenue; one to repay loans taken for expansion is capital. The test now has a narrow role, because the definition of income covers most government subsidies. — Sahney Steel and Press Works Ltd. v. CIT; CIT v. Ponni Sugars and Chemicals Ltd.

cards.f: Does a Hindu undivided family survive when a sole male coparcener holds the joint property with female members?
cards.b: Yes. Joint family property remains such even when held for the time being by a sole male coparcener with female members, so the family can still be assessed as a person separate from its members. — Gowli Buddanna v. CIT

cards.f: Days in India for residence
cards.b: 182 days in the tax year, or 60 days plus 365 days in the four preceding years.

cards.f: Indian income threshold for the 120 day rule and deemed residence
cards.b: Rs. 15,00,000 of income other than income from foreign sources.

cards.f: Indirect transfer thresholds (section 9(10))
cards.b: Indian assets above Rs. 10 crore and at least 50% of total assets; small shareholders at 5% or less are excluded.

cards.f: New regime slabs (section 202(1))
Rebate under section 156
cards.b: Up to Rs. 60,000 where total income is up to Rs. 12,00,000 (new regime); up to Rs. 12,500 where it is up to Rs. 5,00,000 (otherwise).

cards.f: Rule 271: taxable business share of composite income
cards.b: Rubber 35%; coffee grown and cured 25%; coffee grown, cured, roasted and ground 40%; tea 40%.

cards.f: Urban agricultural land distances
cards.b: 2, 6 or 8 kilometres from municipal limits, depending on whether the population is up to one lakh, up to ten lakh, or more.

cards.f: Gifts of money taxable when the yearly total exceeds
Income arises in the course of business, but a specific head covers that kind of income. Which head governs, and why?
cards.b: The specific head. The heads are mutually exclusive and each deals with a particular source, so interest on securities held by a bank in its business had to be computed under the head then provided for interest on securities, not as business income. — United Commercial Bank Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: A company that deals in land builds shops and stalls and lets them. Does its land dealing business turn the rent into business income?
cards.b: No. Rent from buildings the company owns falls under the property head; its business of dealing in land does not move that income out of the specific head. Contrast a company whose main object and whole business is letting (Unit V). — East India Housing and Land Development Trust Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: Who must explain a cash credit in the assessee’s books, and what follows if the explanation fails?
cards.b: The assessee bears the burden of proving the nature and source of the credit. If he fails to explain it satisfactorily, the amount may be treated as his income. — Kale Khan Mohammad Hanif v. CIT

cards.f: Must the tax authorities accept a transaction at face value when the assessee’s explanation is self serving?
cards.b: No. What is apparent is ordinarily real, but the authorities may look at the surrounding circumstances to find the reality, and need not accept a self serving explanation. — CIT v. Durga Prasad More

cards.f: How is an implausible explanation for large credits, such as repeated race winnings, to be tested?
cards.b: Against the test of human probabilities. A claim that large sums were horse race winnings failed that test, and the sums were rightly taxed as unexplained cash credits. — Sumati Dayal v. CIT

cards.f: How do you decide whether a managing director is an employee, whose remuneration is salary, or an agent?
cards.b: Look at the terms of his appointment and the articles. A rough and ready test is whether the company exercises supervisory control over his work; if it does, he is an employee and his remuneration is salary. — Ram Prashad v. CIT

cards.f: Why is “salary” paid by a firm to its working partner not taxed as salary?
cards.b: A partner cannot be an employee of himself and his co partners, so there is no contract of service. The payment is a share of profit, taxed as business income to the extent allowed to the firm. — CIT v. R.M. Chidambaram Pillai

cards.f: Where does the perquisite lie when an employer provides accommodation at a concessional rent?
cards.b: In the concession: the benefit of having accommodation at less than its value. The Act builds this in by taxing only the excess of the prescribed value over the rent recoverable from the employee. — Arun Kumar v. Union of India

cards.f: Under the earlier law, why were stock options subject to a lock in not taxed on exercise? What is the position now?
cards.b: During a lock in the benefit was notional, so under the law then in force it was not a taxable perquisite on exercise. The Act now taxes it specifically on the date of exercise: fair market value then, less the amount paid. — CIT v. Infosys Technologies Ltd.

cards.f: Is an employer’s contribution to a superannuation scheme a perquisite if the employee has no vested right in it?
cards.b: No. Nothing had vested in the employee when the contribution was made, so it was not his perquisite. The Act now taxes employer contributions to such funds above an annual limit, with the accretion on the excess. — CIT v. L.W. Russel

cards.f: If taxable income fits none of the four specific heads, does it escape tax? Can the residuary head take income that a specific head covers?
cards.b: No, and no. Income from other sources is the residuary head: it catches income of every kind, not excluded from total income, that no other head charges. But because the heads are mutually exclusive, it cannot absorb income that a specific head covers; that income must be computed under its own head.

cards.f: Trace the path from income to tax payable. Where do head deductions, Chapter VIII deductions and tax deducted at source fit?
cards.b: Fix residential status and scope; leave out exempt income; compute each head with its own deductions; add clubbed income; set off losses to reach gross total income; subtract Chapter VIII deductions to reach total income; apply rates, rebate, reliefs, surcharge and cess; then give credit for tax deducted or collected at source and advance tax.

cards.f: A minor child has income. When is it NOT clubbed with the parent’s income?
cards.b: When it comes from the child’s own work, or from activities involving the child’s skill, talent, specialised knowledge or experience, or when the minor has a specified disability. Other income, such as interest on a deposit gifted by a parent, is clubbed, subject to a small exclusion for each child.

cards.f: What happens when an assessee cannot satisfactorily explain a credit, investment, asset or expenditure?
cards.b: It is deemed income, taxed at a special flat rate with no deduction or set off against it. For a loan, the creditor must also explain the source; for share capital of a company in which the public are not substantially interested, the resident shareholder must. The burden of explanation lies on the assessee.

cards.f: When is salary taxed: when earned, when due or when received?
cards.b: When due or received, whichever is earlier. Salary due is taxed even if unpaid; advance salary is taxed on receipt and not again when due; arrears are taxed when paid if not taxed earlier, with relief available for bunching. The method of accounting does not apply to salary.

cards.f: Distinguish an allowance from a perquisite.
cards.b: An allowance is money paid to the employee for a purpose, such as rent or travel; it is part of salary unless a specific entry excludes it. A perquisite is a benefit in kind or an obligation of the employee met by the employer, such as a rent free flat, stock options or school fees, valued under the Rules.

cards.f: Distinguish salary from profits in lieu of salary.
cards.b: Salary rewards services under the contract: wages, allowances, perquisites, pension. Profits in lieu of salary are other employment linked receipts: compensation on termination or modification of terms, amounts from a person before joining or after leaving his employment, fund payments beyond the employee’s own contributions, and Keyman insurance sums. Both are taxed under the head Salaries.

cards.f: How does the house rent allowance exemption confine relief to a genuine rent burden?
cards.b: It applies only if rent is actually paid for accommodation the employee occupies and does not own. The exempt amount is the least of the allowance received, rent paid in excess of 10% of salary, and 50% of salary in the named cities (40% elsewhere). It is not available under the new regime.

cards.f: Under the 2025 Act, are gratuity, commuted pension and leave encashment exempt income? Do they survive the new regime?
cards.b: Not exemptions: they are part of salary and then deducted, within limits, under the section 19 Table, along with retrenchment and voluntary retirement compensation. The new regime withdraws only the tax on employment entry, so these deductions, and the larger standard deduction, remain available.

cards.f: A person passes income, or the asset that yields it, to someone else. When is the income still taxed as his?
cards.b: When he passes on only the income and keeps the asset, revocably or not; or when he transfers the asset revocably. A transfer not revocable during the transferee’s or beneficiary’s lifetime shifts the income if he derives no benefit, until a power to revoke arises. Separate rules apply to a spouse, son’s wife and minor child.

cards.f: How does leaving the new regime work for a person without business income, compared with one who has it?
cards.b: The new regime is the default. Without business income, a person may opt out, or not, afresh each year when filing the return. With business income, he opts out by the due date, the choice continues for later years, and it can be withdrawn only once.

cards.f: Standard deduction from salary
cards.b: Rs. 75,000 under the new regime, Rs. 50,000 otherwise, or the salary if less.

cards.f: Employer contributions taxable as perquisite above
cards.b: Rs. 7,50,000 a year in aggregate (section 17(1)(h)).

cards.f: Voluntary retirement compensation deduction
cards.b: The compensation or Rs. 5,00,000, whichever is less, once in a lifetime.

cards.f: Retrenchment compensation: notified amount
cards.b: Not less than Rs. 50,000.

cards.f: Rate on unexplained income (section 195)
cards.b: 30%, as amended by the Finance Act, 2026 (earlier 60%).

cards.f: Minor child’s clubbed income excluded
cards.b: Rs. 1,500 per child (Schedule III, Sl. No. 17).

cards.f: Who is the “owner” for the house property head when title and the right to the income come apart?
cards.b: The person entitled to receive the income from the property in his own right. Where property had vested in a custodian, the registered holder had no right to its income and was not its owner for this head. — R.B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala v. CIT

cards.f: A buyer has paid the price, is in possession and collects the rent, but the sale deed is unregistered. Is the buyer the owner?
cards.b: Yes. A person who has paid for the property, is in possession and receives the rent in his own right is the owner for this head, even without a registered sale deed. — CIT v. Podar Cement (P) Ltd.

cards.f: A building is let together with furniture or machinery. When does the rent cease to be house property income?
cards.b: When the two lettings are inseparable. The income is then business income or income from other sources, not house property income; the Act now states this rule expressly. — Sultan Brothers (P) Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: When was rent from letting property held to be business income, and how far does that view survive?
cards.b: Where letting was a company’s main object and whole business, its rent was business income (also Rayala Corporation). Now income from letting a residential house by its owner is house property income only, so the view can matter only for commercial property let as a business. — Chennai Properties and Investments Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: Where a rent control law applies, can the expected rent be taken at the market rent if no standard rent has actually been fixed?
cards.b: No. The expected rent cannot exceed the standard rent determinable under that law, even if no standard rent has actually been fixed. The Court followed the same view taken on rateable value for municipal tax. — Mrs. Sheila Kaushish v. CIT

cards.f: Why is house property taxed on annual value rather than on rent received?
cards.b: Ownership of a building is itself a source able to yield income; a notional charge treats owners who let and owners who do not more equally; and annual value is easy to estimate, with a flat 30% deduction instead of checking repairs. The law softens the charge for self occupied houses and unsold stock.

cards.f: How is annual value found, and how do vacancy and municipal taxes adjust it?
cards.b: Take the higher of expected rent (limited by standard rent under rent control) and actual rent received or receivable, leaving out unrealised rent. If vacancy pushes actual rent below expected rent, take actual rent. Then deduct municipal taxes actually paid by the owner in the year, whatever year they relate to.

cards.f: What three conditions must be met before income is charged under house property?
cards.b: (1) The property is a building or land appurtenant to it, not vacant land alone; (2) the assessee is its owner, including a deemed owner; (3) it is not occupied for his own business or profession whose profits are taxable. A tenant who sub lets is not the owner.

cards.f: Why does the Act tax some people who are not the legal owners of a building as “deemed owners”?
cards.b: Because they really enjoy the property, or have shifted it within the family: a transferor to a spouse (not under an agreement to live apart) or minor child (not a married daughter) without adequate consideration; an impartible estate holder; an allottee under a house building scheme; a buyer in possession under part performance; a lessee for twelve years or more.

cards.f: Why are actual repair bills irrelevant to house property income, and how is the interest deduction limited?
cards.b: Because the only deductions are a flat 30% of annual value, whatever is spent, and interest on borrowed capital, on an accrual basis (pre construction interest in five instalments). For a self occupied house interest is capped at Rs. 2,00,000 or Rs. 30,000 in all, and nil under the new regime; a let out house has no cap.

cards.f: When does a house have a nil annual value, and when is that benefit lost?
cards.b: When the owner occupies it as his residence or cannot actually occupy it for any reason, for up to two houses of his choice. The benefit is lost if the house is let at any time in the year or he derives any other benefit from it. Co owners each get it individually.

cards.f: How are recovered arrears of rent and a house property loss treated?
cards.b: Arrears and unrealised rent recovered later are taxed in the year of receipt, less 30%, even if the assessee no longer owns the property. A loss is set off against other house property income, then other heads up to Rs. 2,00,000 a year (not under the new regime); the rest is carried forward against house property income only.

cards.f: Interest caps for self occupied houses
cards.b: Rs. 2,00,000 if bought or built with a loan and completed within five years, with certificate; otherwise Rs. 30,000.

cards.f: House property loss
cards.b: Set off against other heads up to Rs. 2,00,000 a year; balance carried forward for eight tax years.

cards.f: Nil annual value for unlet stock in trade property
cards.b: Up to two years from the end of the financial year in which the completion certificate is obtained.

cards.f: What, in the ordinary sense, makes an activity a ‘business’?
cards.b: A real, substantial and systematic or organised course of activity carried on with a set purpose. That is the ordinary sense; the statutory definition goes further and also reaches an isolated adventure in the nature of trade. — Narain Swadeshi Weaving Mills v. Commissioner of Excess Profits Tax

cards.f: When can a single, isolated transaction be business, and how do you decide?
cards.b: When it is an adventure in the nature of trade. Weigh together the intention to resell at a profit when buying, the nature and quantity of the commodity, work done to improve or market it, and how it was financed. No single factor is decisive. — G. Venkataswami Naidu and Co. v. CIT

cards.f: What is the ‘enduring benefit’ test, and how much weight does it carry?
cards.b: Expenditure made once and for all to bring into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade is capital, in the absence of special circumstances. It is a strong guide, not a rule of law, and later cases refuse to treat it as conclusive. — British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. v. Atherton

cards.f: A cement company pays for a quarry lease and for protection from competition during it. Capital or revenue, and why?
cards.b: Capital: both secure an enduring advantage that forms part of the profit making structure. Fixed capital earns profit by being kept; circulating capital by being parted with. — Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: Can a payment that brings a lasting advantage still be revenue?
cards.b: Yes. Buying loom hours (the right to work more looms) was revenue because it let the existing business run more efficiently, without adding to its capital structure. The enduring benefit test is not conclusive. — Empire Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: Know how bought to improve production of an existing product: capital or revenue?
cards.b: Revenue: it helps the existing business work better rather than creating or extending the profit making structure. No single test decides the question. — Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: Does ‘wholly and exclusively for the business’ mean ‘necessarily’?
cards.b: No. Expenditure incurred voluntarily, without any legal necessity, is deductible if it is incurred for the business. The test is purpose, not compulsion. — Sassoon J. David and Co. (P) Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: How wide is ‘for the purpose of the business’, and where does it stop?
cards.b: Wider than ‘for earning profits’: it includes carrying on, preserving and protecting the business. But it needs a link with the business itself, so estate duty paid by a company on deceased shareholders’ shares was not deductible. — CIT v. Malayalam Plantations Ltd.

cards.f: Whose view decides commercial expediency: the businessman’s or the Revenue’s?
cards.b: The businessman’s. Interest on borrowed money lent interest free to a sister concern for commercial expediency was deductible; the Revenue cannot put itself in the businessman’s armchair. — S.A. Builders Ltd. v. CIT (Appeals)

cards.f: Can a company deduct gifts to people whose own conduct rules forbid them to accept such gifts?
cards.b: No. Benefits to a person whose acceptance violates the law, rules or guidelines governing his conduct are never ‘wholly and exclusively’ for the business, even if only the recipient’s rules are broken (freebies to doctors). The Act now says so expressly. — Apex Laboratories (P) Ltd. v. Deputy CIT

cards.f: Must an assessee prove that a written off debt has actually become irrecoverable?
cards.b: No. Since the amendment of the earlier law, writing the debt off as irrecoverable in the accounts is enough, provided it was taken into account as income or lent in a money lending business. The 2025 Act keeps this. — TRF Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: Must a bank close each borrower’s account before a bad debt counts as written off?
cards.b: No. Debiting the bad debt to the profit and loss account and reducing loans and advances in the balance sheet by the same amount is a valid write off, even if individual accounts stay open. — Vijaya Bank v. CIT

cards.f: Does a provision for bad loans become a write off because the regulator requires it?
cards.b: No. A provision, even one made under Reserve Bank directions, is not a write off and is not deductible as a bad debt; the debts stay on the books. — Southern Technologies Ltd. v. Joint CIT

cards.f: Does the disallowance for failure to deduct tax reach sums already paid during the year?
cards.b: Yes. ‘Payable’ is not confined to sums still outstanding at the year end, so the disallowance applies to amounts paid during the year as well as amounts payable at its close. — Palam Gas Service v. CIT

cards.f: Why is the disallowance of large cash payments constitutionally valid?
cards.b: It pursues a legitimate aim, checking unaccounted money, and its exceptions for genuine cases keep it reasonable rather than arbitrary. — Attar Singh Gurmukh Singh v. Income Tax Officer

cards.f: Does the relief for paying taxes and fund contributions by the return due date apply to past years?
cards.b: Yes. The provisions allowing payment up to the due date of the return are curative and so retrospective, for taxes and for employers’ contributions to welfare funds alike. — Allied Motors (P) Ltd. v. CIT; CIT v. Alom Extrusions Ltd.

cards.f: Unclaimed trade deposits are moved to the profit and loss account. Are they taxable, and on what basis?
cards.b: Yes, as trading receipts: received in the course of trade, they became the assessee’s own money once transferred. This rests on the character of the receipt, not on any earlier deduction. — CIT v. T.V. Sundaram Iyengar and Sons Ltd.

cards.f: Is a debtor’s own write back of a trading liability a ‘remission or cessation’?
