cards.b: Not under the old law: remission needs the creditor’s act, and cessation needs operation of law or a bilateral act. Parliament reversed this; the 2025 Act expressly taxes a unilateral write off of a trading liability that was deducted. — CIT v. Sugauli Sugar Works (P) Ltd.

cards.f: Is the waiver of a loan taken to buy capital assets a remission of a trading liability?
cards.b: No. The deemed profit rule claws back an earlier deduction, so it needs a deduction allowed for the liability, and none was claimed for the loan. The Court’s further view that a business benefit must be in kind does not fit the 2025 Act, which covers cash benefits too. — CIT v. Mahindra and Mahindra Ltd.

cards.f: How does tax treat an illegal business: its profits, its losses and its penalties?
cards.b: Its profits are taxable, since tax does not ask whether a business is lawful, and a loss incidental to the business may be allowed. But a penalty for breaking the law is not deductible, and expenditure for an unlawful purpose is expressly barred. — CIT v. S.C. Kothari; Haji Aziz and Abdul Shakoor Bros. v. CIT

cards.f: How do you decide whether an item is ‘plant’ for depreciation?
cards.b: By function: plant includes any apparatus used to carry on the business, other than stock in trade, so technical drawings used as tools of the trade qualified. The Act adds ships, vehicles and books, but excludes buildings, livestock, tea bushes, and furniture and fittings. — CIT v. Taj Mahal Hotel; Scientific Engineering House (P) Ltd. v. CIT

cards.f: Besides trading profits, what kinds of receipts does the Act expressly charge as business income?
cards.b: Receipts that might otherwise escape as capital or non cash: compensation on ending a management, agency or business contract; non compete fees (but not a transfer of the right to manufacture); export incentives; business benefits, whether or not convertible into money; partners’ allowed salary and interest; Keyman policy sums; and stock converted into a capital asset, at market value.

cards.f: Capital or revenue expenditure: what is the working rule?
cards.b: Acquiring, extending or improving the profit making structure is capital; running the business or keeping the existing structure working is revenue. Enduring benefit is a guide, not a conclusive test, and an advantage that only makes the existing business run more efficiently is revenue.

cards.f: What must an expense satisfy to qualify under the general deduction?
cards.b: It must be (1) outside the specific and special deduction provisions, (2) not capital, (3) not personal, and (4) laid out wholly and exclusively for the business or profession. Even then, the Act bars offences and prohibited purposes, prohibited benefits, compounding, settling notified contraventions, corporate social responsibility spending and political party advertisements.

cards.f: What conditions must an asset meet before depreciation is allowed?
cards.b: It must be a tangible asset or a listed intangible (know how, patents, copyrights, trademarks, licences, franchises and similar rights), but not goodwill; owned wholly or partly, dominion and use in one’s own right being enough; and used for the business, with only a fair proportion for part business use.

cards.f: How does the block of assets system work, and what is ‘actual cost’?
cards.b: Assets with the same rate form a block. Written down value = opening value + actual cost of additions − sale price or scrap value of assets sold, discarded or destroyed (never below nil), and depreciation runs on the block, not asset by asset. Actual cost excludes subsidies, GST credit and cash payments above the daily limit.

cards.f: When is a bad debt deductible?
cards.b: When (1) it is written off as irrecoverable in the accounts, a provision not being enough, and (2) it was taken into account in computing income of that or an earlier year, or is money lent in the ordinary course of a banking or money lending business.

cards.f: What is the actual payment rule, and how does the return due date soften it?
cards.b: Taxes and fees, employer fund contributions, leave encashment, bonus, interest to specified lenders and railway dues are deductible only when paid. Payment after the year ends but by the return due date counts for the year of liability, except late dues to micro and small enterprises. Interest converted into a loan is not payment.

cards.f: What is the common logic of the deemed profit provisions?
cards.b: They claw back earlier tax relief when its basis disappears: remission or cessation of a deducted trading liability (even by unilateral write off), balancing charge, excess on sale of a research asset, bad debt recovered beyond the unallowed part, and withdrawal from a special reserve. They apply even after the business ends.

cards.f: How does presumptive taxation work, and what is the catch?
cards.b: Income is deemed at a set rate of turnover or receipts, or per vehicle for goods carriages, though the assessee may declare more; no further deductions are allowed, and depreciation is treated as allowed. Declaring less, with income above the exemption limit, brings books and audit, and a small business that leaves early cannot return for five years.

cards.f: Can an assessee choose when to take depreciation, and what happens when profits are too low to absorb it?
cards.b: No choice: depreciation applies whether or not it is claimed, so it cannot be held back for a more profitable year (reversing the earlier view that it was optional). Depreciation the year’s profits cannot absorb is not lost: it is added to the next year’s allowance and carried forward without time limit.

cards.f: How are a firm’s payments of interest and remuneration to its partners treated, for the firm and for the partner?
cards.b: A firm may deduct remuneration to working partners, and interest to any partner, only if the deed authorises it for that period and it is within the statutory limits. The partner is taxed as business income only on the amount the firm was allowed, so the disallowed part is taxed once, in the firm.

cards.f: Cash payment limit for disallowance
cards.b: Rs. 10,000 a day to a person (Rs. 35,000 for goods carriages).

cards.f: Partner remuneration and interest limits
cards.b: On the first Rs. 6,00,000 of book profit or in case of loss, Rs. 3,00,000 or 90% of book profit, whichever is higher; 60% of the balance; interest up to 12% simple.

cards.f: Pension scheme contribution deductible for the employer
cards.b: Up to 14% of the employee’s salary (section 29(1)(b)).

cards.f: Additional depreciation
cards.b: 20% of actual cost; 10% plus 10% if used for less than 180 days in the first year.

cards.f: Provision for bad and doubtful debts
cards.b: Banks up to 8.5% of total income plus 10% of average rural advances; foreign banks, public financial institutions and NBFCs up to 5%.

cards.f: Presumptive taxation rates (section 58)
cards.b: Business: 6% of digital and 8% of other turnover (up to Rs. 2 crore or Rs. 3 crore). Goods carriages: Rs. 1,000 per ton or Rs. 7,500 a month per vehicle. Professions: 50% of receipts (up to Rs. 50 lakh or Rs. 75 lakh).

cards.f: Books of account thresholds (section 62)
cards.b: Income above Rs. 1,20,000 or turnover above Rs. 10 lakh; Rs. 2,50,000 and Rs. 25 lakh for individuals and Hindu undivided families.

cards.f: Tax audit thresholds (section 63)
cards.b: Business turnover above Rs. 1 crore (Rs. 10 crore if cash receipts and payments are each within 5%); professional receipts above Rs. 50 lakh.

about:
This material follows your syllabus unit by unit. Each topic gives the basic idea, the statutory provisions, the leading cases and exam points, and each unit ends with practice questions.

How to read the references

  1. “Section” alone means a section of the Income Tax Act, 2025 (“the 2025 Act”). “1961 Act” means the Income Tax Act, 1961, which the 2025 Act repealed from 1 April 2026 (section 536(1)).
  2. “Schedule” means a Schedule to the 2025 Act, and “Sl. No.” means the serial number in its Table. “Rules” means the Income Tax Rules, 2026.
  3. Most leading cases were decided under the 1961 Act or the 1922 Act. Each is linked here to the corresponding provision of the 2025 Act.

Sources and verification

  1. Statutory text. Every section number, definition, rate and limit was checked against the SCC Online text of the 2025 Act, as amended up to Act 21 of 2026, including the Finance Act, 2026 (Act 4 of 2026).
  2. Other facts. The legislative history of the Act, the Income Tax Rules, 2026 (including Rules 271 and 279), the Sixteenth Finance Commission and several leading judgments were checked against published sources.
  3. Case citations are from standard law reports. Confirm them on a database before quoting them in written work. Four recent cases are cited by name and year only.
  4. This is study material, not legal advice.

  2. Previous year (section 3) is now the tax year (section 3); assessment year (2(9)) has no counterpart.
  3. Charge, scope, residence, deemed receipt and deemed accrual (sections 4, 5, 6, 7 and 9) keep the same numbers; section 5A is now section 10.
  4. Exemptions (section 10) are now section 11 with Schedules II to VII; section 10(10), (10A), (10AA), (10B) and (10C) are now deductions in section 19.
  5. Heads of income (section 14) is now section 13; section 14A is now section 14.
  6. Salaries: sections 15, 17(1), 17(2), 17(3) and 16 are now sections 15, 16, 17, 18 and 19.
  7. House property: sections 22, 23, 24, 25A, 26 and 27 are now sections 20 to 25.
  8. Business: section 28 is 26; sections 30 and 31 are 28; section 32 is 33; section 36(1) clauses are spread over sections 29 to 32; section 37(1) is 34; section 40 is 35; section 40A is 36; section 43B is 37; section 41 is 38; sections 43(1) and 43(6) are 39 and 41; sections 35D, 35, 35AD and 44A are 44, 45, 46 and 50; section 43CA is 53; sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE are 58; sections 44AA and 44AB are 62 and 63; section 145 is 276.
  9. Other sources (sections 56 to 58) are now sections 92 to 94; clubbing (sections 60 to 65) is now sections 96 to 100; unexplained income (sections 68 to 69D) is now sections 102 to 106, and section 115BBE is section 195.

  11. Rebate (87A), relief (89) and treaties (90) are now sections 156, 157 and 159; the new regime (115BAC) is section 202; the General Anti Avoidance Rule (sections 95 to 102) is sections 178 to 184.
appB:
1. Residence: 182 days; or 60 days plus 365 days in the four preceding years; 120 days for visiting citizens and persons of Indian origin with income (other than from foreign sources) above Rs. 15,00,000; deemed residence for citizens not taxed elsewhere with such income above Rs. 15,00,000.
  2. Not ordinarily resident: non resident in nine of ten preceding years, or 729 days or less in seven preceding years; or 120 to 181 days of stay for citizens and persons of Indian origin with such income above Rs. 15,00,000.
  3. Indirect transfer: Indian assets above Rs. 10 crore and at least 50% of total assets; small shareholders at 5% or less excluded.
  4. New regime slabs: nil up to Rs. 4,00,000, then 5%, 10%, 15%, 20% and 25% for each further Rs. 4,00,000, and 30% above Rs. 24,00,000. Rebate: up to Rs. 60,000 (income up to Rs. 12,00,000, new regime) or Rs. 12,500 (income up to Rs. 5,00,000, otherwise).
  5. Salary: standard deduction Rs. 75,000 (new regime) or Rs. 50,000; voluntary retirement compensation up to Rs. 5,00,000; retrenchment notified amount at least Rs. 50,000; employer contributions taxable above Rs. 7,50,000; commuted pension one third or one half; house rent allowance limit 50% or 40% of salary and rent paid less 10% of salary.
  6. House property: 30% deduction; interest on self occupied houses up to Rs. 2,00,000 or Rs. 30,000; pre construction interest in five instalments; two self occupied houses; set off against other heads up to Rs. 2,00,000; carry forward eight years.
  7. Business: cash payments above Rs. 10,000 a day (Rs. 35,000 for goods carriages) disallowed; 30% disallowance for failure to deduct tax from payments to residents; partner remuneration limits Rs. 6,00,000, Rs. 3,00,000, 90% and 60%, and interest 12%; pension scheme contributions up to 14% of salary; half rate depreciation below 180 days; additional depreciation 20%; bank provisions 8.5% plus 10% of rural advances, others 5%.
  8. Presumptive, books and audit: 6% and 8% up to Rs. 2 crore (Rs. 3 crore); ten goods carriages, Rs. 1,000 per ton and Rs. 7,500 a month; professions 50% up to Rs. 50 lakh (Rs. 75 lakh); books above Rs. 1,20,000 or Rs. 10 lakh (Rs. 2,50,000 or Rs. 25 lakh for individuals and Hindu undivided families); audit above Rs. 1 crore (Rs. 10 crore) or Rs. 50 lakh for professions.
  9. Other: gifts of money taxable above Rs. 50,000 a year; unexplained income taxed at 30%; urban agricultural land within municipalities of at least 10,000 population or within 2, 6 or 8 kilometres; minor child’s clubbed income exempt up to Rs. 1,500 per child; substantial interest 20%.
